sounds.name: Acid Squelch
sounds.ref: In the style of Phuture — "Acid Tracks"
sounds.blurb: Squelchy, sliding bass line where the filter does all the talking.
sounds.how: One sawtooth goes into a low-pass filter with a lot of resonance. Envelope 2 snaps the filter open and shut on every note, and the resonance turns that snap into the "squelch". Overdrive after the filter roughens it up, and a little portamento makes the notes slide into each other.

steps.title: One sawtooth, an octave down
steps.why:
Start with one bright, buzzy oscillator pitched low. Acid bass is a single plain wave, with all the character added later by the filter.
- OSC MIX −5 (OSC 1 only): OSC is short for oscillator, the part that makes the raw tone. The Neutron crossfades its two oscillators instead of giving each a level knob; fully left means only Oscillator 1 is heard.
- SHAPE 2 (saw): the middle of the morph is a sawtooth, which carries every harmonic and gives the filter plenty to chew on. Left of 2 gets hollower (pulse), right gets softer (triangle, sine).
- RANGE 16’: footage comes from organ pipes; 16’ is an octave below 8’, which puts the line in bass territory.
- TUNE 0: centred, so the oscillator plays in tune with the keys. This knob covers about an octave each way, so it is easy to knock.
- Listen for: a raw, bright buzz. The filter is still wide open at 5 kHz, so nothing squelches yet.

steps.title: Low-pass, nearly shut, lots of resonance
steps.why:
Now the filter shuts most of that buzz away. The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) removes part of the sound; here it rests almost closed, waiting for an envelope to open it.
- MODE low-pass: keeps what is below the cutoff and removes the brightness above it. It is a 12 dB per octave filter, gentler than a Moog’s, so a little buzz still leaks through.
- FREQ 3.8 (161 Hz): the cutoff, and where the filter rests between notes. This low, the note is a dull thud. Turn right to let the buzz back in; this is the knob to ride by hand once the pattern plays.
- RESO 7.8: resonance, a boost in a narrow band right at the cutoff. This is the squelch. Lower it for a plain plucky bass; near maximum the filter starts to whistle.
- KEY TRK off: key tracking would make the cutoff follow the notes. Off, every note gets the same filter.
- Listen for: not much yet. The resonance only shows once the cutoff moves; sweep FREQ slowly and you will hear it sing.

steps.title: Let Envelope 2 snap the filter open
steps.why:
This is where the squelch appears. An envelope is a shape that runs once per note; Envelope 2 is wired inside to the filter, so it kicks the cutoff up at the start of every note and lets it fall back.
- ENV DEPTH 6 (60%): ENV is short for envelope. This sets how far Envelope 2 lifts the cutoff above 161 Hz, which is the size of the “wow” on each note. It only pushes upwards.
- A 0 ms (env 2): attack. The filter jumps open the instant a key goes down, so the bite lands on the beat.
- D 110 ms: decay, how fast it closes again. Short is a tight blip; long is a lazy sweep.
- S 0%: sustain. At zero the filter always closes fully, so every note gets the same “wow” however long it is held.
- R 18 ms: release after you let go. Short, so there is no filter tail.
- Listen for: a vocal “wow” on each note as the resonant peak sweeps down. Turn ENV DEPTH and D while repeating one note to hear the size and length change.

steps.title: Tight loudness
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes the volume of each note. It is wired inside to the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier), the stage that opens and closes the sound, so other synths would call this the amp envelope.
- A 0 ms (env 1): instant attack, so the note speaks straight away and lines up with the filter snap.
- D 360 ms, S 70%: after the peak the level eases down over about a third of a second to 70% and holds there. Held notes lose a little weight rather than droning on at full level.
- R 18 ms: a very short release. Notes stop almost as soon as the key comes up, so the gaps in the pattern stay clean.
- Listen for: crisp gaps between notes. Raise R to 6 or so and the notes smear together and the pattern loses its bounce; set it back to 3.

steps.title: Overdrive and slide
steps.why:
The last step adds the rasp and the slide that acid lines are known for.
- DRIVE 5.5: the overdrive sits after the filter, so it distorts the resonant peak itself and exaggerates it. That is a large part of the acid rasp. Turn it back to 1 to hear the cleaner line underneath.
- TONE 5.5: just right of centre. Left rolls off the top for a rounder sound; right thins the bass and adds bite.
- LEVEL 7: the overdrive’s output. Everything passes through here, so it works as a volume control; at zero the synth is silent.
- PORTA TIME 1.2 (140 ms): portamento, a pitch slide from each note to the next. Here it applies to every note.
- Listen for: each note bending into the next, with a gritty edge on the squelch. Flip DRIVE between 1 and 5.5 for a quick A/B.

context.vcf.freq: In this sound the cutoff is where the filter rests between notes. This is the knob to ride by hand while the pattern plays.
context.vcf.reso: This is the squelch. Lower it and the line turns into a plain plucky bass; near maximum the filter starts to whistle.
context.vcf.envDepth: The size of the "wow" on each note.
context.env2.d: The length of the "wow". Short is a tight blip; long is a lazy sweep.
context.od.drive: Distortion after the filter exaggerates the resonant peak, which is a large part of the acid rasp.
context.porta.time: The slide between notes. Here it applies to every note.

tweaks.try: Sweep slowly between 2.5 and 6 while the pattern plays
tweaks.hear: The classic acid build: from muffled blips to a bright, screaming line.
Short decays sound percussive; long ones let each note open out.
A hollower, more rubbery tone — the other classic acid waveform. Stop halfway for a blend of the two.
Much dirtier, with the resonant peak squashed into a snarl.

sounds.name: Random Filter Steps
sounds.ref: In the style of 70s sci-fi "computer" sounds
sounds.blurb: Hold one note and the filter jumps to a new random setting several times a second.
sounds.how: The sample-and-hold takes a reading of white noise at a steady rate and holds it until the next reading, giving a stepped random voltage. On the Neutron that voltage goes nowhere until you patch it. One cable from S&H to FREQ MOD sends it to the filter cutoff, and high resonance makes each step sound like a different pitch.

steps.title: A pulse wave to filter
steps.why:
A plain, hollow tone to start, so the filter steps later on are easy to pick out.
- OSC MIX −5 (OSC 1 only): OSC is short for oscillator, the part that makes the raw tone. Fully left on the crossfade means only Oscillator 1 is heard.
- SHAPE 1 (pulse): one step left of the sawtooth on the morph. A pulse sounds hollower and reedier than a saw, and its gaps between harmonics make filter changes stand out.
- WIDTH 5 (50% duty): pulse width. At the centre the pulse is a square, the hollowest setting; either side it gets thinner and more nasal.
- RANGE 16’: an octave below 8’, low enough that there are plenty of harmonics above the note for the filter to pick out.
- Listen for: a hollow, woody buzz. Turn WIDTH either side of 5 to hear it thin out, then return it to 5.

steps.title: Resonant low-pass, part closed
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) takes away brightness. Its cutoff here is the centre point the random steps will jump around.
- MODE low-pass: keeps what is below the cutoff and removes what is above.
- FREQ 5 (387 Hz): the centre of the random steps. Higher and the steps sit in a brighter, squeakier range; lower and they sound deeper.
- RESO 7: resonance, a boost in a narrow band at the cutoff. This high, it picks out one harmonic at each position, so every jump will sound like a new pitch.
- ENV DEPTH 0: ENV is short for envelope. At zero, Envelope 2 does not move the cutoff, so only the random voltage will.
- Listen for: a darker tone with a slight ring around 387 Hz. Sweep FREQ by hand to preview the kind of movement the random steps will make.

steps.title: Patch S&H to FREQ MOD
steps.why:
One cable brings the random voltage to the filter. S&H stands for sample and hold: it reads white noise at a steady rate and holds each reading until the next, giving a random staircase of voltages. On the Neutron it goes nowhere until you patch it.
- S&H → FREQ MOD: FREQ MOD is the filter’s cutoff modulation input. It is normally fed by the LFO (low-frequency oscillator); this cable replaces the LFO, so the stepped random voltage is now what moves the cutoff.
- Listen for: nothing new yet. MOD DEPTH, which sets how much of the FREQ MOD input reaches the cutoff, is still at 0. The next step turns it up.

steps.title: Set how far and how fast
steps.why:
Now the filter starts jumping. These three knobs set how far, how often and how smoothly.
- MOD DEPTH 5.5 (55%): scales whatever arrives at FREQ MOD, which is now the S&H. This is the size of the random jumps. Low keeps them close to 387 Hz; high throws the cutoff from dark to squeaky.
- RATE (S&H) 6.2 (4.73 Hz): how often a new random value is picked, just under five times a second. The S&H has its own clock, separate from the LFO.
- GLIDE 0: the steps jump cleanly. Turn it up and the cutoff slides between values, more like a drunken LFO than a computer.
- Listen for: hold one note. The tone lands on a new random resonant pitch several times a second, the classic 70s computer burble. Turn GLIDE up briefly to hear the steps melt into slides.

steps.title: Hold the note, add echo
steps.why:
The note is held for the whole effect, and a short echo fills the spaces between steps.
- A 0 / S 100% / R 95 ms (env 1): Envelope 1 shapes loudness. Instant attack, full sustain so a held note stays at full level while the filter steps, and a short release so the note does not stop with a click.
- MIX 3 (30%): the balance of echo against the dry sound. At 0 there is no delay at all.
- TIME 6 (170 ms): short echoes. Each one lands before the next random step arrives, about 210 ms later.
- REPEATS 4.5 (45%): how much echo is fed back, giving two or three audible repeats before it fades. The delay is analogue, so each repeat is a little darker.
- Listen for: each random step followed by fainter copies, which makes the pattern sound busier. Pull MIX to 0 for a dry comparison.

context.sh.rate: How many random steps per second.
context.sh.glide: At zero the filter jumps. Turn it up and it slides between values, more like a drunken LFO than a computer.
context.vcf.modDepth: The size of the random jumps. It scales the FREQ MOD input, which is now the S&H.
context.vcf.reso: High resonance makes each step ring at its own pitch.
context.vcf.freq: The centre the random steps move around.

tweaks.hear: The hard steps turn into smooth random wandering.
The steps blur into a bubbling texture.
Thinner and more vocal, like a talking robot.

tweaks.try: Push to 10 and turn OSC 1 down with noise at 0
tweaks.hear: The filter sings random sine-wave notes on its own.

sounds.name: Audio-Rate Snarl Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of industrial techno — Surgeon, Blawan
sounds.blurb: Aggressive, rasping bass made by wobbling the filter faster than the ear can follow.
sounds.how: The Neutron’s LFO goes far into the audio range. It is already wired to the filter through MOD DEPTH, so no cable is needed. Once the LFO passes about 30 Hz you stop hearing a wobble and start hearing extra, rough overtones — the filter is being modulated as fast as a note. Overdrive then glues it together.

steps.title: Saw and pulse together
steps.why:
Two oscillators blend into a thick, low base for the snarl to work on.
- OSC MIX 0: OSC is short for oscillator, the part that makes the raw tone. The centre of the crossfade gives both an equal share.
- SHAPE 2, RANGE 16’ (osc 1): a sawtooth, bright and full of harmonics, an octave below 8’.
- SHAPE 1, RANGE 32’ (osc 2): a pulse a further octave down, adding sub weight under the saw.
- WIDTH 4 (41%), osc 2: just off square, a touch thinner and more nasal than a pure square.
- TUNE 0 (osc 2): exactly in tune, so the two lock together an octave apart instead of beating.
- Listen for: a heavy, buzzy low note. Turn OSC MIX fully left and fully right to hear each layer on its own, then return it to 0.

steps.title: Filter part closed
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) takes the top off, leaving room for modulation to push the cutoff around.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 4.6 (289 Hz): the cutoff sits medium-low, so most of the saw’s buzz is gone. Higher lets more rasp through later.
- RESO 4: resonance, a moderate peak at the cutoff. It gives the modulation something to grab without whistling.
- ENV DEPTH 4 (40%): ENV is short for envelope, a shape that runs once per note. This sets how far Envelope 2 lifts the cutoff at the start of each note.
- A 0 / D 240 ms / S 30% / R 41 ms (env 2): opens instantly, falls over about a quarter of a second to a low hold, and closes quickly after release.
- Listen for: a short bright bite at the front of each note, settling into a rounder, darker hold.

steps.title: Bring in the LFO, slowly at first
steps.why:
Before the snarl, hear the plain version of the same connection: a slow filter wobble. The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) is a repeating wave you do not hear directly; it moves other settings.
- MOD DEPTH 4.5 (45%): with nothing patched into FREQ MOD, the LFO is wired to the cutoff already, and this knob sets how far it moves it. No cable needed.
- SHAPE (LFO) 0 (sine): the smoothest shape, a steady swing up and down.
- RATE (LFO) 4 (2.00 Hz): two wobbles a second.
- Listen for: hold a note and the tone swings bright and dark twice a second. That is the connection the next step speeds up.

steps.title: Speed the LFO into audio rate
steps.why:
Turning the LFO up into the audio range changes the wobble into a rasp. The Neutron’s LFO keeps going well past where most stop, so it can shake the filter as fast as a note.
- RATE (LFO) 7.4 (100 Hz): at this speed you no longer hear a wobble, you hear extra rough overtones. The rate sets the pitch of the roughness, and because the LFO does not follow the keyboard, each note snarls a little differently.
- KEY SYNC on: restarts the LFO each time a note is played, so every attack begins at the same point and the front of each note stays consistent.
- Listen for: sweep RATE slowly from 4 to 7.4 on a held note. Somewhere around 30 Hz the wobble blurs into a growl. Then try LFO SHAPE towards square for the harshest rasp.

steps.title: Overdrive
steps.why:
Overdrive glues the snarl together, and Envelope 1 gives it a tight bass shape.
- DRIVE 6: distortion after the filter. It thickens the rasp and squashes the level so the snarl stays even.
- TONE 4.5: just left of centre, rolling a little off the top so the distortion is heavy rather than fizzy. Right of centre thins the bass and adds bite.
- LEVEL 7: the overdrive’s output, which everything passes through, so it doubles as a volume control.
- A 0 / S 90% / R 27 ms (env 1): Envelope 1 sets loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). Instant start, near-full hold, and a very short release so notes stop tight.
- Listen for: compare DRIVE at 1 and at 6. The driven version is denser and louder, with the snarl pushed to the front.

context.lfo.rate: Here the LFO runs at about 100 Hz. Its speed sets the pitch of the roughness. It does not follow the keyboard, so each note snarls differently.
context.vcf.modDepth: How hard the LFO shakes the filter. This is the "amount of snarl".
context.lfo.shape: Sine is the smoothest rasp. Square is the harshest.
context.lfo.keySync: Restarts the LFO on each note so the attack is consistent.
context.od.drive: Thickens and compresses the result.

tweaks.hear: A wobble, then a growl, then a metallic ring as the LFO climbs through the audio range.
A harder, buzzier edge.
The snarl becomes a subtle roughness on an otherwise normal bass.

sounds.name: Wobbly Two-Note Keys
sounds.ref: In the style of Boards of Canada — "Roygbiv"
sounds.blurb: Soft, slightly seasick keys that can play two notes at once.
sounds.how: PARAPHONIC gives each oscillator its own note when you hold two keys. The SHAPE knobs sit either side of triangle for a mellow tone. The worn-tape wobble comes from the LFO, turned right down by Attenuator 2 and patched to both oscillators’ pitch. Delay smears it all together.

steps.title: Two mellow oscillators
steps.why:
Two soft oscillators make a mellow base, closer to a worn electric piano than a buzzy synth.
- OSC MIX 0: OSC is short for oscillator, the part that makes the raw tone. The centre of the crossfade gives both an equal share.
- SHAPE 2.6 (osc 1): between saw and triangle, 60% of the way to triangle. Softer than a saw, fuller than a triangle; the morphing SHAPE knob is what makes in-between tones like this possible.
- SHAPE 3.2 (osc 2): mostly triangle with a little sine, a rounder, flute-like tone.
- RANGE 8’ on both: the same octave, in the normal keys range.
- TUNE +0.1 st (osc 2): a tenth of a semitone sharp. When both play the same note they beat slowly, which gives gentle movement.
- Listen for: a slow waver on a held note from the detune. Turn SHAPE 1 towards 2 to hear it brighten, then back.

steps.title: Switch on PARAPHONIC
steps.why:
This switch lets the synth play two notes at once, one on each oscillator.
- PARAPHONIC on: hold two keys and each oscillator takes one; hold one key and both play it. Paraphonic sits between mono and poly: the two notes still share one filter and one amplifier, so a second note added while the first is held does not get its own attack.
- Listen for: hold a key, then add a second. The new note just appears inside the sound already playing. Press both together for a clean two-note chord.

steps.title: Gentle filter with key tracking
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) softens the keys and gives each chord a gentle pluck.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 6.2 (931 Hz): a medium cutoff that takes the edge off the top. Lower is muffled; higher is brighter and more present.
- RESO 2: resonance, just a little, enough to round the pluck without a whistle.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking makes the cutoff follow the notes, so high notes stay as bright as low ones.
- ENV DEPTH 3 (30%): ENV is short for envelope. Envelope 2 lifts the cutoff this much at the start of each chord.
- A 0 / D 540 ms / S 30% / R 330 ms (env 2): opens instantly, closes over about half a second to a low hold, and eases down after release.
- Listen for: a soft brightening at the start of each chord that settles over half a second. Both notes share it, so they pluck together.

steps.title: Soft, ringing loudness
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). Here it gives the keys a soft start and a ringing tail, like an electric piano with the pedal half down.
- A 3.5 (9 ms), env 1: a slightly soft attack that takes the click off without sounding slow.
- D 7 (820 ms), S 60%: the level falls gently over most of a second to 60% and holds, so chords bloom and then settle.
- R 7 (500 ms): half a second of fade after you let go, so one chord rings into the next.
- Listen for: the tail after releasing a chord. Shorten R to hear the keys go dry and choppy, then set it back.

steps.title: Tape wobble: ATT 2 to OSC 1+2
steps.why:
This adds the worn-tape wobble in pitch. The LFO (low-frequency oscillator), a slow wave you do not hear directly, is sent to pitch.
- ATT 2 → OSC 1+2: Attenuator 2 already carries the LFO inside. Patching its output to OSC 1+2, the pitch input for both oscillators, sends that LFO to pitch.
- 2 (ATT 2) at 1: the attenuator sets how much gets through. At 1 it is about half a semitone each way. Keep it low: a full-strength LFO would swing the pitch by octaves. It also feeds pulse width, which only matters on pulse shapes.
- RATE (LFO) 3.3 (0.89 Hz): just under one wobble a second. Below 1 Hz sounds like warped tape.
- SHAPE (LFO) 0 (sine): a smooth swing with no jumps.
- Listen for: a slow, seasick drift in pitch on held chords. Turn ATT 2 to 0 and back up to 1 for an A/B.

steps.title: Delay
steps.why:
An analogue echo sits under the keys and fills the space between chords.
- TIME 6.5 (210 ms): about a fifth of a second between echoes, so they trail close behind each chord. It is a bucket-brigade delay, so each echo is a little darker than the last.
- REPEATS 4 (40%): how much echo is fed back. You hear a few repeats before they die away.
- MIX 2.5 (25%): echoes well behind the dry keys. At 0 there is no delay at all.
- Listen for: short chords leaving a soft trail. The pitch wobble carries into the echoes, which adds to the old-tape feel.

context.osc.para: Gives each oscillator its own note. There is still one filter and one amplifier, so both notes share the same pluck.
context.att.2: Pitch wobble depth. At 1 it is about half a semitone each way. It also feeds pulse width, but that only matters on pulse shapes.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of the wobble. Under 1 Hz sounds like a warped tape.
context.osc1.shape: Between saw and triangle. Turn towards saw for brighter keys, towards sine for something closer to a music box.
context.osc.mix: In paraphonic mode this balances the two notes against each other.

tweaks.hear: The pitch drifts far enough to sound properly out of tune — old, damaged tape.
The second note becomes reedy, and the LFO now also sweeps its pulse width.

tweaks.try: Set to about 2.9 (a fifth up) and switch PARAPHONIC off
tweaks.hear: One key now plays a two-note chord.
The keys wash into a hazy bed.

sounds.name: Dub Chord Stab
sounds.ref: In the style of Basic Channel — dub techno
sounds.blurb: Short, hollow chord stab that trails off into wavering echoes.
sounds.how: Oscillator 2 is tuned a fifth above Oscillator 1, so one key gives a two-note chord. The band-pass filter strips out both the bass and the top, which is the hollow, distant tone of dub techno. The analogue delay does the rest: long-ish repeats timed to the beat, with the LFO gently moving the delay time so the echoes drift in pitch.

steps.title: A fifth apart
steps.why:
Tuning the two oscillators a fifth apart means one key plays a two-note chord, the base of a dub techno stab.
- OSC MIX 0: OSC is short for oscillator, the part that makes the raw tone. The centre of the crossfade gives an equal blend.
- SHAPE 2 on both: sawtooths, bright and full of harmonics for the filter to hollow out.
- RANGE 8’ on both: the same octave.
- TUNE 2.9 (+7 st), osc 2: seven semitones up is a fifth. The knob covers about an octave each way, so watch the readout and stop at +7.
- Listen for: an open, organ-like chord from a single key. Nudge Oscillator 2’s TUNE slightly off +7 and hear it start to beat and sour.

steps.title: Band-pass filter
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is switched to band-pass, which strips out the bass and the top together. That is the hollow, heard-through-a-wall tone of dub techno.
- MODE band-pass: press MODE until the middle lamp lights. Only a band around the cutoff gets through.
- FREQ 6 (805 Hz): the centre of that band, in the mids. This is the main performance control in this style: lower is muffled, higher is thinner and more nasal.
- RESO 4.5: resonance narrows and sharpens the band, making the stab more hollow and focused.
- ENV DEPTH 3.5 (35%): ENV is short for envelope. Envelope 2 lifts the band on each stab.
- A 0 / D 150 ms / S 0% / R 95 ms (env 2): a quick lift that falls away fast, giving each stab a small flick at the front.
- Listen for: the chord losing its low end and its fizz. Switch MODE back to low-pass for a moment to hear the difference.

steps.title: Short stab
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). With no sustain, every note is a short burst however long the key is held.
- A 0 ms (env 1): instant start for a sharp, rhythmic hit.
- D 5.2 (180 ms): the stab dies away in under a fifth of a second.
- S 0%: nothing is held, so long and short presses sound the same.
- R 5 (95 ms): a short tail if you let go early.
- Listen for: hold a key and the chord still stops quickly. A short, dry stab leaves room for the echoes that come next.

steps.title: Delay timed to the beat
steps.why:
The delay is where the dub sound lives. Its echoes are timed so they fall between the beats.
- TIME 8.4 (370 ms): about a dotted eighth note at 120 bpm, so echoes land off the beat. It is an analogue bucket-brigade delay, so each repeat comes back darker. At a different tempo, set it by ear.
- REPEATS 6.8 (68%): plenty of feedback for a long echo tail. Near maximum it builds instead of fading.
- MIX 4.5 (45%): nearly as much echo as dry sound.
- Listen for: play a stab on each beat and hear the repeats fill the gaps and slowly darken. Raise REPEATS briefly towards 9 to hear the tail start to build on itself.

steps.title: Make the echoes drift
steps.why:
A slow, shallow movement of the delay time makes the echoes drift in pitch, like a tape echo with a worn motor. The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) provides that movement.
- ATT 2 → DELAY TIME: Attenuator 2 carries the LFO inside. This cable sends it to the delay time input, where it adds to the TIME knob.
- 2 (ATT 2) at 1.5: how far the LFO moves the delay time. Small amounts give drift; large amounts give seasick warble.
- RATE (LFO) 2.5 (0.36 Hz): one slow cycle roughly every three seconds.
- SHAPE (LFO) 0 (sine): a smooth swing with no jumps.
- Listen for: the echo tail bending slightly flat and sharp as it fades. Turn ATT 2 up to 5 to hear it exaggerated, then bring it back.

context.osc2.tune: Tuned a fifth up (+7 semitones) so one key plays a chord.
context.vcf.mode: Band-pass removes lows and highs together. That is the "heard through a wall" tone.
context.vcf.freq: Moves the band up and down. This is the main performance control for this style.
context.delay.repeats: How long the echo tail lasts. Near maximum it builds instead of fading.
context.delay.time: Set to a dotted eighth at 120 bpm. Moving it while echoes are sounding bends their pitch.
context.att.2: How far the LFO moves the delay time. Small amounts give drift; large amounts give seasick warble.

tweaks.try: Sweep slowly between 4.5 and 7.5 as the stabs repeat
tweaks.hear: The chord moves from murky to thin and bright, and the echoes keep the older tone as they fade.

tweaks.try: Push to 9 for a bar, then pull back
tweaks.hear: The echoes pile up into a wash, then settle again.
The stab gets a gritty, saturated edge and drives the delay harder.

tweaks.try: Set to about 1.25 (a minor third up)
tweaks.hear: A darker, minor-sounding stab.

sounds.name: Sync Sweep Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of The Cars — "Let’s Go"
sounds.blurb: Tearing, vocal lead where every note sweeps through its harmonics.
sounds.how: With OSC SYNC on, Oscillator 1 forces Oscillator 2 to restart its wave each cycle. Oscillator 2 can no longer change pitch, so raising its tuning changes its tone instead, adding sharp harmonics. Patching Envelope 2 to Oscillator 2’s pitch does that raising automatically on each note, which is the classic sync sweep.

steps.title: Listen to Oscillator 2 only
steps.why:
The sound in this patch comes from Oscillator 2, so the mix is set to hear it alone.
- OSC MIX 5 (OSC 2 only): OSC is short for oscillator, the part that makes the raw tone. Fully right on the crossfade means only Oscillator 2 is heard. Oscillator 1 still runs silently and will control it once sync is on.
- SHAPE 2 (osc 2): a sawtooth, bright with every harmonic, which is the best raw material for sync.
- RANGE 8’ on both: the same octave, so Oscillator 1 sets the pitch the synced oscillator will lock to.
- TUNE 0 (osc 1): centred, so the pitch follows the keys.
- Listen for: a plain, bright saw. Nothing tears yet.

steps.title: Switch on OSC SYNC and raise TUNE
steps.why:
Hard sync makes Oscillator 1 restart Oscillator 2’s wave on every cycle. Oscillator 2 can no longer change pitch, so its TUNE knob changes the tone instead.
- OSC SYNC on: Oscillator 2 now always plays Oscillator 1’s pitch.
- TUNE +4.8 st (osc 2): raising it adds sharp, nasal harmonics without changing the note. Higher gives more and harder harmonics; at 0 the sync is barely heard.
- Listen for: turn Oscillator 2’s TUNE slowly up and down on a held note. The pitch stays put while the tone tears and shifts, almost like a voice.

steps.title: Patch ENV 2 to OSC 2
steps.why:
Patching Envelope 2 to Oscillator 2’s pitch does that tuning sweep automatically on every note. This is the classic sync lead.
- ENV 2 → OSC 2: ENV 2 is Envelope 2 as a voltage; an envelope is a shape that runs once per note. OSC 2 is Oscillator 2’s own pitch input, which changes tone rather than pitch while sync is on. The envelope pushes the tuning up at the start of each note and lets it fall back.
- A 0 ms (env 2): the sweep starts at its sharpest instantly.
- D 6.8 (690 ms): about two-thirds of a second to fall. This is the length of the sweep.
- S 20%: where the sweep comes to rest while a key is held.
- R 5 (95 ms): a quick return after release.
- Listen for: each note starts bright and tearing and slides to mellow. Shorten D for a quick zap, lengthen it for a slow “yeow”.

steps.title: Open filter
steps.why:
The sweep is the sound, so the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is left mostly open and does not move.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 8 (3.5 kHz): trims only the harshest fizz from the top. Lower would dull the sync harmonics you just built.
- RESO 1.5: resonance, just a touch, with no whistle.
- ENV DEPTH 0: ENV is short for envelope. Envelope 2 is busy on the pitch cable; at zero it does not move the cutoff as well.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking makes the cutoff follow the notes, so high notes stay as bright as low ones.
- Listen for: very little change, only slightly less fizz on top. Pull FREQ down to 5 to hear how much of the sweep the filter could hide, then return it to 8.

steps.title: Lead playing feel
steps.why:
The last touches give it a lead-playing feel: a solid note, a slight slide, a little grit and a short echo.
- A 0 / D 150 ms / S 90% / R 95 ms (env 1): Envelope 1 sets loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). Instant start, near-full hold, short tail.
- PORTA TIME 1 (100 ms): portamento, a quick pitch slide from each note to the next.
- DRIVE 3: light overdrive after the filter, adding grit that helps a lead cut through a mix.
- MIX 2 · TIME 240 ms · REPEATS 3.5: a quiet echo about a quarter of a second behind, with a few repeats.
- Listen for: legato phrases gliding between notes with a short echo behind. Blend OSC MIX back towards the centre to add a solid fundamental under the sweep.

context.osc.sync: Locks Oscillator 2 to Oscillator 1’s pitch. Without it, this patch is just an oscillator whose pitch swoops wildly.
context.osc2.tune: With sync on this is a tone control. Higher means more, sharper harmonics.
context.env2.d: The length of the sweep on each note.
context.env2.s: Where the sweep comes to rest while a key is held.
context.osc.mix: Fully right so only the synced oscillator is heard. Blend Oscillator 1 back in for a solid fundamental underneath.

tweaks.hear: Short gives a spitting "pew" at the front of each note; long gives a slow, vocal sweep.
The same tone change the envelope makes, under your control.
Oscillator 1 adds body under the sweep.
The lock is gone: Oscillator 2’s pitch now dives on every note. That is what sync was hiding.

sounds.name: Zap Kick Drum
sounds.ref: In the style of Kraftwerk — "Numbers"
sounds.blurb: Synthesised kick: a sine wave whose pitch dives in a few milliseconds.
sounds.how: An analogue kick is a sine wave that starts high and drops very quickly to a low note, with a short loudness envelope. The Neutron has no knob for "envelope to pitch", so you build it from the patch bay: Envelope 2 goes into Attenuator 2, and Attenuator 2 goes to the pitch of both oscillators. The ATT 2 knob then sets how far the pitch dives.

steps.title: A sine wave
steps.why:
The body of an analogue kick is a pure, low tone, so start with a sine wave and nothing else.
- OSC MIX −5 (OSC 1 only): OSC is short for oscillator, the part that makes the raw tone. Fully left on the crossfade means only Oscillator 1 is heard.
- SHAPE 4 (sine): fully right on the morph. A sine has no harmonics at all, just the fundamental, which is the round thump of a kick. A little towards triangle adds some knock.
- RANGE 16’: an octave below 8’, down where a kick’s weight sits.
- TUNE 0: the final pitch of the kick. Later you can tune it to the key of the track.
- Listen for: a smooth, hooting tone that holds as long as the key is down. It needs a short envelope before it sounds like a drum.

steps.title: Short loudness envelope
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). A drum has no held part, so the note dies away on its own.
- A 0 ms (env 1): full level instantly, for a hard hit.
- D 5.6 (260 ms): the length of the kick’s body, about a quarter of a second. Shorter is a tight, clicky kick; longer is boomier.
- S 0%: nothing is held, so the sound fades out even with the key down.
- R 5.4 (130 ms): the release is set close to the decay, so short and long key presses sound the same.
- Listen for: a short, round “boop” on each key. It still has no punch: the pitch does not move yet.

steps.title: A very fast Envelope 2
steps.why:
Envelope 2 is set up very fast, ready to drive the pitch in the next step. An envelope is a shape that runs once per note.
- A 0 ms (env 2): the envelope starts at full straight away, so the pitch will begin high on the first instant.
- D 3.6 (48 ms): about 50 ms of fall. Long enough to hear as a thump, too short to hear as a falling note. This is the most sensitive control in the patch.
- S 0% · R 30 ms: the envelope always falls to nothing and resets quickly, so repeated hits sound the same.
- Listen for: no change yet. Envelope 2 is only wired to the filter, through ENV DEPTH, which is still at 0.

steps.title: Patch ENV 2 → ATT2 IN, ATT 2 → OSC 1+2
steps.why:
Two cables build the envelope-to-pitch route the Neutron has no knob for.
- ENV 2 → ATT2 IN: Attenuator 2 normally carries the LFO (low-frequency oscillator). This cable replaces the LFO with Envelope 2.
- ATT 2 → OSC 1+2: sends the attenuated envelope to the pitch of both oscillators. OSC 1+2 is the shared pitch input.
- 2 (ATT 2) at 7.5: the attenuator is now your pitch-dive depth. Low is a soft thud; high is a laser zap. Full strength moves pitch a long way, which is why it goes through the attenuator.
- Listen for: each hit now starts with a fast downward swoop into the low sine, the classic synth kick. Sweep ATT 2 from 3 to 9 while playing and hear it go from thud to zap.

steps.title: Click and weight
steps.why:
The filter adds a click to the front and the overdrive adds weight.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 6.5 (1.2 kHz): the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) rests fairly open, trimming the top.
- RESO 0: no resonance, so the filter does not ring or add a pitch of its own.
- ENV DEPTH 3 (30%): ENV is short for envelope. Envelope 2 also lifts the cutoff for its brief 48 ms, adding a click at the attack.
- DRIVE 4.5: overdrive squares off the sine, making the kick harder and louder without making it longer, because it sits before the amplifier.
- TONE 4 · LEVEL 8: TONE slightly left rounds the grit; LEVEL is the overdrive’s output and so the synth’s volume.
- Listen for: a firmer, punchier kick with a tick at the front. Compare DRIVE at 1 and 4.5 to hear how much weight it adds.

context.att.2: How far the pitch dives at the start of each hit. Low is a soft thud; high is a laser zap.
context.env2.d: How long the pitch dive takes. This is the most sensitive control in the patch.
context.env1.d: The length of the kick’s body.
context.osc1.shape: Sine for a clean kick. Towards triangle adds a little knock.
context.od.drive: Squares off the sine for a harder, louder kick.
context.osc1.tune: The final pitch of the kick. Tune it to the track.

tweaks.hear: The dive becomes audible as a falling "pew" — an electro tom or laser.
From a soft, round thud to a sharp zap.

tweaks.try: Raise to 5, set MODE to band-pass and ENV DEPTH to 6
tweaks.hear: Noise plus a tuned thump: the start of a snare.
A distorted, hard techno kick.

sounds.name: Sighing PWM Pad
sounds.ref: In the style of Brian Eno — ambient pads
sounds.blurb: Slow, shimmering pad that starts bright, darkens as you hold it and opens again as it fades.
sounds.how: Two pulse waves have their width swept by the LFO through Attenuator 2, which gives a slow, chorus-like shimmer with no cable needed. The unusual part is the filter: ENV DEPTH only pushes upwards, so to make the filter close during a note you patch the inverter (which carries Envelope 2 upside down) into FREQ MOD. The delay adds space.

steps.title: Two pulse waves, slightly detuned
steps.why:
Two pulse waves an octave apart make the raw material for a shimmering pad.
- OSC MIX 0: OSC is short for oscillator, the part that makes the raw tone. The centre of the crossfade gives both an equal share.
- SHAPE 1 on both (pulse): hollow, reedy waves whose width can be moved, which is where the shimmer will come from.
- RANGE 8’ (osc 1) and 16’ (osc 2): an octave apart, so Oscillator 2 adds a lower layer.
- TUNE +0.1 st (osc 2): a hair of detune, adding a slow beat.
- WIDTH 5 (50%) and 4 (41%): a square on 1, a slightly thinner pulse on 2, so the layers differ in colour.
- PARAPHONIC on: hold two keys and each oscillator plays one, so you can play two-note chords.
- Listen for: a hollow, organ-like tone. Hold two keys to hear each oscillator take a note.

steps.title: Pulse-width modulation with ATT 2
steps.why:
PWM (pulse-width modulation) makes the pulse waves slowly thin and fatten, which sounds like a gentle chorus. The Neutron has no knob marked PWM: ATT 2 is it.
- 2 (ATT 2) at 5.5: Attenuator 2 carries the LFO (low-frequency oscillator) to both oscillators’ pulse width with no cable needed. This knob sets how far the width swings. Too high and the pulses thin out to nothing at the extremes.
- RATE (LFO) 3 (0.63 Hz): the speed of the shimmer, a little more than one sweep every two seconds.
- SHAPE (LFO) 1 (triangle): an even, steady swing, which gives the smoothest shimmer.
- Listen for: a slow swirling on held notes. Turn ATT 2 to 0 and back up to hear the static pulse come alive.

steps.title: Slow loudness
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). Here it makes notes fade in and overlap.
- A 7 (270 ms), env 1: a slow attack, so notes swell in rather than start with a hit.
- D 6 (360 ms), S 90%: after the peak the level barely dips, holding at 90% for as long as the key is down.
- R 8 (1.1 s): more than a second of fade after you let go, so one chord overlaps the next.
- Listen for: notes blooming in and trailing on after release. Play slow chord changes and hear them blend into one another.

steps.title: Bright resting filter
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) starts well open. The next step makes it close during each note, so this sets the brightest point.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 7.6 (2.6 kHz): fairly bright. This is the tone heard at the very start and end of each note.
- RESO 2.5: resonance, a light peak that gives the filter movement a little voice.
- ENV DEPTH 0: ENV is short for envelope. ENV DEPTH only pushes the cutoff upwards, so it stays off here; the downward move is patched next.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking makes the cutoff follow the notes, so the two paraphonic notes stay evenly bright.
- Listen for: a clear, bright pad. Lower FREQ briefly to preview the darker sound it will sink to.

steps.title: Patch INVERT to FREQ MOD
steps.why:
This cable is what makes the pad sigh. ENV DEPTH can only push the cutoff up, so the inverter provides a downward push.
- INVERT → FREQ MOD: the inverter carries Envelope 2 upside down. FREQ MOD is the cutoff modulation input; this cable also removes the LFO that normally feeds it, so the LFO now only moves pulse width.
- MOD DEPTH 5 (50%): scales the inverted envelope, so it sets how far the filter closes while a note is held.
- A 8.6 (1.3 s), env 2: how slowly the pad darkens after a key is pressed.
- D 150 ms · S 100%: the envelope reaches full and stays there, so the pad stays dark while held.
- R 7.5 (750 ms): how slowly it brightens again after release.
- Listen for: each chord starts bright, dulls over a second or so, then opens up again as it fades.

steps.title: Space
steps.why:
A long analogue delay adds space and stands in for reverb.
- TIME 7.5 (280 ms): echoes a little over a quarter of a second apart. It is a bucket-brigade delay, so each repeat comes back darker and blurs into the pad.
- REPEATS 5.5 (55%): moderate feedback, a tail of several echoes.
- MIX 3.5 (35%): echoes clearly present but behind the dry pad.
- Listen for: the space around the pad, especially as notes fade. Pull MIX to 0 and the pad sounds close and dry.

context.att.2: Pulse-width modulation depth. Too high and the pulses thin out to nothing at the extremes.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of the shimmer. The cable into FREQ MOD has removed the LFO from the filter, so here it only moves pulse width.
context.vcf.modDepth: Scales the inverted envelope, so it sets how far the filter closes while you hold a note.
context.env2.a: How slowly the pad darkens after a key is pressed.
context.env2.r: How slowly it brightens again after release.
context.vcf.freq: The brightest point of the pad, heard at the very start and the very end of each note.

tweaks.hear: Held notes sink almost to silence, then bloom when you let go.
Now the inverted envelope lets the bass in as you hold: the pad gains weight instead of losing brightness.
A slower, gentler shimmer.
The pad never fully stops: a drone you can play over.

sounds.name: Detuned Reese Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Kevin Saunderson — "Just Want Another Chance"
sounds.blurb: Dark, slowly churning bass made from two sawtooths tuned slightly apart.
sounds.how: Two sawtooths at almost the same pitch drift in and out of step with each other. When they line up the bass is full; when they oppose each other parts of the tone cancel, and the result is a slow churning that never quite repeats. A low-pass filter keeps only the bottom of that movement, and a very slow LFO, already wired to the filter through MOD DEPTH, opens and closes it a little.

steps.title: Two sawtooths, slightly apart
steps.why:
Two sawtooths tuned slightly apart drift in and out of step, which is the whole Reese effect. When they line up the bass is full; when they oppose, parts of the tone cancel.
- OSC MIX 0: OSC is short for oscillator. At the centre of the crossfade both saws are equal, which gives the deepest cancelling. Off-centre the churn gets shallower.
- SHAPE 2 on both (saw): every harmonic present, so there is a lot to phase against itself.
- RANGE 16’ on both: an octave below 8’, in bass range.
- TUNE 0 (osc 1) and +0.3 st (osc 2): the small gap is the effect. A wider gap churns faster; at zero the movement stops.
- Listen for: hold a note and hear a slow churning that never quite repeats. Turn Oscillator 2’s TUNE back to 0 to hear it go still.

steps.title: Low-pass, mostly closed
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) keeps only the bottom of that movement and turns the churn into a growl.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 4.7 (311 Hz): the buzz goes and you hear mostly low end. Lower is a sub rumble; higher lets the phasing top through.
- RESO 2.5: resonance, a little edge at the cutoff.
- KEY TRK off: key tracking off, so the cutoff stays put whatever note you play.
- ENV DEPTH 0: ENV is short for envelope. Envelope 2 is not moving the filter, so the tone stays steady and the churning is the only motion.
- Listen for: a dark growl that still moves underneath. Turn FREQ up to 7 for a moment to hear the full, buzzy phasing.

steps.title: A very slow LFO on the filter
steps.why:
A very slow LFO (low-frequency oscillator) opens and closes the filter a little, on top of the churn. The LFO is a repeating wave you do not hear directly; it moves other settings.
- MOD DEPTH 2.4 (24%): with nothing patched into FREQ MOD, the LFO already reaches the cutoff. This sets how far it moves it; kept low so it is a gentle drift.
- RATE (LFO) 2.6 (0.40 Hz): one cycle every two and a half seconds.
- SHAPE (LFO) 1 (triangle): an even rise and fall.
- KEY SYNC off: the LFO runs free, so it never lines up with the notes the same way twice.
- Listen for: the bass slowly brightening and darkening over a couple of seconds.

steps.title: Held loudness
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). For a held bass, notes should stay at full weight.
- A 1.5 (1 ms), env 1: a slightly softened attack that takes off the click without losing punch.
- D 150 ms · S 100%: full sustain, so long notes stay at full level and keep filling the low end.
- R 4 (41 ms): a short release, so notes stop cleanly.
- Listen for: long notes holding steady, with only the churn and slow filter moving.

steps.title: Some overdrive
steps.why:
Overdrive after the filter thickens the growl and evens out the dips where the two sawtooths cancel.
- DRIVE 4: moderate distortion. It squashes the loud and quiet moments of the churn closer together, so the bass stays present in a mix.
- TONE 4: below centre keeps the top rounded. Right of centre would thin the bass and add bite.
- LEVEL 7: the overdrive’s output and the synth’s volume, just under the default 8.
- Listen for: compare DRIVE at 1 and 4. The driven version is thicker and steadier in level, with the churn more even.

context.osc2.tune: In this sound the small gap between the oscillators is the whole effect. A wider gap churns faster; at zero the movement stops.
context.osc.mix: At the centre the two sawtooths are equal, which gives the deepest cancelling. Off-centre the churning gets shallower.
context.vcf.freq: How much of the churning you hear. Lower is a sub rumble; higher lets the buzzing, phasing top through.
context.vcf.modDepth: How far the slow LFO moves the cutoff.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of the slow filter movement. It runs free, so it never lines up with the notes the same way twice.
context.od.drive: Thickens the tone and makes the loud and quiet moments of the churning more even.

tweaks.hear: The churning goes from a slow swell to a fast, seasick beating.

tweaks.try: Open slowly from 4 to 7 on a held note
tweaks.hear: The buzzing, phasing upper part of the two sawtooths comes through: the brighter, later style of Reese.
The sub goes and a nasal, hollow growl is left, useful as a layer over a separate sub bass.
A harder, more distorted growl with less difference between loud and quiet moments.

sounds.name: LFO Wobble Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Skream and Benga — 2000s dubstep
sounds.blurb: Heavy bass whose filter opens and closes in time with the beat.
sounds.how: The wobble is the LFO moving the filter cutoff, and on the Neutron that connection is already made: MOD DEPTH sets the amount. A resonant low-pass filter gives each opening a vocal "wow". The LFO’s RATE sets the rhythm of the wobble and its SHAPE sets the character, so those two knobs are what you play.

steps.title: Saw with a square underneath
steps.why:
A sawtooth with a square underneath gives a thick, full bass for the filter to wobble.
- OSC MIX −1.5 (65/35): OSC is short for oscillator. A little left of centre on the crossfade favours Oscillator 1.
- SHAPE 2, RANGE 16’ (osc 1): a sawtooth, bright and buzzy, an octave below 8’.
- SHAPE 1, WIDTH 5, RANGE 16’ (osc 2): a square pulse at the same octave. Its hollow tone adds body under the saw.
- TUNE +0.1 st (osc 2): a slight detune so the two beat gently.
- Listen for: a heavy, buzzy bass note with a slow beat in it. The filter is still open, so it is bright for now.

steps.title: Resonant low-pass, set low
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is set to the middle of the wobble, not the bottom: the LFO will push the cutoff above and below this point.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 4.5 (269 Hz): lower keeps the wobble mostly closed with brief openings; higher keeps it mostly open.
- RESO 5.5: resonance adds the “wow” as the cutoff passes through the harmonics. Too high and the bass thins out.
- KEY TRK off: key tracking off, so every note wobbles the same way.
- ENV DEPTH 0: ENV is short for envelope. Envelope 2 stays off the filter; the LFO does all the moving.
- Listen for: a dark, slightly nasal bass. Sweep FREQ by hand to preview the wobble.

steps.title: Turn up MOD DEPTH
steps.why:
No cable needed. The LFO (low-frequency oscillator), a repeating wave you do not hear directly, already feeds the filter’s FREQ MOD input.
- MOD DEPTH 6 (60%): how far the LFO moves the cutoff, the depth of the wobble. At 6 it swings about three octaves either side of FREQ.
- Listen for: a steady wobble, bright and dark about six times a second at the default LFO speed. Turn MOD DEPTH down to 2 and back up to 6 to hear the depth change.

steps.title: Set the LFO to the beat
steps.why:
The LFO’s RATE sets the rhythm of the wobble and its SHAPE sets the character, so these are the knobs you play.
- RATE (LFO) 4.7 (4.69 Hz): about one wobble per eighth note at 140 bpm. Around 4.13 is quarter notes, 5.09 eighth-note triplets, 5.34 sixteenths. Changing it mid-phrase is the main move in this style.
- SHAPE (LFO) 0 (sine): a round “wow-wow”. Saws give a one-way ramp that snaps back; square switches between closed and open.
- KEY SYNC on: restarts the LFO on each note, so every note starts at the same point of the wobble and stays locked to your playing.
- Listen for: play a note on the beat and the wobble lines up. Try RATE at 4.13 then 5.34 to hear the rhythm halve and double.

steps.title: Loudness and drive
steps.why:
Envelope 1 holds the note at full weight, and overdrive makes the open part of each wobble bark.
- A 0 / S 100% / R 27 ms (env 1): Envelope 1 sets loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). Instant start, full sustain for held notes, short release for clean stops.
- DRIVE 5: overdrive after the filter. It hits hardest when the filter is open, so the bright half of each wobble barks.
- TONE 4.5: slightly left of centre, rounding off the fizz.
- LEVEL 6.5: the overdrive’s output and the synth’s volume, lowered a little.
- Listen for: the open part of each wobble growling. Set DRIVE to 1 and back to 5 for an A/B.

context.lfo.rate: The rhythm of the wobble. At 140 bpm: 4.13 is quarter notes, 4.74 is eighth notes, 5.09 is eighth-note triplets, 5.34 is sixteenths. Changing it during a phrase is the main performance move in this style.
context.lfo.shape: Sine gives a round "wow-wow". Saw and reverse saw give a one-way ramp that snaps back. Square switches between closed and open with nothing in between.
context.lfo.keySync: Restarts the wobble on every note, so the rhythm stays locked to your playing.
context.vcf.modDepth: How far the LFO moves the cutoff. This is the depth of the wobble.
context.vcf.freq: The centre of the wobble. Lower keeps it mostly closed with brief openings; higher keeps it mostly open.
context.vcf.reso: The vocal quality of each opening. Too high and the bass thins out.
context.od.drive: Adds bark to the open half of each wobble.

tweaks.try: Switch between 4.13, 4.74 and 5.09 while the riff plays
tweaks.hear: Quarter-note, eighth-note and triplet wobbles. Changing between them is how wobble bass lines are phrased.
Each wobble now starts open and closes, a "yoi-yoi" instead of a "wow-wow".
A hard on-off chop with no sweep in between.
A shallower wobble that stays dark: more of a throb.

sounds.name: Overdriven Filter Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Daft Punk — "Da Funk"
sounds.blurb: Rasping, distorted lead where each note bites and then closes down.
sounds.how: One sawtooth goes through a resonant low-pass filter that Envelope 2 opens sharply on every note. The OVERDRIVE section comes after the filter, so it distorts the resonant sweep itself and turns a fairly polite sound into a rasp. A little portamento slurs the notes together.

steps.title: One sawtooth
steps.why:
Start with one plain sawtooth. At this point it is bright and simple; the filter and overdrive will give it its character.
- OSC MIX −5 (OSC 1 only): OSC is short for oscillator, the part that makes the raw tone. Fully left on the crossfade means only Oscillator 1 is heard.
- SHAPE 2 (saw): a sawtooth, carrying every harmonic.
- RANGE 8’: the normal playing octave for a lead.
- TUNE 0: centred, so the oscillator plays in tune with the keys.
- Listen for: a bright, plain buzz. Keep this sound in mind to compare with the finished lead.

steps.title: Close the filter and add resonance
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is closed right down with resonance ready to sing once it moves.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 4.4 (250 Hz): the cutoff, and where the filter rests after the envelope. This low, the note is dull. This is the knob to move by hand during a phrase.
- RESO 6: resonance puts a whistle-like peak at the cutoff. It will show once the envelope moves it.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking makes the cutoff follow the notes, so high and low notes stay equally bright.
- Listen for: a muffled, dull note. Sweep FREQ upwards to hear the resonant peak rise through the harmonics.

steps.title: Envelope 2 opens it on each note
steps.why:
Envelope 2 opens the filter sharply on every note. An envelope is a shape that runs once per note.
- ENV DEPTH 5 (50%): ENV is short for envelope. This sets how far Envelope 2 pushes the cutoff up at the start of each note.
- A 0 ms (env 2): the filter snaps open instantly.
- D 5.8 (300 ms): about a third of a second to close down. Shorter is more percussive; longer is a slower sweep.
- S 25%: where the filter settles while a key is held, low so held notes go darker.
- R 4 (41 ms): a quick close after release.
- Listen for: the “wow” at the front of every note as the resonant peak sweeps down.

steps.title: Heavy overdrive
steps.why:
Heavy overdrive is most of this sound’s character. It sits after the filter, so it distorts the resonant sweep itself.
- DRIVE 8: turning it up turns a polite filter sweep into a rasp and exaggerates the resonant peak. Turn it down to 1 to hear the plain filtered saw underneath.
- TONE 6: right of centre thins the bass a little and adds bite. Left of centre is rounder and heavier.
- LEVEL 5.5: distortion makes the sound much louder, so LEVEL comes down to compensate. It is the overdrive’s output, which everything passes through.
- Listen for: each note biting harder and fizzing as the filter sweeps. Swap DRIVE between 1 and 8 for the most obvious A/B in the patch.

steps.title: Loudness and slide
steps.why:
Envelope 1 gives the lead a firm shape, and a little portamento slurs the notes together.
- A 0 / D 150 ms / S 90% / R 27 ms (env 1): Envelope 1 sets loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). Instant start, near-full hold and a short release, so phrases stay tight.
- PORTA TIME 1.3 (170 ms): portamento, a pitch slide from each note to the next. A small amount like this bends each note into the next without sounding lazy.
- Listen for: play a legato phrase and hear the notes slide while each one still bites. Turn PORTA TIME to 0 to hear the notes jump.

context.od.drive: In this sound the overdrive is most of the character. Turn it down to 1 and you hear the plain filtered saw underneath.
context.od.tone: Right of centre thins the bass and adds bite. Left of centre is rounder and heavier.
context.od.level: Turned down to make up for how loud the distortion is.
context.vcf.reso: Puts a peak on the filter sweep. The overdrive exaggerates that peak.
context.vcf.envDepth: How far the filter opens at the start of each note.
context.env2.d: How long each note takes to close down again.
context.vcf.freq: Where the filter rests once the envelope has finished. This is the knob to move by hand during a phrase.
context.porta.time: The slide between notes.

tweaks.try: Pull back to 2, then return to 8
tweaks.hear: The same filter sweep, first clean and then distorted. The difference is what the overdrive adds.

tweaks.try: Sweep slowly from 3.5 to 6.5 over a few bars
tweaks.hear: The line opens from a muffled growl to a bright, tearing lead.
Each note becomes a short bark with a dull body.
From thick and woolly to thin and cutting.

sounds.name: Dark 80s Arpeggio Pluck
sounds.ref: In the style of Kyle Dixon & Michael Stein — "Stranger Things" theme
sounds.blurb: Soft, rounded pluck for steady arpeggios, with echoes filling the gaps.
sounds.how: A sawtooth and a narrow pulse are blended and sent through a low-pass filter that opens only a little on each note, so the pluck is soft and rounded. Both envelopes have no sustain, which makes every note the same short shape however it is played. A very slow LFO on the filter makes the pattern brighten and darken over several bars, and a delay timed to the tempo adds notes between the played ones.

steps.title: Saw plus a narrow pulse
steps.why:
A sawtooth and a narrow pulse blend into a tone with a little reed in it, a good base for a soft arpeggio.
- OSC MIX −1.5 (65/35): OSC is short for oscillator. Slightly left of centre on the crossfade, so the saw leads.
- SHAPE 2, RANGE 8’ (osc 1): a sawtooth in the normal playing octave.
- SHAPE 1, WIDTH 3.5 (37%), osc 2: a pulse narrower than square, which sounds a little reedy. At 5 it would be a hollow square.
- RANGE 8’ · TUNE +0.1 st (osc 2): same octave, with a tiny detune so the blend does not sound static.
- Listen for: a bright, slightly reedy buzz with gentle movement. The filter is still open.

steps.title: A short note shape
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). With no sustain, every note is the same short pluck.
- A 0 ms (env 1): instant start, so each note of the arpeggio is clearly defined.
- D 6.2 (420 ms): the note dies away in under half a second. With sustain at zero, this and the filter decay set the whole shape.
- S 0%: nothing held, even with the key down.
- R 5.5 (140 ms): similar to the decay so short and long presses sound alike.
- Listen for: short plucked notes that fade on their own. Hold a key to check it still dies away.

steps.title: A soft filter pluck
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) rests low and opens only a little on each note. The aim is a rounded “dum”, not a bright “pang”.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 4.6 (289 Hz): where the filter rests. Opening it slowly over many bars is the classic way to build this kind of arpeggio.
- RESO 3: resonance, a little, for a slightly rounded peak.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking keeps higher notes of the pattern from going dull.
- ENV DEPTH 3.8 (38%): ENV is short for envelope. How bright the front of each pluck is; keep it moderate.
- A 0 / D 220 ms / S 0% / R 95 ms (env 2): opens instantly and closes in about a fifth of a second. Shorter is more percussive.
- Listen for: a soft, rounded pluck. Raise ENV DEPTH to 7 to hear it turn bright and hard.

steps.title: Slow movement from the LFO
steps.why:
A very slow LFO (low-frequency oscillator) moves the filter over time, so the pattern brightens and darkens by itself. The LFO is a repeating wave you do not hear directly.
- MOD DEPTH 1.6 (16%): the LFO already feeds FREQ MOD, and this sets how far it moves the cutoff. Kept low for a gradual change.
- RATE (LFO) 1.8 (0.16 Hz): one cycle about every six seconds, heard as a slow change across the pattern rather than a wobble.
- SHAPE (LFO) 0 (sine): a smooth rise and fall.
- Listen for: let a steady arpeggio run for a few bars. It opens and closes gently without you touching anything.

steps.title: Delay timed to the tempo
steps.why:
An analogue delay timed to the tempo adds notes between the played ones.
- TIME 9.5 (540 ms): a dotted eighth note at 84 bpm, so each echo lands between the played notes. At another tempo, adjust it by ear until the echoes fall between the notes.
- REPEATS 4.5 (45%): a few echoes before they fade. Each repeat of the bucket-brigade delay is a little darker.
- MIX 3 (30%): how loud the echoes are against the played notes.
- Listen for: the pattern sounding busier than what you play. Pull MIX to 0 to hear the bare arpeggio.

context.vcf.freq: In this sound this is where the filter rests. Opening it slowly over many bars is the classic way to build this kind of arpeggio.
context.vcf.envDepth: How bright the front of each pluck is.
context.env2.d: How quickly each pluck closes down. Shorter is more percussive.
context.env1.d: The length of each note. With sustain at zero, this and the filter decay set the whole shape.
context.vcf.modDepth: How far the slow LFO moves the filter over time.
context.lfo.rate: Set very slow here, one cycle in about six seconds, so it is heard as a gradual change across the pattern and not as a wobble.
context.delay.time: A dotted eighth note at 84 bpm. If you change the tempo, retune this by ear until the echoes fall between the notes.
context.delay.mix: How loud the echoes are against the played notes.
context.osc2.width: Sets how reedy the pulse layer is. At 5 it is a hollow square.

tweaks.try: Open slowly from 4 to 6.5 while the arpeggio runs
tweaks.hear: The pattern builds from muffled to bright and urgent.
A tighter, more clicky pluck.

tweaks.try: Turn down to 0, then back to 3
tweaks.hear: How much of the pattern’s movement is coming from the echoes.

tweaks.try: Turn fully right for the pulse alone
tweaks.hear: A thinner, more nasal arpeggio.

sounds.name: Random Bleep Melody
sounds.ref: In the style of Raymond Scott and early Aphex Twin — self-playing bleeps
sounds.blurb: Play one key in any rhythm and the synth picks a new random pitch for every note.
sounds.how: The sample-and-hold takes readings of white noise, so its output is a random voltage that stays still between readings. Sent straight to pitch it would jump by several octaves, so it goes through Attenuator 1 first, and the ATT 1 knob sets the range of the melody. A last cable from MIDI GATE to S&H CLOCK makes it take exactly one reading per key press, so your rhythm decides when the pitch changes. The pitches are not tuned to a scale.

steps.title: A soft, pure tone
steps.why:
A soft, plain tone keeps the attention on the pitches, which will soon be picked at random.
- OSC MIX −5 (OSC 1 only): OSC is short for oscillator, the part that makes the raw tone. Fully left on the crossfade means only Oscillator 1 is heard.
- SHAPE 3.5 (triangle/sine): halfway between triangle and sine, a soft, round bleep with few harmonics. Turn towards pulse for a more chip-like tone.
- RANGE 8’: the middle octave, where bleeps sit clearly above a bass line.
- TUNE 0: centred, so the oscillator follows the keys in tune.
- Listen for: a pure, gentle tone, like a sine test signal with a little edge.

steps.title: Short bleeps
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). Here it turns each note into a short bleep.
- A 0 ms (env 1): instant start, so each bleep is clearly defined.
- D 5.2 (180 ms): the length of each bleep, about a fifth of a second.
- S 0%: nothing held, so the bleep dies away even with the key down.
- R 5 (95 ms): a short tail if you let go early.
- Listen for: short, round blips. Tap a rhythm on one key; for now every note is the same pitch.

steps.title: Patch S&H → ATT1 IN and ATT 1 → OSC 1+2
steps.why:
Two cables send a random voltage to pitch, scaled down so it stays musical. S&H stands for sample and hold: it reads white noise at a steady rate and holds each value, giving random steps.
- S&H → ATT1 IN: replaces Attenuator 1’s usual input (Attenuator 2) with the random steps. Straight to pitch they would jump by several octaves.
- ATT 1 → OSC 1+2: adds Attenuator 1’s output to both oscillators’ pitch, on top of the key you play.
- 1 (ATT 1) at 5: the range of the melody, about an octave either side. At 2 it stays within a couple of semitones; at 10 it spans several octaves.
- RATE (S&H) 6 (4.31 Hz) · GLIDE 0: for now the S&H picks a new value about four times a second on its own clock, and jumps without sliding.
- Listen for: pitches changing on their own, out of step with your playing. Hold a key and a note may even change mid-bleep.

steps.title: Patch MIDI GATE → S&H CLOCK
steps.why:
One more cable hands the timing to your playing.
- MIDI GATE → S&H CLOCK: MIDI GATE is high while a key is held. Into S&H CLOCK it replaces the sample and hold’s own clock, so a new reading is taken each time a key goes down, and the RATE knob no longer does anything.
- Listen for: every note now gets one steady random pitch, changing only when you play. Tap a rhythm and you get a new melody each time. The pitches are not tuned to a scale, so expect some sour ones.

steps.title: A little filter and echo
steps.why:
A slight filter pluck rounds each bleep, and a delay repeats the random notes so they overlap into phrases.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 7 (1.7 kHz): the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) trims the top a little.
- RESO 2.5: resonance, a small peak at the cutoff.
- ENV DEPTH 2 (20%): ENV is short for envelope. Envelope 2 lifts the cutoff a little at each note.
- A 0 / D 130 ms / S 0% / R 80 ms (env 2): a quick blip of brightness that falls back as each bleep dies.
- TIME 8.4 (370 ms) · REPEATS 5 · MIX 3.5: a dotted-eighth echo with several repeats, clearly audible behind the dry notes.
- Listen for: the echoes replaying earlier random notes under new ones, which makes the line sound more like a melody. Pull MIX to 0 to compare.

context.att.1: In this sound this is the range of the random melody. At 5 the notes land within about an octave of the key you play; at 2 they stay within a couple of semitones; at 10 they range over several octaves.
context.sh.rate: Does nothing once MIDI GATE is patched into S&H CLOCK. Unplug that cable and this knob sets how often the pitch changes.
context.sh.glide: At zero each note starts on its new pitch. Turn it up and each note slides to its pitch from the previous one.
context.env1.d: The length of each bleep.
context.osc1.shape: Between triangle and sine for a soft bleep. Turn towards pulse for a more chip-like tone.
context.delay.mix: The echoes repeat earlier random notes, which makes the line sound more like a melody.

tweaks.hear: The melody narrows to a few semitones around the played key, more like a nervous trill.
Each bleep swoops to its pitch from the last one.
Hollow, early-computer-game bleeps.
Old notes hang around for longer and pile into a cloud of random pitches.

sounds.name: Metal Clank Percussion
sounds.ref: In the style of Depeche Mode — early-80s metal percussion
sounds.blurb: Short, clanging hit like a struck pipe, made by one oscillator shaking the pitch of the other.
sounds.how: This is frequency modulation. Oscillator 2 is not heard; its output is patched, through Attenuator 1, into Oscillator 1’s pitch. Because that wobble happens hundreds of times a second, you hear it as a cluster of new overtones, not as vibrato. Tuning Oscillator 2 to an awkward interval makes those overtones clash like struck metal. Envelope 2 controls Attenuator 1’s level, so the clang is strongest at the hit and clears as it rings.

steps.title: Hear only Oscillator 1, as a sine
steps.why:
This sound uses FM (frequency modulation): one oscillator shakes the pitch of the other. Start by hearing only the one that will be shaken, as a sine.
- OSC MIX −5 (OSC 1 only): OSC is short for oscillator. Fully left on the crossfade means only Oscillator 1 is heard. Oscillator 2’s own output jack still works whatever the mix.
- SHAPE 4 (sine), RANGE 8’, TUNE 0 (osc 1): a sine has no overtones of its own, so everything you hear later comes from the modulation.
- SHAPE 4, RANGE 16’ (osc 2): Oscillator 2 will be the modulator. A sine gives the cleanest clang; saw or pulse add a gritty buzz.
- TUNE +8.2 st (osc 2): puts it a few semitones below Oscillator 1, at an interval that is deliberately not clean. That clash is what makes it sound like metal.
- Listen for: a plain sine tone. Oscillator 2 is running, but you will not hear it directly.

steps.title: A short hit
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). A struck object has no held part, so the note dies away on its own.
- A 0 ms (env 1): full level instantly, like a strike.
- D 5.6 (260 ms): the length of the whole hit, about a quarter of a second.
- S 0%: nothing held, so the hit fades even with the key down.
- R 5.4 (130 ms): close to the decay, so short and long presses sound alike.
- Listen for: a plain sine “boop”. The clang comes next.

steps.title: Patch OSC 2 → ATT1 IN and ATT 1 → OSC 1
steps.why:
Two cables route Oscillator 2 into Oscillator 1’s pitch. Because that wobble happens hundreds of times a second, you hear it as a cluster of new overtones, not as vibrato.
- OSC 2 → ATT1 IN: replaces Attenuator 1’s usual input with Oscillator 2’s audio.
- ATT 1 → OSC 1: adds it to Oscillator 1’s pitch only.
- 1 (ATT 1) at 9: the modulation depth, how hard Oscillator 2 shakes Oscillator 1. More gives more and harsher overtones; less is closer to a bell.
- Listen for: the “boop” turning into a harsh, clanging hit. Turn ATT 1 slowly from 0 to 9 on repeated hits, then try Oscillator 2’s TUNE: clean intervals (the knob at 0 or 5) ring like a bell, in-between settings clash.

steps.title: Patch ENV 2 → ATT1 CV
steps.why:
Real metal is harshest at the strike and clears as it rings. This cable makes the modulation depth follow an envelope.
- ENV 2 → ATT1 CV: Attenuator 1 is voltage controlled, so it can act as a spare amplifier. This cable replaces its usual control source with Envelope 2, so the modulation is strongest at the hit and fades with the envelope.
- A 0 / D 5.8 (300 ms), env 2: jumps to full on the strike and falls over about a third of a second. This is how long the harsh part of the clang lasts.
- S 0% · R 180 ms: the envelope always falls to nothing, so the tail ends as a purer tone.
- Listen for: each hit starting as a clang and ending as a cleaner sine. Lengthen D and the clang lasts through the whole note.

steps.title: Thin it out
steps.why:
The filter thins the hit so it sounds like a light pipe, not a heavy one, and a very short echo adds a small room.
- MODE high-pass, FREQ 5.8 (695 Hz): the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) now removes everything below the cutoff, taking out the low thump. Higher leaves a thinner tick.
- RESO 2 · ENV DEPTH 0: a little resonance, and ENV (envelope) depth off, so Envelope 2 only works on the clang.
- DRIVE 3: light overdrive for a bit of density.
- TIME 3 (66 ms) · REPEATS 3 · MIX 2: a quick slap, like a hard-walled room.
- Listen for: the hit losing its body and gaining a small room around it. Flip MODE to low-pass briefly to hear how much the high-pass took away.

context.osc2.tune: In this sound this is the character of the metal. Settings that make a clean interval with Oscillator 1 (0 is an octave below it, 5 is the same pitch) give a tuned, bell-like tone; in-between settings give clashing, clangy overtones.
context.att.1: The modulation depth: how hard Oscillator 2 shakes Oscillator 1’s pitch.
context.env2.d: How long the harsh part of the clang lasts before the tone clears.
context.osc2.range: At 16’ the modulator sits just below Oscillator 1. A slower modulator packs the new overtones closer together, which sounds denser and more metallic.
context.env1.d: The length of the whole hit.
context.osc.mix: Fully left so Oscillator 2 is only a modulator. Its OSC 2 output jack still works whatever the mix is set to.
context.vcf.freq: In high-pass mode, turning this up removes more of the body and leaves a thinner tick.
context.osc2.shape: A sine modulator gives the cleanest clang. Saw or pulse add a gritty buzz to it.

tweaks.try: Sweep slowly from 0 to 5 while the pattern plays
tweaks.hear: The hit moves through bell, gong, pipe and anvil tones as the ratio between the oscillators changes.
From a plain ping with a slightly bright front to a dense, harsh clang.
The clang shrinks to a brief tick at the front of an otherwise pure tone.

tweaks.try: Press RANGE on Oscillator 2 until 8’ is lit
tweaks.hear: A faster modulator spreads the new overtones further apart, so the clang becomes thinner and more bell-like.

sounds.name: Electro Snare
sounds.ref: In the style of Afrika Bambaataa & the Soulsonic Force — "Planet Rock"
sounds.blurb: Drum-machine snare: a burst of filtered noise over a short tuned tone.
sounds.how: Early drum machines built a snare from two parts: one or two short tones for the drum’s body and a burst of noise for the rattle of the wires. Here two triangle-wave oscillators give the body, the NOISE knob gives the wires, and a high-pass filter takes the low end off both so it sits above a kick drum. One short envelope shapes the whole hit.

steps.title: A tuned body from two triangles
steps.why:
Early drum machines built a snare from short tones for the drum’s body and noise for the wires. Two triangles make the body here.
- OSC MIX 0: OSC is short for oscillator. The centre of the crossfade gives both an equal share.
- SHAPE 3 on both (triangle): a soft tone with only a few harmonics, closer to a drum skin than a buzzy saw.
- RANGE 8’ on both · TUNE 0 (osc 1): the pitch of the body. The played key also sets it, so pick a key that suits the track.
- TUNE +7.9 st (osc 2): about 8 semitones above Oscillator 1. An interval that is not quite musical sounds more like a drum than a note.
- Listen for: a two-tone chord that holds while the key is down. It needs an envelope to sound like a hit.

steps.title: A short hit
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). With no sustain, every note becomes a short hit.
- A 0 ms (env 1): instant attack, for a sharp hit.
- D 5 (150 ms): the length of the snare. Short is tight and electronic; longer is closer to a loose acoustic drum.
- S 0%: nothing held.
- R 5 (95 ms): kept close to the decay so the snare sounds the same however long the key is held.
- Listen for: a small, tom-like “tok” on each key.

steps.title: Add noise
steps.why:
The noise generator supplies the rattle of the snare wires.
- NOISE 6 (60%): white noise added into the filter along with the oscillators. This is the balance between the wires (noise) and the body (the tones). It runs through the same envelope, so it stops with the body.
- Listen for: a hiss on top of the “tok”, about as loud as the tone. Turn NOISE between 3 and 9 to hear the snare go from tonal to trashy.

steps.title: High-pass filter
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is switched to high-pass, which takes the low end off both parts so the snare sits above a kick drum.
- MODE high-pass: press MODE until the top lamp lights. It removes the bass below the cutoff. Band-pass instead gives a boxier, older-sounding snare.
- FREQ 4.2 (216 Hz): around 4 to 5 keeps some thump; above 6 it is mostly noise.
- RESO 2.5: resonance, a slight ring at the cutoff.
- ENV DEPTH 0 · KEY TRK off: ENV is short for envelope. Neither the envelope nor the keys move the cutoff, so every hit is filtered the same.
- Listen for: the boom leaving the body and the noise getting brighter. Sweep FREQ from 3 to 7 to hear the body thin out.

steps.title: Crunch
steps.why:
Overdrive squashes the hit so it sounds denser and louder without lasting any longer.
- DRIVE 4.5: moderate distortion after the filter. It flattens the peak of the hit and brings the tail up, so the snare hits harder in a mix.
- TONE 5.5: just right of centre, keeping the noise bright. Further right adds more bite.
- LEVEL 7: the overdrive’s output and so the synth’s volume, a little under the default 8.
- Listen for: a fatter, more compressed crack. Set DRIVE to 1 and back to 4.5 to compare.

context.mix.noise: In this sound this is the balance between the wires (noise) and the body (the oscillators).
context.env1.d: The length of the snare. Short is tight and electronic; longer is closer to a loose acoustic drum.
context.env1.r: Kept the same as the decay so the snare sounds the same however long the key is held.
context.osc1.tune: The pitch of the body. The played key also sets it, so tune the snare from the keyboard first.
context.osc2.tune: The second body tone. Its distance from Oscillator 1 changes how "drum-like" or "note-like" the body is.
context.vcf.freq: In high-pass mode, higher removes more body. Around 4 to 5 keeps some thump; above 6 it is mostly noise.
context.vcf.mode: High-pass keeps all the top of the noise. Band-pass narrows it to a boxier, older-sounding snare.
context.od.drive: Squashes the hit so it sounds denser.

tweaks.try: Turn down to 0, then up to 10
tweaks.hear: From a bare tom-like body to a mostly-noise snare. Find the balance you like between the two.
A tight click-snare suited to fast electro patterns.

tweaks.try: Press MODE for band-pass and set FREQ to 6.5
tweaks.hear: A narrower, boxier snare with less sizzle.
The body disappears and you are left with a bright noise burst, close to a clap or an open hat.

sounds.name: Hoover Rave Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Joey Beltram — "Mentasm"
sounds.blurb: Thick, swirling rave lead that swoops down into each note.
sounds.how: The swirl is pulse-width modulation. Attenuator 2 already carries the LFO to both oscillators’ pulse-width inputs, so turning ATT 2 up makes the tone mod and pulse shapes thicken and thin several times a second, much like a chorus. The swoop is Envelope 2 patched to pitch through Attenuator 1: each note starts a few semitones sharp and falls into tune. Patching into ATT1 IN does not disturb Attenuator 2, so the pulse-width modulation carries on.

steps.title: Tone mod on top, pulse an octave below
steps.why:
Both oscillators use shapes that respond to pulse width, because the swirl in this sound comes from moving the width.
- OSC MIX 0: OSC is short for oscillator. The centre of the crossfade gives both an equal share.
- SHAPE 0.4 (tone mod/pulse), osc 1: between the Neutron’s own tone mod wave and a pulse. Both respond to WIDTH; a saw or triangle would ignore the modulation.
- WIDTH 5 (osc 1) · 4 (osc 2): set differently, so the two oscillators are never thin at the same moment.
- RANGE 8’ (osc 1) · 16’ (osc 2): Oscillator 2 is a pulse an octave below, adding weight.
- TUNE +0.1 st (osc 2): a hair sharp for slow beating.
- Listen for: a buzzy, reedy chord of octaves. Static for now.

steps.title: Fast pulse-width modulation with ATT 2
steps.why:
PWM (pulse-width modulation) turns the static tone into a thick swirl. The Neutron has no knob marked PWM: Attenuator 2 carries the LFO (low-frequency oscillator) to both oscillators’ pulse width with no cable.
- 2 (ATT 2) at 7: the PWM depth, how far the LFO thins and thickens both oscillators. This is the amount of swirl.
- RATE (LFO) 5.2 (7.96 Hz): about eight times a second. Around 6 to 10 Hz gives the restless hoover character; slower is a gentle chorus.
- SHAPE (LFO) 1 (triangle): an even sweep of the width.
- KEY SYNC off: the LFO runs free across notes.
- Listen for: a thick, restless churning. Turn ATT 2 to 0 and back up to 7 to hear the swirl appear.

steps.title: Patch ENV 2 → ATT1 IN and ATT 1 → OSC 1+2
steps.why:
Two cables add the swoop: each note starts sharp and falls into tune. Envelope 2, a shape that runs once per note, drives the pitch.
