- ENV 2 → ATT1 IN: replaces Attenuator 1’s usual input with Envelope 2. Attenuator 2 is untouched, so the PWM carries on.
- ATT 1 → OSC 1+2: sends the scaled envelope to both oscillators’ pitch.
- 1 (ATT 1) at 3: how far each note swoops. At 3 it starts about 5 semitones sharp.
- A 0 / D 5.3 (200 ms), env 2: jumps up instantly and falls into tune over a fifth of a second. This is the length of the swoop.
- S 0% · R 41 ms: the pitch always ends exactly in tune.
- Listen for: each note diving down into place. Raise ATT 1 for a bigger dive.

steps.title: Open filter
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is left fairly open so the swirl and swoop come through.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 7.4 (2.2 kHz): trims only the harshest top.
- RESO 2: resonance, just a little.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking makes the cutoff follow the notes, so high notes stay bright.
- ENV DEPTH 0: ENV is short for envelope. Left at zero so Envelope 2 only moves the pitch, not the filter.
- Listen for: a slightly smoother top. Lower FREQ to 5 briefly to hear how much the filter could hide.

steps.title: Slide, drive and a short echo
steps.why:
The last step adds slide, grit and a short echo for width.
- A 0 / S 100% / R 63 ms (env 1): Envelope 1 sets loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). Instant start, full hold, short release.
- PORTA TIME 2 (400 ms): portamento, a slow pitch slide from note to note, on top of the swoop from Envelope 2.
- DRIVE 4 · TONE 5 · LEVEL 6.5: overdrive thickens the swirl; LEVEL is lowered a little.
- TIME 4 (91 ms) · REPEATS 2.5 · MIX 2: a short, quiet echo that widens the sound.
- Listen for: legato notes gliding into each other with a swoop at each attack. Turn PORTA TIME to 0 to hear the slide go.

context.att.2: In this sound this is the pulse-width modulation depth: how far the LFO thins and thickens both oscillators. It is the amount of swirl.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of the swirl. Around 6 to 10 Hz gives the restless hoover character; slower sounds like a gentle chorus.
context.att.1: How far each note swoops down into tune. At 3 it starts about 5 semitones sharp.
context.env2.d: How long the swoop takes.
context.osc1.shape: Between tone mod and pulse. Both respond to pulse width; a saw or triangle here would ignore the modulation.
context.osc2.width: Set off-centre so the two oscillators are never thin at the same moment.
context.porta.time: The slide between notes, on top of the swoop from Envelope 2.
context.vcf.envDepth: Left at zero so Envelope 2 only moves the pitch.

tweaks.try: Turn down to 0, then back up to 7
tweaks.hear: Without pulse-width modulation the sound is flat and static. The swirl is all from this one knob.
Each note dives from almost an octave above: a much more exaggerated swoop.
A slow, siren-like fall into each note.
The swirl relaxes into a slow, wide chorus.

sounds.name: Slow Brass Swell
sounds.ref: In the style of Vangelis — "Blade Runner" main titles
sounds.blurb: Broad synth brass that opens slowly on each note, with gentle vibrato and long echoes.
sounds.how: Synth brass is mostly a filter shape. Two sawtooths supply the raw buzz, and Envelope 2 opens the low-pass filter slowly, so each note starts dull and swells brighter the way a brass player’s note does. The vibrato is the LFO, turned right down by Attenuator 2 and patched to pitch. A long delay stands in for the reverb on the records.

steps.title: Two sawtooths, slightly detuned
steps.why:
Two sawtooths supply the raw buzz for synth brass.
- OSC MIX 0: OSC is short for oscillator, the part that makes the raw tone. The centre of the crossfade gives both an equal share.
- SHAPE 2 on both (saw): every harmonic present, the brassy buzz.
- RANGE 8’ on both: the same octave.
- TUNE +0.1 st (osc 2): a touch sharp, so the two beat slowly and the sound gets wider, like a small section.
- Listen for: a bright, buzzy tone with a slow shimmer. The filter is still open, so it sounds more like a raw synth than brass.

steps.title: A filter that opens slowly
steps.why:
Synth brass is mostly a filter shape. The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) starts low and Envelope 2 opens it slowly, the way a brass player’s note swells.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 3.8 (161 Hz): the dull starting point of each note.
- RESO 1.5 · KEY TRK on: little resonance, and key tracking so high notes stay bright.
- ENV DEPTH 5.5 (55%): ENV is short for envelope. Envelope 2 opens the filter by more than four octaves. This is how bright the peak of the swell gets.
- A 7.2 (330 ms), env 2: the speed of the swell, the most important control for the brass character.
- D 1.2 s · S 55% · R 330 ms: after the peak it settles slowly to a medium brightness while held.
- Listen for: each note starting dull and blooming brighter. Set Envelope 2’s A to 0 and it becomes a snap.

steps.title: Loudness slightly softened
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). It fades in quicker than the filter, so the note starts straight away but dull.
- A 6.3 (140 ms), env 1: a short, soft fade-in.
- D 360 ms · S 90%: the level barely dips, holding at 90%.
- R 6.8 (420 ms): notes tail off over nearly half a second.
- Listen for: the note arriving before the brightness does. Release a chord and hear it fade gently.

steps.title: Vibrato: patch ATT 2 → OSC 1+2
steps.why:
Vibrato is the LFO (low-frequency oscillator), a slow wave you do not hear directly, moving pitch.
- ATT 2 → OSC 1+2: Attenuator 2 already carries the LFO. This cable adds its output to both oscillators’ pitch. It also feeds pulse width, which does nothing on sawtooths.
- 2 (ATT 2) at 0.9: the vibrato depth, a little under half a semitone each way. Keep it below 1: at full level the LFO would bend the pitch by two octaves.
- RATE (LFO) 4.9 (5.32 Hz): vibrato speed, about five times a second.
- SHAPE (LFO) 0 (sine): a smooth, even waver.
- Listen for: a gentle waver on held notes. Turn ATT 2 to 0 and back to 0.9 to compare.

steps.title: Long delay
steps.why:
A long analogue delay leaves a trail behind each note, standing in for the reverb on the records.
- TIME 9.2 (490 ms): nearly half a second between echoes, so they are heard as distinct repeats.
- REPEATS 5.5 (55%): the length of the trail, several fading echoes. Each repeat of the bucket-brigade delay is a little darker.
- MIX 3.5 (35%): echoes clearly present behind the dry brass.
- DRIVE 2: a touch more overdrive than the default, adding slight warmth.
- Listen for: slow phrases leaving a long trail. Pull MIX to 0 and the brass sounds close and dry.

context.env2.a: In this sound this is the speed of the swell. It is the most important control for the brass character.
context.vcf.envDepth: How bright the peak of the swell gets.
context.env2.s: How bright a held note stays after the swell has peaked.
context.vcf.freq: The dull starting point of each note.
context.att.2: Vibrato depth. At 0.9 it is a little under half a semitone each way. It also feeds pulse width, which does nothing on sawtooths.
context.lfo.rate: Vibrato speed, about 5 Hz here.
context.env1.a: The loudness fade-in. Kept shorter than the filter attack so the note starts straight away but dull.
context.delay.repeats: The length of the trail behind each note.

tweaks.hear: The swell becomes a quick "bwap": a punchy brass stab.
A very slow opening over a second or more, closer to a pad.
A wide, exaggerated vibrato.
The swell gains a nasal, slightly whistling edge as the filter opens.

sounds.name: Tremolo Electric Keys
sounds.ref: In the style of Portishead — "Roads"
sounds.blurb: Mellow electric-piano-like keys whose loudness pulses, and still dies away to silence.
sounds.how: Tremolo is the LFO moving loudness. The obvious patch, LFO into VCA CV, removes Envelope 1 from the amplifier, so the note never ends. Here a summer adds the two together: Envelope 1 into one input, the LFO into the other, and the sum into VCA CV. To stop the LFO leaking through after the note has died, it passes through Attenuator 1, which Envelope 2 opens and closes. The tremolo therefore fades out with the note.

steps.title: Two soft oscillators, two notes
steps.why:
Two soft oscillators make a mellow, electric-piano-like tone that can play two notes.
- OSC MIX 0: OSC is short for oscillator. The centre of the crossfade gives both an equal share.
- SHAPE 3.4 (osc 1): between triangle and sine, soft and round.
- SHAPE 3 (osc 2): a triangle, a little brighter.
- RANGE 8’ on both · TUNE +0.1 st (osc 2): the same octave, with a hair of detune for slow movement.
- PARAPHONIC on: hold two keys and each oscillator takes one note. Both still share one filter and one amplifier.
- Listen for: a gentle, flute-like tone. Hold two keys for a two-note chord.

steps.title: Two matching piano-like envelopes
steps.why:
Both envelopes are set the same, piano-like shape. Envelope 1 is loudness; Envelope 2 gives a small filter pluck now and will control the tremolo later.
- Both envelopes, D 8 (1.9 s), S 35%: A 0 and R 180 ms on each. Instant attack, a long fall to a quiet hold, a medium release. Matching them matters later: if Envelope 2 outlasts Envelope 1, the tremolo leaks through after the note.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 5.8 (695 Hz): the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) keeps the tone mellow.
- RESO 1 · KEY TRK on: barely any resonance; key tracking keeps high notes bright.
- ENV DEPTH 2.5 (25%): ENV is short for envelope. A gentle lift on each key.
- Listen for: a soft pluck that fades over a couple of seconds, like an electric piano.

steps.title: Patch ENV 1 → SUM 1(A) and SUM 1 → VCA CV
steps.why:
Tremolo means loudness pulsing. The VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) is normally driven by Envelope 1 alone; these cables put a summer in that path so a second signal can be added.
- ENV 1 → SUM 1(A): Envelope 1 goes into the first input of summer 1, which adds its two inputs together.
- SUM 1 → VCA CV: VCA CV (control voltage) sets loudness. This cable replaces the built-in Envelope 1 connection with the summer’s output.
- Listen for: no change at all. With only Envelope 1 in the summer, the sound is the same. The point is that the summer now has a free second input.

steps.title: Patch ATT 1 → SUM 1(B)
steps.why:
Now the LFO (low-frequency oscillator), a slow repeating wave, is added to loudness.
- ATT 1 → SUM 1(B): Attenuator 1 is normally fed from Attenuator 2, which carries the LFO, so the LFO arrives with one cable. This adds it to Envelope 1 in the summer.
- 2 (ATT 2) at 7 · 1 (ATT 1) at 6.5: the two tremolo depth controls, one after the other. ATT 2 also feeds pulse width, which does nothing on these shapes.
- RATE (LFO) 4.9 (5.64 Hz): tremolo speed, about five and a half pulses a second.
- SHAPE (LFO) 0 (sine): a smooth pulse. Square gives a hard on-off chop.
- Listen for: the loudness pulsing. Then listen to the end of a note: the LFO keeps opening the amplifier after Envelope 1 has finished, so the note never quite stops.

steps.title: Patch ENV 2 → ATT1 CV
steps.why:
This cable fixes the leak, so the tremolo fades out with the note.
- ENV 2 → ATT1 CV: Attenuator 1 is voltage controlled. This replaces its usual control source with Envelope 2, so the LFO only gets through while Envelope 2 is up, and in proportion. Because Envelope 2 matches Envelope 1, the tremolo shrinks as the note decays and stops when it stops.
- Listen for: the pulsing strongest at the start of a note and fading with it, then true silence after release. Envelope 2’s sustain now also sets how deep the tremolo is on a held note.

steps.title: A little echo
steps.why:
A quiet analogue delay adds some depth behind the keys.
- TIME 7 (240 ms): echoes about a quarter of a second behind.
- REPEATS 3.5 (35%): a few repeats before they fade, each a little darker.
- MIX 2 (20%): kept low, so it is depth rather than an obvious echo.
- Listen for: a little space around the keys. Pull MIX to 0 and they sound closer and drier.

context.att.2: In this sound this is the LFO level going into Attenuator 1, so it is one of two tremolo depth controls. It also feeds pulse width, which does nothing on triangle and sine shapes.
context.att.1: The other tremolo depth control: the level of the LFO sent into the summer. Envelope 2 scales it further through ATT1 CV.
context.lfo.rate: Tremolo speed, about 5.5 Hz here.
context.lfo.shape: Sine is a smooth pulse. Square is a hard on-off chop, as on some old amplifiers.
context.env2.r: Keep this no longer than Envelope 1’s release. If Envelope 2 outlasts Envelope 1, the LFO leaks through after the note has ended.
context.env2.s: Sets how deep the tremolo is on a held note, as well as how bright the held note is.
context.env1.d: How long a held note takes to fall to its quiet sustain level.
context.osc.para: Lets two held keys sound as two notes, one per oscillator.

tweaks.hear: From a slight shimmer in the level to a deep throb.
A lazy 2 Hz pulse, closer to a 60s guitar amplifier’s tremolo.
The smooth pulse becomes a stutter.

tweaks.try: Raise to 8 and play short notes
tweaks.hear: The fault this patch avoids: Envelope 2 outlasts the note, and the LFO lets short bursts of sound through after each key is released.

sounds.name: Filter Whistle Theremin
sounds.ref: In the style of The Beach Boys — "Good Vibrations"
sounds.blurb: Pure, gliding whistle played from the keys. The oscillators are not used at all: the filter makes the sound.
sounds.how: With RESO at maximum the filter rings continuously at its cutoff frequency, giving a sine-like whistle. KEY TRK makes the cutoff follow the keyboard, so the whistle plays in tune, and FREQ becomes the tuning knob. OSC MIX is a crossfade and cannot silence both oscillators, so a cable into VCF IN replaces them. The LFO is already wired to the cutoff, so MOD DEPTH is the vibrato, and PORTA TIME gives the slide between notes.

steps.title: Make the filter ring
steps.why:
In this sound the filter makes the tone, not the oscillators. With resonance at maximum, the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) rings on its own at its cutoff, giving a sine-like whistle.
- MODE low-pass: the usual filter type; the whistle comes from the resonant peak whatever the mode.
- RESO 10: resonance fully up. Near maximum the filter self-oscillates. Below about 9.3 the whistle dies away, so keep it right at the top.
- ENV DEPTH 0: ENV is short for envelope. Envelope 2 does not move the cutoff, so the whistle holds one pitch.
- Listen for: a high whistle at the cutoff, about 5 kHz, mixed in with the buzz of the oscillator. Turn FREQ and hear the whistle follow it.

steps.title: Patch ENV 2 → VCF IN
steps.why:
A cable into the filter’s audio input silences the oscillators, leaving only the whistle.
- ENV 2 → VCF IN: VCF IN is the filter’s audio input, normally the oscillator mix plus noise. OSC MIX is a crossfade and cannot silence both oscillators, so this cable replaces them. Envelope 2, as a very short blip, gives the filter a small kick at each note that keeps the ringing strong.
- A 0 / D 1.5 (8 ms), env 2: a blip of a few milliseconds. Keep it very short or it is heard as a thump.
- S 0% · R 1.5 (5 ms): the blip always ends at once.
- Listen for: the buzz gone and only the pure whistle left, with a tiny tick at each key.

steps.title: Play it in tune
steps.why:
Two settings make the whistle playable in tune, so FREQ becomes the tuning knob.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking makes the cutoff, and so the whistle, follow the keyboard. Off, every key plays the same pitch.
- FREQ 4.5 (261 Hz): about 4.46 puts the whistle at concert pitch. Every change here transposes the whole instrument.
- Listen for: a simple tune on the keys coming out as a pure whistle. If it sounds out of tune with other instruments, nudge FREQ very slightly.

steps.title: Soft starts and slides
steps.why:
A theremin player’s hand never starts or stops a note sharply, and moves between pitches in a slide. Envelope 1 and portamento copy that.
- A 5.6 (69 ms), env 1: Envelope 1 sets loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). A slightly slow attack hides the start of each note and the tick of the blip.
- D 150 ms · S 100%: full sustain, so held notes stay at full level.
- R 5.8 (180 ms): a soft fade after release.
- PORTA TIME 2.4 (580 ms): portamento, the pitch sliding between keys over about half a second.
- Listen for: notes swooping from one to the next. Play two keys far apart to hear the long slide.

steps.title: Vibrato from MOD DEPTH
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator), a slow wave you do not hear directly, is already wired to the cutoff. Because the cutoff is the pitch here, a tiny amount is vibrato.
- MOD DEPTH 0.1 (1%): vibrato depth. Keep it tiny: 0.12 is under a semitone each way.
- RATE (LFO) 4.9 (5.64 Hz) · SHAPE 0 (sine): a smooth waver about five and a half times a second.
- DRIVE 0 · LEVEL 6.5: no overdrive, to keep the whistle pure. Raising DRIVE squares it towards a hollow, clarinet-like tone.
- TIME 280 ms · REPEATS 4 · MIX 2.5: a quiet echo for space.
- Listen for: a singing, wavering whistle with a soft trail. Set MOD DEPTH to 0 to hear the vibrato go.

context.vcf.reso: In this sound maximum resonance is what makes the filter sing. Below about 9.3 the whistle dies away and the patch goes almost silent.
context.vcf.freq: The tuning knob. 4.46 is concert pitch; every change here transposes the whole instrument.
context.vcf.keyTrk: Makes the whistle follow the keyboard. Switch it off and every key plays the same pitch.
context.vcf.modDepth: Vibrato depth, because the LFO is moving the cutoff and the cutoff is the pitch. Keep it tiny: 0.12 is under a semitone each way.
context.lfo.rate: Vibrato speed.
context.porta.time: The slide between notes.
context.env2.d: The length of the blip that kicks the filter. Keep it very short or it is heard as a thump.
context.od.drive: At zero to keep the whistle as pure as possible. Raising it squares the tone off towards a hollow, clarinet-like sound.

tweaks.hear: A wide, wobbling, B-movie vibrato.
Long, swooping slides between notes.

tweaks.try: Turn slowly by hand on a held note
tweaks.hear: The pitch moves smoothly with the knob: you are playing the filter directly.
The pure whistle becomes hollow and reedy.

sounds.name: Gated Trance Pulse
sounds.ref: In the style of 90s trance gates and Giorgio Moroder’s pulsing sequences
sounds.blurb: Hold one key and the synth chops it into a run of even sixteenth notes.
sounds.how: The envelopes normally start when a key goes down. Here the square-wave LFO starts them instead, so a held note is re-struck on every LFO cycle. Sent straight to the gate inputs the LFO would pulse for ever, keys or no keys, so on its way to Envelope 1 it passes through Attenuator 1, and MIDI GATE controls that attenuator. The pulses only get through while a key is held.

steps.title: Two detuned sawtooths
steps.why:
Two bright, detuned sawtooths make a wide tone for the pulses.
- OSC MIX 0: OSC is short for oscillator. The centre of the crossfade gives both an equal share.
- SHAPE 2 on both (saw): every harmonic present, bright and cutting.
- RANGE 8’ on both: the same octave.
- TUNE +0.2 st (osc 2): a little sharp, so the two beat and the sound gets wider.
- Listen for: a bright, slightly chorused buzz that holds as long as the key is down.

steps.title: A short, plucky shape
steps.why:
Both envelopes are made short and plucky. An envelope is a shape that runs once each time it is triggered.
- A 0 / D 94 ms / S 50% / R 30 ms (env 1): Envelope 1 sets loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). A quick drop to half level, then a very short release. With the release, the decay sets how long each pulse lasts.
- A 0 / D 110 ms / S 0% / R 41 ms (env 2): a quick filter pluck that always closes fully.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 5 (387 Hz): the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) rests fairly dark. Opening it slowly over many bars is the standard trance build.
- RESO 3.5 · KEY TRK on: a little resonance; the cutoff follows the keys.
- ENV DEPTH 4 (40%): ENV is short for envelope. How bright the front of each pluck is.
- Listen for: one pluck per key press, for now.

steps.title: A square LFO at sixteenth notes
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) will do the re-striking. It needs a square shape to act as a gate.
- SHAPE (LFO) 3 (square): the wave is either high or low. A gate input fires when a signal passes half level, and a square gives a clean on and off.
- RATE (LFO) 5.3 (9.25 Hz): the speed of the pulses, sixteenth notes at 138 bpm. Around 4.73 gives eighth notes.
- KEY SYNC on: restarts the LFO on each key press, so the first pulse lands with the key.
- Listen for: nothing new yet. The LFO still only reaches the filter through MOD DEPTH, which is at 0.

steps.title: Patch LFO → ATT1 IN, MIDI GATE → ATT1 CV, ATT 1 → E.GATE 1
steps.why:
Three cables let the LFO re-strike Envelope 1, but only while a key is held.
- ATT 1 → E.GATE 1: E.GATE 1 is Envelope 1’s trigger input. This replaces the keyboard gate, so Envelope 1 starts whenever Attenuator 1’s output goes high.
- LFO → ATT1 IN: Attenuator 1 now carries the LFO, replacing its usual input.
- MIDI GATE → ATT1 CV: MIDI GATE is high while a key is held. It controls Attenuator 1’s level, so the pulses only pass while you hold a key.
- 1 (ATT 1) at 8: must stay above about 5, since the gate input needs more than half level. Below that the pulses stop.
- Listen for: a held key now chopped into even sixteenth notes. Turn ATT 1 below 5 and the chopping stops.

steps.title: Patch MULT 1 → E.GATE 2
steps.why:
One more cable makes the filter pluck restart on every pulse too, so each chop gets its own bright front.
- MULT 1 → E.GATE 2: the MULT outputs carry a copy of the LFO. E.GATE 2 is Envelope 2’s trigger input, and this cable replaces its usual gate. Envelope 2 now fires on every pulse. It keeps running with no key held, but you cannot hear that, because Envelope 1 keeps the amplifier shut.
- Listen for: each pulse now starting with a small “wow” of brightness, instead of only the first. Raise ENV DEPTH to exaggerate it.

steps.title: Delay between the pulses
steps.why:
An analogue delay puts quieter echoes in the gaps between pulses.
- TIME 7.9 (330 ms): about a dotted eighth at 138 bpm, so the echoes fall off the pulse grid and fill the spaces.
- REPEATS 5 (50%): several repeats, each a little darker.
- MIX 3 (30%): echoes behind the dry pulses.
- Listen for: a busier, rolling rhythm from one held key. Pull MIX to 0 to hear the bare gate.

context.lfo.rate: In this sound this is the speed of the pulses. At 138 bpm: 4.73 is eighth notes, 5.33 is sixteenths.
context.lfo.shape: Must be at or near square. The gate inputs fire when the signal goes above half level, and a square wave gives a clean on and off.
context.lfo.keySync: Starts the pulse train on the key press so the rhythm lines up with your playing.
context.att.1: The level of the LFO reaching E.GATE 1. Below about 5 it never gets above half level and the pulses stop.
context.env1.d: With the release, sets how long each pulse lasts. Short for a tight chop; longer and the pulses start to join up.
context.env2.d: The length of the filter pluck on each pulse.
context.vcf.freq: The resting brightness of the pulses. Opening it slowly over many bars is the standard trance build.
context.vcf.envDepth: How bright the front of each pulse is.

tweaks.try: Open slowly from 4 to 7.5 while a note is held
tweaks.hear: The pulses build from a dull throb to a bright, buzzing chop.
Half speed: eighth-note pulses, closer to a Moroder-style bass sequence.

tweaks.try: Turn down below 5, then back up to 8
tweaks.hear: The pulses stop completely, then return. The gate input only responds once the signal passes half level.

tweaks.try: Reduce to 0 and set D to 3.8
tweaks.hear: Each pulse becomes a very short tick, leaving more room for the echoes.

sounds.name: Dub Siren
sounds.ref: In the style of King Tubby — Jamaican sound-system sirens
sounds.blurb: Rising and falling alarm tone that trails off into long, murky echoes.
sounds.how: A dub siren is a simple oscillator whose pitch is swept up and down by an LFO, played through a tape echo. On the Neutron the LFO reaches pitch through Attenuator 2 and one cable, and the ATT 2 knob sets how wide the sweep is. The delay, with REPEATS set high, does the rest: each burst of siren keeps echoing long after the key is released.

steps.title: A square wave, up high
steps.why:
A simple square wave is the tone of the original siren boxes.
- OSC MIX −5 (OSC 1 only): OSC is short for oscillator. Fully left on the crossfade means only Oscillator 1 is heard.
- SHAPE 1 (pulse) · WIDTH 5 (50%): a pulse with the width centred is a square, hollow and a little harsh.
- RANGE 8’ · TUNE 0: the normal octave, in tune with the keys. Play high on the keyboard for a siren.
- Listen for: a steady, hollow buzz. The siren movement comes next.

steps.title: Patch ATT 2 → OSC 1+2
steps.why:
One cable sends the LFO (low-frequency oscillator), a repeating wave you do not hear directly, to pitch.
- ATT 2 → OSC 1+2: Attenuator 2 already carries the LFO. This cable adds its output to both oscillators’ pitch.
- 2 (ATT 2) at 4.5: the width of the pitch sweep, about 6 semitones each way. Attenuator 2 also still feeds pulse width, so the square thins and fattens a little as the pitch moves.
- Listen for: the pitch swinging up and down quickly at the default LFO speed of about 6 Hz. Turn ATT 2 up and down to hear the sweep widen and narrow.

steps.title: Choose the sweep
steps.why:
The LFO’s speed and shape are what you play on a siren.
- RATE (LFO) 4.6 (3.99 Hz): about four sweeps a second. Sweeping it by hand while a note sounds is the classic way to play it.
- SHAPE (LFO) 1 (triangle): an even rise and fall. Saw rises and drops back; square jumps between two notes like a two-tone alarm.
- KEY SYNC on: starts every burst from the same point of the sweep.
- Listen for: an even “wee-woo”. Try turning RATE slowly while holding a key, then sweep SHAPE through saw and square.

steps.title: Take the edge off
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) takes the edge off so the siren sits behind a mix instead of on top of it.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 7 (1.7 kHz): rounds the square wave. Lower it for a more distant sound.
- RESO 3: resonance, a little peak at the cutoff.
- ENV DEPTH 0: ENV is short for envelope. Envelope 2 does not move the filter.
- A 0 / S 100% / R 41 ms (env 1): Envelope 1 sets loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). Full level while the key is held, a quick stop after.
- Listen for: the siren sounding rounder and less piercing.

steps.title: Long, heavy echo
steps.why:
The delay does most of the work in dub: each burst keeps echoing long after the key is released.
- TIME 8.5 (390 ms): long gaps between echoes. Moving it while echoes sound bends their pitch, like tape.
- REPEATS 7.5 (75%): high feedback, so the echoes carry on. Near maximum they build instead of fading.
- MIX 4.5 (45%): nearly as much echo as dry sound.
- DRIVE 3: a little more grit, which also pushes the delay harder.
- Listen for: play a short burst and let it trail off. Each echo comes back duller than the last, as from tape. Turn TIME while the tail sounds to bend it.

context.att.2: In this sound this is the width of the pitch sweep. It also moves the pulse width slightly, which adds to the wobble in the tone.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of the siren. Sweeping it by hand while a note sounds is the classic way to play it.
context.lfo.shape: Triangle is an even rise and fall. Saw rises and drops back. Square jumps between two notes like a two-tone alarm.
context.lfo.keySync: Starts every burst from the same point of the sweep.
context.delay.repeats: How long the echoes carry on. Near maximum they build up instead of fading.
context.delay.time: The gap between echoes. Moving it while echoes are sounding bends their pitch.
context.vcf.freq: How bright the siren is. Lower it for a more distant sound.

tweaks.try: Sweep from 3.5 up to 6 while holding a note
tweaks.hear: The siren speeds up from a slow wail to a fast warble.
A two-note alarm instead of a sweep.
Repeated rising swoops, like a laser gun.

tweaks.try: Play a burst, release, then turn TIME slowly while the echoes ring
tweaks.hear: The echoes bend up or down in pitch as the delay time changes.

sounds.name: Distorted Dark Drone
sounds.ref: In the style of Tim Hecker — distorted ambient drones
sounds.blurb: Low, gritty drone that carries on sounding with no key held and never quite settles.
sounds.how: VCA BIAS holds the amplifier open, so the oscillators sound all the time and the keyboard only chooses the pitch. Two low oscillators an octave and a fifth apart go through a dark, resonant filter that a very slow LFO opens and closes, and heavy overdrive turns the result to grit. To stop it sounding static, the sample-and-hold, smoothed by its GLIDE knob, is patched through Attenuator 1 to Oscillator 2’s pitch, so the tuning between the two oscillators drifts at random.

steps.title: Two low oscillators an octave and a fifth apart
steps.why:
Two low oscillators a fifth apart make a heavy base for the drone.
- OSC MIX 0: OSC is short for oscillator. The centre of the crossfade gives both an equal share.
- SHAPE 2, RANGE 32’ (osc 1): a sawtooth at the lowest octave, buzzy and deep.
- SHAPE 2.5, RANGE 16’ (osc 2): halfway between saw and triangle, a softer layer an octave up.
- TUNE +7 st (osc 2): a fifth up, which with the octave puts it a fifth plus an octave above Oscillator 1. At 0 it would be a plain octave.
- Listen for: a deep, open, organ-like chord from one key.

steps.title: Hold the amplifier open
steps.why:
VCA BIAS holds the amplifier open, so the sound never stops. VCA stands for voltage-controlled amplifier, the stage that sets loudness.
- VCA BIAS 5 (50%): the amplifier stays half open with no key held, so the oscillators sound all the time and the keyboard only picks the pitch. At zero the patch becomes a pad that only sounds while keys are held.
- A 8 (720 ms), env 1: Envelope 1 still adds to the bias, so each key press is a slow swell on top.
- D 360 ms · S 60%: the swell settles back a little while held.
- R 8.5 (1.7 s): the swell fades slowly after release.
- Listen for: the drone carrying on after you let go. Each key press swells up out of it.

steps.title: Dark filter, slowly moving
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) makes the drone dark, and a very slow LFO opens and closes it.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 4.6 (289 Hz): the overall darkness of the drone.
- RESO 4 · ENV DEPTH 0: some resonance for body; ENV (envelope) depth off, so only the LFO moves the cutoff.
- MOD DEPTH 3 (30%): the LFO (low-frequency oscillator) already feeds FREQ MOD; this sets how far it moves the cutoff.
- RATE (LFO) 1.5 (0.11 Hz) · SHAPE 0 (sine): about nine seconds per cycle, a slow tide.
- NOISE 2.5 (25%): a layer of hiss under the oscillators, for air. The overdrive later turns it grainy.
- Listen for: the drone slowly opening and closing over many seconds, with a faint hiss.

steps.title: Patch S&H → ATT1 IN and ATT 1 → OSC 2
steps.why:
Two cables make the tuning between the oscillators drift at random, so the drone never settles. S&H stands for sample and hold: it takes readings of white noise and holds each one.
- S&H → ATT1 IN: replaces Attenuator 1’s usual input with the random voltage.
- ATT 1 → OSC 2: adds it to Oscillator 2’s pitch only.
- 1 (ATT 1) at 1: how far Oscillator 2 drifts, under a semitone, enough to make the fifth go slowly in and out of tune.
- RATE (S&H) 2 (0.66 Hz): a new target about every one and a half seconds.
- GLIDE 10 (1.0 s): the voltage slides to each target instead of jumping, so the pitch wanders.
- Listen for: a slow beating that speeds up and slows down as the fifth drifts. Set GLIDE to 0 to hear it jump instead.

steps.title: Grit and long echoes
steps.why:
Heavy overdrive turns the drone to grit, and long echoes smear it together.
- DRIVE 6.5: blends the two oscillators into one gritty mass and brings out new tones between them. It also roughens the noise.
- TONE 4: left of centre, keeping the grit dark.
- LEVEL 5: pulled back to make up for the extra loudness of the drive.
- TIME 540 ms · REPEATS 7 · MIX 4: long echoes with plenty of repeats, well mixed in.
- VOLUME 6.5: main output, lowered slightly as the drone never stops.
- Listen for: a thick, grainy wall of sound. Compare DRIVE at 1 and 6.5.

context.vca.bias: In this sound this is what makes it a drone: the amplifier never closes. Turn it to zero and the patch becomes a slow pad that only sounds while keys are held.
context.att.1: How far the random voltage pushes Oscillator 2 out of tune.
context.sh.rate: How often the random drift picks a new target.
context.sh.glide: How slowly the drift moves to each new target. At zero the pitch would jump instead of wander.
context.osc2.tune: The interval between the two oscillators. 2.92 is a fifth; 0 is an octave; small offsets from either give slow beating.
context.vcf.freq: The overall darkness of the drone.
context.vcf.modDepth: How far the slow LFO opens and closes the filter.
context.od.drive: Overdrive blends the two oscillators into one gritty mass and brings out new tones between them.
context.mix.noise: A layer of hiss under the oscillators, which the overdrive turns into a rough, grainy surface.

tweaks.hear: Oscillator 2 wanders by several semitones and the drone becomes uneasy and sour.
The drone stops between key presses, and each note becomes a slow swell.
From a clean, organ-like hum to a wall of distortion.
The bass drops away and a hollow, distant roar is left.

sounds.name: Closed Noise Hi-Hat
sounds.ref: In the style of The Normal — "Warm Leatherette" and other synth-made drum kits
sounds.blurb: Very short tick of high-pitched hiss: a closed hi-hat made from the noise generator.
sounds.how: A closed hi-hat is a very short burst of hiss with all the low end removed. Early synth-pop records, made before drum machines were affordable, often built their hats this way from a synth’s noise generator. OSC MIX is a crossfade and cannot turn both oscillators off, so one cable from the NOISE output into VCF IN replaces the whole oscillator mix with white noise. A high-pass filter near 10 kHz keeps only the top of the hiss, and Envelope 1 cuts it to about 35 ms.

steps.title: Patch NOISE → VCF IN
steps.why:
A closed hi-hat is a very short burst of hiss with the low end removed. One cable swaps the oscillators for white noise.
- NOISE → VCF IN: VCF IN is the audio input of the filter (VCF, voltage-controlled filter), normally the oscillator mix plus the NOISE knob. OSC MIX is a crossfade and cannot silence both oscillators, so this cable replaces the whole mix with white noise. The NOISE jack is always full strength, and the NOISE knob no longer does anything.
- Listen for: a steady roar of white noise for as long as a key is held.

steps.title: High-pass, right at the top
steps.why:
The filter is switched to high-pass and set right at the top, so only the thin sizzle is left.
- MODE high-pass: press MODE until the top lamp lights. It removes everything below the cutoff.
- FREQ 9.4 (9.7 kHz): only hiss above about 9.7 kHz gets through. Lower lets in more body, towards a shaker.
- RESO 2.5: resonance, a small peak that gives the hiss a slightly metallic centre.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking; the cutoff follows the keys. Below middle C gives a heavier hat, above it a thinner one. G below middle C drops the cutoff to about 7 kHz.
- ENV DEPTH 0: ENV is short for envelope; the envelope does not move the filter.
- Listen for: the roar replaced by a thin “tss”.

steps.title: Cut it to a tick
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). A very short shape turns the hiss into a tick.
- A 0 ms (env 1): instant start.
- D 3.2 (35 ms): the length of the hat. Around 3 is tightly closed; 5 to 6 is an open hat.
- S 0%: nothing held.
- R 3.2 (21 ms): as short as the decay, so holding the key makes no difference.
- Listen for: a crisp “tk” on each key. Try D at 5.5 to hear it open up, then set it back.

steps.title: Bite
steps.why:
A little overdrive makes the tick denser and gives it edge.
- DRIVE 3: light distortion, which thickens the short burst.
- TONE 7: well right of centre, removing more low end after the filter and adding bite.
- LEVEL 8: the overdrive’s output and so the synth’s volume, at its default.
- Listen for: a sharper, denser tick that cuts through more. Compare TONE at 5 and at 7.

context.vcf.freq: In this sound this is how thin the hat is. At 9.4 only hiss above about 9.7 kHz gets through; lower settings let in more body and it starts to sound like a shaker.
context.vcf.keyTrk: Lets you play heavier and lighter hats from different keys. The riff uses G below middle C for the accents, where the cutoff drops to about 7 kHz.
context.vcf.reso: A small peak at the cutoff, which gives the hiss a slightly metallic centre.
context.env1.d: The length of the hat. Around 3 is tightly closed; 5 to 6 is an open hat.
context.env1.r: Kept the same as the decay so short and long key presses sound alike.
context.mix.noise: Does nothing here. The cable into VCF IN has taken the mixer, and this knob with it, out of the signal path.
context.od.tone: Right of centre removes more low end after the filter.

tweaks.try: Lengthen to 5.5 and set R to 5.5
tweaks.hear: The tick opens out into a "tsss": an open hi-hat from the same patch.
More of the body of the noise comes through and the hat turns into a shaker.
The hiss gains a ringing pitch at the cutoff, closer to a struck piece of metal.
The very top is removed as well as the bottom, leaving a duller, narrower tick.

sounds.name: Metallic Open Hi-Hat
sounds.ref: In the style of the Roland TR-808 — open hi-hat and cymbal
sounds.blurb: Sizzling, metallic open hat built from clashing square waves instead of noise.
sounds.how: The 808 makes its hats and cymbal from six square-wave oscillators tuned so that they clash, then filters away everything but the top. The Neutron has two oscillators, not six, so the LFO fills in the rest: running at about 700 Hz as a square wave, it flips the pitch of both oscillators between two values hundreds of times a second. The ear hears that as a dense cluster of unrelated tones. A high-pass filter keeps only the sizzle, and a decay of about half a second makes it an open hat.

steps.title: Two square waves that clash
steps.why:
The 808 builds its hats from square waves tuned to clash. Start with two.
- OSC MIX 0: OSC is short for oscillator. The centre of the crossfade gives both an equal share.
- SHAPE 1 · WIDTH 5 on both: pulse waves with the width centred, which are square waves.
- RANGE 8’ on both · TUNE 0 (osc 1): the same octave, in tune with the keys.
- TUNE +7.3 st (osc 2): just off a clean fifth, so the two never blend into one note. Clean intervals sound more like a note; in-between settings sound more like metal.
- Listen for: play high on the keyboard. You hear a harsh two-note buzz.

steps.title: An open-hat length
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). A half-second decay makes it an open hat.
- A 0 ms (env 1): instant start.
- D 6.3 (460 ms): the length of the hat, just under half a second. Short for closed; long for a cymbal.
- S 0%: nothing held.
- R 5 (95 ms): shorter than the decay, so letting go early chokes the hat, like closing the pedal.
- Listen for: a two-note buzz that rings and fades. Release early and it cuts short.

steps.title: Patch ATT 2 → OSC 1+2 and speed the LFO up
steps.why:
The Neutron has two oscillators, not six, so the LFO (low-frequency oscillator) fills in the rest by flipping both pitches hundreds of times a second.
- ATT 2 → OSC 1+2: Attenuator 2 carries the LFO. This cable adds it to both oscillators’ pitch.
- 2 (ATT 2) at 6: depth. The pitch jumps about 10 semitones either side. More is noisier and less pitched. It also flips the pulse width, adding to the clutter.
- SHAPE (LFO) 3 (square): the pitch jumps between two values, which sounds like extra oscillators.
- RATE (LFO) 9.1 (710 Hz): an audio-rate modulator. Its speed sets how closely packed the tones are; it does not follow the keyboard.
- KEY SYNC off: the LFO runs free.
- Listen for: the buzz breaking up into a clangorous cluster.

steps.title: Keep only the sizzle
steps.why:
A high-pass filter keeps only the sizzle at the top of the cluster.
- MODE high-pass, FREQ 9.2 (8.4 kHz): the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) removes everything below the cutoff, including the pitched part. Lower it and the hat becomes a clanging cymbal or gong.
- RESO 2.5: resonance, a small peak at the cutoff.
- ENV DEPTH 0 · KEY TRK off: ENV is short for envelope. Neither the envelope nor the keys move the cutoff.
- NOISE 3 (30%): a little hiss under the square waves, softening the most obviously pitched moments.
- Listen for: the clang reduced to a metallic sizzle. Sweep FREQ down to 6 to hear the cymbal body return.

steps.title: Edge
steps.why:
Overdrive with a bright TONE makes the hat denser and brighter.
- DRIVE 3: light distortion to thicken the sizzle.
- TONE 6.5: right of centre, thinning any remaining low end and adding bite.
- LEVEL 8: the overdrive’s output and the synth’s volume, at its default.
- Listen for: a fuller, crisper hat. Compare DRIVE at 1 and 3.

context.lfo.rate: In this sound the LFO is an audio-rate modulator, at about 700 Hz. Its speed sets how closely packed the clashing tones are. It does not follow the keyboard.
context.lfo.shape: Square makes the pitch jump between two values, which sounds like extra oscillators. Sine or triangle sweep it smoothly and sound more like a bell.
context.att.2: The modulation depth: how far the LFO throws the pitch of both oscillators. More is noisier and less pitched.
context.osc2.tune: The clash between the two oscillators. Clean intervals such as 0 or 2.92 sound more like a note; in-between settings sound more like metal.
context.env1.d: The length of the hat. Short for closed, long for a cymbal.
context.env1.r: How quickly the hat is choked when the key is released.
context.vcf.freq: How much of the pitched body is removed. Lower it and the hat becomes a clanging cymbal or gong.
context.mix.noise: A little hiss under the square waves, to soften the most obviously pitched moments.

tweaks.try: Shorten to 3.5 and set R to 3.5
tweaks.hear: A closed hat with the same metallic colour.
A long crash-cymbal wash.
The cluster of tones spreads out and tightens, from a trashy clang to a fine sizzle.
The pitched body returns: a small, clanging cymbal or a struck bin lid.

sounds.name: Falling Electronic Tom
sounds.ref: In the style of the Simmons SDS-V — 80s electronic toms
sounds.blurb: Round "doom" whose pitch falls as it rings, with a short burst of noise for the stick.
sounds.how: The 80s electronic tom is a plain tone whose pitch bends downwards during the hit, plus a little noise at the front. The Neutron has no "envelope to pitch" knob, so Envelope 2 goes to pitch through Attenuator 1, and the ATT 1 knob sets how far the pitch falls. The same envelope also opens the filter, so the noise is only heard in the first instant. Different keys give high, middle and floor toms.

steps.title: A triangle wave
steps.why:
An electronic tom is a plain tone whose pitch falls as it rings. Start with a triangle, nearly as pure as a sine but with a little more knock.
- OSC MIX −5 (OSC 1 only): OSC is short for oscillator. Fully left on the crossfade means only Oscillator 1 is heard.
- SHAPE 3 (triangle): soft, with a few quiet harmonics. Towards sine is rounder; towards saw is buzzier and less drum-like.
- RANGE 16’: an octave below 8’, where toms sit. Different keys will give high, middle and floor toms.
- TUNE 0: in tune with the keys.
- Listen for: a soft, steady hoot that holds while the key is down.

steps.title: A drum-length note
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). A drum has no held part, so the note dies away on its own.
- A 0 ms (env 1): full level instantly, like a stick hit.
- D 6 (360 ms): the length of the tom, about a third of a second.
- S 0%: nothing held, so it fades even with the key down.
- R 5.8 (180 ms): a short tail if you let go early.
- Listen for: a short, level “boop”. It needs the pitch fall to sound like a tom.

steps.title: Patch ENV 2 → ATT1 IN and ATT 1 → OSC 1+2
steps.why:
The Neutron has no knob for envelope to pitch, so two cables build one. Envelope 2, a shape that runs once per note, bends the pitch.
- ENV 2 → ATT1 IN: replaces Attenuator 1’s usual input (Attenuator 2) with Envelope 2.
- ATT 1 → OSC 1+2: adds Attenuator 1’s output to both oscillators’ pitch.
- 1 (ATT 1) at 3.4: how far the pitch falls, about 6 semitones. Around 2 is a natural drum; 5 and above is the exaggerated “pew” of disco toms.
- A 0 / D 6.2 (420 ms), env 2: the fall starts at once and takes about 400 ms.
- S 0% · R 220 ms: the pitch always lands on the played note.
- Listen for: each hit starting sharp and falling as it rings, the classic 80s “doom”.

steps.title: Stick noise through a closing filter
steps.why:
A burst of noise at the front adds the sound of the stick, and the filter hides it again almost at once.
- NOISE 3.5 (35%): white noise added into the filter, the stick sound.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 5.2 (448 Hz): the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) rests low enough that the noise is hidden and the triangle is soft.
- RESO 2 · KEY TRK off: a little resonance; key tracking off, so the cutoff stays put across keys.
- ENV DEPTH 5 (50%): ENV is short for envelope. Envelope 2 also opens the filter by about four octaves at the hit, so it now does two jobs: bending the pitch and letting the noise through for an instant.
- Listen for: a brief “tch” at the front that is gone by the time the tone rings.

steps.title: Weight
steps.why:
Overdrive rounds the triangle off and makes the tom louder without making it longer.
- DRIVE 3.5: moderate distortion. It squares the triangle slightly, giving more body and punch.
- TONE 4.5: slightly left of centre, keeping the grit rounded.
- LEVEL 8: the overdrive’s output and so the synth’s volume, at its default.
- Listen for: a fuller, punchier tom. Play three keys an octave apart to hear a high, middle and floor tom.

context.att.1: In this sound this is how far the pitch falls during each hit. Around 2 is a natural drum; 5 and above is the exaggerated "pew" of disco toms.
context.env2.d: How long the fall takes. Envelope 2 is doing two jobs here: it bends the pitch and it closes the filter.
context.env1.d: The length of the tom.
context.mix.noise: The stick sound at the front of the hit.
context.vcf.envDepth: How far the filter opens at the start. It sets how bright and how long the stick noise is.
context.vcf.freq: Where the filter rests once the hit has rung out. Low enough that the noise is hidden and the triangle’s tone is soft.
context.osc1.shape: Triangle for a soft tom. Towards sine is rounder; towards saw is buzzier and less drum-like.

tweaks.hear: The pitch falls by more than an octave: the swooping disco tom.
The fall happens in a flash and the tom becomes a tight, punchy knock.
Much more stick and rattle, halfway to a snare.

tweaks.try: Lengthen to 7.2 and set R to 7
tweaks.hear: A long, booming floor tom.

sounds.name: Noise Burst Hand Clap
sounds.ref: In the style of the Roland TR-808 — hand clap
sounds.blurb: Drum-machine clap: three very fast bursts of filtered noise and a short tail.
sounds.how: One burst of noise sounds like a snare, not a clap. A clap is several people hitting slightly apart, and drum machines copy that with a few bursts about 10 ms apart followed by a tail. Here white noise goes through a band-pass filter, and the square-wave LFO, at about 85 Hz, re-starts Envelope 1 on every cycle while the key is down. Each re-start is a burst; the release after the last one is the tail. How long you hold the key sets how many bursts there are, and the riff holds it for three.

steps.title: Patch NOISE → VCF IN
steps.why:
A clap starts with noise. One cable swaps the oscillators for white noise.
- NOISE → VCF IN: VCF IN is the audio input of the filter (VCF, voltage-controlled filter), normally the oscillator mix. This cable replaces it, so the oscillators go silent and the filter receives white noise at full strength. No knob sets the level on this path, and the NOISE knob no longer does anything.
- Listen for: a steady roar of hiss for as long as a key is held.

steps.title: Band-pass around 1 kHz
steps.why:
Band-pass turns the hiss into the mid-range “chh” of a clap.
- MODE band-pass: press MODE until the middle lamp lights. It keeps a band around the cutoff and removes the rest.
- FREQ 6.4 (1.1 kHz): the pitch of the clap. Around 1 kHz is the usual place; higher is thinner and snappier.
- RESO 3.5: resonance narrows the band and gives it a slight ring.
- ENV DEPTH 0 · KEY TRK off: ENV is short for envelope. Neither the envelope nor the keys move the cutoff.
- Listen for: the roar narrowed to a papery, mid-range hiss.

steps.title: A spike with a tail
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). Here it makes a sharp spike followed by a quieter tail.
- A 0 ms (env 1): instant start.
- D 2 (13 ms): very fast. It has to be shorter than the gap between bursts, or the bursts merge.
- S 2.5 (25%): the level of the tail compared with the spikes.
- R 6.2 (260 ms): the length of the tail after the last burst.
- Listen for: a sharp crack that drops to a quieter hiss while held, then fades out on release. One burst sounds more like a snare than a clap.

steps.title: A square LFO at about 85 Hz
steps.why:
A clap is several people hitting slightly apart. The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) will supply those repeated bursts, and needs a square shape to act as a gate.
- SHAPE (LFO) 3 (square): either high or low, so a gate input sees a clean on and off.
- RATE (LFO) 7.3 (85 Hz): one cycle lasts about 12 ms, the gap between bursts. Slower spreads them into a flam; faster blurs them into one hit.
- KEY SYNC on: restarts the LFO on each key press, so the first burst lands with the key.
- Listen for: no change yet. The LFO is not connected to the envelope.

steps.title: Patch LFO → ATT1 IN, MIDI GATE → ATT1 CV, ATT 1 → E.GATE 1
steps.why:
Three cables let the LFO re-start Envelope 1, but only while a key is held. Each re-start is a burst.
- ATT 1 → E.GATE 1: E.GATE 1 is Envelope 1’s trigger input. This replaces the keyboard gate, so Envelope 1 re-starts each time Attenuator 1’s output goes high.
- LFO → ATT1 IN: Attenuator 1 now carries the LFO, replacing its usual input.
- MIDI GATE → ATT1 CV: MIDI GATE is high while a key is held, and here it opens Attenuator 1, so pulses pass only while you hold.
- 1 (ATT 1) at 8: must stay above about 5, since a gate input needs more than half level to fire.
- Listen for: a quick flurry of bursts, then the tail. How long you hold sets how many bursts; hold for about three.

steps.title: A small room
steps.why:
A tiny room and some overdrive finish the clap.
- DRIVE 5.5 · TONE 5.5 · LEVEL 9: overdrive thickens the bursts; LEVEL is raised above the default 8.
- TIME 0 (25 ms): the shortest delay time, so the echoes are close enough to sound like a room, not separate repeats.
- REPEATS 3 (30%) · MIX 2 (20%): a few quiet repeats, like the slap of a small room.
- Listen for: a denser clap with a hint of space around it. Pull MIX to 0 to hear it dry.

context.lfo.rate: In this sound this is the gap between the bursts. At 7.26 (85 Hz) they are about 12 ms apart. Slower spreads them into a flam; faster blurs them into one hit.
context.lfo.shape: Must be at or near square so the gate input sees a clean on and off.
context.lfo.keySync: Starts the first burst exactly on the key press.
context.att.1: The level of the LFO pulses reaching E.GATE 1. Below about 5 they never pass half level and only silence is left.
context.env1.d: How quickly each burst drops away. It has to be shorter than the gap between bursts or they merge.
context.env1.s: The level of the tail compared with the spikes.
context.env1.r: The length of the tail after the last burst.
context.vcf.freq: The pitch of the clap. Around 1 kHz is the usual place; higher is thinner and snappier.
context.delay.time: At its minimum, so the echoes are close enough together to sound like a room and not like separate repeats.

tweaks.hear: The bursts move apart to about 25 ms and you can count them: more of a drum roll than a clap. The riff’s short key press now only fits two.
From a dry, tight clap to one with a long, washy tail.
A thinner, brighter clap that cuts through more.
The band narrows and the clap takes on a hollow, pitched "tock".

sounds.name: Two-Tone Cowbell
sounds.ref: In the style of the Roland TR-808 — cowbell
sounds.blurb: Short, hollow "tonk" made from two square waves a rough fifth apart.
sounds.how: The 808 cowbell is two square-wave oscillators at about 540 Hz and 800 Hz, put through a band-pass filter and given a short envelope. That interval is a little narrower than a true fifth, which is why it sounds like a bell and not like a chord. The Neutron has exactly the parts needed: two pulse oscillators, a band-pass mode and a fast envelope. No cables are required.

steps.title: Two square waves, 6.8 semitones apart
steps.why:
The 808 cowbell is two square waves a slightly flat fifth apart. That interval is why it sounds like a bell, not a chord.
- OSC MIX 0: OSC is short for oscillator. The centre of the crossfade gives both an equal share.
- SHAPE 1 · WIDTH 5 on both: pulse waves with the width centred, which are square waves.
- RANGE 8’ on both · TUNE 0 (osc 1): the same octave. The played key moves both tones together, so tune the cowbell from the keyboard first.
- TUNE +6.8 st (osc 2): a slightly flat fifth. On the C sharp an octave above middle C that gives about 550 Hz and 820 Hz. A true fifth sounds like a chord; further away is more like an agogo.
- Listen for: a harsh two-note buzz.

steps.title: A short hit
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). A fast decay turns the two tones into a hit.
- A 0 ms (env 1): instant start.
- D 4.8 (130 ms): the length of the hit, about an eighth of a second.
- S 0%: nothing held.
- R 4.8 (80 ms): short, so long key presses do not ring on.
- Listen for: the buzz becoming a short “tonk”.

steps.title: Band-pass at the upper tone
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is switched to band-pass and set near the upper tone. That leaves the hollow, boxy middle.
- MODE band-pass: press MODE until the middle lamp lights. It takes away the low thump and the fizzy top together.
- FREQ 6.1 (866 Hz): near the upper tone, the classic setting. Lower favours the lower tone and sounds duller.
- RESO 4.5: resonance narrows the band and adds a little ring.
- KEY TRK off: key tracking off, so the band stays put across keys.
- Listen for: the tonk turning hollow and woody, like a real cowbell.

steps.title: A harder strike
steps.why:
A very fast push on the filter gives each hit a brighter strike at the front.
- ENV DEPTH 2 (20%): ENV is short for envelope. Envelope 2 pushes the band upwards briefly. This sets how bright the strike is.
- A 0 / D 3 (29 ms), env 2: the push lasts only a few milliseconds.
- S 0% · R 18 ms: it always falls straight back.
- Listen for: a small “tk” at the start of each hit. Raise ENV DEPTH to 5 to exaggerate it, then set it back.

steps.title: Crunch
steps.why:
Overdrive after the filter squares the hit off and makes it louder.
- DRIVE 4: moderate distortion. It squashes the hit so it sounds harder.
- TONE 6: right of centre, thinning the low end and adding bite.
- LEVEL 8: the overdrive’s output and the synth’s volume, at its default.
- Listen for: a harder, more cutting cowbell. Compare DRIVE at 1 and 4.

context.osc2.tune: In this sound this is the interval that makes it a cowbell. 2.83 is 6.8 semitones. At 2.92 (a true fifth) it sounds like a chord; further away it sounds more like an agogo or a clang.
context.osc1.tune: Moves the lower tone. The played key moves both tones together, so tune the cowbell from the keyboard first.
context.vcf.freq: Where the band sits. Near the upper tone is the classic setting; lower favours the lower tone and sounds duller.
context.vcf.reso: Narrows the band and adds ring.
context.env1.d: The length of the hit.
context.vcf.envDepth: The brightness of the strike at the very front.
context.od.drive: Squashes the hit so it sounds harder.

tweaks.hear: The bell moves through sour, chord-like and clangy intervals. 2.83 is where it sounds most like the drum machine.

tweaks.try: Shorten to 3.6 and set R to 3.6
tweaks.hear: A dry click, close to a clave or a rimshot.
A more pitched, ringing bell.
The low thump comes back and the hit sounds like a small tuned drum.

sounds.name: Long Boom Kick Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of the Roland TR-808 kick — Miami bass and trap
sounds.blurb: Long, tuned sub boom that is a kick drum and a bass line in one. The oscillators are not used.
sounds.how: The 808 kick is not an oscillator: it is a filter-like circuit set just short of ringing on its own, struck by a short pulse so that it rings and dies away. The Neutron can do the same. With RESO just below the point where the filter whistles without stopping, a very short Envelope 2 patched into VCF IN strikes it once per key press. KEY TRK makes the ring follow the keyboard, so the boom plays in tune, and RESO sets how long it lasts.

steps.title: Set the filter just short of ringing
steps.why:
The 808 kick is a filter-like circuit struck so that it rings and dies away. The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) can do the same when set just short of ringing on its own.
- MODE low-pass: the resonant peak does the work.
- RESO 9.2: resonance just below the point, about 9.3, where the filter whistles continuously. Here it only rings for a moment when something hits it. This knob is the length of the boom and is very sensitive.
- ENV DEPTH 0: ENV is short for envelope. Envelope 2 does not move the cutoff.
- Listen for: the oscillator with a sharp, whistling edge on top.

steps.title: Patch ENV 2 → VCF IN
steps.why:
A cable into the filter’s audio input silences the oscillators and strikes the filter with a single thump.
- ENV 2 → VCF IN: VCF IN is the filter’s audio input, normally the oscillators and noise; this cable replaces them. Envelope 2, as a short blip, strikes the filter once per key press.
- A 0 / D 1.6 (9 ms), env 2: a blip of about 10 ms. There is no depth knob on this path: D sets how hard the filter is struck. Too long and it muffles the start.
- S 0% · R 6 ms: the blip always ends at once.
- Listen for: a short, high “pip” on each key.

steps.title: Tune it and let it follow the keys
steps.why:
Key tracking and a low cutoff make the pip into a tuned sub boom.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking makes the ring follow the keyboard, so the boom can play a bass line. Off, every key gives the same drum.
- FREQ 4.5 (261 Hz): about 4.46 is concert pitch. FREQ is the tuning knob; any change transposes the boom.
- Listen for: play low. The pip has become a deep boom that rings and dies away. Low notes ring for longer than high ones.

steps.title: Keep the amplifier open long enough
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). The filter’s ring is the sound, so Envelope 1 only has to stay out of the way.
- A 0 ms (env 1): instant, so the strike is not softened.
- D 8.2 (2.2 s) · S 0%: a two-second decay while the key is held, long enough for the boom to ring out.
- R 6.5 (330 ms): short key presses cut the boom off cleanly. This is how trap bass lines are phrased: the length of each key press is the length of each note.
- Listen for: short taps giving short booms and held keys letting them ring.

steps.title: A knock at the front
steps.why:
A little envelope on the cutoff adds a knock that helps the kick cut through.
- ENV DEPTH 1.5 (15%): ENV is short for envelope. The same Envelope 2 blip now also pushes the cutoff, and so the pitch, up for the first few milliseconds. This is the size of the knock.
- Listen for: a short click-like knock at the start of each boom. Raise ENV DEPTH to 4 to hear it grow into a zap, then set it back.

steps.title: Overdrive for small speakers
steps.why:
A pure sine this low is hard to hear on small speakers. Overdrive adds overtones above it.
- DRIVE 5: moderate distortion. It adds harmonics so the boom can be heard on phones and laptops, and evens out its level as it dies away.
- TONE 3.5: left of centre, keeping the added overtones rounded rather than fizzy.
- LEVEL 7: the overdrive’s output and the synth’s volume, a little under the default.
- Listen for: the boom sounding louder and more present, especially on small speakers. Compare DRIVE at 1 and 5.

context.vcf.reso: In this sound this is the length of the boom, and the knob is very sensitive here. At 9 it is a tight kick of under half a second; at 9.2 it rings for about a second; from about 9.3 the filter never stops and only Envelope 1 ends the note. Low notes ring for longer than high ones.
context.vcf.freq: The tuning knob. 4.46 is concert pitch; any change transposes the boom.
context.vcf.keyTrk: Makes the boom follow the keys so it can play a bass line. Switch it off and every key gives the same drum.
context.env2.d: The length of the pulse that strikes the filter. Longer hits harder and adds a thump; too long and it muffles the start.
context.vcf.envDepth: The size of the pitch knock at the front of each hit.
context.env1.r: How quickly the boom is cut off when you let go of a key. This is how trap bass lines are phrased: the length of each key press is the length of each note.
context.od.drive: Adds overtones so the boom can be heard on small speakers, and evens out its level as it dies away.

tweaks.try: Move in small steps between 8.8 and 9.25
tweaks.hear: From a short, tight kick to a long boom that rings into the next note.
A much bigger pitch drop at the front: closer to a techno kick or a zap.
The distorted, buzzing sub of modern trap.
Each boom slides to its pitch from the previous note, because the keyboard signal that steers the filter is glided too.

sounds.name: Hollow Sequencer Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Eurythmics — "Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This)"
sounds.blurb: Firm, hollow bass for steady eighth-note lines, with the same quick pluck on every note.
sounds.how: The record is from 1983, long before the Neutron: its bass line came from early-80s analogue synths driven by a sequencer, so every note had the same length and the same filter pluck. To get close, Oscillator 1’s SHAPE sits halfway between pulse and saw, which is hollow and buzzy at once, and Oscillator 2 adds a square wave an octave below. Envelope 2 gives each note a quick pluck, and a slow LFO moves the pulse width slightly so repeated notes do not sound identical.

steps.title: Half pulse, half saw, with a square below
steps.why:
Oscillator 1 is set halfway between pulse and saw, hollow and buzzy at once, with a square an octave below.
- OSC MIX −1.5 (65/35): OSC is short for oscillator. A little left of centre on the crossfade keeps Oscillator 1 in front and the sub behind.
- SHAPE 1.5 (pulse/saw), osc 1: the readout shows a 50% blend, with the hollow middle of a square and the buzz of a saw. Towards 1 is a purer square; towards 2 a plain saw.
- WIDTH 5 on both: centred, so the pulse parts are square.
- RANGE 16’ (osc 1) · 32’ (osc 2): Oscillator 2 is a sub-octave under Oscillator 1.
- SHAPE 1 · TUNE 0 (osc 2): a plain square, exactly in tune.
- Listen for: a firm, hollow, buzzy bass.

steps.title: Low-pass, part closed
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) makes the note round and dull, ready for the pluck.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 5 (387 Hz): where the filter rests after each pluck. This is the knob to open slowly over a long build.
- RESO 3: resonance, a little, giving the pluck some definition.
- KEY TRK off: key tracking off, so low and high notes in the bass line stay equally dark.
- Listen for: a warm, rounded bass with the buzz tucked away.

steps.title: The same pluck on every note
steps.why:
Envelope 2 gives every note the same quick pluck, the sequenced feel of the original.
- ENV DEPTH 4.2 (42%): ENV is short for envelope. Envelope 2 opens the filter by about three and a half octaves. This is how bright the front of each note is.
- A 0 / D 5 (150 ms), env 2: opens instantly, closes in about 150 ms. Short is tight and percussive.
- S 1.5 (15%) · R 27 ms: settles low while held; closes quickly after.
- Listen for: the “bow” at the front of each note. Play steady eighth notes and hear each one match.

steps.title: Even, clipped notes
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). Even, clipped notes are a large part of the sequenced feel.
- A 0 ms (env 1): instant start.
- D 5.5 (240 ms) · S 60%: a quarter-second dip to 60% while held.
- R 3.2 (21 ms): a very short release, so each note stops as soon as the key does and the notes stay separate.
- Listen for: clean gaps between notes. Raise R to 6 and the line blurs.

steps.title: Slow pulse-width movement and some drive
steps.why:
PWM (pulse-width modulation) moves the pulse width slowly, so repeated notes are never quite identical. Overdrive adds weight.
- 2 (ATT 2) at 3: the Neutron has no knob marked PWM. Attenuator 2 carries the LFO (low-frequency oscillator) to both pulse-width inputs with no cable. It only acts on the pulse part of each tone.
- RATE 3.5 (1.12 Hz), SHAPE 1: the LFO as a triangle, about one slow, even sweep a second.
- DRIVE 3.5 · TONE 4.5 · LEVEL 7: moderate overdrive, slightly rounded, a touch below the default level.
- Listen for: a subtle shift in colour from note to note, and more weight. Turn ATT 2 to 0 to hear the notes go static.

context.osc1.shape: In this sound the halfway position gives the hollow-but-buzzy tone. Towards 1 is a purer square; towards 2 is a plain saw bass.
context.osc2.range: At 32’ Oscillator 2 is a sub-octave under Oscillator 1.
context.osc.mix: The balance between the main tone and the sub-octave.
context.vcf.freq: Where the filter rests after each pluck. This is the knob to open slowly over a long build.
context.vcf.envDepth: How bright the front of each note is.
context.env2.d: How quickly each pluck closes. Short is tight and percussive.
context.env1.r: Kept very short so the notes are separate.
context.att.2: Pulse-width modulation depth. It only acts on the pulse part of each oscillator’s tone.

tweaks.try: Open slowly from 4.5 to 7 while the riff plays
tweaks.hear: The line goes from a dull thump to a bright, buzzing sequence.
From a hollow square bass to a full saw bass, with every blend in between.
Each note becomes a click followed by a dull body: tighter and more mechanical.
The sub-octave takes over and the line gets heavier and less defined.

sounds.name: Resonant Sweep Growl
sounds.ref: In the style of Rush — "Tom Sawyer"
sounds.blurb: One long low note that starts as a bright snarl and growls its way down to a dark hum.
sounds.how: The original was an Oberheim OB-X polysynth; here is how to get close on the Neutron. The growl is a resonant low-pass filter closing slowly. Resonance boosts a narrow band at the cutoff, and as Envelope 2 lets the cutoff fall over a couple of seconds, that band passes down through the harmonics of the note one after another. A saw and a pulse, slightly detuned, give it plenty of harmonics to pass through.

steps.title: A saw and a pulse, slightly apart
steps.why:
A saw and a pulse, slightly apart, give the sweep plenty of harmonics to pass through.
- OSC MIX 0: OSC is short for oscillator. The centre of the crossfade gives both an equal share.
- SHAPE 2 · RANGE 16’ (osc 1): a sawtooth in the bass octave.
- SHAPE 1 · WIDTH 4 (41%), osc 2: a slightly narrow pulse. Its harmonics differ from the saw’s, giving the resonant peak more to pick out.
- RANGE 16’ · TUNE +0.1 st (osc 2): the same octave, a touch sharp, so the two beat slowly and the sweep never sounds quite the same twice.
- Listen for: a thick, buzzy low note with a slow beat.

steps.title: Filter nearly shut, RESO high
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is nearly shut with high resonance, ready to sweep.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 3.6 (139 Hz): where the sweep ends up. This low, only a dark hum is left. Any lower and the note almost disappears.
- RESO 7: resonance, a strong peak at the cutoff. This is the growl. Lower gives a plain darkening; near maximum the peak whistles.
- KEY TRK off: key tracking off, so the cutoff does not follow the keys.
- Listen for: a dark hum. The resonance shows once the cutoff moves.

steps.title: A long, slow fall from Envelope 2
steps.why:
Envelope 2 opens the filter wide and lets it fall slowly, so the resonant peak steps down through the harmonics one after another.
- ENV DEPTH 7 (70%): ENV is short for envelope. The filter opens by more than five octaves at the start of the note. This is how bright the note starts.
- A 0 ms (env 2): the sweep starts wide open instantly.
- D 8.3 (2.4 s): how long the sweep takes, about two and a half seconds.
- S 0% · R 220 ms: the filter always closes fully to the hum.
- Listen for: hold a low note. It starts as a bright snarl and growls its way down to a dark hum.

steps.title: Full, held loudness
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). Full sustain keeps the note loud for the whole sweep.
- A 0 ms (env 1): instant start.
- D 150 ms · S 100%: full level while held, so the fading brightness is the only change.
- R 5.8 (180 ms): about a fifth of a second to fade after release.
- Listen for: the note staying loud while the filter does all the moving.

steps.title: Drive
steps.why:
Overdrive after the filter exaggerates the resonant peak and turns the sweep into a snarl.
- DRIVE 4.5: moderate distortion. The resonant peak barks as it moves.
- TONE 5: centred.
- LEVEL 6.5: brought down to make up for the extra loudness of the drive.
- Listen for: a rougher, more aggressive sweep. Compare DRIVE at 1 and 4.5.

context.vcf.reso: In this sound this is the growl. Lower it and the sweep is a plain darkening; near maximum the peak whistles over the note.
context.env2.d: How long the sweep takes. About 2.4 seconds here.
context.vcf.envDepth: How bright the note starts.
context.vcf.freq: Where the sweep ends up. Any lower and the note almost disappears at the end.
context.osc2.tune: A small detune, so the harmonics shift slowly and the sweep never sounds quite the same twice.
context.osc2.width: A slightly narrow pulse has a different set of harmonics from the saw, which gives the peak more to pick out.
context.od.drive: Distortion after the filter makes the resonant peak bark.

tweaks.hear: From a quick "yow" of under a second to a sweep that takes most of four seconds.
First a plain darkening with no growl, then a sweep with a whistling, vocal peak.
The filter now opens slowly before it closes: a rising and falling "wow".
A rougher, louder snarl with the peak squashed into the distortion.

sounds.name: Bright Staccato Pulse Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of a-ha — "Take On Me"
sounds.blurb: Bright, bouncy lead with a short note shape, for fast riffs.
sounds.how: The record’s lead was made on mid-80s polyphonic synths, so this is a way to get close with one voice. The tone is a narrow pulse wave with a sawtooth beside it: thin, bright and a little nasal. Both envelopes fall quickly to a low level, so every note has a bright front and then gets out of the way, which is what lets a fast riff sound clean. A delay set to the eighth note fills the spaces.

steps.title: A narrow pulse with a saw beside it
steps.why:
A narrow pulse with a sawtooth beside it gives a thin, bright, slightly nasal lead.
- OSC MIX −1 (60/40): OSC is short for oscillator. Slightly left of centre on the crossfade favours the pulse; the saw adds body.
- SHAPE 1 · WIDTH 3 (32%), osc 1: a pulse narrower than a square, thinner and more nasal. At 5 it is a hollow square; towards 1 very thin and reedy.
- RANGE 8’ · TUNE 0 (osc 1): normal playing octave, in tune.
- SHAPE 2 · RANGE 8’ · TUNE +0.1 st (osc 2): a sawtooth a touch sharp, for slight movement.
- Listen for: a bright, reedy buzz. Sweep Oscillator 1’s WIDTH between 1 and 5 to hear the character change.

steps.title: A short note shape
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). Here each note has a bright front and then gets out of the way.
- A 0 ms (env 1): instant start.
- D 5.2 (180 ms): how quickly each note drops back. This is what keeps a fast riff clean.
- S 4 (40%): the level held notes settle to. Short notes are all attack.
- R 4.5 (63 ms): a short release.
- Listen for: short notes punchy and held notes falling back after the first instant.

steps.title: Bright filter with a small pluck
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) stays fairly bright, with a small pluck at each note.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 7 (1.7 kHz): the resting brightness.
- RESO 2: resonance, a touch.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking keeps the top of the riff as bright as the bottom.
- ENV DEPTH 3 (30%): ENV is short for envelope. Envelope 2 opens the filter by about two and a half octaves.
- A 0 / D 100 ms / S 20% (env 2): the brightness lasts about 100 ms and settles low; R 41 ms closes it quickly.
- Listen for: a crisp, bright front on each note of a fast riff.

steps.title: Delay on the eighth note
steps.why:
An analogue delay set to the eighth note fills the spaces.
- TIME 6.2 (190 ms): one eighth note at 160 bpm. Retune it by ear at a different tempo.
- REPEATS 3 (30%): a few repeats.
- MIX 2 (20%): a quiet echo landing on the next eighth.
- Listen for: the riff sounding busier than you play it. Pull MIX to 0 to compare.

steps.title: A little drive
steps.why:
A little overdrive adds edge without making the lead heavy.
- DRIVE 2.5: light distortion.
- TONE 6: right of centre, thinning the low end and adding bite.
- LEVEL 7.5: the overdrive’s output and the synth’s volume, just under the default.
- Listen for: a brighter, slightly edgier lead that cuts through. Compare DRIVE at 1 and 2.5.

context.osc1.width: In this sound this is the character of the lead. At 3 it is thin and nasal; at 5 it is a hollow square; towards 1 it becomes very thin and reedy.
context.osc.mix: The balance of pulse against saw. The saw adds body.
context.env1.d: How quickly each note drops back. This is what keeps a fast riff clean.
context.env1.s: The level that held notes settle to.
context.vcf.envDepth: The brightness of the front of each note.
context.vcf.keyTrk: Keeps high notes as bright as low ones.
context.delay.time: One eighth note at 160 bpm. Retune it by ear if you change the tempo.

tweaks.hear: From a thin, reedy buzz to a round, hollow square.
Every note becomes a pluck, closer to a harpsichord or a sequencer line.

tweaks.try: Raise to 4 with LFO RATE at 4.5
tweaks.hear: The pulse width starts to move and the lead thickens, as a chorus would make it.
The echoes become a second part answering the riff.

sounds.name: Growing Wobble Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Tame Impala — wobbly, detuned synth leads
sounds.blurb: Detuned, sliding lead whose notes start steady and begin to waver the longer you hold them.
sounds.how: Two sawtooths about a quarter of a semitone apart give the woozy, slightly sour tone. The waver is vibrato: the LFO reaches pitch through both attenuators and one cable. To keep short notes in tune, Attenuator 1 is also put under the control of Envelope 2, which has a slow attack. Vibrato therefore fades in over about half a second, and because Envelope 2 also drives ENV DEPTH, the note brightens as it starts to wobble.

steps.title: Two sawtooths, clearly detuned
steps.why:
Two clearly detuned sawtooths give a woozy, slightly sour tone.
- OSC MIX 0: OSC is short for oscillator. The centre of the crossfade gives both an equal share.
- SHAPE 2 on both (saw) · RANGE 8’: bright sawtooths in the lead octave.
- TUNE 0 (osc 1) · +0.2 st (osc 2): about a quarter of a semitone apart, more than you would use for a pad. With the knob at 0.03 it is a polite chorus; at 0.2 it is plainly out of tune.
- Listen for: fast beating between the two, which gives the sour, woozy edge.

steps.title: Held notes that slide
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier), and portamento makes the notes slide.
- A 1 (1 ms), env 1: near-instant, just enough to take off a click.
- D 360 ms · S 85%: held notes stay close to full level.
- R 5.8 (180 ms): about a fifth of a second of fade.
- PORTA TIME 1.6 (260 ms): portamento, so every note bends in from the last one.
- Listen for: legato phrases sliding from note to note.

steps.title: A filter that opens as you hold
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) opens slowly as you hold a note: short notes stay mellow, long notes brighten.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 6.6 (1.2 kHz): the resting, mellow tone.
- RESO 2.5 · KEY TRK on: a little resonance; key tracking keeps high notes bright.
- ENV DEPTH 2 (20%): ENV is short for envelope. How much a held note brightens as Envelope 2 rises, about an octave and a half.
- A 7.5 (440 ms), env 2: nearly half a second to rise, so the brightness arrives late.
- D 150 ms · S 100% · R 95 ms: full sustain, so the filter stays open while held.
- Listen for: hold a note and it opens up after a moment. Play short notes and they stay dark.

steps.title: Vibrato: patch ATT 1 → OSC 1+2
steps.why:
Vibrato is the LFO (low-frequency oscillator), a slow wave you do not hear directly, moving pitch through both attenuators.
- ATT 1 → OSC 1+2: Attenuator 1’s input is normally Attenuator 2’s output, which carries the LFO, so the LFO passes through both. This cable adds it to both oscillators’ pitch.
- 2 (ATT 2) at 2.5 · 1 (ATT 1) at 3.2: both knobs set the depth, about half a semitone each way.
- RATE (LFO) 4.8 (5.02 Hz) · SHAPE 0 (sine): a smooth waver about five times a second.
- KEY SYNC off: the LFO runs free.
- Listen for: a steady waver on every note, even short ones, all the time.

steps.title: Patch ENV 2 → ATT1 CV
steps.why:
This cable makes the vibrato grow over each note instead of being there all the time.
- ENV 2 → ATT1 CV: Attenuator 1 is voltage controlled. This replaces its usual control source (the ASSIGN output) with Envelope 2, so the vibrato is only as deep as Envelope 2 is high. The ATT 1 knob still sets the depth it grows to.
- Listen for: each note starting steady, then the wobble and the brightness arriving together over the first half second. Short notes stay in tune. Envelope 2’s attack now sets how long both take.

steps.title: Echo and a little dirt
steps.why:
A medium delay smears the slides together, and some overdrive roughens the tone.
- TIME 7 (240 ms): echoes about a quarter of a second behind.
- REPEATS 4.5 (45%): how long the echoes of each slide hang around.
- MIX 3 (30%): echoes clearly present behind the lead.
- DRIVE 3 · TONE 4.5 · LEVEL 7: light, slightly rounded grit, with the level just under the default.
- Listen for: sliding phrases trailing into each other. Pull MIX to 0 to hear the dry lead.

context.osc2.tune: In this sound the wide detune is the sour, woozy part of the tone. At 0.03 it is a polite chorus; at 0.2 it is plainly out of tune.
context.att.1: The depth the vibrato grows to on a held note. Envelope 2 scales it from zero through ATT1 CV.
context.att.2: The level of the LFO going into Attenuator 1, so it is a second depth control for the same vibrato.
