context.env2.a: How long the wobble and the brightness take to arrive. About 440 ms here.
context.vcf.envDepth: How much a held note brightens as Envelope 2 rises.
context.lfo.rate: Vibrato speed, about 5 Hz.
context.porta.time: The slide between notes.
context.delay.repeats: How long the echoes of each slide hang around.

tweaks.hear: The wobble is there almost from the start of every note, and fast passages sound seasick.
Held notes swing by more than a semitone each way: badly warped tape.
A slow, drunken drift of about 1 Hz instead of a vibrato.
From a gentle chorus to two oscillators that plainly disagree.

sounds.name: Chorused String Machine
sounds.ref: In the style of Joy Division — "Love Will Tear Us Apart"
sounds.blurb: Thin, shimmering synthetic strings that can play two notes at once.
sounds.how: The original was a 1970s string machine, an ARP Omni. String machines get their shimmer from a built-in chorus: a very short delay whose time is kept moving, so the delayed copy is always slightly out of tune with the dry sound. The Neutron’s delay can do that. TIME goes almost to its minimum, about 30 ms, MIX goes to half, and the LFO, turned right down by Attenuator 2, is patched into DELAY TIME. Two bright sawtooths with a soft attack supply the string tone, and PARAPHONIC gives two-note chords.

steps.title: Two sawtooths, two notes
steps.why:
Two bright sawtooths supply the string tone, and PARAPHONIC allows two-note chords.
- OSC MIX 0: OSC is short for oscillator. The centre of the crossfade gives both an equal share.
- SHAPE 2 on both (saw) · RANGE 8’: bright, buzzy tones in the same octave.
- TUNE +0.1 st (osc 2): a touch sharp, for slow beating.
- PARAPHONIC on: hold two keys and each oscillator takes one. Both notes share one filter and one amplifier.
- Listen for: a bright, buzzy tone. Hold two keys to hear a two-note chord.

steps.title: A bowed attack
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). A slow attack copies the start of a bowed note.
- A 7 (270 ms), env 1: the bowed fade-in. Shorter is more like an organ; longer is more like a pad.
- D 360 ms · S 90%: held chords stay near full level.
- R 6.8 (420 ms): just under half a second of fade, so chords overlap a little.
- Listen for: chords swelling in and trailing into each other.

steps.title: Bright and thin
steps.why:
String machines have very little low end. The filter keeps things bright, and the overdrive’s TONE thins the bass.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 7.3 (2.1 kHz): the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is fairly open.
- RESO 1 · KEY TRK on: barely any resonance; key tracking keeps high notes bright.
- ENV DEPTH 0: ENV is short for envelope. The envelope does not move the filter.
- DRIVE 1.5 · TONE 7 · LEVEL 8: little distortion; TONE well right of centre removes low end.
- Listen for: a thinner, brighter tone, closer to a string machine than a synth.

steps.title: A 30 ms delay at half mix
steps.why:
A very short delay at half mix is the first half of a chorus.
- TIME 0.6 (30 ms): so short you do not hear an echo. The delayed copy blends with the dry sound and makes it slightly hollow.
- REPEATS 1.5 (15%): kept low, so the short delay does not ring like a metal pipe.
- MIX 5 (50%): dry and delayed sounds equal, which gives the strongest chorus.
- Listen for: a slightly hollow, thicker tone. It is static until the next step moves the delay time.

steps.title: Chorus: patch ATT 2 → DELAY TIME
steps.why:
Moving the delay time bends the pitch of the delayed copy, and mixed with the dry sound that is a chorus. The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) moves it.
- ATT 2 → DELAY TIME: Attenuator 2 carries the LFO. This cable adds it to the TIME knob. It also feeds pulse width, which does nothing on sawtooths.
- 2 (ATT 2) at 2: the chorus depth. The delay time moves about 2 ms either side, bending the copy by about a tenth of a semitone.
- RATE 3.2 (0.80 Hz), SHAPE 1: the LFO as a triangle, a slow, even movement. Under 1 Hz is a slow ensemble effect; 5 Hz and above is more of a vibrato.
- Listen for: a slow shimmer on held chords. Turn ATT 2 to 0 and back to hear it.

context.att.2: In this sound this is the chorus depth: how far the LFO moves the delay time. It also feeds pulse width, which does nothing on sawtooths.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of the shimmer. Under 1 Hz is a slow ensemble effect; 5 Hz and above is more of a vibrato.
context.delay.time: Kept very short so the delay is heard as thickening and not as an echo.
context.delay.mix: At 5 the dry and delayed sounds are equal, which gives the strongest chorus.
context.delay.repeats: Low, so the short delay does not ring like a metal pipe.
context.env1.a: The bowed fade-in. Shorter is more like an organ; longer is more like a pad.
context.od.tone: Right of centre removes low end, as a string machine has.
context.osc.para: Lets two held keys sound as two notes. They share one filter and one amplifier.

tweaks.try: Turn down to 0, then back to 2
tweaks.hear: Without the moving delay time the sound is static and slightly hollow. The shimmer is all from this one cable.
The delayed copy goes plainly out of tune: a seasick, detuned ensemble.
The short delay starts to ring, like playing inside a metal pipe, and the LFO makes that ring waver.
Darker, more distant strings.

sounds.name: Slowing Laser Zaps
sounds.ref: In the style of Jean-Michel Jarre — "Oxygène" zaps and sweeps
sounds.blurb: Hold a key for a volley of falling "pew" sounds that starts as a blur and slows to single shots.
sounds.how: Effects like these were made on the patchable synths of the 1970s; here is one way to get close on the Neutron. Each zap is a resonant filter swept quickly downwards. The LFO, set to a reverse sawtooth, is already wired to the cutoff through MOD DEPTH, so every LFO cycle is one zap. The volley slows down because Envelope 2 is patched into LFO RATE: at the start of the note it pushes the LFO 16 times faster, and as it decays the zaps spread out.

steps.title: A low pulse as raw material
steps.why:
A plain low pulse gives the filter plenty of harmonics to pick out.
- OSC MIX −5 (OSC 1 only): OSC is short for oscillator. Fully left on the crossfade means only Oscillator 1 is heard.
- SHAPE 1 · WIDTH 5: a pulse with the width centred, a square wave.
- RANGE 32’: the lowest octave, a deep buzz with closely packed harmonics.
- TUNE 0: in tune with the keys.
- Listen for: a plain, low, hollow buzz.

steps.title: Filter almost whistling
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is set almost at the point where it sings on its own.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 6 (805 Hz): the centre of each sweep to come.
- RESO 9: resonance close to about 9.3, where the filter whistles by itself. This is how pure the zap is: lower gives more of the buzzing oscillator and less whistle.
- ENV DEPTH 0 · KEY TRK off: ENV is short for envelope. Neither the envelope nor the keys move the cutoff.
- Listen for: the buzz with a strong, ringing peak at about 800 Hz.

steps.title: A falling ramp from the LFO
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator), a repeating wave you do not hear directly, is already wired to the cutoff. With a falling ramp, every cycle is one zap.
- MOD DEPTH 6 (60%): how far each zap sweeps, about three octaves either side of FREQ.
- SHAPE (LFO) 4 (reverse saw): jumps up and ramps down, giving falling zaps. A saw gives rising ones; triangle a siren.
- RATE (LFO) 4.2 (2.52 Hz): about two and a half zaps a second.
- KEY SYNC on: each note starts at the top of a sweep.
- Listen for: a steady “pew, pew, pew” while the key is held.

steps.title: Patch ENV 2 → LFO RATE
steps.why:
One cable makes the volley start fast and slow down.
- ENV 2 → LFO RATE: Envelope 2, a shape that runs once per note, is added to the RATE knob. At full height it raises the LFO by four octaves, from 2.5 Hz to about 40 Hz.
- A 0 / D 7.6 (1.4 s), env 2: starts at full and falls over about a second and a half. There is no depth knob on this path, so D sets how long the slowing takes.
- S 0%: the zaps always settle to the RATE knob’s speed. Raise it and a held note stays fast.
- R 95 ms: quick reset after release.
- Listen for: each note starting as a blur of zaps that slows to single shots.

steps.title: Hold it open and add echo
steps.why:
Full sustain keeps the volley going, and a delay scatters the zaps.
- A 0 / S 100% / R 95 ms (env 1): Envelope 1 sets loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). Full level for as long as the key is held.
- DRIVE 2 · LEVEL 6: a touch of grit, with the level lowered.
- TIME 210 ms · REPEATS 5.5 · MIX 3.5: echoes with plenty of repeats, well mixed in. REPEATS sets how long they carry on.
- Listen for: a spray of zaps with echoes between them, thinning out as the volley slows.

context.lfo.rate: In this sound this is the speed the zaps slow down to. Envelope 2 adds up to four octaves on top of it at the start of each note.
context.lfo.shape: Reverse saw gives falling zaps. Saw (2) gives rising ones; triangle gives a siren.
context.vcf.modDepth: How far each zap sweeps. At 6 it is three octaves either side of FREQ.
context.vcf.reso: How pure the zap is. Lower it and you hear more of the buzzing oscillator and less of the whistle.
context.vcf.freq: The centre of each sweep.
context.env2.d: How long the volley takes to slow down.
context.env2.s: At zero the zaps always settle to the RATE knob’s speed. Raise it and a held note stays fast.
context.delay.repeats: How long the echoes of the zaps carry on.

tweaks.hear: The zaps rise instead of fall: "whup, whup, whup".
A brief rattle at the start of the note, then steady shots.

tweaks.try: Raise to 8 and set S to 10
tweaks.hear: The reverse effect: slow single shots that speed up into a blur while the key is held.
The filter sings on its own and each zap is a pure falling whistle over the buzz.

sounds.name: Chopped Organ Filter
sounds.ref: In the style of The Who — "Won’t Get Fooled Again"
sounds.blurb: Held organ-like chords that a square-wave LFO chops into a steady rhythm.
sounds.how: The original was a home organ played through the filter of an EMS VCS3 synthesiser, with the synth’s LFO opening and shutting the filter in a steady rhythm under the held chords. On the Neutron a square pulse and a triangle make a plain organ-like tone, PARAPHONIC allows two-note chords, and the LFO is already wired to the filter through MOD DEPTH. A square LFO shape makes the filter jump between open and nearly shut with nothing in between.

steps.title: A plain organ tone, two notes
steps.why:
A square pulse and a soft triangle-sine make a plain organ-like tone, with two notes available.
- OSC MIX −0.5 (55/45): OSC is short for oscillator. Just left of centre on the crossfade, favouring the square slightly.
- SHAPE 1 · WIDTH 5 (osc 1): a square wave, hollow like a drawbar organ.
- SHAPE 3.5 (osc 2): between triangle and sine, a softer second voice.
- RANGE 8’ on both · TUNE 0 (osc 2): the same octave, in tune.
- PARAPHONIC on: hold two keys and each oscillator takes one note. Both share one filter and one amplifier.
- Listen for: a hollow, organ-like tone. Hold two keys for a chord.

steps.title: On and off like an organ key
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). Like an organ key, the note is simply on while the key is down.
- A 1 (1 ms), env 1: near-instant, just enough to avoid a click.
- D 150 ms · S 100%: full sustain, so there is no dip.
- R 3.5 (27 ms): stops almost at once on release.
- Listen for: chords starting and stopping cleanly with no shape of their own.

steps.title: Resonant low-pass at the halfway point
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is set to the middle of the chop, not the bottom: the LFO will push the cutoff above and below it.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 5.4 (519 Hz): the halfway point between open and shut. Raise it and the shut half lets more through.
- RESO 4.5: resonance adds a nasal peak to the open half of each chop.
- KEY TRK off · ENV DEPTH 0: ENV is short for envelope. Neither the keys nor the envelope move the cutoff; the LFO will.
- Listen for: a darker, slightly nasal organ.

steps.title: A square LFO on the filter
steps.why:
No cable needed: the LFO (low-frequency oscillator), a repeating wave you do not hear directly, already reaches the cutoff through MOD DEPTH. A square shape chops the filter open and shut.
- MOD DEPTH 5 (50%): the cutoff jumps about two and a half octaves each way, to about 2.9 kHz when the LFO is high and 90 Hz when low.
- SHAPE (LFO) 3 (square): a hard chop with nothing in between. Towards saw ramps open; sine gives a smooth wobble.
- RATE (LFO) 4.7 (4.53 Hz): one open-and-shut cycle per eighth note at 136 bpm.
- KEY SYNC on: each chord starts on the open half. Off, the chop runs free under your playing, as on the record.
- Listen for: held chords chopped into a steady rhythm.

steps.title: Echo and a little drive
steps.why:
An echo fills the gaps and a little drive adds the grit of an overloaded organ amplifier.
- TIME 8 (330 ms): a dotted eighth at 136 bpm, so quiet copies of the chops land in the gaps.
- REPEATS 3 (30%) · MIX 2 (20%): a few quiet repeats.
- DRIVE 3.5 · TONE 5.5 · LEVEL 7: moderate, slightly bright grit, with the level just under the default.
- Listen for: a busier, grittier rhythm. Pull MIX to 0 to hear the bare chop.

context.lfo.rate: In this sound this is the rhythm of the chop. At 136 bpm: 4.11 is quarter notes, 4.71 is eighth notes, 5.31 is sixteenths.
context.lfo.shape: Square gives a hard chop. Turn towards saw (2) for a chop that ramps open, or to sine (0) for a smooth wobble.
context.lfo.keySync: Starts the rhythm again on each chord. Switch it off and the chop runs free under your playing, as it did on the record.
context.vcf.modDepth: How far apart the open and shut settings are.
context.vcf.freq: The halfway point between open and shut. Raise it and the shut half lets more through.
context.vcf.reso: Adds a nasal peak to the open half of each chop.
context.osc.para: Lets two held keys sound as two notes, one per oscillator.

tweaks.hear: Eighth-note and sixteenth-note chopping.

tweaks.try: Turn to 2.5, between saw and square
tweaks.hear: Each chop gains a short upward sweep as it opens, which sounds more like a picked note.

tweaks.try: Sweep between 4.5 and 7 while chords are held
tweaks.hear: The shut half goes from near silence to a muted organ, so the chop becomes less severe.
A thinner chop that alternates between a bright band and a low murmur.

sounds.name: Fast Looping Filter Sequence
sounds.ref: In the style of Pink Floyd — "On the Run"
sounds.blurb: Eight quick notes round and round, with the filter slowly opening and closing over the loop.
sounds.how: The original was an EMS Synthi AKS playing an eight-note loop from its built-in sequencer at high speed while the filter was turned by hand. The Neutron has no sequencer, so the riff (or your own sequencer) plays the notes and the synth supplies the tone: a sawtooth through a resonant low-pass filter with a very short pluck on each note. A slow LFO, already wired to the filter through MOD DEPTH, stands in for the hand on the filter knob.

steps.title: One sawtooth
steps.why:
Everything starts from one bright oscillator. The notes in this loop go by at about eleven a second, so a single, simple source keeps each one clear instead of a thick blur.
- OSC MIX −5: a crossfader between the two oscillators. Fully left is Oscillator 1 only; turn right and Oscillator 2 fades in as 1 fades out.
- SHAPE saw: SHAPE morphs through five waves. The sawtooth carries every harmonic, the buzziest raw material, and plenty for the filter to work on later.
- RANGE 8’, TUNE 0: the octave in organ-pipe feet (8’ is the highest of the three) and exactly in tune.
- Listen for: a plain, buzzy tone. Play the riff now and the notes blur into each other, which the next step fixes.

steps.title: Very short notes
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes the loudness of each note (it is wired to the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier). Here it turns every note into a short blip, so the fast loop stays separate and rhythmic.
- A 0: full volume at once, so each note lands right on time.
- D 110 ms, S 0: with no sustain the note fades to silence over about a tenth of a second even while the key is held. Longer decay and the notes start to overlap.
- R 41 ms: a short fade after the key comes up, so nothing hangs over into the next note.
- Listen for: the riff turning from a smear into a string of separate ticks. Turn D up towards 6 and hear the notes run into each other.

steps.title: Resonant filter with a tiny pluck
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) takes brightness away. In low-pass it keeps what is below the cutoff and trims what is above. Envelope 2, the filter envelope, gives each note a quick flick of brightness.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 5.4 (about 520 Hz): the resting point is quite dark, so most of the buzz is gone between flicks.
- RESO 5.5: resonance, a boost right at the cutoff. Above half it gives the notes a rubbery, vocal ring; higher gets more whistly.
- KEY TRK Off: the cutoff stays put whatever note you play.
- ENV DEPTH 3: how far Envelope 2 pushes the cutoff up, about two and a half octaves.
- Envelope 2 A 0, D 57 ms, S 0, R 35 ms: an instant, very short flick that falls straight back.
- Listen for: a “tik” at the front of each note, then a rounder, rubbery body. Sweep Envelope 2’s D to lengthen or shorten the tik.

steps.title: A slow LFO turns the filter for you
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) is a slow wave that moves other settings instead of being heard. It stands in for the hand turning the filter knob on the original.
- MOD DEPTH 4: how far the LFO moves the cutoff. With nothing patched the LFO is already wired here, so no cable is needed. At 4 it swings about two octaves either way around 520 Hz.
- RATE 1.9 (0.18 Hz): one open-and-close every five and a half seconds or so. Faster and it becomes a wobble; slower and the loop changes almost too gradually to notice.
- SHAPE triangle: an even rise and fall, so the sweep has no sudden jumps.
- KEY SYNC Off: the LFO runs free and does not restart on each note, so the sweep drifts across the loop rather than lining up with it.
- Listen for: the loop going from muffled to bright and back on its own. Turn MOD DEPTH to 0 and ride FREQ by hand to play the sweep yourself.

steps.title: Hiss and drive
steps.why:
The last touches add air and bite. The noise gives a breathy layer, and the overdrive stops the resonance sounding thin and polite.
- NOISE 2: white noise mixed in before the filter. Because it passes through the filter too, it gets louder as the sweep opens, a little like a hi-hat fading in and out.
- DRIVE 3.5: the overdrive sits after the filter. A moderate amount adds grit and bite to the resonant peak; more gets fuzzier.
- TONE 5.5: just right of centre, a little brighter. Left would round it off.
- LEVEL 7: the overdrive’s output, which every sound passes through. Down a touch to allow for the extra drive.
- Listen for: a soft hiss on every note that swells as the sweep opens. Turn NOISE back to 0 to compare.

context.vcf.freq: In this sound this is the centre of the slow sweep. Turn MOD DEPTH to zero and ride this knob by hand to play it as the record was made.
context.vcf.modDepth: How far the slow LFO moves the filter.
context.lfo.rate: The length of one open-and-close cycle, about five and a half seconds here. It runs free, so the sweep does not line up with the loop.
context.vcf.reso: The rubbery, vocal quality of each note. Higher is more whistly as the sweep passes through.
context.env2.d: The length of the "tik" at the front of each note.
context.env1.d: The length of each note. Much longer and the notes run into each other.
context.mix.noise: A breathy layer that follows the filter, a little like a hi-hat that fades in and out.

tweaks.try: Set MOD DEPTH to 0 and sweep FREQ between 4 and 7.5 by hand
tweaks.hear: The same rise and fall, under your control and in time with the music if you want it to be.
A whistling peak travels up and down through the loop.
The sweep now thins the loop out and fills it in again, instead of dulling and brightening it.
The breathy tick becomes a steady noise pulse riding on top of the notes.

sounds.name: Random-Speed Wobble Solo
sounds.ref: In the style of Brian Eno with Roxy Music — the synth solo on "Editions of You"
sounds.blurb: Unruly solo voice whose pitch and filter shake at a speed that keeps changing at random.
sounds.how: Eno’s solos with Roxy Music were played on an EMS VCS3, a small patchable synth, with the modulation pushed until the pitch was barely under control. Here the LFO shakes the pitch through Attenuator 2 and the filter through MOD DEPTH. The unstable part comes from one more cable: the sample-and-hold’s random steps go into LFO RATE, so several times a second the LFO jumps to a new speed, anywhere from a slow lurch to a buzz. Overdrive and a short echo roughen it up.

steps.title: A raw pulse-and-saw tone
steps.why:
The raw voice for a solo that has to cut through a band. One oscillator only, with its wave set between two shapes to get a tone no switch would give.
- OSC MIX −5: the crossfader between the two oscillators, fully left for Oscillator 1 alone.
- SHAPE 1.5 (pulse → saw 50%): SHAPE morphs smoothly between five waves. Halfway between pulse and sawtooth gives the saw’s brightness with some of the pulse’s hollowness.
- WIDTH 4 (41% duty): pulse width. A little off square, slightly thinner and more nasal. It colours the in-between shapes too.
- RANGE 8’, TUNE 0: the highest of the three octave settings, in tune.
- Listen for: a bright, slightly hollow buzz. Turn SHAPE towards 2 and it goes plain sawtooth; towards 1 it goes hollow and reedy.

steps.title: Resonant filter, held notes
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is set so that any movement of the cutoff will be easy to hear later, and Envelope 1, the loudness envelope, is set for held solo notes.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 6.5 (about 1.2 kHz): a middling cutoff that takes the fizz off but keeps it forward.
- RESO 5: resonance at half, a clear peak at the cutoff. Any sweep of the cutoff will sound vocal.
- ENV DEPTH 0: Envelope 2 does not move the filter. All the movement will come from the LFO.
- KEY TRK On: the cutoff follows the keys, so high notes stay as bright as low ones.
- Envelope 1 A 0, D 150 ms, S 100%, R 63 ms: instant start, full level while held, a quick fade at the end.
- Listen for: a steady, slightly nasal tone that holds as long as the key does.

steps.title: Patch ATT 2 → OSC 1+2, and turn up MOD DEPTH
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator), a wave that moves other settings, now shakes both pitch and filter. One cable does the pitch; the filter needs only a knob.
- Cable ATT 2 → OSC 1+2: Attenuator 2 already carries the LFO. This adds its output to both oscillators’ pitch.
- 2 (Attenuator 2) at 3: the depth of that pitch wobble, about three semitones either side. It also moves the pulse width slightly, which adds to the unsteadiness.
- RATE 5.5 (11 Hz), SHAPE triangle: a fast, even wobble, well past a gentle vibrato.
- KEY SYNC Off: the wobble runs free across notes.
- MOD DEPTH 3: the same LFO moves the cutoff an octave and a half each way, no cable needed.
- Listen for: a wide, seasick vibrato with the tone wah-ing in step. Turn the ATT 2 knob down to hear the filter wobble alone.

steps.title: Patch S&H → LFO RATE
steps.why:
S&H (sample and hold) takes a reading of noise at regular intervals and holds it, giving random steps. Here those steps change the LFO’s speed, which is where the solo gets unruly.
- Cable S&H → LFO RATE: adds the random steps to the RATE knob’s setting. A full step moves the LFO four octaves, so from 11 Hz it can land anywhere from about 0.7 Hz to 180 Hz. No knob sets the depth of this path.
- RATE (S&H) 6 (4.31 Hz): about four new speeds a second. Slower and each speed lasts longer; faster and it turns to chaos.
- GLIDE 0: the speed jumps. Turn it up and the LFO speeds up and slows down smoothly instead.
- Listen for: the vibrato lurching, racing and now and then turning into a buzz as the LFO is thrown into the audio range.

steps.title: Overdrive and a short echo
steps.why:
Grit and a short echo make it sound like a solo on a record rather than a test tone.
- DRIVE 5: overdrive after the filter. It adds grit and keeps the level more even as the filter is shaken. Less is cleaner; more is fuzzier.
- TONE 5.5, LEVEL 6.5: slightly bright, with the output level brought down to allow for the drive.
- TIME 5.5 (150 ms): an analogue delay. Short enough to thicken the line rather than repeat whole phrases.
- REPEATS 3: only one or two echoes before they die away.
- MIX 2.5: echoes quiet against the dry sound.
- Listen for: a rougher, fuller line with a quick shadow after each note. Turn MIX to 0 to hear it dry.

context.att.2: In this sound this is how far the LFO bends the pitch. It also moves the pulse width slightly, which adds to the unsteadiness.
context.lfo.rate: The centre speed of the wobble. The random steps push it up to four octaves faster or slower than this.
context.sh.rate: How often the LFO is thrown to a new speed.
context.sh.glide: At zero the speed jumps. Turn it up and the LFO speeds up and slows down smoothly instead.
context.vcf.modDepth: How far the same LFO moves the cutoff. When the LFO is thrown into the audio range this turns into a rasp.
context.od.drive: Grit, and a more even level while the filter is being shaken.

tweaks.hear: From a nervous vibrato to pitch swings of most of an octave.
The wobble now accelerates and brakes smoothly instead of jumping between speeds.
The pitch trills between two notes at random speeds, more like a faulty computer.
Each speed lasts a second or so, so you can play phrases that fit round the changes.

sounds.name: Filter FM Clang
sounds.ref: In the style of Brian Eno — VCS3 "treatments" and ring-modulator clangs on early Roxy Music records
sounds.blurb: Hollow, bell-like clang with overtones that do not belong to the note, made by shaking the filter with a second oscillator.
sounds.how: The EMS VCS3 Eno used has a ring modulator, which multiplies two signals and gives clanging tones that are not in either one. The Neutron has no ring modulator, but it can get close. Oscillator 2 is taken out of the mix and patched into FREQ MOD, so it moves the filter cutoff hundreds of times a second. With high resonance the filter turns that movement into new overtones around Oscillator 1’s note. Both oscillators follow the keyboard, so the clang keeps the same character on every key.

steps.title: Hear only Oscillator 1
steps.why:
The sound starts as one soft tone, with Oscillator 2 kept out of the mix so it can be used purely as a modulator later.
- OSC MIX −5: the crossfader between the two oscillators, fully left, so only Oscillator 1 is heard.
- SHAPE triangle: SHAPE morphs between five waves. The triangle has few harmonics, a soft, round tone, so anything the filter adds will stand out clearly.
- RANGE 8’, TUNE 0: the highest octave setting, in tune.
- Listen for: a soft, flute-like tone with little edge to it.

steps.title: A ringing filter
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is set to ring. The ringing peak is what will turn Oscillator 2’s movement into new overtones.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 6 (about 800 Hz): where the ringing peak sits, and so where the added overtones will be strongest.
- RESO 8: resonance, a boost at the cutoff. At 8 the filter nearly rings on its own. Below about 5 the clang later would fade to a slight roughness.
- KEY TRK On: the peak follows the notes, so the effect keeps the same character on every key.
- ENV DEPTH 0: no envelope sweep on the filter.
- Listen for: a nasal edge on the triangle. That is all for now.

steps.title: Set up Oscillator 2 as the modulator
steps.why:
Oscillator 2 is set up as the modulator. It is silent in the mix, so this step changes nothing you hear yet.
- SHAPE (osc 2) sine: the purest wave, which gives the cleanest clang. Towards saw or pulse the modulator brings harmonics of its own and the result is harsher and noisier.
- RANGE 8’: the same octave as Oscillator 1.
- TUNE (osc 2) 3.2 (+7.7 semitones): an interval that is not a simple ratio. That gives the most bell-like, out-of-tune overtones. Later, this knob changes which overtones appear, not the pitch you hear.

steps.title: Patch OSC 2 → FREQ MOD
steps.why:
Oscillator 2 now shakes the filter cutoff hundreds of times a second. The ringing filter turns that into overtones that are not in either oscillator, close to the clang of a ring modulator.
- Cable OSC 2 → FREQ MOD: FREQ MOD normally carries the LFO. This cable replaces it with Oscillator 2.
- MOD DEPTH 4: scales what reaches FREQ MOD, so here it is the amount of clang. At 4 the cutoff swings two octaves either side at the speed of a musical note. At 0 you are back to the plain triangle.
- Listen for: no sweep, but a hollow, metallic clang, because the filter is being retuned faster than the ear can follow. Turn osc 2 TUNE slowly to hear the overtones reshuffle while the pitch stays put.

steps.title: Struck, then fading
steps.why:
Envelope 1, which sets loudness, turns the clang into something struck. A long echo carries each hit on.
- Envelope 1 A 0, D 970 ms, S 30%, R 420 ms: an instant hit, a fall of about a second to a low held level, and a long fade after release, like a struck bar.
- DRIVE 2, LEVEL 7: overdrive after the filter, kept light so the clang stays clear. LEVEL is the stage’s output.
- TIME 8.5 (390 ms): a long gap between echoes.
- REPEATS 5, MIX 3: several echoes, fairly quiet against the dry hit.
- Listen for: each note ringing out and dying away, with echoes trailing it. Tap single notes and let them decay.

context.vcf.modDepth: In this sound this is the amount of clang. It scales the FREQ MOD input, which is now Oscillator 2. At zero you are back to a plain triangle.
context.osc2.tune: The interval between the modulator and the note. It changes which overtones appear, not the pitch you hear.
context.osc2.shape: A sine gives the cleanest clang. Towards saw or pulse the modulator has harmonics of its own and the result is harsher and noisier.
context.vcf.reso: The filter has to ring for the effect to be strong. Below about 5 the clang fades to a slight roughness.
context.vcf.freq: Where the ringing peak sits, and so where the added overtones are strongest.
context.osc.mix: Fully left keeps Oscillator 2 out of the sound, so it acts only as a modulator.

tweaks.try: Sweep slowly from 0 to 5 on a held note
tweaks.hear: The overtones slide against the note. At 0 (the same pitch) it is smooth and buzzy; in between it is bell-like and sour.
From a slight metallic edge to a harsh, broken-radio tone.

tweaks.try: Press RANGE on Oscillator 2 until it shows 32’
tweaks.hear: The modulator drops two octaves and the clang turns into a fast, gritty flutter.
The body of the triangle goes and mostly the added overtones are left.

sounds.name: Rising and Falling Swoops
sounds.ref: In the style of Hawkwind — the electronic swoops on "Silver Machine"
sounds.blurb: Press a key and the tone climbs two octaves; let go and it falls back, with echoes trailing behind.
sounds.how: Space-rock swoops are an oscillator swept up and down by hand through an echo unit. This patch makes the key do the sweeping. MIDI GATE is a voltage that is high while a key is down and zero otherwise. The slew limiter slows that sudden on-and-off into a gradual rise and fall, Attenuator 1 sets its size, and the result is added to the pitch of both oscillators. A long release lets you hear the fall after you let go, and the delay repeats everything.

steps.title: A smooth, plain tone
steps.why:
A pure tone makes the pitch movement the whole event. The noise adds the hiss of worn equipment.
- OSC MIX −5: the crossfader, fully left for Oscillator 1 only.
- SHAPE 3.6 (triangle → sine 60%): SHAPE blends between neighbouring waves. Near sine is a clean whistle. Turn it towards saw for a rougher, siren-like swoop.
- RANGE 8’, TUNE 0: the highest octave setting, in tune.
- NOISE 1.5: a little white noise mixed in under the tone.
- Listen for: a plain whistle with a faint hiss behind it.

steps.title: Let the note ring on after the key
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness. The pitch will fall after you let go of the key, so the note has to go on sounding long after release. The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is set just to take the edge off.
- Envelope 1 A 6 ms: a slightly soft start, no click.
- D 150 ms, S 100%: full level while the key is held.
- R 1.9 s: a release of nearly two seconds. Shorten it and the fall is cut off.
- Low-pass, FREQ 7.2 (1.9 kHz), RESO 2.5: a gentle trim of the top with a slight peak.
- ENV DEPTH 0: no filter envelope.
- Listen for: notes that fade slowly after you let go.

steps.title: Patch MIDI GATE → SLEW IN
steps.why:
The slew limiter smooths sudden jumps into slides. Feeding it the key gate turns the on-and-off of each key press into a gradual rise and fall.
- Cable MIDI GATE → SLEW IN: MIDI GATE is high while a key is down and zero otherwise. Nothing is connected to the slew limiter until you patch it.
- SLEW 7.5 (410 ms): how long each rise and each fall takes, about half a second. Lower and the swoop is quicker; higher and it is lazier.
- Listen for: nothing new yet. The SLEW output goes nowhere until the next step.

steps.title: Patch SLEW → ATT1 IN and ATT 1 → OSC 1+2
steps.why:
The slowed gate is scaled and sent to pitch. Now every key press makes the tone climb, and every release makes it fall.
- Cable SLEW → ATT1 IN: replaces Attenuator 1’s usual input (Attenuator 2) with the slewed gate.
- Cable ATT 1 → OSC 1+2: adds Attenuator 1’s output to the pitch of both oscillators.
- 1 (Attenuator 1) at 8: the height of the swoop, about two octaves. At 10 it is more than three.
- Listen for: hold a key and the pitch rises over half a second; let go and it falls back as the release fades. Play short and long notes to hear how far each rise gets.

steps.title: Echo
steps.why:
The analogue delay repeats every swoop. The pitch is always moving, so each echo lands at a different pitch from the one before and they stack into a trail.
- TIME 8 (330 ms): the gap between echoes. Moving it while echoes sound bends their pitch as well.
- REPEATS 7: a lot of feedback, so the trail lasts a long time.
- MIX 4.5: echoes almost as loud as the dry tone.
- DRIVE 2.5, LEVEL 7: light overdrive for some warmth; LEVEL is the stage’s output, which also sets how hard the delay is driven.
- Listen for: a spiral of echoes after each swoop. Turn TIME while it rings to bend them.

context.slew.time: In this sound this is how long each rise and each fall takes.
context.att.1: The height of the swoop. At 8 it is about two octaves; at 10 it is more than three.
context.env1.r: How long the note lasts after you let go. Shorten it and the fall is cut off.
context.osc1.shape: Near sine for a clean whistle. Turn towards saw for a rougher, siren-like swoop.
context.delay.repeats: How long the trail of echoes lasts.
context.delay.time: The gap between echoes. Moving it while echoes sound bends their pitch as well.
context.mix.noise: A little hiss under the tone.

tweaks.hear: Each swoop takes well over a second, and short key presses only get part of the way up.
The swoop shrinks to about two-thirds of an octave: more of a slow bend than a take-off.
The echoes stop dying away and build into a wall of sliding tones. Pull it back before it gets too loud.
The tone never stops, so you hear the whole fall every time and the keys only trigger the swoops.

sounds.name: Feedback Grind Drone
sounds.ref: In the style of Throbbing Gristle and Cabaret Voltaire — abrasive feedback and noise
sounds.blurb: Harsh, grinding drone in which the synth’s own distorted output is fed back into its filter.
sounds.how: Early industrial groups got much of their sound from wiring equipment back into itself. The patch bay allows the same thing. A summer adds two signals: the oscillator mix, and the overdrive’s output brought back through Attenuator 1. The sum goes into VCF IN, so the sound goes round the filter and overdrive again and again. With enough feedback the loop howls at the filter’s cutoff, and the oscillator fights it. The LFO, running at audio rate, shakes the cutoff so the howl turns to a grind. VCA BIAS keeps it sounding with no key held.

steps.title: A very low pulse, always on
steps.why:
A low, rattling pulse is the base of the drone. The VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) is held partly open so it keeps sounding between keys.
- OSC MIX −5: the crossfader, fully left for Oscillator 1 only.
- SHAPE pulse, WIDTH 3 (32% duty): a narrow pulse, thinner and more nasal than a square.
- RANGE 16’, TUNE 0: an octave down. On the low notes it runs at under 30 Hz, heard as a buzzing rattle more than a note.
- VCA BIAS 4.5: holds the amplifier part open whatever the envelope is doing, so the drone never stops.
- Envelope 1 A 270 ms, S 60%, R 1.1 s: the loudness envelope, with D at 360 ms. On top of the bias, each key press becomes a slow swell.
- Listen for: a rattle that sounds with no key held, swelling when you play.

steps.title: Band-pass with resonance, and heavy overdrive
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) and the overdrive are set up before the feedback loop is closed. The filter will choose the pitch of the howl, and the overdrive will stop it growing without limit.
- MODE Band-pass, FREQ 5.4 (about 520 Hz): only a band around 520 Hz gets through. FREQ is the main knob to play by hand later.
- RESO 6: a strong peak. More makes the loop howl more easily and more purely.
- ENV DEPTH 0, KEY TRK Off: the filter stays put.
- DRIVE 6.5: heavy overdrive. It will be inside the loop, so more drive means more gain round it and a more crushed result.
- TONE 4.5, LEVEL 5: a touch dark, with the output pulled back. LEVEL also scales what is fed back.
- Listen for: a thin, nasal, gritty buzz.

steps.title: Patch OSC MIX → SUM 1(A) and SUM 1 → VCF IN
steps.why:
This step only makes room for a second input to the filter, by putting a summer (which adds two signals) in front of it.
- Cable SUM 1 → VCF IN: replaces the filter’s usual input with the summer’s output.
- Cable OSC MIX → SUM 1(A): puts the oscillators into the summer’s first input, so the sound comes through as before.
- Listen for: almost no change. The one difference: NOISE no longer reaches the filter, because noise joins after the OSC MIX jack.

steps.title: Patch OVERDRIVE → ATT1 IN and ATT 1 → SUM 1(B)
steps.why:
The loop is closed. The synth’s own overdriven output goes back into the filter, round and round, until it howls.
- Cable OVERDRIVE → ATT1 IN: replaces Attenuator 1’s usual input with the overdrive output.
- Cable ATT 1 → SUM 1(B): adds it to the oscillators on their way into the filter.
- 1 (Attenuator 1) at 6.5: the feedback amount. Below about 3 it only thickens the tone. From about 3.5 the loop howls by itself near the cutoff, about 500 Hz. At 6.5 the howl is as loud as the pulse wave, which keeps knocking it off balance.
- Listen for: a howl that fights the rattle. Turn ATT 1 slowly up from 0 to hear the point where it takes off, then play FREQ.

steps.title: Shake the cutoff at audio rate
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator) normally makes slow movements, but on the Neutron it runs into the audio range. Here it shakes the cutoff fast enough to turn the howl into a grind.
- RATE 6.8 (about 50 Hz): too fast to hear as a trill. Slow it down and the grind becomes a rhythm.
- SHAPE square: the cutoff, and the howl with it, jumps between two settings.
- MOD DEPTH 2.5: the LFO is still wired to the filter through this knob. At 2.5 the two settings are about two and a half octaves apart.
- Listen for: a rough grind with a low buzz in it that does not follow the keys. Turn RATE down past 5 to hear the jumps separate.

steps.title: Echo and level
steps.why:
The analogue delay gives the grind a metallic ring, and the main level comes down because the patch is loud.
- TIME 3 (66 ms): a very short delay, too close to hear as separate echoes.
- REPEATS 6.5: high feedback, so the short echoes pile up and ring like a metal tank.
- MIX 3: enough to colour it without swamping the dry sound.
- VOLUME 6: the main output, down a little.
- Listen for: a clanging, boxy resonance behind the drone. Turn MIX to 0 to hear it dry.

context.att.1: In this sound this is the feedback amount. Below about 3 it only thickens the tone; above that the loop howls by itself, louder the further you go.
context.vcf.freq: The pitch of the howl. This is the main knob to play by hand.
context.vcf.reso: How easily the loop howls, and how pure the howl is.
context.od.drive: The overdrive is inside the loop. More drive means more gain round the loop and a more crushed result.
context.od.level: Also inside the loop: it scales what is fed back as well as what you hear.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of the audio-rate shake on the filter. Slow it down and the grind becomes a rhythm.
context.vcf.modDepth: How hard the LFO shakes the cutoff.
context.vca.bias: Keeps the amplifier open so the drone sounds with no key held.
context.mix.noise: Has no effect while a cable is in VCF IN, because noise is mixed in after the OSC MIX jack.

tweaks.try: Turn down to 0, then bring it up slowly to 8
tweaks.hear: A plain filtered pulse, then a thickening, then the howl taking over.
The howl follows the knob up and down like a badly behaved microphone.
The shake slows to about 3.5 Hz and the howl trills between its two pitches in a steady rhythm.
More bass gets round the loop and the drone becomes heavier and more blunt.

sounds.name: Sustained Fuzz Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Robert Fripp — sustained fuzz guitar lines with King Crimson and on David Bowie’s "Heroes"
sounds.blurb: Thick, singing lead that swells into each note and holds it for as long as the key is down.
sounds.how: The original is an electric guitar through a fuzz box, played so that notes sustain and bloom instead of dying away. A synth can borrow the shape. Envelope 1 has a slow attack, so there is no pick noise, and full sustain. The overdrive is turned up high, which flattens the wave and gives the fuzz. The filter is set fairly dark and Envelope 2 opens it slowly, so each note gets brighter as it holds. Portamento joins the notes up.

steps.title: Saw with a triangle underneath
steps.why:
Two oscillators give the lead its body. The main one is a slightly softened sawtooth; the second is a triangle underneath.
- OSC MIX −2 (70% / 30%): the crossfader between the two oscillators, a little left of centre, so Oscillator 1 leads.
- SHAPE (osc 1) 2.3 (saw → triangle 30%): SHAPE blends between waves. A saw with some triangle mixed in is a touch less fizzy.
- SHAPE (osc 2) triangle: soft and round, adding weight rather than brightness.
- RANGE 8’ on both: the same octave.
- TUNE (osc 2) +0.1 semitone: a touch sharp, so the two beat slowly against each other.
- Listen for: a full buzz with a slow, gentle movement in it on held notes.

steps.title: Swell in, hold, fade
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness. A slow attack removes the pluck, which is most of what makes a note sound bowed or sustained rather than picked.
- A 6.5 (170 ms): each note swells in over about a sixth of a second. Shorter gets pluckier; longer gets pad-like.
- D 150 ms, S 100%: full level for as long as the key is held.
- R 6.2 (260 ms): notes fade after you let go instead of stopping dead.
- Listen for: no hard front on the notes. Turn A to 0 to hear the pluck come back.

steps.title: A dark filter that opens slowly
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is set fairly dark, and Envelope 2, the filter envelope, opens it slowly, so each held note gets brighter the way a sustained guitar note blooms.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 6.3 (about 1 kHz): the tone at the very start of each note, quite dark.
- RESO 2: a slight peak, no squelch.
- KEY TRK On: high notes stay as bright as low ones.
- ENV DEPTH 2.5: how much brighter a held note gets, about two octaves.
- Envelope 2 A 480 ms, S 100%: a slow rise of about half a second, then it holds fully open (D 150 ms, R 220 ms).
- Listen for: hold a note and hear it brighten. Change Envelope 2’s A to make the bloom quicker or slower.

steps.title: Heavy overdrive
steps.why:
The overdrive is where the fuzz comes from. It sits after the filter and before the amplifier, so the grit stays the same as a note fades.
- DRIVE 8: squashes the wave almost flat, adding the buzz of a fuzz box. It also keeps the level the same from start to end of a note.
- TONE 3.5: left of centre for a rounded, woolly fuzz. Right is thinner and more piercing.
- LEVEL 5.5: the output of the stage, brought down to make up for the extra loudness.
- Listen for: a thick, singing sustain. Sweep TONE to hear it go from woolly to cutting.

steps.title: Slide between notes, add echo
steps.why:
Portamento joins the notes up, and a long, quiet echo adds depth behind the line.
- PORTA TIME 1.5 (220 ms): each note slides into the next over about a fifth of a second. At 0 the pitch jumps.
- TIME 8.8 (430 ms): a long gap, so echoes land clearly after each phrase.
- REPEATS 4.5, MIX 2.5: a few echoes, kept quiet under the dry line.
- Listen for: notes that bend from one to the next, and a soft trail after you stop.

context.env1.a: In this sound the slow attack removes the pluck, which is most of what makes it sound bowed or sustained.
context.od.drive: The fuzz. It also keeps the level the same from the start of a note to its end.
context.od.tone: Left of centre for a rounded, woolly fuzz. Right of centre is thinner and more piercing.
context.vcf.envDepth: How much brighter a held note gets.
context.vcf.freq: The tone at the very start of each note.
context.porta.time: The slide between notes.

tweaks.hear: From a warm, slightly gritty lead to a flat-topped, buzzing fuzz.
The bloom takes more than a second, so only long notes reach full brightness.
The overdrive mixes the two pitches and produces a rough, low growl beneath them, as a fuzz box does with two strings.
Long slides between notes, closer to a slide guitar.

sounds.name: New-Vowel-Each-Note Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Zapp and the wider P-Funk family — talk-box lead lines
sounds.blurb: Nasal, mouth-like lead that seems to say a different vowel on each note.
sounds.how: A talk box sends a synth’s sound up a tube into the player’s mouth, and the mouth shapes it into vowels. A vowel is mostly a matter of where the strongest band of the sound sits. Here a narrow pulse wave goes through a resonant band-pass filter, which gives one strong band. The sample-and-hold is patched to the cutoff and clocked by MIDI GATE, so every new note moves the band to a new random place and holds it there: a new vowel per note. Envelope 2 adds a short upward slide at the start, like a mouth opening.

steps.title: A narrow, buzzy pulse
steps.why:
A thin, buzzy source is the raw material for a voice. A narrow pulse has strong upper harmonics, which is what a mouth-shaped filter needs to work on.
- OSC MIX −3.5 (85% / 15%): the crossfader between the two oscillators, mostly Oscillator 1.
- SHAPE (osc 1) pulse, WIDTH 2.5 (28% duty): SHAPE picks the wave; WIDTH thins the pulse. Narrow has the buzz of a voice; at 5 (a square) it is hollower and less vocal.
- SHAPE (osc 2) saw, RANGE 16’, TUNE 0: a little sawtooth an octave below Oscillator 1’s 8’, for weight.
- Listen for: a reedy, nasal buzz. Sweep WIDTH from 2.5 to 5 to hear it lose its voice-like edge.

steps.title: Resonant band-pass
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is switched to band-pass, which keeps only a band around the cutoff. A vowel is mostly a matter of where that strongest band sits.
- MODE Band-pass: press MODE until the middle lamp lights.
- FREQ 5.8 (about 700 Hz): the centre of the band, and later the middle vowel that the random ones spread around.
- RESO 7: resonance narrows and boosts the band. Higher is more nasal and more like speech; lower is closer to a plain filtered lead.
- KEY TRK Off: the band stays put whatever note you play.
- Listen for: sweep FREQ by hand and hear it move through “oo”, “oh”, “ah” and “ee”.

steps.title: Patch S&H → FREQ MOD
steps.why:
S&H (sample and hold) takes a reading of noise and holds it, giving a random voltage that steps to a new value each tick. Sent to the filter, each step is a new vowel.
- Cable S&H → FREQ MOD: replaces the LFO that normally feeds FREQ MOD with the random steps.
- MOD DEPTH 2.4: how different the vowels are from each other. At 2.4 the band moves up to 1.2 octaves either side of FREQ, roughly 300 Hz to 1.6 kHz.
- RATE (S&H) 6 (4.31 Hz): about four new vowels a second for now, on the S&H’s own clock.
- GLIDE 4 (10 ms): a very short slide from one vowel to the next instead of an instant jump.
- Listen for: the vowel changing by itself, not in time with your playing. The next step fixes that.

steps.title: Patch MIDI GATE → S&H CLOCK
steps.why:
The sample-and-hold now takes its reading when you play, so every note gets its own vowel and keeps it.
- Cable MIDI GATE → S&H CLOCK: MIDI GATE is high while a key is down. It replaces the S&H’s own clock, so the RATE knob stops doing anything, and no knob sets a depth here.
- Listen for: one new vowel as each key goes down, held for the whole note. Notes that overlap do not send a new gate, so play them slightly apart to change the vowel.

steps.title: A mouth-opening slide, some drive
steps.why:
Envelope 2, the filter envelope, gives each note a short upward slide at the front, like a mouth opening. Envelope 1 sets the loudness, and drive and glide finish the line.
- ENV DEPTH 2: lets Envelope 2 push the band up by about an octave and a half at the start of each note, the “y” or “w” before the vowel.
- Envelope 2 A 39 ms, D 220 ms, S 20%, R 63 ms: a quick rise, then a fall back to near the vowel.
- Envelope 1 A 1 ms, S 90%, R 63 ms: a clean start and nearly full level while held.
- DRIVE 4.5, TONE 5, LEVEL 7.5: overdrive thickens the narrow band so it sounds less thin.
- PORTA TIME 0.8 (64 ms): a short pitch slide between notes.
- Listen for: a “wah” shape at the start of each note. Set ENV DEPTH to 0 to hear the vowels arrive flat.

context.vcf.modDepth: In this sound this is how different the vowels are from each other. It scales the FREQ MOD input, which is now the sample-and-hold.
context.vcf.freq: The middle vowel that the random ones spread around.
context.vcf.reso: How narrow the band is. Higher is more nasal and more like speech; lower is closer to a plain filtered lead.
context.sh.glide: A short slide from the last vowel to the new one. At zero the change is instant.
context.sh.rate: Does nothing once MIDI GATE is patched into S&H CLOCK.
context.osc1.width: A narrow pulse has the buzz of a voice. At 5 (a square) the tone is hollower and less vocal.
context.vcf.envDepth: The size of the upward slide at the front of each note.

tweaks.try: Turn down to 0, then up to 4
tweaks.hear: At 0 every note says the same vowel. At 4 the vowels range from a closed "oo" to a thin "ee".
Each note slides slowly from the previous vowel to its own, like "ow" or "ay".
The band narrows until it almost whistles, and the words become more exaggerated.
From a thin, reedy buzz to a hollow square. The vowels are clearest with a narrow pulse.

sounds.name: Heavy Gliding Saw Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Gary Numan and Tubeway Army — "Are ‘Friends’ Electric?"
sounds.blurb: Big, buzzing lead of two sawtooths an octave apart, sliding slowly from note to note.
sounds.how: Numan’s early records lean on a Minimoog playing slow, heavy lines with the oscillators stacked and the glide turned up. The same recipe works here. Two sawtooths an octave apart, the lower one a touch out of tune, give a thick buzz. The filter is left fairly open with only a small envelope, because the weight comes from the oscillators and not from filter movement. PORTA TIME makes every note slide into the next.

steps.title: Two sawtooths an octave apart
steps.why:
The weight of this lead comes from two sawtooths stacked an octave apart and slightly out of tune with each other.
- OSC MIX 0 (50% / 50%): the crossfader between the two oscillators, set to the centre for an equal blend. Towards Oscillator 2 it gets heavier and darker.
- SHAPE saw on both: SHAPE morphs through five waves; the sawtooth is the brightest and buzziest.
- RANGE 8’ and 16’: Oscillator 2 sits an octave below Oscillator 1.
- TUNE (osc 2) +0.1 semitone: a small detune, so the two beat slowly. More detune beats faster and sounds more out of tune.
- Listen for: a slow beating in held notes, which is what makes the tone sound large.

steps.title: Filter mostly open
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is left fairly open, because the weight comes from the oscillators, not from filter movement. Envelope 2, the filter envelope, adds only a little bite.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 6.7 (about 1.3 kHz): overall brightness, high enough for the buzz of the saws to come through.
- RESO 1.5: a small peak, no squelch.
- KEY TRK Off: the cutoff does not follow the keys.
- ENV DEPTH 1.8: Envelope 2 opens the filter a further octave and a half at the start of each note.
- Envelope 2 A 0, D 540 ms, S 50%, R 95 ms: an instant opening that settles halfway.
- Listen for: a slight edge on the front of each note, then a steady buzz.

steps.title: Organ-like loudness
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness, and here it is set like an organ: the note is simply on while the key is down.
- A 1 ms: nearly instant, without a click.
- D 150 ms, S 100%: full level for the whole held note.
- R 80 ms: a short fade after release.
- Listen for: notes that start and stop cleanly and hold at a steady level.

steps.title: Slow glide
steps.why:
Portamento, set with PORTA TIME, makes the pitch slide from each note to the next. In a slow line the slide becomes part of the tune.
- PORTA TIME 2 (400 ms): each move takes about four tenths of a second. At 0 it is a plain, solid synth lead; higher and wide jumps take noticeably longer to arrive.
- Listen for: the pitch swooping between notes, most obvious on large jumps. Play a slow line and try PORTA TIME at 0 to compare.

steps.title: A little drive
steps.why:
The overdrive, which sits after the filter, thickens the two saws and adds some edge.
- DRIVE 4: moderate drive. Higher settings turn the beating between the oscillators into a growl.
- TONE 4.5: a little left of centre, so it does not get thin or fizzy.
- LEVEL 7: the output of the stage, a touch down to allow for the drive.
- Listen for: a fuller, slightly gritty buzz. Push DRIVE to 7 to hear the growl.

context.porta.time: In this sound the slide is a large part of the character. At zero it is a plain, solid synth lead.
context.osc2.tune: The small detune makes the two oscillators beat slowly. More detune beats faster and sounds more out of tune.
context.osc.mix: The balance between the upper and lower octave. Towards Oscillator 2 it gets heavier and darker.
context.vcf.freq: Overall brightness. It is kept fairly high so the buzz of the sawtooths comes through.
context.vcf.envDepth: The slight bite at the start of each note.
context.od.drive: Thickens the tone. Higher settings turn the beating between the oscillators into a growl.

tweaks.hear: From no slide at all to long, lazy swoops of about a second.
The beating speeds up and the lead sounds wider and less stable.
A dark, heavy tone closer to a bass, with the buzz removed.
Only the lower octave is left, and the thickness from the beating disappears.

sounds.name: Scooping Rubber Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Funkadelic — "(Not Just) Knee Deep"
sounds.blurb: Rubbery funk bass in which every note starts flat and bends quickly up to pitch.
sounds.how: P-Funk synth bass lines bend and slide like a rubber band. The Neutron has no knob that sends an envelope to pitch, so the bend is patched. The inverter normally carries Envelope 2 upside down: it drops to its lowest point as the note starts and rises back to zero as Envelope 2 decays. Sent through Attenuator 1 to the pitch of both oscillators, that makes each note begin several semitones flat and scoop up. The same Envelope 2 also snaps the resonant filter open, so the scoop and the "wow" happen together.

steps.title: Pulse and saw, low
steps.why:
Two low oscillators at the same pitch give a thick, buzzy bass tone for the filter and pitch bends to work on.
- OSC MIX −2 (70% / 30%): the crossfader between the two oscillators, a little left, so Oscillator 1 leads.
- SHAPE (osc 1) 1.4 (pulse → saw 40%), WIDTH 4: SHAPE blends neighbouring waves; this is mostly pulse with some saw. WIDTH slightly off square.
- SHAPE (osc 2) saw: adds brightness underneath.
- RANGE 16’ on both: an octave below the default, in bass range.
- TUNE (osc 2) +0.1 semitone: very slightly sharp, for thickness.
- Listen for: a full, buzzy bass with a slight slow movement on held notes.

steps.title: Resonant filter with a quick envelope
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) sits low with resonance, and Envelope 2, the filter envelope, snaps it open on every note. That is the “wow”.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 5 (about 390 Hz): where the filter rests once the envelope has died away.
- RESO 5.5: resonance just above half, which gives the movement its rubbery, vocal quality.
- KEY TRK Off: the cutoff does not follow the keys.
- ENV DEPTH 4: how far Envelope 2 opens the cutoff, about three octaves. It does not change the pitch scoop added later.
- Envelope 2 A 0, D 200 ms, S 0, R 63 ms: an instant opening that falls quickly back.
- Listen for: a quick “wow” at the start of each note.

steps.title: Patch INVERT → ATT1 IN and ATT 1 → OSC 1+2
steps.why:
The Neutron has no knob that sends an envelope to pitch, so the scoop is patched. The inverter carries Envelope 2 upside down: it drops as the note starts and rises back to zero as Envelope 2 decays.
- Cable INVERT → ATT1 IN: replaces Attenuator 1’s usual input (Attenuator 2) with the upside-down envelope.
- Cable ATT 1 → OSC 1+2: adds it to the pitch of both oscillators.
- 1 (Attenuator 1) at 3: how far below pitch each note starts, about five semitones. At 5 it is about an octave.
- Listen for: every note starting flat and bending up to pitch, in step with the filter’s “wow”, because Envelope 2 drives both. Change Envelope 2’s D to lengthen both together.

steps.title: Punchy loudness and a little slide
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness, set tight for a funk line. A touch of portamento lets notes lean into each other.
- A 0: full level at once, for punch.
- D 360 ms, S 70%: a small dip after the hit, then a solid held level.
- R 35 ms: notes stop cleanly, leaving gaps in the groove.
- PORTA TIME 1 (100 ms): a short slide between notes, separate from the scoop.
- Listen for: tight, punchy notes with the scoop on top and a slight slur between them.

steps.title: Drive
steps.why:
The overdrive, after the filter, rounds off the resonant peak and adds weight to the low end.
- DRIVE 4: moderate grit. More gets fuzzier and more compressed.
- TONE 4.5: slightly dark, keeping the bottom full.
- LEVEL 7.5: the output of the stage.
- Listen for: a thicker, rounder bass. Set DRIVE to 0 to hear the thinner, whistlier peak without it.

context.att.1: In this sound this is how far below pitch each note starts. At 3 it is about five semitones; at 5 it is about an octave.
context.env2.d: The length of both the scoop and the filter’s "wow", because Envelope 2 drives both.
context.vcf.envDepth: The size of the filter’s "wow". It does not change the pitch scoop.
context.vcf.reso: The rubbery, vocal quality of the filter movement.
context.vcf.freq: Where the filter rests once the envelope has died away.
context.porta.time: A slide between notes, separate from the scoop.

tweaks.hear: From no bend, through a funky scoop, to a comic octave swoop on every note.
The scoop and the filter sweep both slow down, so each note yawns up to pitch.
Held notes now stay flat and bright, and only reach true pitch after you let go. It shows that the inverter follows Envelope 2 exactly.
A much more pronounced, squelching "wow".

sounds.name: Bubbling Resonance Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Parliament — "Flash Light"
sounds.blurb: Fat funk bass in which each note starts with a resonant "bwip" and settles into a round tone.
sounds.how: Bernie Worrell played the "Flash Light" bass on a Minimoog. This version uses a Neutron trick to get the bubbling front of each note. Normally resonance is fixed by the RESO knob. Here Envelope 2 is patched into the RES jack, so resonance rises sharply at the start of each note and falls away with the envelope. The same envelope opens the cutoff through ENV DEPTH, so the note starts bright and whistling and ends round and plain.

steps.title: A saw with a square an octave below
steps.why:
A sawtooth with a square an octave below gives a fat funk bass: buzz on top and a solid, hollow bottom.
- OSC MIX −1.5 (65% / 35%): the crossfader between the two oscillators, a little left, so the saw leads.
- SHAPE (osc 1) saw, RANGE 16’: bright and buzzy, an octave below the default.
- Osc 2 pulse, WIDTH 5, RANGE 32’: the lowest octave, a hollow square that fills in the sub.
- TUNE (osc 2) 0: in tune with Oscillator 1.
- Listen for: a big, buzzy bass. Turn OSC MIX left and right to hear the balance between the saw and the square.

steps.title: Low filter, modest resonance
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is set to the tone each note settles to: low and round with only a slight edge.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 4.7 (about 300 Hz): the resting tone. Lower is rounder and more of a sub bass.
- RESO 3: resonance, a boost at the cutoff. Keep it at 3.5 or below, because a later cable adds to it and too much tips into a whistle.
- KEY TRK Off: the cutoff does not follow the keys.
- Listen for: a dark, round bass with little movement.

steps.title: Envelope 2 opens the filter
steps.why:
Envelope 2, the filter envelope, gives each note a short, bright front by pushing the cutoff up and letting it fall back.
- ENV DEPTH 4.5: how far the cutoff jumps, more than three octaves.
- Envelope 2 A 0: opens instantly on the beat.
- D 220 ms: the length of the bright front. Longer makes a slower “wow”.
- S 15%: how much extra brightness a held note keeps.
- R 63 ms: a quick close after release.
- Listen for: a bright “wow” at the start of each note, then the tone rounding off.

steps.title: Patch ENV 2 → RES
steps.why:
Resonance is usually fixed by the RESO knob. This cable lets Envelope 2 raise it on each note too, so the front of every note whistles and bubbles before settling.
- Cable ENV 2 → RES: adds Envelope 2 to the RESO setting; it does not replace anything. No knob sets its depth. At the envelope’s peak it is like turning RESO from 3 up to about 8.5, just short of whistling, then it falls back as the envelope decays.
- Listen for: the front of each note changing from a bright “wow” to a sharper, bubbling “bwip”. ENV DEPTH changes the cutoff jump but not this resonance movement.

steps.title: Tight loudness, drive and slide
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness and keeps the notes tight. Drive and a short glide finish the funk feel.
- Envelope 1 A 0, D 360 ms, S 80%, R 35 ms: instant attack, a solid held level and a quick stop, so notes stay separate.
- DRIVE 3.5, TONE 4.5, LEVEL 7.5: overdrive after the filter fattens the low end; TONE slightly dark keeps it round.
- PORTA TIME 0.8 (64 ms): short slides between notes.
- Listen for: punchy notes with clean gaps and a slight slur between them.

context.vcf.reso: In this sound this is the resonance each note settles to. Envelope 2 adds to it, so keep it at 3.5 or below or the peak will tip into a whistle.
context.env2.d: The length of the "bwip": Envelope 2 drives both the cutoff and the resonance.
context.env2.s: How much extra brightness and resonance a held note keeps.
context.vcf.envDepth: How far the cutoff jumps at the start of each note. The resonance movement is not affected by this knob.
context.vcf.freq: The resting tone. Lower is rounder and more of a sub bass.
context.osc.mix: The balance between the sawtooth and the square an octave below.

tweaks.hear: The front of each note now crosses into self-oscillation and you hear a brief falling whistle.
From a tiny click of resonance to a long, vowel-like sweep.
The cutoff stays put and only the resonance moves: a subtle sharpening at the front of each note.
The low end goes and the bubbling front becomes the whole sound, closer to a clavinet.

sounds.name: Sliding Fretless-Style Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Japan — Mick Karn’s fretless bass on "Tin Drum"
sounds.blurb: Soft, round bass that slides between notes and swells slightly after each one starts.
sounds.how: The original is a fretless bass guitar, not a synth: with no frets the player slides freely between notes, and each note has a soft "mwah" as it blooms. Here a tone between triangle and sine supplies the roundness, PORTA TIME gives the slides, and Envelope 2 with a slow attack opens the filter a little after each note starts. The patch cable sets how much the filter follows the keyboard. The KEY TRK button is all or nothing, but ASSIGN carries the keyboard pitch as a voltage, and through FREQ MOD the MOD DEPTH knob can dial in any amount.

steps.title: A round tone with a little edge
steps.why:
A round tone is the base of a fretless-style bass, with a little sawtooth blended in so the filter has something to shape.
- OSC MIX −3 (80% / 20%): the crossfader, mostly Oscillator 1. More to the right adds edge.
- SHAPE (osc 1) 3.3 (triangle → sine 30%): SHAPE blends between waves. Between triangle and sine is soft and round; towards saw it is more like a fretted bass played with a pick.
- SHAPE (osc 2) saw, TUNE 0: a quiet, bright layer at the same pitch.
- RANGE 16’ on both: bass octave.
- Listen for: a soft, round, slightly woody bass tone.

steps.title: Long slides
steps.why:
Portamento makes every note slide from the one before. On a fretless bass that slide is the signature.
- PORTA TIME 2.2 (480 ms): about half a second per slide. Wide jumps become long, audible glides. Try shorter values for faster lines.
- Listen for: the pitch sliding between every pair of notes, most obvious on big intervals.

steps.title: The "mwah"
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) rests fairly low, and Envelope 2, the filter envelope, opens it a moment after each note starts. That delayed bloom is the “mwah”.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 5.9 (about 750 Hz): the cutoff at middle C.
- RESO 3.5: a slightly vocal edge on the swell.
- KEY TRK Off: tracking is set by cable in the next step instead.
- ENV DEPTH 2.2: the size of the bloom.
- Envelope 2 A 63 ms: the brightness arrives just after the note starts.
- D 420 ms, S 30%, R 95 ms: it eases back to a lower level while held.
- Listen for: each note opening up just after it begins. Change Envelope 2’s A to move the “mwah”.

steps.title: Patch ASSIGN → FREQ MOD
steps.why:
KEY TRK is all or nothing. This cable gives a partial amount instead, so high notes do not sound dull without getting as bright as full tracking would make them.
- Cable ASSIGN → FREQ MOD: ASSIGN carries the keyboard pitch as a voltage. It replaces the LFO that normally feeds FREQ MOD.
- MOD DEPTH 1: how closely the cutoff follows the keys. 2 would be exactly octave for octave; 1 is half as much; 0 is none.
- FREQ set higher: the voltage is zero at middle C and negative below it, so in the bass register it pulls the cutoff down. That is why FREQ sits a little higher than you might expect. It follows the slides too.
- Listen for: high notes keeping some brightness. Set MOD DEPTH to 0 and play up the neck to hear them go dull.

steps.title: Soft start, gentle drive
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness, with just enough attack to take the click off. The drive stays gentle to keep it round.
- Envelope 1 A 2.5 (3 ms): a few milliseconds to soften the start.
- D 540 ms, S 70%: a slow dip to a solid held level.
- R 95 ms: a short fade after release.
- DRIVE 2.5, TONE 3.5, LEVEL 8: low overdrive with TONE left of centre adds warmth without edge.
- Listen for: soft, round notes with no click at the start.

context.porta.time: In this sound the slide is what suggests a fretless neck. Try shorter values for faster lines.
context.vcf.modDepth: How closely the cutoff follows the keyboard, because FREQ MOD now carries the keyboard pitch. 0 is none, 1 is half, 2 is full.
context.env2.a: The delay before each note blooms. This is the "mwah".
context.vcf.envDepth: The size of the bloom.
context.vcf.freq: The cutoff at middle C. Bass notes sit below this because the keyboard voltage is negative down there.
context.osc1.shape: Between triangle and sine for roundness. Towards saw is more like a fretted bass played with a pick.
context.osc.mix: How much of Oscillator 2’s sawtooth is blended in for edge.

tweaks.try: Compare 0, 1 and 2 while the riff plays
tweaks.hear: At 0 the low and high notes pass through the same fixed filter, so the high ones are duller. At 2 every note is equally bright.
From quick fingered slides to slow glides that barely arrive before the next note.
The bloom arrives later and more slowly: an exaggerated "mwaaah".
More sawtooth: a brighter, more nasal bass with a stronger filter swell.

sounds.name: Slowly Opening Sequence
sounds.ref: In the style of Tangerine Dream — "Phaedra" and "Rubycon"
sounds.blurb: Steady, echoing bass sequence whose filter opens over a quarter of a minute, then shuts and starts again.
sounds.how: Tangerine Dream’s mid-70s records are built on a Moog modular sequencer looping a short bass pattern while the filter is opened very gradually. The Neutron has no sequencer, so the riff (or your own sequencer) plays the notes. The slow opening is an LFO set to a rising sawtooth at its slowest speeds. The cable matters: the normal LFO connection swings both above and below the FREQ setting, but LFO UNI only goes upwards from zero, so FREQ becomes the closed position and the ramp only ever opens the filter from there. An echo timed to the pattern doubles the notes.

steps.title: Saw and square together
steps.why:
Two oscillators at the same pitch give the thick, slightly hollow tone of a big modular bass.
- OSC MIX −1.5 (65% / 35%): the crossfader between the two oscillators, a little left, so the saw leads.
- SHAPE (osc 1) saw: bright and buzzy.
- SHAPE (osc 2) pulse, WIDTH 5: a square, hollow and woody.
- RANGE 16’ on both: an octave down, in bass range.
- TUNE (osc 2) +0.1 semitone: a touch sharp, so the two beat slowly against each other.
- Listen for: a full bass tone with a slow swirl on held notes.

steps.title: Short notes
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness. With no sustain each sixteenth note becomes a separate thump, which a fast sequence needs.
- A 0: the note hits at once.
- D 150 ms, S 0: it fades to silence over about 150 ms even with the key held.
- R 49 ms: a quick tail after release.
- Listen for: the pattern turning into clear, separate notes. Turn D up and the notes run together.

steps.title: Filter nearly shut, with a small pluck
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) starts nearly shut. Envelope 2, the filter envelope, gives each note a small pluck so the pattern stays audible even at its darkest.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 4.5 (about 270 Hz): the closed position, where each cycle of the sweep will start.
- RESO 4.5: a vocal peak that will travel upwards as the filter opens.
- KEY TRK Off: cutoff fixed.
- ENV DEPTH 2.5: Envelope 2 flicks the filter open a couple of octaves.
- Envelope 2 A 0, D 94 ms, S 0, R 49 ms: an instant, short flick.
- Listen for: muffled notes with a small pluck at the front of each.

steps.title: Patch LFO UNI → FREQ MOD
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator), a slow wave that moves other settings, becomes a very slow ramp that opens the filter over about 16 seconds.
- Cable LFO UNI → FREQ MOD: the normal LFO feed swings above and below FREQ. LFO UNI only goes upwards from zero, so FREQ becomes the closed position and the ramp only opens from there.
- MOD DEPTH 7: the top of the ramp is three and a half octaves above FREQ, about 3 kHz.
- SHAPE (lfo) saw: opens slowly and snaps shut. Reverse saw (4) snaps open and closes slowly; triangle (1) is even.
- RATE (lfo) 1 (0.06 Hz): one cycle every 16 seconds. At 0 about 50 seconds; at 2 about 5.
- KEY SYNC Off: the ramp runs free.
- Listen for: the pattern brightening steadily, the peak rising with it, then snapping shut.

steps.title: Echo in time
steps.why:
The analogue delay doubles the pattern, and a little drive adds weight.
- TIME 8.4 (370 ms): about a dotted eighth at 120 bpm, so each echo lands between the played notes. At another tempo, retune it by ear until the echoes fall between the notes.
- REPEATS 5, MIX 3.5: several echoes at a clear but lower level.
- DRIVE 3.5, TONE 4.5, LEVEL 7.5: moderate overdrive, slightly dark, for body.
- Listen for: the pattern sounding twice as busy. Turn MIX to 0 to hear the plain line.

context.lfo.rate: In this sound this is how long one opening takes: about 16 seconds at 1, about 50 seconds at 0, about 5 seconds at 2.
context.lfo.shape: Saw (2) opens slowly and snaps shut. Reverse saw (4) snaps open and closes slowly. Triangle (1) opens and closes evenly.
context.vcf.modDepth: How far the ramp opens the filter above FREQ.
context.vcf.freq: The closed position, where each cycle starts. With LFO UNI the filter never goes below this.
context.vcf.envDepth: The small pluck on each note, which keeps the pattern audible when the filter is closed.
context.vcf.reso: Adds a vocal peak that travels upwards as the filter opens.
context.delay.time: Set to a dotted eighth at 120 bpm. If you change the tempo, retune this by ear until the echoes fall between the notes.

tweaks.hear: The whole opening takes about three seconds, so you can hear the shape of the ramp quickly.
The filter closes as slowly as it opened, with no snap.
A whistling peak climbs through the pattern as the filter opens.

tweaks.try: Turn down to 0, then back to 3.5
tweaks.hear: Without the echo the pattern is half as busy. The extra notes are all echoes.

sounds.name: Bubbling Pinged Filter
sounds.ref: In the style of Talking Heads — the bubbling synth texture on "Once in a Lifetime"
sounds.blurb: Hold a key for a stream of short, watery "bloops", each at a different random pitch.
sounds.how: This patch has no oscillator in it. A filter with resonance set just below the point of whistling rings briefly when it is hit with a sudden voltage step, like a tapped wine glass. The LFO, set to a reverse sawtooth, is patched into VCF IN, and its sudden upward jump once per cycle is the tap. A copy of the LFO from MULT 1 clocks the sample-and-hold at the same moment, and the sample-and-hold moves the cutoff, so every bloop rings at a new pitch. The keys only open the amplifier and, through KEY TRK, shift the whole stream up or down.

steps.title: A filter on the edge of whistling
steps.why:
This patch has no oscillator in the final sound. The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) itself will make the bloops, by ringing each time it is tapped, so it is set right on the edge of whistling.
- MODE Band-pass, FREQ 6.2 (about 930 Hz): the middle pitch of the bloops.
- RESO 9: how long each bloop will ring. At 8 they are dull taps; from about 9.3 the filter sings without stopping.
- KEY TRK On: lets the keyboard shift the whole stream. An octave up the keys is an octave up in the bloops.
- ENV DEPTH 0: no envelope sweep.
- Envelope 1 S 100%, A 0, D 150 ms, R 95 ms: the loudness envelope holds the amplifier fully open while a key is down.
- Listen for: for now, the sawtooth still, with a strong whistle on top.

steps.title: Patch LFO → VCF IN
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator), normally a slow modulation wave, is fed straight into the filter as its sound source. Its sudden jump once per cycle is the tap that makes the filter ring.
- Cable LFO → VCF IN: replaces the oscillators and noise at the filter’s input, so you no longer hear them. No knob sets its level.
- SHAPE (lfo) reverse saw: jumps up, then ramps slowly down. The ramp is too slow to hear; each jump is one bloop. Square (3) would give two taps per cycle, one up and one down.
- RATE (lfo) 5.2 (about 8 Hz): the number of bloops per second.
- KEY SYNC Off: the stream runs free.
- Listen for: eight identical, watery bloops a second while a key is held.

steps.title: Patch S&H → FREQ MOD
steps.why:
S&H (sample and hold) takes readings of noise and holds each one, giving random steps. Sent to the cutoff, the steps scatter the bloops across different pitches.
- Cable S&H → FREQ MOD: replaces the LFO that normally feeds FREQ MOD with the random steps.
- MOD DEPTH 3: how widely the pitches are scattered, up to an octave and a half either side of FREQ.
- RATE (S&H) 6 (4.31 Hz): for now the S&H runs on its own clock.
- GLIDE 0: each new pitch jumps. Turn it up and each bloop bends from the last pitch to its own, which sounds more like water.
- Listen for: bloops at different pitches, but some change pitch part-way through, because the two clocks do not line up.

steps.title: Patch MULT 1 → S&H CLOCK
steps.why:
The S&H is now clocked by the LFO itself, so it takes a new reading at exactly the moment the filter is tapped.
- Cable MULT 1 → S&H CLOCK: MULT copies whatever is at its input, which is the LFO when nothing is patched there. This replaces the S&H’s own clock, so its RATE knob stops doing anything.
- Listen for: every bloop now having exactly one pitch, with no mid-bloop jumps. Try LFO RATE to speed the stream up or slow it down.

steps.title: Level and echo
steps.why:
The ringing is quiet, so the overdrive stage brings it up. A short echo fills the gaps.
- DRIVE 4, TONE 5, LEVEL 8: overdrive after the filter raises the level of the bloops and firms them up. LEVEL is the stage’s output, which everything passes through.
- TIME 6.2 (190 ms): an analogue delay, short enough that echoes fall between the real bloops.
- REPEATS 4.5, MIX 3: a few echoes, quieter than the dry sound.
- Listen for: extra, softer bloops scattered between the real ones. Turn MIX to 0 to hear the plain stream.

context.lfo.rate: In this sound this is the number of bloops per second, about 8 here.
context.lfo.shape: Reverse saw gives one sharp jump per cycle. Square (3) gives two taps per cycle, one up and one down.
context.vcf.reso: How long each bloop rings. At 8 they are dull taps; from about 9.3 the filter sings without stopping.
context.vcf.freq: The middle pitch of the bloops.
context.vcf.modDepth: How widely the pitches are scattered. It scales the FREQ MOD input, which is now the sample-and-hold.
context.sh.glide: At zero each bloop has a steady pitch. Turn it up and each one bends from the last pitch to its own, which sounds more like water.
context.sh.rate: Does nothing once MULT 1 is patched into S&H CLOCK.
context.vcf.keyTrk: Lets the keyboard shift the whole stream: an octave up the keys is an octave up in the bloops.

tweaks.hear: Each bloop bends into its pitch: a dripping, bubbling sound.
From slow single drips to a fast, chattering burble.
The bloops go from short, dry taps to long, singing pings that overlap.
Each tap gains a low thump beneath the ring, like a tuned drum.

sounds.name: Phased Notch Pad
sounds.ref: In the style of Gong and Steve Hillage — phased, drifting space-rock pads
