sounds.blurb: Bright two-note pad with a hollow gap that drifts slowly up and down through it, like a phaser pedal.
sounds.how: 1970s space rock ran string machines and synths through phaser pedals, which cut moving gaps out of the sound. The Neutron’s MODE button offers low-pass, band-pass and high-pass, but the patch bay can make a fourth type. The VCF 2 jack always carries a different filter type from the main output: with MODE on low-pass, it carries high-pass. Add the two in a summer and you have everything below the cutoff plus everything above it, with a gap at the cutoff itself. That is a notch filter. Send the sum into OD IN and move the cutoff with a slow LFO, and the gap drifts through the pad.

steps.title: Two bright sawtooths, two notes
steps.why:
A notch is easiest to hear on a sound with lots of harmonics, so two bright sawtooths start the pad. PARAPHONIC lets it play two-note chords.
- OSC MIX 0 (50% / 50%): the crossfader between the two oscillators, at the centre for an equal blend.
- SHAPE saw, RANGE 8’ on both: bright, buzzy, same octave.
- TUNE (osc 2) +0.1 semitone: slightly sharp, so held notes beat gently.
- PARAPHONIC On: hold two keys and each oscillator takes one. They still share one filter and one amplifier.
- Listen for: a bright, buzzy two-note chord.

steps.title: Slow loudness
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness. A slow attack and long release let chords fade in and overlap, as a pad should.
- A 7.2 (330 ms): each chord swells in over a third of a second.
- D 360 ms, S 90%: nearly full level while held.
- R 7.5 (750 ms): chords fade out slowly, running into the next one.
- Listen for: soft swells instead of hard starts. Shorten R to hear the chords separate.

steps.title: Low-pass in the middle of the range
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is set to low-pass in the middle of the range. MODE has to be low-pass here, because that makes the second filter output, VCF 2, carry high-pass for the next step.
- MODE Low-pass: on high-pass, VCF 2 would be band-pass and the sum would be something else.
- FREQ 6 (about 800 Hz): later the centre of the gap’s travel.
- RESO 2.5: will set the width of the gap. Low gives a wide, obvious gap; high a narrow one that is harder to hear.
- KEY TRK Off, ENV DEPTH 0: the cutoff stays fixed.
- Listen for: for now, just a dull pad.

steps.title: Patch VCF 1 → SUM 1(A), VCF 2 → SUM 1(B), SUM 1 → OD IN
steps.why:
Adding low-pass and high-pass together gives everything below the cutoff plus everything above it, with a gap at the cutoff itself. That is a notch filter, a type the MODE button does not offer.
- Cable SUM 1 → OD IN: replaces the overdrive’s usual input (the filter’s main output) with summer 1.
- Cables VCF 1 → SUM 1(A), VCF 2 → SUM 1(B): put the low-pass and high-pass outputs into the summer. No knob sets the balance: they are added equally.
- Listen for: the pad suddenly bright again, because the highs are back, but with a hollow gap around 800 Hz.

steps.title: Move the gap with the LFO
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator), a slow wave that moves other settings, carries the gap up and down through the chord, like a phaser pedal.
- MOD DEPTH 3.5: the LFO is still wired to the cutoff through this knob. At 3.5 the gap travels an octave and three-quarters each way.
- RATE (lfo) 2.2 (0.25 Hz): one cycle about every four seconds.
- SHAPE (lfo) triangle: an even sweep up and down.
- KEY SYNC Off: the sweep runs free across chords.
- Listen for: a slow “swoosh” through the held chord. Turn MOD DEPTH to 0 and the gap stops at 800 Hz.

steps.title: Space
steps.why:
Drive stays low so the gap stays clean, and a long echo adds space.
- DRIVE 1.5, TONE 5.5, LEVEL 6.5: nearly clean. Distortion after a notch fills the gap back in. LEVEL sets the volume from the stage.
- TIME 8.5 (390 ms): a long analogue delay.
- REPEATS 5, MIX 3: several echoes, below the dry pad.
- Listen for: the sweeping chord trailing into a wash of echoes. Turn DRIVE up to 6 to hear the notch fade.

context.vcf.mode: In this sound MODE must be on low-pass, so that VCF 2 carries high-pass and the two add up to a notch. On high-pass, VCF 2 is band-pass and the sum is something else.
context.vcf.reso: The width of the gap. Low RESO gives a wide, obvious gap; high RESO gives a narrow one that is harder to hear.
context.vcf.freq: The centre of the gap’s travel.
context.vcf.modDepth: How far the LFO carries the gap up and down.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of the sweep, about four seconds per cycle here.
context.od.drive: Kept low. Distortion after a notch fills the gap back in.
context.osc.para: Lets two held keys sound as two notes, one per oscillator.

tweaks.hear: The gap goes from wide and hollow to a thin slot that is barely audible.
A faster, more obvious phaser sweep, twice a second.
VCF 2 changes to low-pass, so the sum is now a low-pass with a boosted band: a darker pad with a moving peak instead of a moving gap.
The distortion restores the missing harmonics and the phasing mostly disappears.

sounds.name: Flanged Pulse Keys
sounds.ref: In the style of The Cure — the flanged sound of "A Forest" and "Seventeen Seconds"
sounds.blurb: Plain, cold keyboard tone with a metallic sweep moving slowly through it.
sounds.how: On those records the flanging came from effects units, mostly on guitar and bass; this patch gets a similar sweep from the Neutron’s own delay. A flanger is a very short delay, under about 15 ms, mixed equally with the dry sound while its time moves slowly. The TIME knob stops at 25 ms, which is too long. The DELAY TIME jack can push it lower, but only with a voltage that goes downwards. So LFO UNI, which runs from zero upwards, goes through the inverter to become zero downwards, and that sweeps the delay from 25 ms down to about 9 ms and back. High REPEATS make the sweep ring.

steps.title: A thin pulse with a saw
steps.why:
Flanging needs plenty of harmonics to work on, so the tone starts thin and bright: a narrow pulse with a sawtooth at the same pitch.
- OSC MIX −2 (70% / 30%): the crossfader between the two oscillators, a little left.
- SHAPE (osc 1) pulse, WIDTH 3.5 (37% duty): a slightly nasal pulse. Narrower is thinner and brighter, which shows the flanging more.
- SHAPE (osc 2) saw, TUNE +0.1: a sawtooth a touch sharp.
- RANGE 8’ on both: same octave.
- Listen for: a plain, cold, buzzy tone.

steps.title: Simple keyboard shape
steps.why:
Envelope 1 (loudness) and the VCF (voltage-controlled filter, with Envelope 2 as its envelope) are set for simple keyboard playing.
- Envelope 1 A 0.5, D 820 ms, S 50%, R 220 ms: an instant start, a slow fall to half level, a moderate fade on release.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 7.2 (about 1.9 kHz): fairly open. Flanging is clearest on a bright sound.
- RESO 1.5, KEY TRK On: a slight peak, and high notes stay bright.
- ENV DEPTH 1.5, Envelope 2 D 360 ms, S 20%: a slight pluck at the start of each note.
- Listen for: a plain keyboard sound, a little brighter at the front of each note.

steps.title: The shortest delay, at half mix
steps.why:
A flanger is a very short delay mixed equally with the dry sound. Here the analogue delay is set as short as its knob allows.
- TIME 0 (25 ms): the longest the delay will get later; a cable will only shorten it. Keep it near 0: above about 2 the effect turns into a wobbly doubling.
- REPEATS 6.5: feeds the delay back into itself. Low is gentle and hollow; high is metallic and jet-like.
- MIX 5: dry and delayed equal, which gives the deepest effect.
- Listen for: a fixed, slightly metallic colour, like playing in a short pipe.

steps.title: Patch LFO UNI → INVERT IN
steps.why:
25 ms is too long for flanging, and the DELAY TIME jack can only push it lower with a voltage that goes downwards. So the LFO (low-frequency oscillator) is turned upside down first.
- Cable LFO UNI → INVERT IN: LFO UNI runs from zero upwards. This replaces the inverter’s usual input, Envelope 2, so INVERT now runs from zero down to full negative and back.
- RATE (lfo) 2.5 (0.36 Hz): about three seconds per cycle, the speed of the sweep.
- SHAPE (lfo) triangle: an even sweep up and down.
- KEY SYNC Off: runs free.
- Listen for: no change yet, because INVERT is not connected to anything.

steps.title: Patch INVERT → DELAY TIME
steps.why:
The inverted LFO now shortens the delay and lets it lengthen again. The moving, hollow sweep this makes is flanging.
- Cable INVERT → DELAY TIME: adds the inverted LFO to the TIME knob’s setting. No knob sets its depth. At full negative it shortens the delay by one and a half octaves, from 25 ms to about 9 ms.
- Listen for: the metallic colour climbing and falling once every three seconds. Hold a chord and turn REPEATS between 3 and 8 to hear it go from a gentle swirl to a jet-like whoosh.

context.delay.time: In this sound this is the longest the delay gets. The inverted LFO only shortens it from here. Keep it near zero: above about 2 the effect turns into a wobbly doubling.
context.delay.repeats: How strongly the sweep rings. Low is a gentle, hollow movement; high is a metallic, jet-like whoosh.
context.delay.mix: At 5 dry and delayed are equal, which gives the deepest flanging.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of the sweep, about three seconds per cycle here.
context.lfo.shape: Triangle gives an even sweep up and down.
context.osc1.width: A narrower pulse is thinner and brighter, which shows the flanging more.
context.vcf.freq: Overall brightness. Flanging is clearest on a bright sound.

tweaks.hear: From a soft, chorus-like movement to a sharp, ringing sweep.
One sweep takes about nine seconds, so it sounds less like an effect and more like the tone slowly changing.
The delay is now long enough to hear as a separate, slightly out-of-tune copy: doubling instead of flanging.
Only the delayed sound is left. Most of the hollow sweep goes, and what remains is a gentle pitch wobble with a faint ring from REPEATS.

sounds.name: Soft Sustained Electric Keys
sounds.ref: In the style of Radiohead — "Everything in Its Right Place" ("Kid A")
sounds.blurb: Warm, rounded keys with a soft front and a long sustain, playing two-note chords over a quiet echo.
sounds.how: The tone is kept plain on purpose. Oscillator 1 sits between triangle and sine, which is close to the rounded tone of an electric piano, and Oscillator 2 is a slightly brighter blend, a touch sharp. PARAPHONIC gives each of two held keys its own oscillator. A low-pass filter at about 600 Hz keeps it warm, and Envelope 2 opens it by two octaves for the first third of a second, so each chord starts a little brighter and then settles. A small amount of overdrive thickens the tone, and the delay repeats each chord quietly behind the next one.

steps.title: Two rounded oscillators
steps.why:
The tone is kept plain on purpose: two rounded oscillators close to the tone of an electric piano, with just a little edge.
- OSC MIX −1.5 (65% / 35%): the crossfader between the two oscillators, a little left.
- SHAPE (osc 1) 3.4 (triangle → sine 40%): SHAPE blends between waves. Almost no buzz. Towards 2 (saw) is brighter and reedier; towards 4 is pure and organ-like.
- SHAPE (osc 2) 2.7 (saw → triangle 70%): mostly triangle with some saw left in, for a little edge.
- RANGE 8’ both, TUNE osc 1 0, osc 2 +0.1: osc 2 a hair sharp, so the two drift slowly.
- Listen for: a soft, round tone with a gentle slow movement.

steps.title: Switch on PARAPHONIC
steps.why:
PARAPHONIC sits between mono and poly: two notes at once, one per oscillator, sharing one filter and one amplifier.
- PARAPHONIC On: hold two keys and each oscillator takes one. Hold one key and both play it. Both notes get the same envelope, so a second key played while the first is held does not get its own attack.
- Listen for: two-note chords. Oscillator 2’s slightly brighter shape is now the tone of the second note.

steps.title: A warm filter that opens a little on each chord
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) keeps it warm, and Envelope 2, the filter envelope, opens it briefly on each chord, like a key struck a bit harder.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 5.6 (about 600 Hz): the main warmth control, where the filter rests once the front has passed.
- RESO 1.5: a slight peak only.
- KEY TRK On: higher chords do not sound duller than low ones.
- ENV DEPTH 2.5: Envelope 2 opens the filter by two octaves; more makes the front brighter.
- Envelope 2 A 0, D 300 ms, S 20%, R 140 ms: the brighter front lasts about a third of a second.
- Listen for: a slightly brighter start on each chord that settles to a warm tone.

steps.title: Soft front, long sustain
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness: a soft front, then a long, slow fall to a held level.
- A 2.5 (3 ms): just enough to remove the click.
- D 7.5 (1.2 s): the note falls slowly after the start.
- S 5 (50%): a held chord settles at half level. Lower is more like a piano; higher more like an organ.
- R 6.5 (330 ms): chords overlap slightly when you move between them.
- Listen for: chords that bloom and then sink gently while held.

steps.title: A little drive and a quiet echo
steps.why:
A little overdrive thickens the tone, and a quiet analogue delay repeats each chord faintly under the next.
- DRIVE 2.5, TONE 4.5, LEVEL 7.5: thickens without audible distortion; TONE slightly dark keeps it warm.
- TIME 7.6 (290 ms): the gap between echoes.
- REPEATS 4.5: a few echoes.
- MIX 3: the level of the echo, low under the dry keys.
- Listen for: a soft shadow of each chord behind the next one. Turn MIX to 0 to hear the keys dry.

context.osc1.shape: In this sound 3.4 is a blend of triangle and sine. Turn towards 2 (saw) for a brighter, reedier key; towards 4 for a pure, organ-like tone.
context.osc2.shape: A little sawtooth in Oscillator 2 gives the chord some edge. In paraphonic mode this is the tone of the second note.
context.osc.para: Gives each of two held keys its own oscillator. One filter and one amplifier are shared, so both notes get the same envelope.
context.vcf.freq: Where the filter rests once the front of the chord has passed. This is the main warmth control.
context.vcf.envDepth: How much brighter the front of each chord is than the rest of it.
context.env2.d: How long the brighter front lasts.
context.env1.s: The level a held chord settles at. Lower makes it more like a piano; higher more like an organ.
context.delay.mix: The level of the echo under the dry keys.

tweaks.hear: From muffled and distant to clear and slightly reedy.
A harder strike at the front of each chord, closer to a plucked sound.
When one key plays both oscillators, the slow drift becomes an obvious, faster beating.
The echoes last long enough to blur the chords into each other.

sounds.name: Filter Feedback Screech
sounds.ref: In the style of Daft Punk — "Rollin’ & Scratchin’"
sounds.blurb: High, rasping screech from a ringing band-pass filter, made harsher by feeding the distorted sound back to the filter’s own cutoff.
sounds.how: That track is built around a resonant filter pushed until it squeals, then distorted. Here a low sawtooth goes into the band-pass filter with RESO at 9.2, just below the point where the filter whistles on its own (about 9.3). Every cycle of the sawtooth knocks the filter into ringing, so you hear a high ring at the cutoff, broken up at the speed of the low note, and the bass itself is gone. Heavy overdrive turns that into a hard buzz. One cable then sends the overdrive’s output back into FREQ MOD, so the ring bends its own cutoff on every cycle. That distorts the shape of the ring: it gains overtones, gets harsher and drops a little in pitch. Envelope 2 raises the cutoff during each note, so the screech climbs.

steps.title: One low sawtooth
steps.why:
A low sawtooth is the raw material, but you will not hear it as a bass in this patch. Its job is to hit the filter with a sharp edge 30 to 50 times a second.
- OSC MIX −5: the crossfader, fully left for Oscillator 1 only.
- SHAPE saw: SHAPE morphs through five waves; the saw has a sharp edge once per cycle.
- RANGE 16’, TUNE 0: an octave down. The range sets how fast the saw hits the filter, which becomes the speed of the rasp.
- Listen for: a plain, low, buzzy saw.

steps.title: Band-pass, resonance just below whistling
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is set to band-pass with resonance just below the point where it whistles on its own. Every cycle of the saw knocks it into ringing.
- MODE Band-pass: press MODE until the BP lamp lights.
- FREQ 6.2 (about 930 Hz): the pitch of the screech. It does not follow the keyboard.
- RESO 9.2: the filter starts to whistle by itself at about 9.3. Below about 8 the ring dies quickly and you hear more rasp than pitch.
- KEY TRK Off, ENV DEPTH 0: the cutoff stays fixed.
- Listen for: the bass gone, leaving a ring with a rasp at the speed of the low note. Play another key: the rasp changes speed, the ring stays put.

steps.title: Heavy overdrive
steps.why:
Heavy overdrive turns the ring into a hard buzz.
- DRIVE 8: flattens the ring and brings up the rasp between the peaks. It will also be inside the feedback loop next, where more drive makes the screech harsher.
- TONE 6.5: right of centre adds bite.
- LEVEL 5.5: down because heavy drive is loud. The next cable is taken after LEVEL, so this knob will change the feedback amount too.
- Listen for: a hard, rasping buzz. Sweep TONE to hear it go from dull to piercing.

steps.title: Patch OVERDRIVE → FREQ MOD
steps.why:
One cable feeds the sound back to its own cutoff, so the ring bends the filter on every cycle. That distorts the ring: it gains overtones, gets harsher and drops a little in pitch.
- Cable OVERDRIVE → FREQ MOD: replaces the LFO that normally feeds FREQ MOD with the overdrive’s output.
- MOD DEPTH 6: scales whatever arrives at FREQ MOD, so it is now the feedback amount. At 0 the patch is a plain distorted ring.
- Listen for: turn MOD DEPTH up from 0 and hear the ring get brighter and harsher while its pitch sags a little.

steps.title: Make the screech climb
steps.why:
Envelope 2, the filter envelope, raises the cutoff during each note, so the screech climbs. Envelope 1 sets the loudness.
- ENV DEPTH 2: how far the screech climbs, about one and a half octaves.
- Envelope 2 A 7.5 (440 ms): how long the climb takes, just under half a second.
- D 360 ms, S 100%, R 41 ms: it holds at the top while the key is down.
- Envelope 1 A 0, S 100%, R 27 ms: full level while held, a quick stop.
- Listen for: held notes climbing from about 900 Hz towards 2.8 kHz. Short notes only get the start of the climb.

context.vcf.modDepth: In this sound this is the feedback amount: how far the overdrive’s output moves the cutoff. At 0 the patch is a plain distorted ring. Higher settings add overtones and pull the pitch of the ring down.
context.vcf.reso: How long the filter rings after each cycle of the sawtooth. Below about 8 the ring dies away quickly and you hear more rasp than pitch. Above 9.3 the filter whistles continuously and the rasp goes.
context.vcf.freq: The pitch of the screech before the envelope lifts it. It does not follow the keyboard.
context.osc1.range: Sets how fast the sawtooth hits the filter, which is the speed of the rasp.
context.od.drive: The overdrive is inside the feedback loop. More drive makes the signal that bends the cutoff squarer, which makes the screech harsher.
context.od.level: The cable is taken after LEVEL, so this knob changes the feedback amount as well as the volume.
context.vcf.envDepth: How far the screech climbs during a held note.

tweaks.try: Sweep slowly from 0 to 10 on a held note
tweaks.hear: The ring gains overtones and gets steadily harsher and brighter, while its pitch falls by a few semitones.

tweaks.try: Move between 5 and 7.5 while the riff plays
tweaks.hear: The screech moves from a mid-range honk to a thin, piercing squeal.
The filter now whistles by itself, so most of the rasp gives way to a continuous, siren-like squeal.
Every note starts at the top of the shriek instead of climbing to it.

sounds.name: Band-Pass Buzz Bass with Clean Sub
sounds.ref: In the style of Air — "Sexy Boy" ("Moon Safari")
sounds.blurb: Nasal, buzzing, overdriven bass with a clean low note added underneath it.
sounds.how: Air used a Korg MS-20 on "Moon Safari", a semi-modular synth like the Neutron. The MS-20 has a high-pass filter followed by a low-pass filter, and both distort easily, so its basses are often a buzzing band of mid frequencies. The Neutron’s band-pass mode followed by the overdrive gives a similar tone, but band-pass removes the low end. The patch bay puts it back: Oscillator 2 is taken from its own jack, past the filter and the overdrive, and added to the buzz in a summer just before the amplifier.

steps.title: One sawtooth at 16’
steps.why:
One sawtooth goes into the filter. OSC MIX must stay fully left for this whole patch, because Oscillator 2 will be brought in another way.
- OSC MIX −5: the crossfader between the two oscillators, fully left, so only Oscillator 1 reaches the filter. Turn it up and Oscillator 2 would also go through the filter and overdrive.
- SHAPE saw: SHAPE morphs through five waves; the saw is the brightest.
- RANGE 16’, TUNE 0: an octave down, in bass range.
- Listen for: a full, buzzy saw bass.

steps.title: Band-pass with resonance
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) goes to band-pass, which keeps only a band of mid frequencies. That is what makes the tone nasal, standing in for the MS-20’s high-pass and low-pass filters in a row.
- MODE Band-pass: press MODE until the BP lamp lights.
- FREQ 5.6 (about 600 Hz): the centre of the band. Lower is a throatier growl; higher a thin rasp.
- RESO 4.5: narrows and boosts the band, more vocal.
- KEY TRK Off: the band stays put.
- ENV DEPTH 2.5, env 2 D 240 ms, S 30%: with an instant attack, Envelope 2 moves the band up two octaves at the start of each note.
- Listen for: a nasal, quieter tone. The weight of the bass has gone.

steps.title: Overdrive for the buzz
steps.why:
The overdrive, which comes after the filter, turns the nasal band into a hard buzz and brings the level back up.
- DRIVE 7: the amount of buzz. It acts on the filtered saw only; the sub added later skips it.
- TONE 5.5: a little bright, for bite.
- LEVEL 8.5: the stage’s output, up to restore the level lost in the filter.
- Listen for: a hard, buzzing mid-range bass. Lower DRIVE to hear it go back to thin and nasal.

steps.title: Firm note shape with a short slide
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness for a firm bass line, and a short slide joins the notes.
- Envelope 1 A 0, D 360 ms, S 80%, R 35 ms: instant attack, high sustain and a short release, so notes hit and stop cleanly.
- PORTA TIME 1 (100 ms): each note slides into the next over about a tenth of a second. It moves both oscillators, so the sub will slide with the buzz.
- Listen for: tight notes with a quick slur between them.

steps.title: Set Oscillator 2 up as the sub
steps.why:
Oscillator 2 is set up as the clean sub. Nothing changes yet, because OSC MIX is fully left and nothing else carries it to the output.
- SHAPE (osc 2) triangle: round with a little definition. Sine is purer; sawtooth would give a second, unfiltered bass.
- RANGE 16’, TUNE 0: the same octave and pitch as Oscillator 1.

steps.title: Patch the sub round the filter
steps.why:
Four cables take Oscillator 2 round the filter and the overdrive and add it back in just before the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier), so the low end returns under the buzz.
- Cable SUM 1 → VCA IN: replaces the amplifier’s usual input, the overdrive, with summer 1.
- Cable OVERDRIVE → SUM 1(A): puts the buzz back in.
- Cable OSC 2 → ATT1 IN: replaces Attenuator 1’s usual input (Attenuator 2) with Oscillator 2.
- Cable ATT 1 → SUM 1(B): adds it to the buzz.
- 1 (Attenuator 1) at 3.5: the level of the sub. At 0 you hear the thin band-pass buzz alone.
- Listen for: a clean, solid low note under the buzz. Sweep ATT 1 from 0 to hear the weight come back.

context.vcf.mode: Band-pass is what makes the tone nasal. It stands in for the MS-20’s high-pass and low-pass filters in a row.
context.vcf.freq: The centre of the band that gets through. Lower is a throatier growl; higher is a thin rasp.
context.vcf.reso: Narrows and boosts the band, which makes the buzz more vocal.
context.od.drive: The amount of buzz. It acts on the filtered sawtooth only, because the sub joins after it.
context.att.1: In this sound this is the level of the clean sub. At 0 you hear the thin band-pass buzz on its own.
context.osc2.shape: The tone of the sub. Triangle is round with a little definition; sine is purer; sawtooth gives a second, unfiltered bass.
context.osc.mix: Must stay fully left. Turn it up and Oscillator 2 also goes through the filter and the overdrive.
context.porta.time: The slide between notes. It moves both oscillators, so the sub slides with the buzz.

tweaks.hear: From a thin, nasal buzz to a bass with far more low end than buzz.

tweaks.try: Sweep between 5 and 7.5 while the riff plays
tweaks.hear: The buzz changes vowel, from "oh" to "ee", while the sub underneath stays exactly the same.
The sub drops an octave below the buzz. On small speakers it may almost disappear.
A much fuzzier, more broken-up buzz. The sub does not distort, because it never passes through the overdrive.

sounds.name: Staircase Bleep Arpeggio
sounds.ref: In the style of Kraftwerk — the bleeping patterns of "Computer World" ("Home Computer", "Pocket Calculator")
sounds.blurb: Play one key over and over and the bleeps climb a staircase of equal steps, then start again from the bottom.
sounds.how: This builds on the random bleep patch, where the sample-and-hold takes one reading of white noise per note and sends it to pitch. Here the noise is swapped for the LFO, set to a rising ramp that takes one second. Each new note catches the ramp a little higher than the note before, so repeated notes climb in equal steps and drop back when the ramp restarts. Attenuator 1 sets the size of the steps. The pattern is mechanical and repeats, but the LFO is not locked to the tempo, so it shifts very slowly against the beat.

steps.title: A square wave
steps.why:
A square wave gives the hollow, plain tone of early computer sound, a good fit for a mechanical bleep pattern.
- OSC MIX −5: the crossfader between the two oscillators, fully left for Oscillator 1 only.
- SHAPE pulse, WIDTH 5 (50% duty): SHAPE picks the wave; WIDTH at the centre makes the pulse a square. Narrower gets thinner and more nasal.
- RANGE 8’, TUNE 0: the highest octave setting, in tune.
- Listen for: a hollow, woody beep.

steps.title: Short bleeps
steps.why:
Envelope 1 (loudness) makes every note a short bleep, and the VCF (voltage-controlled filter), with Envelope 2 as its envelope, sharpens the front of each one.
- Envelope 1 A 0, D 94 ms, S 0, R 41 ms: no sustain, so each note dies in about 90 ms however long the key is held. D is the length of each bleep.
- Low-pass, FREQ 7 (1.7 kHz), RESO 2.5: fairly open, with a slight peak.
- KEY TRK On: high notes stay as bright as low ones.
- ENV DEPTH 2, Envelope 2 A 0, D 67 ms, S 0: a quick push of brightness at the start.
- Listen for: short, crisp bleeps with clean gaps between them.

steps.title: Patch S&H to pitch, one reading per note
steps.why:
S&H (sample and hold) takes a reading of its input and holds it. Here it takes one reading per key press and sends it to pitch. Three cables set that up.
- Cable S&H → ATT1 IN: replaces Attenuator 1’s usual input (Attenuator 2) with the sample-and-hold.
- Cable ATT 1 → OSC 1+2: adds it to the pitch of both oscillators.
- Cable MIDI GATE → S&H CLOCK: replaces the S&H’s own clock, so its RATE knob no longer matters and one reading is taken each time a key goes down.
- 1 (Attenuator 1) at 5.1: the size of each pitch step. About 4 gives whole tones, 5.1 minor thirds, higher gives wide leaps.
- Listen for: the S&H is still reading noise, so the same key plays a random pitch each time.

steps.title: Patch LFO → S&H IN
steps.why:
The noise the S&H reads is swapped for the LFO (low-frequency oscillator) as a one-second rising ramp. Each new note catches the ramp a little higher, so the random pitches become a staircase.
- Cable LFO → S&H IN: replaces the white noise. No knob sets its level; ATT 1 still sets the step size.
- SHAPE (lfo) saw: climbs then drops. Reverse saw falls, triangle goes up and back, square jumps between two pitches.
- RATE (lfo) 3.4 (1 Hz): at eight notes a second, eight steps per staircase. At ATT 1 5.1 that is three semitones a step, two octaves in all, centred on your key.
- KEY SYNC Off: must stay off, or every note restarts the ramp and every reading is the same.
- Listen for: repeated notes climbing in equal steps and dropping back. The LFO is not locked to the tempo, so the pattern shifts slowly; a rest skips a step.

steps.title: Echo in time
steps.why:
The analogue delay is timed to the pattern, so the echoes fill the gaps between bleeps.
- TIME 8.4 (370 ms): about three sixteenth notes at 120 bpm, so each echo lands between played notes.
- REPEATS 4: a few repeats that die away.
- MIX 2.5: echoes clearly quieter than the dry bleeps.
- Listen for: a busier, interlocking pattern. Turn MIX to 0 to hear only the played staircase.

context.att.1: In this sound this is the size of each pitch step. About 4 gives whole tones, 5.1 gives minor thirds, and higher settings give wide leaps.
context.lfo.rate: The length of the ramp, and so the number of notes per staircase. At 1 Hz with eight notes a second there are eight steps. It is not locked to the tempo, so the pattern shifts slowly.
context.lfo.shape: The outline the notes trace. Sawtooth climbs, reverse sawtooth falls, triangle goes up and back down, and square jumps between two pitches.
context.lfo.keySync: Must stay off. With it on, every note restarts the ramp and every reading is the same.
context.env1.d: The length of each bleep.
context.sh.rate: Does nothing here: the cable into S&H CLOCK has replaced the internal clock.

tweaks.hear: The bleeps climb for half a second and come back down for half a second.
Four steps of six semitones instead of eight steps of three: a faster, more angular pattern.
The steps shrink to whole tones and the staircase covers just over an octave instead of two.

tweaks.try: Lengthen to 5.5 with Envelope 1’s R at 5
tweaks.hear: The bleeps become short notes that overlap the next step, more like a fast melody than a row of blips.

sounds.name: Punchy Bass with an Octave on Top
sounds.ref: In the style of Depeche Mode — "Enjoy the Silence" ("Violator")
sounds.blurb: Round, firm bass with a quick pluck, and a quieter square wave an octave up that keeps it clear on small speakers.
sounds.how: A sawtooth at 16’ is the body of the sound. Oscillator 2 adds a square wave one octave higher at a lower level, which is what lets the line be heard when the low notes themselves are not. The low-pass filter rests at about 290 Hz and Envelope 2 opens it by three octaves for about 130 ms, giving each note a rounded pluck. A little overdrive evens the notes out.

steps.title: A saw with a square an octave above
steps.why:
A low sawtooth is the body, and a quieter square an octave above lets the line be heard on small speakers when the low notes themselves are not.
- OSC MIX −2 (70% / 30%): the crossfader between the two oscillators. Further right is clearer but lighter.
- SHAPE (osc 1) saw, RANGE 16’: the buzzy body, an octave down.
- SHAPE (osc 2) pulse, WIDTH 5, RANGE 8’: a hollow square one octave above. Set both to 16’ for a thicker bass with no upper octave.
- TUNE 0 on both: in tune.
- Listen for: the upper octave adding definition, not weight. Turn OSC MIX fully left to hear the line lose its outline.

steps.title: Low-pass, mostly closed
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) rests mostly closed, so between plucks the note is dull and round.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 4.6 (about 290 Hz): where the filter rests after the pluck. Lower is rounder and deeper.
- RESO 3: a mild peak that will give the pluck a slight “ow”.
- KEY TRK Off: the cutoff does not follow the keys.
- Listen for: a dark, soft bass with little top.

steps.title: A rounded pluck
steps.why:
Envelope 2, the filter envelope, opens the filter on each note and closes it again at once. That is the rounded pluck.
- ENV DEPTH 4: how bright the front of each note is, just over three octaves up.
- Envelope 2 A 0: instant.
- D 130 ms: the length of the pluck. Shorter is a click; longer a “wow”.
- S 15%, R 41 ms: settles low, closes quickly.
- Listen for: each note starting bright and rounding off straight away.

steps.title: Firm loudness
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness: firm and even, so held notes stay solid and short ones stop cleanly.
- A 0: full level at once, for punch.
- D 360 ms, S 70%: a small dip after the hit, then a steady level.
- R 27 ms: a very short release, leaving clean gaps between notes.
- Listen for: a tight, even line. Hold one note long to hear it keep its weight.

steps.title: A little overdrive
steps.why:
The overdrive, which comes after the filter, adds weight and evens the line out.
- DRIVE 3: a little grit. It also makes low and high notes more equal in level.
- TONE 4.2: left of centre, keeping the top rounded.
- LEVEL 7: the stage’s output.
- Listen for: a fuller, more even bass. Set DRIVE to 0 to compare.

context.osc.mix: In this sound this is the balance between the low sawtooth and the square an octave above it. Further right is clearer but lighter.
context.osc2.range: At 8’ Oscillator 2 sits an octave above Oscillator 1. Set both to 16’ for a thicker bass with no upper octave.
context.vcf.freq: Where the filter rests after the pluck. Lower is rounder and deeper.
context.vcf.envDepth: How bright the front of each note is.
context.env2.d: The length of the pluck.
context.od.drive: Weight, and more even levels across the line.

tweaks.hear: From the saw alone, deep and plain, to a bass led by the hollow upper octave.
The pluck turns into a slower "wow" on each note.
A brighter, more forward bass that takes up more room in a mix.
The upper octave becomes thin and nasal and cuts through more.

sounds.name: Bubbling Arpeggio Pluck
sounds.ref: In the style of Duran Duran — "Rio" and "Hungry Like the Wolf"
sounds.blurb: Short, bright, slightly wet-sounding pluck for fast arpeggios, with an echo that fills the gaps.
sounds.how: On "Rio" the pattern came from the arpeggiator of a Roland Jupiter-4; here the riff is written out and the Neutron supplies the tone. A narrow pulse wave goes into a low-pass filter that is nearly closed, with a fair amount of resonance. Envelope 2 opens the filter by more than three octaves and shuts it again in about 60 ms, and with the resonance that fast sweep gives each note its "bloop". A slow LFO, already wired to the filter through MOD DEPTH, makes the run of notes brighter and darker over a few seconds, and a delay timed to the riff adds notes in between the played ones.

steps.title: A narrow pulse
steps.why:
A narrow pulse gives a thin, quick tone that suits fast arpeggios.
- OSC MIX −5: the crossfader between the two oscillators, fully left for Oscillator 1.
- SHAPE pulse, WIDTH 3.5 (37% duty): thinner and more nasal than a square. At 5 (a square) it is rounder and more hollow.
- RANGE 8’, TUNE 0: the highest octave setting, in tune.
- Listen for: a thin, reedy buzz.

steps.title: Short notes
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness. With no sustain every note is a pluck however long the key is held.
- A 0: instant start.
- D 150 ms, S 0: the length of each note, fading to silence.
- R 80 ms: nearly as long as the decay, so very short notes are not cut off.
- Listen for: separate plucks. Hold a key and the note still dies away.

steps.title: Nearly closed filter, fast envelope
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) sits nearly closed with resonance, and Envelope 2, the filter envelope, sweeps it open and shut very fast. That sweep through the resonance is the “bloop”.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 4.8 (about 330 Hz): nearly closed at rest.
- RESO 5.5: lower and the notes become dry ticks; higher and they chirp.
- KEY TRK On: high notes are not duller than low ones.
- ENV DEPTH 4.5: opens the filter over three and a half octaves.
- Envelope 2 A 0, D 57 ms, S 0, R 35 ms: closes in about 60 ms. D is the most sensitive control: a few tenths change the character.
- Listen for: the resonant peak passing down through the harmonics at the front of each note.

steps.title: A slow LFO on the filter
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator), a slow wave that moves other settings, makes the whole run of notes brighter and darker over a few seconds, so it does not sound the same on every pass.
- MOD DEPTH 1.5: the LFO is already connected to the cutoff; this sets how much. At 1.5 it is three-quarters of an octave either way.
- RATE (lfo) 2.4 (0.32 Hz): one cycle about every three seconds.
- SHAPE (lfo) sine: a smooth rise and fall.
- KEY SYNC Off: runs free across notes.
- Listen for: the arpeggio slowly brightening and darkening. Set MOD DEPTH to 0 to hear it static.

steps.title: Delay on three sixteenths
steps.why:
The analogue delay is timed so that echoes fall on sixteenths the riff has already moved on from, making the pattern sound denser than it is played.
- TIME 8.1 (340 ms): about three sixteenth notes at 132 bpm.
- REPEATS 3.5: a few repeats.
- MIX 2.5: echoes below the dry plucks.
- Listen for: extra notes filling the gaps. Turn MIX to 0 to hear only the played line.

context.osc1.width: In this sound a narrow pulse keeps the pluck thin. At 5 (a square) it is rounder and more hollow.
context.vcf.reso: This turns a plain pluck into a "bloop". Lower it and the notes become dry ticks; raise it and they start to chirp.
context.vcf.envDepth: How far the filter opens at the start of each note.
context.env2.d: How fast the filter closes again. This is the most sensitive control here: a few tenths either way changes the character.
context.vcf.modDepth: How much the slow LFO moves the brightness of the whole pattern.
context.env1.d: The length of each note.

tweaks.hear: From a dry click to a slower, more liquid "bwow" on each note.
Each note chirps, and the arpeggio starts to sound like dripping water.

tweaks.try: Sweep between 4 and 6.5 as the riff plays
tweaks.hear: The pattern goes from soft and distant to bright and close.
The gaps open up and you hear how simple the played part is.

sounds.name: Breathy Soft Horn Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Marc Almond and Soft Cell — "Say Hello, Wave Goodbye"
sounds.blurb: Soft, rounded lead like a muted horn, with a faint roughness of breath in the tone.
sounds.how: A horn-like synth tone is a sawtooth through a low-pass filter that opens a moment after the note starts, the way a blown note takes a moment to speak. Envelope 2 has an attack of about 50 ms for that. The breath comes from the patch bay: white noise is patched into FREQ MOD, so the cutoff is jittered very quickly by a small random amount. You do not hear hiss added on top. Instead the note itself gets a slightly rough, airy surface, and only while it sounds.

steps.title: One sawtooth
steps.why:
A sawtooth is the starting point for brass and reed tones because it carries every harmonic.
- OSC MIX −5: the crossfader between the two oscillators, fully left for Oscillator 1 only.
- SHAPE saw: SHAPE morphs through five waves; the saw is the brightest.
- RANGE 8’, TUNE 0: the highest octave setting, in tune.
- Listen for: a bright, buzzy tone. The filter will soften it next.

steps.title: A filter that opens just after the note starts
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) starts dark, and Envelope 2, the filter envelope, opens it a moment after the note starts, the way a blown note takes a moment to speak.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 4.6 (about 290 Hz): the darkest point, heard at the very start and end of each note.
- RESO 1.5: a small peak, no squelch.
- KEY TRK On: high notes do not go dull.
- ENV DEPTH 3.2: opens it by two and a half octaves.
- Envelope 2 A 47 ms: how long the note takes to speak. Shorter is more like a trumpet; longer a soft horn.
- D 540 ms, S 60%, R 95 ms: settles to a held brightness.
- Listen for: a “bw” at the start of each note.

steps.title: Soft loudness and a little glide
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness, set soft, and a glide joins the notes like a player moving between them without tonguing.
- A 3.5 (9 ms): takes the edge off the start.
- D 360 ms, S 85%: nearly full level while held.
- R 95 ms: a short fade.
- PORTA TIME 1.5 (220 ms): each note slides into the next over about a fifth of a second.
- Listen for: a soft start and slurred moves between notes.

steps.title: Patch NOISE → FREQ MOD
steps.why:
White noise is patched to the cutoff, so the filter is jittered very quickly by a small random amount. You do not hear hiss added on top: the note itself gets a rough, airy surface, and only while it sounds.
- Cable NOISE → FREQ MOD: replaces the LFO that normally feeds FREQ MOD with white noise.
- MOD DEPTH 2.2: the amount of breath. At 2.2 the cutoff moves up to 1.1 octaves either way, thousands of times a second. Above about 5 the note turns hoarse.
- The NOISE knob is not used: it adds noise to the sound itself, while the cable only uses it to move the filter.
- Listen for: a fine roughness on long notes. Turn MOD DEPTH to 0 and back to compare.

steps.title: A quiet echo
steps.why:
A quiet analogue delay gives the lead some room.
- TIME 8 (330 ms): a clear gap before each echo.
- REPEATS 3.5: a few repeats.
- MIX 2: low in the mix, so it sits behind the dry line.
- Listen for: a faint echo after each phrase, most obvious when you stop.

context.vcf.modDepth: In this sound this is the amount of breath: how far the noise jitters the cutoff. Above about 5 the note turns hoarse.
context.env2.a: How long the note takes to "speak". Shorter is more like a trumpet; longer is more like a soft horn or a bowed note.
context.vcf.envDepth: How much the filter opens as the note speaks.
context.env2.s: The brightness the note holds at while the key is down.
context.vcf.freq: The darkest point of the tone, heard at the very start and end of each note.
context.porta.time: The slide between notes.
context.mix.noise: Not used here. This knob adds noise to the sound itself; the cable uses the noise only to move the filter.

tweaks.hear: From a clean, smooth horn to a hoarse, rasping one.
A quick, brassy "ba" at one end and a slow swell into each note at the other.
Actual hiss joins the note, like air escaping round a mouthpiece. Compare it with the roughness the cable gives, which is part of the note instead of a layer on top.
A hollower, more clarinet-like tone.

sounds.name: Deep Rounded Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Pet Shop Boys — "West End Girls"
sounds.blurb: Deep, smooth bass with a soft front and a slight slide between notes.
sounds.how: The depth comes from keeping the top off. Oscillator 1 is set halfway between sawtooth and triangle, which already has less buzz than a saw, and Oscillator 2 adds a sine at the same pitch for a solid fundamental. The low-pass filter rests at about 215 Hz and Envelope 2 opens it gently, so each note has a soft "doo" and no click. A short portamento joins the notes up.

steps.title: A soft saw with a sine beside it
steps.why:
The depth comes from keeping the top off. Both oscillators are already soft before the filter does anything.
- OSC MIX −1 (60% / 40%): the crossfader between the two oscillators, a little left. Further right is deeper and plainer.
- SHAPE (osc 1) 2.5 (saw → triangle 50%): SHAPE blends between waves; halfway is a saw with the edge taken off. Towards 2 buzzier, towards 3 softer.
- SHAPE (osc 2) sine: no harmonics at all, a solid fundamental.
- RANGE 16’ on both, TUNE 0: bass octave, in tune.
- Listen for: a bass that is already rounded.

steps.title: Low-pass, well closed
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is set well closed, so only the bottom few harmonics of each note get through.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 4.2 (about 215 Hz): the main depth control. Lower and the bass is felt more than heard.
- RESO 1: almost no peak, keeping it smooth.
- KEY TRK Off: the cutoff does not follow the keys.
- Listen for: a deep, dark tone with nothing sharp on top.

steps.title: A gentle opening on each note
steps.why:
Envelope 2, the filter envelope, opens the filter gently on each note. This is a soft “doo”, not a pluck.
- ENV DEPTH 2.5: how much each note opens at the front, two octaves.
- Envelope 2 A 0, D 240 ms: opens at once and settles over about a quarter of a second.
- S 20%, R 63 ms: a little extra brightness held, closing quickly after release.
- Listen for: a slight “doo” at the start of each note. Raise ENV DEPTH and it turns into a pluck.

steps.title: Soft front, held level
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness: a soft front and a solid held level.
- A 2 (2 ms): just long enough to remove the click a low sine would otherwise make. Longer makes the bass late and soft.
- D 540 ms, S 80%: long notes stay solid.
- R 63 ms: a short tail.
- Listen for: no click at the start, and held notes keeping their weight.

steps.title: A short slide
steps.why:
A short portamento joins the notes up.
- PORTA TIME 0.8 (64 ms): a slide of about 60 ms. Too short to hear as a swoop, long enough to make the line smooth. Higher and it becomes an obvious glide.
- Listen for: a smoother line, most noticeable on wide jumps. Set PORTA TIME to 0 to compare.

context.osc1.shape: In this sound the halfway position gives a saw with the edge taken off. Towards 2 it gets buzzier; towards 3 it gets softer still.
context.osc.mix: The balance between the soft saw and the pure sine. Further right is deeper and plainer.
context.vcf.freq: The main depth control. Lower and the bass is felt more than heard.
context.vcf.envDepth: How much each note opens at the front.
context.env1.a: Just long enough to avoid a click. Longer makes the bass late and soft.
context.porta.time: The slide between notes.

tweaks.hear: From a sub bass you mostly feel to a rounder bass with a clear pitch.
Only the sine is left: very deep and very plain, and hard to hear on small speakers.
Each note swoops into the next, a rubbery effect.
The overdrive adds harmonics back on top, so the line is easier to follow on small speakers.

sounds.name: Tight Sequenced Bass with a Click
sounds.ref: In the style of Vince Clarke — the sequenced bass lines on Yazoo’s "Upstairs at Eric’s" and early Erasure
sounds.blurb: Short, dry, exact bass note with a hard click at the front, made for fast sequenced lines.
sounds.how: Everything here is about the first 30 ms. One square wave goes into a low-pass filter that rests almost shut. Envelope 2 throws it open by more than five octaves and closes it again in about 35 ms, which is too fast to hear as a sweep: you hear a click. After the click the note is a dull, short thump, because Envelope 1 also has a fast decay and a low sustain. Because both envelopes restart identically on every note, a sequenced line sounds perfectly even.

steps.title: One square wave
steps.why:
One square wave gives a hollow, firm base for a tight sequenced bass.
- OSC MIX −5: the crossfader between the two oscillators, fully left for Oscillator 1 only.
- SHAPE pulse, WIDTH 5 (50% duty): a square. Narrower is thinner and buzzier.
- RANGE 16’, TUNE 0: an octave down, in tune.
- Listen for: a hollow, woody bass tone.

steps.title: Filter almost shut, some resonance
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) rests almost shut, so after the click the note is a dull thump.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 4 (about 190 Hz): the tone of the note after the click.
- RESO 4: will give the click a pitch of its own. Higher turns “tk” into “tyew”.
- KEY TRK Off: the cutoff does not follow the keys.
- Listen for: a muffled, round thump.

steps.title: A 35 ms filter envelope
steps.why:
Envelope 2, the filter envelope, throws the filter wide open and shuts it in about 35 ms. That is too fast to hear as a sweep: you hear a click.
- ENV DEPTH 6.5: the size of the click, just over five octaves, enough to open the filter completely for an instant.
- Envelope 2 A 0: instant.
- D 3.2 (35 ms): the length of the click. By 4.5 it becomes a pluck you can hear closing.
- S 0, R 21 ms: nothing held.
- Listen for: the hard “tk” at the front of each note. Sweep Envelope 2’s D to hear it turn into a pluck.

steps.title: Short, dry loudness
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness: short and dry, so a sequenced line sounds perfectly even.
- A 0: instant.
- D 180 ms, S 30%: a quick fall to a low level.
- R 3 (18 ms): very short, so each note stops dead when the key does. Separate notes are what make a line sound sequenced.
- Listen for: tight, even notes with clean gaps.

steps.title: A touch of drive
steps.why:
A touch of overdrive, after the filter, brings up the body of the note after the click, so the two are closer in level.
- DRIVE 3.5: moderate grit and weight.
- TONE 5: neutral.
- LEVEL 7: the stage’s output.
- Listen for: a slightly fatter thump behind the click. Set DRIVE to 0 to hear the body drop back.

context.env2.d: In this sound this is the length of the click. At 3.2 it is about 35 ms. By 4.5 it has become a pluck you can hear closing.
context.vcf.envDepth: The size of the click. At 6.5 the filter opens all the way for an instant.
context.vcf.freq: The tone of the note after the click.
context.vcf.reso: Gives the click a pitch. Higher settings turn "tk" into "tyew".
context.env1.r: Kept very short so notes are separate, which is what makes a line sound sequenced.
context.osc1.width: A square. Narrower is thinner and buzzier.

tweaks.hear: From a tiny tick, through a hard click, to a rounded pluck.

tweaks.try: Open slowly from 4 to 6.5 while the riff plays
tweaks.hear: The body of each note brightens until the click is no longer separate from it.
A buzzier, fuller bass with the same click.
Every note becomes a very short blip, whatever its written length.

sounds.name: Slow Tones with Drifting Brightness
sounds.ref: In the style of Brian Eno — "Discreet Music" and "Music for Airports"
sounds.blurb: Soft, slow notes that fade in and out over long echoes, while the brightness wanders without ever repeating.
sounds.how: "Discreet Music" was made by feeding a synthesiser into a long tape delay, and "Music for Airports" from tape loops of different lengths that never line up the same way twice. This patch borrows both ideas on a small scale. Two near-sine oscillators with slow envelopes play into the delay at its longest time with high REPEATS. The brightness is moved by two unrelated sources added in a summer: a sine LFO that takes eight seconds, and the sample-and-hold, which picks a new random value about every two seconds and slides to it. Their sum does not repeat.

steps.title: Two soft oscillators, two notes
steps.why:
Two soft oscillators start the sound with very little brightness, so the slow filter movement later has room to be heard. PARAPHONIC lets notes overlap.
- OSC MIX 0 (50% / 50%): the crossfader between the two oscillators, at the centre for an equal blend.
- SHAPE 3.3 and 3.6: SHAPE blends between waves. Both sit between triangle and sine, soft and round, with Oscillator 2 a little purer.
- RANGE 8’, TUNE 0 on both: same octave, in tune.
- PARAPHONIC On: a second key can sound while the first is still held, each on its own oscillator.
- Listen for: a soft, flute-like tone with almost no edge.

steps.title: Slow in, slower out
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness: slow in and slower out. The VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) is also held very slightly open.
- A 7.6 (480 ms): each note fades in over about half a second.
- D 820 ms, S 80%: a gentle settle to a high held level.
- R 8.6 (1.9 s): nearly two seconds to fade after release.
- VCA BIAS 0.5: holds the amplifier open a little, so a trace of sound keeps feeding the delay between notes.
- Listen for: notes that swell in and fade out slowly, overlapping one another.

steps.title: A half-closed filter
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is set half-closed and still. The next step sets it wandering.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 5.4 (about 520 Hz): a dull, soft tone.
- RESO 1.5: a slight peak only.
- KEY TRK On: the cutoff follows the keys, so high notes are not duller.
- ENV DEPTH 0: no envelope movement.
- Listen for: a dull, fixed tone.

steps.title: Patch LFO → SUM 1(A), S&H → SUM 1(B), SUM 1 → FREQ MOD
steps.why:
Two unrelated sources move the brightness, added together in a summer: the LFO (low-frequency oscillator), a regular slow wave, and S&H (sample and hold), which picks random values. Their sum never repeats.
- Cables LFO, S&H → SUM 1 → FREQ MOD: the LFO goes into SUM 1(A) and the S&H into SUM 1(B), and the sum replaces the LFO that normally feeds FREQ MOD. No knob sets the balance.
- MOD DEPTH 2.5: scales the sum. Each source can move the cutoff up to an octave and a quarter.
- RATE (lfo) 1.6, SHAPE sine, KEY SYNC Off: one smooth cycle every eight seconds.
- RATE (S&H) 1.5: a new random target about every two seconds.
- GLIDE 10 (1 s): slides to each target. Lower it and the brightness jumps in steps.
- Listen for: a held note opening and closing slowly with no fixed pattern.

steps.title: The longest delay, high repeats
steps.why:
The analogue delay at its longest, with high repeats, lets new notes sound over the fading remains of the old ones.
- TIME 10 (640 ms): the longest the Neutron’s delay goes.
- REPEATS 7.5: each note keeps coming back for several seconds, each repeat a little duller. Above about 9 the echoes stop dying away.
- MIX 4.5: echoes nearly as loud as the dry notes.
- Listen for: a slow wash of overlapping echoes. Play sparse notes and leave space.

context.vcf.modDepth: In this sound this scales the sum of the LFO and the S&H, so it sets how far the brightness wanders. At 2.5 each of them can move the cutoff by up to an octave and a quarter.
context.lfo.rate: The slow, regular part of the movement: one cycle every eight seconds here.
context.sh.rate: How often the random part picks a new target.
context.sh.glide: At maximum the random part slides over about a second. Lower it and the brightness starts to jump in steps.
context.vca.bias: Holds the amplifier slightly open so the delay is always being fed a trace of sound.
context.delay.repeats: How long each note lingers. Above about 9 the echoes stop dying away.
context.env1.a: How slowly each note fades in.
context.env1.r: How slowly it fades out after the key is released.

tweaks.hear: Notes hang on for much longer and start to pile up into a slowly changing chord.
The tone swings from almost inaudible to quite bright.
The random part now jumps, and you hear sudden changes of brightness in the echoes.
The last note never stops: a drone that the delay smears into a bed.

sounds.name: Two-Note Brass Stab
sounds.ref: In the style of Prince — "1999" and the Minneapolis synth-brass sound
sounds.blurb: Bright, punchy synth-brass stab for two-note chords, with a brief smear of detune at the front of each hit.
sounds.how: In early-80s Minneapolis funk, polyphonic synths (Prince’s were Oberheims) played the parts a horn section would have. The brass tone is two sawtooths and a low-pass filter that Envelope 2 opens over about 30 ms and then closes, which gives the "bap". PARAPHONIC gives two-note chords. A real section never hits a note exactly together, so the patch bay adds a smear: Envelope 2 also goes through Attenuator 1 to Oscillator 2’s pitch, pushing it slightly sharp at the peak of each hit and letting it fall back into tune.

steps.title: Two sawtooths, two notes
steps.why:
Two sawtooths give the bright, buzzy raw material of synth brass, and PARAPHONIC lets it play two-note chords.
- OSC MIX 0 (50% / 50%): the crossfader between the two oscillators, at the centre.
- SHAPE saw, RANGE 8’ on both: bright, same octave.
- TUNE (osc 2) +0.1 semitone: a small fixed detune that stays after the smear added later has gone.
- PARAPHONIC On: two held keys get one oscillator each, sharing one filter and one amplifier.
- Listen for: a bright, buzzy two-note chord.

steps.title: The brass filter shape
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) and Envelope 2, the filter envelope, make the brass shape. The short attack on the filter is what separates brass from a pluck.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 5 (about 390 Hz): dark at rest.
- RESO 1.5, KEY TRK On: a slight peak; high chords stay bright.
- ENV DEPTH 4.5: how bright the peak of each stab is, more than three and a half octaves up.
- Envelope 2 A 4.8 (32 ms): the brightness arrives just after the note starts. At 0 it becomes a pluck; above about 6 a swell.
- D 360 ms, S 0, R 63 ms: closes over about a third of a second.
- Listen for: “bap”, not “tik”.

steps.title: Punchy loudness
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness: tight stabs, with held chords settling to a moderate level.
- A 2 (2 ms): a very short attack, enough to avoid a click.
- D 420 ms, S 60%: after the hit, the level drops back.
- R 49 ms: a short release, so stabs stop cleanly.
- Listen for: punchy, short stabs. Hold a chord to hear it settle down.

steps.title: Patch ENV 2 → ATT1 IN, ATT 1 → OSC 2
steps.why:
A real horn section never hits exactly together. This patch pushes Oscillator 2 slightly sharp at the peak of each hit and lets it fall back into tune.
- Cable ENV 2 → ATT1 IN: replaces Attenuator 1’s usual input (Attenuator 2) with Envelope 2.
- Cable ATT 1 → OSC 2: adds it to Oscillator 2’s pitch only.
- 1 (Attenuator 1) at 1.2: the size of the smear, about a semitone at the peak. At 0 there is none. Envelope 2’s D also sets how long the return to tune takes.
- Listen for: on one key, the two oscillators beat quickly for a moment and settle. On two keys, one note of the chord arrives slightly sharp, like a player overshooting.

steps.title: Some drive
steps.why:
The overdrive, after the filter, adds bite to the front of each stab.
- DRIVE 3.5: two notes through one overdrive produce extra tones between them, so the chord rubs a little. That is part of the rough edge.
- TONE 5.5: slightly bright.
- LEVEL 7: the stage’s output.
- Listen for: a grittier, more aggressive stab. Set DRIVE to 0 for a cleaner, politer sound.

context.env2.a: In this sound this short attack is the brass character. At 0 the stab becomes a pluck; above about 6 it becomes a swell.
context.env2.d: How long the brightness lasts. It also sets how long Oscillator 2 takes to come back into tune.
context.vcf.envDepth: How bright the peak of each stab is.
context.att.1: The size of the pitch smear on Oscillator 2. At 1.2 it is about a semitone at the peak. At 0 there is none.
context.osc2.tune: A small fixed detune that stays after the smear has gone.
context.osc.para: Gives each of two held keys its own oscillator. With PARAPHONIC on, the smear only affects the note Oscillator 2 is playing.
context.od.drive: Two notes through one overdrive produce extra tones between them, which is part of the rough edge.

tweaks.hear: From a clean, exact stab to a loose, sour blare at the front of each hit.
A hard pluck, then brass, then a slow "wah" into each chord.
Held chords stay bright, but Oscillator 2 now also stays about half a semitone sharp, because the same envelope drives its pitch.
A darker, more distant section.

sounds.name: Pulse Lead with Envelope-Swept Width
sounds.ref: In the style of Howard Jones — "What Is Love?" and "New Song"
sounds.blurb: Bright, bouncy pulse lead whose tone goes from hollow to thin inside every note.
sounds.how: A pulse wave’s tone depends on its width: near 50% it is hollow and full, and as it narrows it gets thin and nasal. Normally the LFO moves the width, through Attenuator 2. Here one cable replaces that with Envelope 2 on Oscillator 1, so the width is swept once per note. WIDTH is set narrow, the envelope widens it at the start, and as the envelope falls the pulse narrows again. The filter stays nearly still, so the change you hear is the oscillator’s own. Oscillator 2 adds a quiet square an octave below for body.

steps.title: A narrow pulse over a quiet square
steps.why:
A pulse wave’s tone depends on its width: near 50% it is hollow and full, narrower is thin and nasal. Oscillator 1 starts narrow; Oscillator 2 adds a square underneath for body.
- OSC MIX −2.5 (75% / 25%): the crossfader, keeping Oscillator 2 at about a quarter.
- SHAPE (osc 1) pulse, WIDTH 1.2 (16% duty): thin and nasal. Later this is the width each note ends up at.
- SHAPE (osc 2) pulse, WIDTH 5, RANGE 16’: a square an octave below. Its width will not move.
- RANGE (osc 1) 8’, TUNE 0 on both: in tune.
- Listen for: a thin, reedy tone with some weight under it.

steps.title: A springy note shape
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness: a springy shape where short notes bounce and held notes drop back a little.
- A 0: instant start.
- D 360 ms, S 65%: falls to about two-thirds level.
- R 80 ms: a short release.
- Listen for: bouncy short notes and a slight dip on held ones.

steps.title: Patch ENV 2 → PW 1
steps.why:
Normally the LFO moves the pulse width, through Attenuator 2. Here Envelope 2 takes its place on Oscillator 1, so the width is swept once per note.
- Cable ENV 2 → PW 1: replaces Attenuator 2 at Oscillator 1’s pulse-width input. No knob sets its depth: a full envelope widens the pulse by 45% of the cycle. ATT 2 still feeds Oscillator 2.
- Envelope 2 A 0, D 420 ms: each note starts at about 61% duty, close to a square, and narrows over about 400 ms. D sets how long hollow takes to turn thin.
- S 20%, R 63 ms: held notes rest at about 25%, 9% wider than WIDTH.
- Listen for: the tone going from hollow to thin inside each note, although the filter is not moving.

steps.title: Open filter
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) stays fairly open and nearly still, so the change you hear is the oscillator’s own.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 7.4 (about 2.2 kHz): bright.
- RESO 1.5: a slight peak only.
- KEY TRK On: high notes stay bright.
- ENV DEPTH 1: less than an octave of extra brightness at the front. Kept low on purpose, so the pulse width does the work.
- Listen for: a brighter version of the same moving tone.

steps.title: Eighth-note echo and a little drive
steps.why:
An echo in time makes the riff bounce, and a little drive adds edge.
- TIME 7.1 (250 ms): about one eighth note at 120 bpm.
- REPEATS 3, MIX 2: one or two quiet echoes.
- DRIVE 2.5, TONE 5.5, LEVEL 7.5: light overdrive after the filter, slightly bright.
- Listen for: each note answered by a softer copy an eighth later. Turn MIX to 0 to hear the riff dry.

context.osc1.width: In this sound this is the width the pulse ends up at once the envelope has fallen. The envelope only ever widens it from here.
context.env2.d: How long the tone takes to go from hollow to thin.
context.env2.s: Where the width rests while a key is held. At 2 it is 9% wider than the WIDTH knob’s setting.
context.att.2: No longer reaches Oscillator 1’s pulse width, because the cable has replaced it there. It still feeds Oscillator 2’s.
context.vcf.envDepth: Kept low on purpose, so the pulse width does the work.
context.osc.mix: How much of the lower square is mixed in. Its width does not move.

tweaks.hear: A quick "pyow" at the front of each note at one end, a slow change across the whole note at the other.
The sweep now runs the other way round: each note starts thin, because the envelope pushes the pulse past square to 95%, and fills out as it falls back towards 50%.
Held notes stay wide and hollow instead of thinning out.

tweaks.try: Raise to 6 with the LFO RATE at 4
tweaks.hear: Only the lower square shimmers, because the LFO now reaches Oscillator 2’s width alone.

sounds.name: Two-Speed PWM String Line
sounds.ref: In the style of Gary Numan — "Cars"
sounds.blurb: Thin, bright, slightly cold string line, thickened by two pulse waves whose widths move at different speeds.
sounds.how: On the record the high string line was a Polymoog, a fully polyphonic keyboard. One voice can suggest that ensemble sound with pulse-width modulation: a pulse whose width keeps moving sounds like two detuned oscillators. This patch does it twice, at two speeds. Attenuator 2 already carries the LFO to both PW inputs. A cable from the sample-and-hold into PW 2 replaces the LFO on Oscillator 2 only, so Oscillator 1 moves in a regular cycle and Oscillator 2 wanders at random. The two never move together, which is what stops it sounding like one oscillator with an effect on it.

steps.title: Two square waves
steps.why:
Two static square waves are the starting point. On their own they sound hollow and plain; the next two steps set their widths moving.
- OSC MIX 0 (50% / 50%): the crossfader between the two oscillators, at the centre.
- SHAPE pulse, WIDTH 5 on both: squares. WIDTH on osc 2 is also the centre its later random movement wanders around.
- RANGE 8’ on both: same octave.
- TUNE (osc 2) +0.1 semitone: a small fixed detune.
- Listen for: a hollow, reedy, slightly beating tone.

steps.title: Turn up ATT 2 for pulse-width modulation
steps.why:
PWM (pulse-width modulation) means moving the pulse width with the LFO (low-frequency oscillator). The Neutron has no knob marked PWM: Attenuator 2 is that knob, already wired to both oscillators’ widths.
- 2 (Attenuator 2) at 5: the PWM depth. Each pulse swings between about 36% and 64% duty.
- RATE (lfo) 3.9 (1.78 Hz): the speed of the movement.
- SHAPE (lfo) triangle: an even back-and-forth.
- KEY SYNC Off: runs free.
- Listen for: the hollow tone turning into a moving, chorus-like one. Turn ATT 2 to 0 and back to compare.

steps.title: Patch S&H → PW 2
steps.why:
S&H (sample and hold) takes random readings of noise. Patched to Oscillator 2’s width, it makes that oscillator wander at random while Oscillator 1 keeps its regular cycle. The two never move together.
- Cable S&H → PW 2: replaces Attenuator 2 at Oscillator 2’s pulse-width input. No knob sets its depth. ATT 2 is now depth for Oscillator 1 only.
- RATE (S&H) 4.5 (2.14 Hz): a new random target about twice a second.
- GLIDE 8 (220 ms): smooths the steps into slides, which also keeps the width away from its extremes most of the time. At 0 the width jumps with a small click-like change.
- Listen for: the movement becoming less regular and thicker.

steps.title: A bowed note shape and a bright, thin filter
steps.why:
Envelope 1 (loudness) gives a bowed shape, and the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) and overdrive tone keep it bright and thin, as a string machine has very little bass.
- Envelope 1 A 120 ms, S 90%, R 330 ms: a soft swell in (D 360 ms), a third of a second to fade.
- Low-pass, FREQ 7.6 (2.6 kHz), RESO 1: well open.
- KEY TRK On, ENV DEPTH 0: steady brightness across the keyboard.
- DRIVE 1.5, LEVEL 8: nearly clean.
- TONE 6.8: right of centre thins the low end.
- Listen for: a bright, cold string line that swells in.

steps.title: A little echo
steps.why:
A little analogue delay puts some space behind the line.
- TIME 8 (330 ms): a clear gap before the echo.
- REPEATS 3: one or two echoes.
- MIX 2: low in the mix.
- Listen for: a faint trail after each phrase, most obvious when you stop playing.

context.att.2: In this sound this is the pulse-width modulation depth for Oscillator 1 only. The cable has taken Oscillator 2’s width away from it.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of Oscillator 1’s regular movement.
context.sh.rate: How often Oscillator 2’s width is given a new random target.
context.sh.glide: Smooths Oscillator 2’s width changes. At 0 the width jumps, and you hear a small click-like change of tone twice a second.
context.osc2.width: The centre that the random movement wanders around.
context.osc2.tune: A small fixed detune on top of the movement.
context.od.tone: Right of centre to thin the low end.

tweaks.hear: Oscillator 2’s tone now changes in sudden steps instead of wandering.
Oscillator 1 goes from a fixed square to a deep, seasick sweep. Around 5 is closest to an ensemble.
The random movement speeds up into a nervous shimmer.

tweaks.try: Switch PARAPHONIC on and hold two keys
tweaks.hear: Two-note chords, one note with regular movement and one with random movement.

sounds.name: Mellow Gliding Lead with Delay
sounds.ref: In the style of Zero 7 — "Destiny" and "In the Waiting Line" ("Simple Things")
sounds.blurb: Warm, soft-edged lead that slides between notes and trails a long, quiet echo.
sounds.how: Nothing in this sound is sharp. Oscillator 1 sits between triangle and sine, and Oscillator 2 adds a quiet triangle an octave below for warmth. The low-pass filter takes off what little edge remains, a soft attack removes the click, and portamento of about a third of a second makes the notes slide into each other. The LFO, already wired to the filter through MOD DEPTH, gives a slow, shallow pulse in the brightness. A long delay with a fair number of repeats fills the spaces a slow melody leaves.

steps.title: A near-sine with a triangle below
steps.why:
Nothing in this sound is sharp. A soft triangle leads, with a quiet triangle an octave below for warmth.
- OSC MIX −3 (80% / 20%): the crossfader, keeping Oscillator 2 to about a fifth: warmth under the note, not a second voice.
- SHAPE (osc 1) 3.3 (triangle → sine 30%): mostly triangle. Towards 2 (saw) reedier and more present; at 4 a pure sine.
- SHAPE (osc 2) triangle, RANGE 16’: an octave lower.
- RANGE (osc 1) 8’, TUNE 0 on both: in tune.
- Listen for: a soft, round, flute-like tone.

steps.title: Soft front, gentle fade
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness: a soft start and a gentle fade.
- A 4.5 (24 ms): rounds the start of each note. Longer is softer still.
- D 540 ms, S 75%: a small settle to a high level.
- R 6.5 (330 ms): each note fades instead of stopping.
- Listen for: no click at the front, and a soft tail on every note.

steps.title: Glide
steps.why:
Portamento, set with PORTA TIME, makes the pitch slide from each note to the next.
- PORTA TIME 1.8 (320 ms): a slide of about a third of a second. It applies to every note, not only overlapping ones. Shorter is tighter; longer gets lazier.
- Listen for: the wide steps in the riff turning into slow swoops.

steps.title: A warm filter with a slow pulse
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) takes off what little edge remains, and the LFO (low-frequency oscillator) gives the brightness a slow, shallow pulse that stands in for vibrato.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 6 (about 800 Hz), RESO 1: warm, no peak.
- KEY TRK On, ENV DEPTH 0: follows the keys, no envelope movement.
- MOD DEPTH 1: the LFO is already wired here; at 1 it moves the cutoff half an octave either way.
- RATE (lfo) 4.6 (4 Hz), SHAPE sine: a smooth, steady pulse. KEY SYNC Off lets it run free.
- Listen for: a soft tremble in the brightness on held notes. Set MOD DEPTH to 0 to hear it still.

steps.title: A long, quiet echo
steps.why:
A long, quiet analogue delay fills the spaces a slow melody leaves.
- TIME 8.6 (410 ms): a long gap between echoes.
- REPEATS 5: how long the trail lasts. The delay dulls each repeat a little, so they sit behind the note.
- MIX 3.5: echoes below the dry lead.
- Listen for: a trail of softer copies after each phrase.

context.osc1.shape: In this sound 3.3 is a soft triangle. Towards 2 (saw) the lead gets reedier and more present; at 4 it is a pure sine.
context.osc.mix: How much of the lower octave is mixed in.
context.porta.time: The slide between notes. It applies to every note, not only overlapping ones.
context.vcf.modDepth: The depth of the slow pulse in brightness.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of that pulse, about 4 Hz here.
context.delay.repeats: How long the echo trail lasts.
context.env1.a: How soft the start of each note is.

tweaks.hear: From clean steps to long, lazy slides that barely arrive before the next note.
Some sawtooth comes in and the lead gets a reedy edge.
The echoes become as loud as the notes and the melody blurs into a wash.
The pulse in the brightness becomes an obvious "wow-wow" on held notes.

sounds.name: Delay-Time Scratch
sounds.ref: In the style of Herbie Hancock — "Rockit"
sounds.blurb: Each key press jerks the sound backwards and then whips it forwards, like a record being pulled back and let go.
sounds.how: The scratching on the record is a DJ moving a vinyl record by hand, which slows, reverses and speeds up whatever is on it. An analogue delay can do something similar. While the delay time is getting longer, the sound inside it plays back slower, and if it lengthens fast enough it plays backwards. While the time is getting shorter, the sound plays back faster and higher. So this patch listens to the delay only, with MIX at 10, and patches Envelope 2 into DELAY TIME. Every note-on stretches the delay quickly and lets it shrink back. The thing being scratched is a nasal, noisy tone from the band-pass filter.

steps.title: Sawtooth and noise
steps.why:
A scratch is easiest to hear on a sound with some hiss and grain in it, so the source is a sawtooth with noise.
- OSC MIX −5: the crossfader between the two oscillators, fully left for Oscillator 1.
- SHAPE saw, RANGE 8’, TUNE 0: bright and buzzy, in tune.
- NOISE 3.5: white noise mixed in. The grain makes the speed changes easier to hear later.
- Listen for: a buzzy tone with a clear hiss on it.

steps.title: Band-pass for a vocal tone
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) in band-pass mode turns the saw and noise into something like a shouted “ah”, a common thing to scratch.
- MODE Band-pass: only a band around the cutoff gets through.
- FREQ 6.4 (about 1.1 kHz): the vowel of the sound being scratched.
- RESO 5.5: narrows and boosts the band, more vocal.
- KEY TRK Off, ENV DEPTH 0: the band stays put.
- Listen for: a nasal, noisy “ah”.

steps.title: Plain on-off loudness
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness as plain on and off, and the overdrive brings the level back up.
- Envelope 1 A 0, D 150 ms, S 100%: full level for as long as the key is held.
- R 140 ms: a short fade.
- DRIVE 4.5, TONE 5.5, LEVEL 8: overdrive after the filter restores the level lost to band-pass and roughens it.
- Listen for: a louder, grittier “ah” that holds steady.

steps.title: Listen to the delay only
steps.why:
The analogue delay is set so you hear only its output. The pitch changes will happen inside the delay, and any dry sound would cover them up.
- MIX 10: no dry sound at all. It must stay at 10 for this patch.
- REPEATS 0: each note is heard once.
- TIME 7.6 (290 ms): the resting delay. Longer makes the later scratch more extreme.
- Listen for: every note arriving late, about a third of a second after the key.

steps.title: Patch ENV 2 → DELAY TIME
steps.why:
While the delay time lengthens, the sound inside plays back slower, and if fast enough, backwards. While it shortens, it plays faster and higher. Envelope 2 now does that on every key press.
- Cable ENV 2 → DELAY TIME: adds Envelope 2 to the TIME setting. No knob sets its depth: a full envelope stretches it from 290 ms towards 830 ms.
- Envelope 2 A 47 ms: how quickly the delay stretches. Shorter gives a sharper backwards jerk.
- D 240 ms: how quickly it shrinks back, setting the forward rush. Here about twice normal speed, an octave up.
- S 0, R 140 ms: nothing held.
- Listen for: a backwards gulp on each key press, then a fast, high rush. The delay holds roughly the last third of a second, so what gets jerked about is mostly the end of the note before; the new note then arrives running fast and settles to its proper pitch.

context.delay.mix: In this sound this must be at 10. The pitch changes only happen inside the delay, and any dry sound covers them up.
context.delay.time: The resting delay, and the size of the scratch: the longer it is, the faster the delay time changes when the envelope hits, and the more extreme the speed changes.
context.env2.a: How quickly the delay stretches. Shorter gives a sharper backwards jerk.
context.env2.d: How quickly the delay shrinks back, which sets how high and how long the forward rush is.
context.delay.repeats: At 0 each scratch is heard once. Turn it up and the scratches are scratched again on the next key press.
context.vcf.freq: The vowel of the sound being scratched.
context.mix.noise: Adds grain, which makes the speed changes easier to hear.

tweaks.hear: Small, quick pitch wobbles at one end; big, slurring scratches that arrive late at the other.
The forward rush is shorter and higher, more of a "wik".
Old scratches come round again and are scratched a second time, which quickly gets chaotic.

tweaks.try: Move between 5.5 and 7.5 while the riff plays
tweaks.hear: The scratched sound changes from "oh" to "ee".

sounds.name: Dry Jazz-Funk Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Herbie Hancock — "Chameleon"
sounds.blurb: Short, slightly nasal bass with a quick filter snap, played like a bass guitar.
sounds.how: That bass line was played by hand on an ARP Odyssey, a small two-oscillator synth with the same 12 dB per octave kind of filter as the Neutron. The tone is a pulse wave with a sawtooth underneath. Envelope 2 opens the filter for about a tenth of a second at the start of each note, which gives the "bow" at the front, and the notes are kept short and dry. There is no delay and only a little drive.

steps.title: Pulse on top of a sawtooth
steps.why:
A pulse wave on top of a sawtooth gives a bass that is both nasal and weighty, played dry like a bass guitar.
- OSC MIX −2 (70% / 30%): the crossfader between the two oscillators, left of centre, so the pulse leads.
- SHAPE (osc 1) pulse, WIDTH 5: a square, where the nasal, hollow part of the tone comes from.
- SHAPE (osc 2) saw, TUNE +0.1: a sawtooth underneath for weight, a touch sharp.
- RANGE 16’ on both, TUNE (osc 1) 0: bass octave.
- Listen for: a hollow, buzzy bass with a slight slow movement in it.

steps.title: Low-pass with some resonance
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is set low with some resonance. On its own this is dull; the next step opens it.
- MODE Low-pass: the Neutron’s filter is 12 dB per octave, gentler and buzzier than a Moog-style one, the same kind as on the ARP Odyssey.
- FREQ 4.2 (about 220 Hz): where the filter rests between snaps. Lower is rounder; higher is buzzier.
- RESO 3.5: adds a slight quack once the filter moves.
- KEY TRK Off: the cutoff does not follow the keys.
- Listen for: a dull, round bass.

steps.title: A quick snap from Envelope 2
steps.why:
Envelope 2, the filter envelope, snaps the filter open at the start of each note and lets it fall back. That puts the “bow” on the front.
- ENV DEPTH 5: how far each snap opens the filter.
- Envelope 2 A 0: instant, on the beat.
- D 4.6 (110 ms): how long the snap lasts, so how much “bow” each note has. Longer gets more “wow”.
- S 15%, R 27 ms: settles low; closes fast.
- Listen for: a short, quacky “bow” on every note. Sweep Envelope 2’s D to change it.

steps.title: Short, dry notes
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness: short and dry, so a note stops the moment you lift the key, as on a bass played by hand.
- A 0: instant.
- D 240 ms, S 60%: a quick dip to a solid level.
- R 3 (18 ms): very short, so notes stop when you lift your finger.
- Listen for: tight notes with clean gaps. Play the riff staccato and legato to hear the difference.

steps.title: A little drive, no echo
steps.why:
A little overdrive and no echo keep it dry and in the pocket.
- DRIVE 2.5: thickens the low notes slightly.
- TONE 5, LEVEL 8: neutral tone, near full output.
- MIX (delay) 0: no echo at all.
- Listen for: a slightly fuller bass that still sounds dry. Set DRIVE to 0 to compare.

context.osc1.shape: Pulse. This is where the nasal part of the tone comes from.
