context.osc.mix: Left of centre: mostly the pulse, with the sawtooth underneath.
context.vcf.freq: Where the filter rests between snaps. Lower is rounder; higher is buzzier.
context.vcf.envDepth: How far each note’s snap opens the filter.
context.env2.d: How long the snap lasts. This sets how much "bow" each note has.
context.vcf.reso: Adds the slight quack to the snap.
context.env1.r: Very short, so notes stop when you lift your finger.

tweaks.hear: At 3.8 the snap is only a click. At 6 each note says a slow "wow".
The pulse thins out and the bass gets more nasal and cutting.
The quack at the front of each note becomes obvious.

sounds.name: Upside-Down Keyboard Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Weather Report — Joe Zawinul’s inverted 2600
sounds.blurb: Brassy lead on a keyboard that runs backwards: play up the keys and the pitch goes down.
sounds.how: Zawinul set one of his two ARP 2600s so the keyboard was inverted, with middle C staying put and everything else mirrored around it. Familiar fingerings then produced lines he would never have played otherwise. Two cables do it here. ASSIGN carries the keyboard pitch; the inverter turns it upside down; and the OSC 1+2 input adds two octaves of pitch change for every octave of signal. One octave up the keys therefore gives plus one octave from the key itself and minus two from the cable, which comes to one octave down.

steps.title: Two sawtooths, slightly apart
steps.why:
Two sawtooths, slightly apart, give the brassy raw tone.
- OSC MIX 0 (50% / 50%): the crossfader between the two oscillators, at the centre for an equal blend.
- SHAPE saw on both: SHAPE morphs through five waves; the saw is the brightest.
- RANGE 8’ on both: same octave.
- TUNE osc 1 0, osc 2 +0.2: Oscillator 2 about a fifth of a semitone sharp, for a thicker, brassier tone.
- Listen for: a bright, buzzy tone with a gentle beating.

steps.title: A brass-style filter
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) and Envelope 2, the filter envelope, make it sound blown instead of plucked.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 5 (about 390 Hz): dark at rest.
- RESO 2.5: a mild peak.
- KEY TRK Off: switched on, the filter would follow the keys you press, not the pitch you hear, once the keyboard is inverted.
- ENV DEPTH 4.5: how far the filter opens on each note.
- Envelope 2 A 39 ms: the short delay before full brightness that gives the blown, brassy start.
- D 360 ms, S 50%, R 41 ms: settles halfway while held.
- Listen for: a brassy “bwah” at the front of each note.

steps.title: Sustained notes with a short slide
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness, set for held notes, and portamento joins them.
- Envelope 1 A 6 ms: a clean start.
- D 150 ms, S 90%: notes hold at nearly full level.
- R 41 ms: a short tail.
- PORTA TIME 1.2 (140 ms): each note slides into the next. After the next step the slides run in the mirrored direction too.
- Listen for: smooth, sustained lead notes that glide together.

steps.title: Patch ASSIGN → INVERT IN, INVERT → OSC 1+2
steps.why:
Two cables turn the keyboard upside down. ASSIGN carries the keyboard pitch; the inverter flips it; OSC 1+2 adds two octaves of pitch for every octave of signal. One octave up the keys gives +1 from the key and −2 from the cable: one octave down.
- Cable ASSIGN → INVERT IN: replaces the inverter’s usual input, Envelope 2, with the keyboard pitch.
- Cable INVERT → OSC 1+2: adds the flipped pitch to both oscillators.
- Listen for: play the riff before and after. The keys have not changed, but the melody runs the other way up. Middle C is the one note that stays where it was.

context.osc2.tune: Slight detune for a thicker, brassier tone.
context.vcf.envDepth: How far the filter opens on each note.
context.env2.a: The short delay before full brightness. It gives the blown, brassy start.
context.porta.time: Joins the notes. The slide runs in the mirrored direction too.
context.vcf.keyTrk: Off. Switched on, the filter would follow the keys you press, not the pitch you hear.

tweaks.hear: The filter follows your hands, not the pitch: notes get brighter as they get lower, which no acoustic instrument does.

tweaks.try: Unplug INVERT → OSC 1+2 and plug it into OSC 2 instead
tweaks.hear: Only Oscillator 2 is mirrored. The two oscillators move in opposite directions and meet at middle C.
Long slides that are hard to predict, because your hand moves one way and the pitch the other.

sounds.name: Droid Chirps and Whistles
sounds.ref: In the style of Ben Burtt — R2-D2 in Star Wars
sounds.blurb: Chattering whistles that swoop to a new random pitch on every hit.
sounds.how: The droid’s voice was patched on an ARP 2600 and mixed with a human voice. The synth part is a pure whistle whose pitch never stays still. Here the sample-and-hold makes a new random voltage about nine times a second, GLIDE turns the jumps between them into quick slides, and Attenuator 1 sets how wide the jumps are before they reach the pitch of the oscillators. Envelope 2 goes through Attenuator 2 to Oscillator 1, so each hit also starts high and drops: a chirp. Play short, uneven notes on any one key.

steps.title: A pure whistle
steps.why:
A pure whistle is the raw material. A sine has no harmonics, so the filter is left open and the overdrive clean.
- OSC MIX −5: the crossfader, fully left for Oscillator 1 only.
- SHAPE sine: SHAPE fully right. Towards triangle it gets slightly reedy.
- RANGE 8’, TUNE +6 st: TUNE shifts the pitch by up to about an octave; here up about six semitones, the centre of the whistle’s range.
- Low-pass, FREQ 8.5 (5 kHz), RESO 0: the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is wide open, with ENV DEPTH at 0, as a sine has nothing to filter.
- DRIVE 0: overdrive off for a clean tone.
- Listen for: a clean, high whistle.

steps.title: Short notes
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness. Full sustain means the length of each whistle is the length of your key press.
- A 0: instant start.
- D 150 ms, S 100%: full level while held.
- R 95 ms: a quick fade after release.
- Listen for: whistles that start and stop with your fingers. Play short, uneven notes.

steps.title: Patch S&H → ATT1 IN, ATT 1 → OSC 1+2
steps.why:
S&H (sample and hold) takes readings of noise and holds them, giving random voltages. Sent to pitch, it makes the whistle hop about on its own.
- Cable S&H → ATT1 IN: replaces Attenuator 1’s usual input (Attenuator 2) with the random steps.
- Cable ATT 1 → OSC 1+2: adds them to both oscillators’ pitch.
- RATE (S&H) 7.5 (8.69 Hz): a new target nearly nine times a second. Faster is more agitated.
- 1 (Attenuator 1) at 6: how wide the random pitch range is.
- Listen for: hold a key and the whistle jumps between random pitches.

steps.title: Turn the hops into slides
steps.why:
GLIDE smooths the S&H’s steps, so the pitch swoops between targets instead of jumping. This is the difference between a computer bleep and a whistle.
- GLIDE 7 (100 ms): about a tenth of a second to reach each new value. At 0 it steps; higher and it swoops more lazily.
- Listen for: the hops turning into quick, chattering slides.

steps.title: Patch ENV 2 → ATT2 IN, ATT 2 → OSC 1
steps.why:
Envelope 2 goes to Oscillator 1’s pitch through Attenuator 2, so each hit starts high and falls: a chirp at the front.
- Cable ENV 2 → ATT2 IN: replaces Attenuator 2’s usual input, the LFO, with Envelope 2.
- Cable ATT 2 → OSC 1: adds it to Oscillator 1’s pitch.
- 2 (Attenuator 2) at 6: how high each chirp starts before it falls.
- Envelope 2 A 0, D 150 ms, S 0, R 95 ms: an instant peak that falls over about 150 ms. D sets how long each chirp takes to fall.
- Listen for: a quick downward “tweet” on every key press, on top of the random slides.

steps.title: A short echo
steps.why:
A short analogue delay makes the chatter sound as if it is in a room.
- TIME 4 (91 ms): a very short gap.
- REPEATS 2: a single quick repeat.
- MIX 2.5: quiet against the dry whistle.
- Listen for: a small slap-back after each chirp. Turn MIX to 0 to hear it dry.

context.osc1.shape: Sine, for a clean whistle. Towards triangle it gets slightly reedy.
context.sh.rate: How often the pitch picks a new target. Faster is more agitated.
context.sh.glide: How long the pitch takes to reach each new target. At 0 it steps; higher up it swoops.
context.att.1: How wide the random pitch range is.
context.att.2: How high each chirp starts before it falls.
context.env2.d: How long each chirp takes to fall.
context.osc1.tune: The centre of the whistle’s range.

tweaks.hear: At 0 the pitch steps like a computer. At 8 it never quite arrives and turns into a slow, sad warble.

tweaks.try: Sweep from 5 to 9 while you hold a key
tweaks.hear: The chatter goes from thoughtful to frantic.

tweaks.try: Raise to 8 and shorten Envelope 2’s D to 4
tweaks.hear: Each hit becomes a sharp downward "pew".

tweaks.try: Set MODE to band-pass, FREQ to 7, RESO to 6 and SHAPE to 2
tweaks.hear: A sawtooth through a resonant band-pass: the whistle turns into a nasal, more voice-like squawk.

sounds.name: Distorted Rubber Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Mr. Oizo — "Flat Beat"
sounds.blurb: Fat, overdriven bass that bends into each note and honks as the filter closes.
sounds.how: That bass came from a Korg MS-20, a small semi-modular with a resonant filter that distorts when pushed. Three things make the sound: a low pulse wave, a resonant filter that closes over about a quarter of a second on each note, and heavy overdrive after it. Portamento of nearly half a second makes the pitch bend from each note into the next, which is the rubbery part.

steps.title: A low pulse with a sawtooth an octave below
steps.why:
A low pulse leads, with a sawtooth an octave below for the floor.
- OSC MIX −1.5 (65% / 35%): the crossfader between the two oscillators, left of centre, so the pulse leads.
- SHAPE (osc 1) pulse, WIDTH 5, RANGE 16’: a hollow square in bass range.
- SHAPE (osc 2) saw, RANGE 32’: the lowest octave setting, an octave below Oscillator 1, for weight.
- TUNE 0 on both: in tune.
- Listen for: a deep, hollow bass with a buzzy floor.

steps.title: Resonant filter that closes on each note
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) sits low with strong resonance, and Envelope 2, the filter envelope, opens it wide and lets it honk shut on each note.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 3.6 (about 140 Hz): dark at rest.
- RESO 6.5: the honk, which the overdrive will squash into dirt.
- KEY TRK Off: cutoff fixed.
- ENV DEPTH 5.5: how far the filter opens at the start of each note.
- Envelope 2 A 0, D 240 ms, S 20%, R 41 ms: D is how long it takes to close, the length of each “wow”.
- Listen for: a resonant “wow” on every note.

steps.title: Heavy overdrive
steps.why:
Heavy overdrive after the filter is where most of the character comes from.
- DRIVE 8.5: flattens the peaks the resonance makes, which is where the dirt comes from. Lower it and the sound turns polite.
- TONE 3.5: below centre, keeping the distortion fat, not fizzy.
- LEVEL 5.5: brought down to make up for the extra loudness.
- Listen for: a fat, dirty honk. Sweep DRIVE from 2 to 8.5 to hear it go from clean to crushed.

steps.title: Bend into every note
steps.why:
Portamento makes the pitch bend from each note into the next. That is the rubbery part.
- PORTA TIME 2.2 (480 ms): nearly half a second, so the pitch is still moving when each note starts. Shorter tightens the line; at 0 notes jump.
- Listen for: every note bending into place, most obvious on wide jumps.

steps.title: Held notes that stop short
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness: held notes stay fat and stop short.
- A 0: instant start.
- D 360 ms, S 80%: a small dip to a high held level.
- R 27 ms: a quick release, so notes stop almost as soon as you let go.
- Listen for: solid held notes and clean stops between them.

context.vcf.reso: The honk. The overdrive then squashes it, which makes the dirt.
context.vcf.envDepth: How far the filter opens at the start of each note.
context.env2.d: How long the filter takes to close: the length of each "wow".
context.od.drive: Most of the character is here. Lower it and the sound turns polite.
context.od.tone: Below centre, to keep the distortion fat and not fizzy.
context.porta.time: The bend between notes.
context.osc2.range: An octave below Oscillator 1, for weight.

tweaks.hear: At 3 it is a clean squelchy bass. At 10 the resonance is crushed into a square, buzzing honk.
At 0 the rubber goes and the notes are rigid. At 4 the line slurs like a slowed-down record.

tweaks.try: Move between 3 and 5 while the riff plays
tweaks.hear: The honk moves from a low "oo" to an open "ah".

sounds.name: Buzzing Glam Riff Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Goldfrapp — "Strict Machine"
sounds.blurb: Hard, buzzing riff bass with a fixed nasal edge, a little like a fuzz guitar.
sounds.how: Will Gregory’s glam sounds came from a Korg MS-20 pushed until it buzzed. The Neutron gets to a similar place with oscillator sync. With OSC SYNC on, Oscillator 2 is forced to restart in step with Oscillator 1, so it always plays Oscillator 1’s note, and its own TUNE knob changes the tone instead: turning it up adds a hard, nasal buzz at a fixed spot. Here it is set and left alone, not swept. Overdrive adds the fuzz, and a swung riff does the rest.

steps.title: Two sawtooths at 16’
steps.why:
Two sawtooths start the riff bass. Oscillator 2 will carry the character, so the mix leans towards it.
- OSC MIX 3 (20% / 80%): the crossfader between the two oscillators, right of centre: mostly Oscillator 2, with Oscillator 1 for weight.
- SHAPE saw on both: the brightest, buzziest wave.
- RANGE 16’ on both, TUNE (osc 1) 0: bass octave.
- Listen for: a thick, buzzy saw bass.

steps.title: Sync on, Oscillator 2 tuned up
steps.why:
Hard sync makes Oscillator 2 restart in step with Oscillator 1, so it always plays Oscillator 1’s note. Its own TUNE knob then changes the tone instead of the pitch.
- OSC SYNC On: Oscillator 2 is locked to Oscillator 1’s pitch.
- TUNE (osc 2) 3.2 (+7.7 st): where the buzz sits. Higher is thinner and more nasal; here it is set and left alone, not swept.
- Listen for: no pitch change, but a hard, nasal buzz that stays the same on every note. Turn osc 2 TUNE slowly to hear the tearing sync sweep.

steps.title: Filter mostly open
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is left open enough to let the buzz through, with a small push from Envelope 2, the filter envelope.
- MODE Low-pass, FREQ 6.2 (about 930 Hz): open enough for the sync buzz.
- RESO 2: a slight peak.
- KEY TRK Off: the cutoff does not follow the keys.
- ENV DEPTH 2.5, env 2 D 150 ms, S 40%: a little extra bite at the start of each note.
- Listen for: a slightly brighter front on each note.

steps.title: Fuzz
steps.why:
The overdrive, after the filter, adds the fuzz, a little like a fuzz guitar.
- DRIVE 6.5: heavy grit.
- TONE 5.5: just above centre, a touch bright.
- LEVEL 6: brought down to allow for the drive.
- Listen for: a hard, fuzzy buzz. Set DRIVE to 1 to hear the clean sync tone underneath.

steps.title: Firm notes with a slight slur
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness for a firm riff, and a short slide blurs the joins.
- Envelope 1 A 0, D 150 ms, S 90%: full-level held notes.
- R 27 ms: a short release, so notes stop cleanly.
- PORTA TIME 0.8 (64 ms): about 60 ms of slide between notes.
- Listen for: tight notes with a slight slur. Play a swung riff to hear it groove.

context.osc.sync: On. Oscillator 2 is locked to Oscillator 1’s pitch, so its TUNE knob changes tone, not pitch.
context.osc2.tune: Where the buzz sits. Higher is thinner and more nasal.
context.osc.mix: Right of centre: mostly the synced oscillator, with Oscillator 1 for weight.
context.od.drive: The fuzz.
context.vcf.freq: Open enough to let the buzz through.

tweaks.try: Turn slowly from 0 to 5 while the riff plays
tweaks.hear: The buzz climbs through the tone like a wah pedal, while the notes stay where they are.
Oscillator 2 goes back to playing its own pitch, a little over a fifth above: a sour power chord instead of a buzz.
Only the plain sawtooth is left, which shows how much of the character is the synced oscillator.

sounds.name: Pad with Opposite Drifting Detune
sounds.ref: In the style of Aphex Twin — "#3" (known as "Rhubarb") from "Selected Ambient Works Volume II"
sounds.blurb: Soft, slow pad whose two oscillators drift apart and back together, so the beating between them speeds up and slows down by itself.
sounds.how: A fixed detune beats at one steady speed, and the ear soon notices the pattern. Here the detune itself moves. The LFO, turned almost to nothing by Attenuator 2, goes into MULT to make two copies. One copy pushes Oscillator 1’s pitch. The other goes through the inverter first, so it pushes Oscillator 2 the opposite way by the same amount. As the LFO rises the oscillators move apart; as it falls they meet, cross and move apart the other way. The pitch you hear stays centred because the two always move by equal amounts. Both oscillators sit between triangle and sine, and a half-closed filter and slow envelopes keep everything soft.

steps.title: Two soft oscillators in unison
steps.why:
Both oscillators (the circuits that make the raw tone) start on the same soft wave at the same pitch. The movement comes later from the patch bay, so for now this is a plain, round tone with no buzz.
- SHAPE 3.3 and 3.5 (triangle towards sine): the Neutron’s SHAPE knob morphs between waves. Between triangle and sine there are very few harmonics, so the pad stays soft. Turn towards saw for a brighter, more string-like pad.
- RANGE 8’ and TUNE 0 on both: same octave, no detune from the knobs. The detune arrives in step 4.
- OSC MIX −1.5 (65 / 35): a crossfader, not two level knobs. At dead centre the two waves could cancel completely when they oppose each other and the note would drop out; with Oscillator 1 louder it only dips.
- Listen for: a steady, flute-like tone. Turn OSC MIX to the centre later, once the drift is patched, and the dips get deeper.

steps.title: Slow in, slow out
steps.why:
Envelope 1 is wired to the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier), so it shapes the loudness of each note. Slow settings at both ends turn separate notes into a pad that overlaps itself.
- A 7.8 (590 ms): attack, the fade-in. Slow enough that nothing starts with a hit; shorter makes it an organ, longer makes it a swell.
- D 7 (820 ms), S 8 (80%): after the fade-in the level falls a little to the sustain and holds while the key is down.
- R 9 (2.6 s): release, the fade after you let go. Long, so each chord is still ringing as the next one fades in.
- Listen for: play two chords one after the other. The first hangs on under the second instead of stopping.

steps.title: A half-closed filter that opens a little
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) sets how bright the pad is. Here it is half closed for softness, and a slow second envelope opens it a little as each note grows.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 5.8 (about 700 Hz): keeps the lows, cuts the top. Most of the softness comes from here; turn right for a brighter pad.
- RESO 1: resonance, a boost at the cutoff. Just a trace, so the filter has a slight edge without ringing.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking, so the cutoff follows the keyboard and high notes are no duller than low ones.
- ENV DEPTH 2 with Envelope 2 at A 1.2 s, D 1.9 s, S 60%, R 1.7 s: Envelope 2 lifts the cutoff slightly. Its slow attack means each note brightens over its first second instead of plucking.
- Listen for: hold a note and hear it open up gently after it has faded in.

steps.title: Patch ATT 2 → MULT, MULT 1 → OSC 1, MULT 2 → INVERT IN, INVERT → OSC 2
steps.why:
The patch bay makes the detune move. One slow LFO (low-frequency oscillator, a wave too slow to hear that moves other settings) pushes the two oscillators’ pitches in opposite directions, so they drift apart and back while the note stays centred.
- ATT 2 → MULT, MULT 1 → OSC 1: Attenuator 2 already carries the LFO, so its output is the LFO at the level of its knob. MULT copies it; one copy goes to Oscillator 1’s pitch.
- MULT 2 → INVERT IN, INVERT → OSC 2: the other copy is turned upside down, so Oscillator 2 moves the opposite way by the same amount.
- 2 at 0.4: must stay very low. A full-strength LFO would move the pitch by two octaves; here each oscillator moves by well under a semitone.
- LFO RATE 1 (0.06 Hz), SHAPE sine, KEY SYNC off: about 16 seconds per cycle. A sine lingers at its widest and passes quickly through unison.
- Listen for: hold one note. The beating starts slow, speeds up, slows to nothing and starts again.

steps.title: Delay for space
steps.why:
The last stage adds space behind the pad and makes sure the overdrive adds no grit.
- DRIVE 0: the overdrive is always in the signal path. At zero it is close to clean, which suits a soft pad.
- TIME 8.5 (390 ms): long gaps, so you hear echoes rather than a thickening.
- REPEATS 5 (50%): a handful of echoes, each quieter and darker than the one before, because this is an analogue bucket-brigade delay.
- MIX 3 (30%): the echoes sit well behind the notes. More MIX pushes the pad further back in the mix.
- Listen for: short chords leaving a soft trail that fills the gaps between them.

context.att.2: In this sound this is the width of the detune. At 0.35 the oscillators are at most a sixth of a semitone apart. It also feeds pulse width, but that only matters on pulse shapes, and there are none here.
context.lfo.rate: How long the detune takes to open, close and open the other way: 16 seconds here.
context.lfo.shape: A sine slows down at each end, so the detune lingers at its widest and passes quickly through unison.
context.osc1.shape: Between triangle and sine. Turn towards saw for a brighter, more string-like pad.
context.osc.mix: Sets how deep the dips in the beating are. At the centre the two oscillators can cancel each other completely; off centre they cannot.
context.vcf.freq: The overall brightness. Most of the softness comes from here.
context.vcf.envDepth: How much each note brightens as Envelope 2 slowly rises.
context.env1.a: How slowly each note fades in.
context.env1.r: How slowly it fades out after the key is released.
context.delay.mix: How loud the echoes are behind the notes.

tweaks.hear: At its widest the beating becomes fast and slightly sour, then calms again as the oscillators come back together.
The detune opens and closes every three seconds, which sounds more like a slow chorus effect.
The oscillators now meet at a different point in the LFO’s cycle, and the beating is clearly faster on one side of that point than on the other.

tweaks.try: Switch PARAPHONIC on and hold two keys
tweaks.hear: Two-note chords, where the interval between the notes goes slowly in and out of tune.

sounds.name: Pad with Worn-Tape Echoes
sounds.ref: In the style of Boards of Canada — "Olson"
sounds.blurb: Warm two-note pad that stays in tune while its echoes waver in pitch, like a tape machine that cannot hold its speed.
sounds.how: Changing a delay’s time while sound is inside it bends the pitch of the echoes, the way a tape does when it slows down and speeds up. This patch does that on purpose and keeps it random. The sample-and-hold picks a new random voltage about every two seconds, and its GLIDE knob turns the steps into slow slides. That voltage goes through Attenuator 1, turned down low, into DELAY TIME. The notes you play are untouched; only the echoes drift a little sharp and then a little flat. With MIX at half, the steady note and its drifting echo together sound like a slow, uneven chorus. A trace of noise under the oscillators stands in for tape hiss.

steps.title: Two mellow oscillators, two notes
steps.why:
Two soft oscillators (the circuits that make the raw tone) give a warm, slightly hollow base, and paraphonic mode lets you hold two notes at once.
- OSC MIX 0 (50 / 50): a crossfader, so the centre is an equal blend of both.
- SHAPE osc 1 2.7 (saw towards triangle): a saw with most of its buzz taken off. Turn left for more bite.
- SHAPE osc 2 3 (triangle), both RANGE 8’: a plain triangle underneath for body, tuned a hair sharp (too little to show on the chip).
- PARAPHONIC on: two held keys each get their own oscillator. They still share one filter and one amplifier, so both notes fade together.
- Listen for: hold two keys a few notes apart and both sound, one on each oscillator. Turn OSC MIX fully left and only one of the two notes remains.

steps.title: Soft loudness
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). Soft settings take the edge off the start and let chords overlap.
- A 7.2 (330 ms): a third of a second to fade in, so there is no click at the front.
- D 7 (820 ms), S 8 (80%): the level eases down slightly after the fade-in and holds.
- R 8.6 (1.9 s): nearly two seconds of fade after you let go. Shorter makes the chords stop; longer blurs them together.
- Listen for: change chords and hear the old one fading under the new one.

steps.title: Warm filter and a little hiss
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) warms the tone, and a little noise goes in with the oscillators to stand in for tape hiss.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 6.2 (about 930 Hz): cuts the top off for a warm, dull-edged pad. Turn right for a brighter, more present sound.
- RESO 1.5: resonance, a small lift at the cutoff that gives the filter a faint edge.
- KEY TRK on, ENV DEPTH 0: the cutoff follows the keyboard, and no envelope moves it, so the tone stays steady.
- NOISE 1.5 (15%): white noise added before the filter. The filter darkens it into a quiet hiss that follows the notes through the envelope.
- Listen for: a faint hiss that appears and fades with each chord.

steps.title: A long delay, mixed high
steps.why:
A long, loud delay sets up the echoes that the patch will bend later. For now they are clean copies of the chord.
- DRIVE 0: no grit from the overdrive stage.
- TIME 8.5 (390 ms): long enough to hear distinct echoes.
- REPEATS 6 (60%): plenty of repeats. Each one is darker than the last, as on an analogue bucket-brigade delay.
- MIX 5 (50%): the echo is as loud as the note, which is where the chorus-like thickening will be strongest.
- Listen for: hold a chord and let go. The echoes are in tune, one after another. Remember this; the next step makes them waver.

steps.title: Patch S&H → ATT1 IN and ATT 1 → DELAY TIME
steps.why:
The patch bay adds slow, random tape wobble to the echoes. The S&H (sample and hold) makes a random voltage, which gently moves the delay time; changing the time while sound is inside the delay bends the echoes’ pitch.
- S&H → ATT1 IN: the random voltage replaces Attenuator 1’s usual input.
- ATT 1 → DELAY TIME: adds it to the TIME knob. Knob 1 at 1 keeps it small, a fraction of a semitone; more makes the echoes go audibly out of tune.
- S&H RATE 1.5 (0.52 Hz): a new random target about every two seconds.
- GLIDE 10 (1.0 s): slides to each target instead of jumping. At zero each jump would chirp.
- Listen for: hold a chord. The echoes drift a little flat, then sharp, and later repeats wander further than early ones.

context.att.1: In this sound this is how far the random voltage moves the delay time, and so how far out of tune the echoes go. At 1 it is a small fraction of a semitone.
context.sh.rate: How often the drift picks a new target: about every two seconds here.
context.sh.glide: How slowly the delay time moves to each new target. At zero the time would jump, and each jump is heard as a short chirp in the echoes.
context.delay.mix: At half, the dry note and the echo are equally loud, which is where the chorus-like thickening is strongest.
context.delay.repeats: Each repeat passes through the drifting delay again, so later echoes are further out of tune than early ones.
context.delay.time: The gap before the echo. The random voltage is added to this setting.
context.mix.noise: A quiet hiss under the oscillators. It goes through the filter, the envelope and the delay with them.
context.osc.para: Gives each oscillator its own note. There is still one filter and one amplifier, so both notes fade together.
context.vcf.freq: The overall warmth of the pad.

tweaks.hear: The echoes swing well out of tune: a badly damaged tape.
The delay time now jumps to each new value, and every jump makes a short chirp in the echoes.
Only the echoes are left. Everything arrives late and nothing is quite in tune.
A clear layer of hiss that swells with each chord.

sounds.name: Drone with a Slow Overtone Sweep
sounds.ref: In the style of Éliane Radigue — "Kyema" ("Trilogie de la Mort")
sounds.blurb: Steady low drone that needs no key held, with a quiet whistle above it that climbs and descends through the overtones one at a time.
sounds.how: A sawtooth contains every harmonic: tones at whole-number multiples of the note’s pitch, stacked above it. Normally they blend into one sound. A low-pass filter with high resonance boosts a narrow band at its cutoff, so whichever harmonic sits there stands out from the rest. Move the cutoff very slowly and the harmonics are picked out one after another, like a slow scale above the drone. The LFO, already wired to the filter through MOD DEPTH, does the moving: a triangle wave that takes about half a minute per cycle. VCA BIAS holds the amplifier open, so the keys only choose the pitch.

steps.title: A low sawtooth with a soft partner
steps.why:
The two oscillators (the circuits that make the raw tone) set up a low drone with plenty of harmonics for the filter to pick out later.
- SHAPE osc 1 2 (saw), RANGE 16’: a sawtooth contains every harmonic, so it is the raw material for the sweep. 16’ is an octave below normal.
- SHAPE osc 2 3 (triangle), RANGE 16’: a softer wave a hair sharp (too little to show on the chip), adding weight at the bottom and a very slow beat.
- OSC MIX −2 (70 / 30): a crossfader leaning towards the saw. Turn right and the drone gets rounder, with fewer harmonics to find.
- Listen for: a bright, buzzy low note. The filter is still wide open, so every harmonic blends into one sound.

steps.title: Hold the amplifier open
steps.why:
The VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) sets loudness. Here it is held part open so the drone sounds with no key held, and the keys add swells and choose pitch.
- VCA BIAS 5 (50%): holds the amplifier open whatever the envelope does. At zero the drone would only sound while a key is down.
- Envelope 1 at A 1.2 s, D 820 ms, S 40%, R 2.6 s: adds to the bias, so each key press is a slow swell on top of the drone that settles back.
- PORTA TIME 3 (900 ms): portamento, a slide in pitch from one note to the next. Turn it down for a jump.
- Listen for: let go of all keys and the drone carries on. Press a new key and the pitch slides there.

steps.title: A narrow resonant peak
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) becomes a narrow peak that picks one harmonic out of the saw and makes it whistle above the drone.
- MODE low-pass, RESO 8.6: resonance boosts a narrow band at the cutoff. At 8.6 it is just short of whistling by itself. Lower it and the harmonics blend back; above about 9.3 the filter sings on its own and stops following them.
- FREQ 6 (about 800 Hz): with KEY TRK on this is the cutoff at middle C. On the low D of the riff the peak lands near 450 Hz, that note’s sixth harmonic.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking keeps the peak on the same harmonic as you change note.
- ENV DEPTH 0: no envelope moves the cutoff.
- Listen for: the drone with one steady overtone ringing above it.

steps.title: Let the LFO move the peak, very slowly
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator, a slow wave that moves other settings) is already wired to the cutoff, so turning up MOD DEPTH walks the peak through the harmonics one at a time.
- MOD DEPTH 2 (20%): how far the LFO moves the cutoff. An octave each way, from about the third harmonic up to the twelfth. Wider and the top of the sweep fades, as a saw’s high harmonics are quieter.
- RATE 0.4 (0.03 Hz): one trip up and down every half minute or so.
- SHAPE 1 (triangle): moves at an even speed, so each overtone gets the same time. A sine would linger at the ends.
- KEY SYNC off: the LFO runs free; key presses do not restart it.
- Listen for: the whistle stepping from one overtone to the next, like a slow scale, rather than a smooth glide.

steps.title: Level, air and space
steps.why:
The last stage keeps the loud resonant peak under control and adds air and space.
- DRIVE 0, LEVEL 4.5: the overdrive is always in the path. No drive keeps it clean, and LEVEL comes down because the resonant peak is loud.
- NOISE 1 (10%): a trace of white noise gives the peak something to ring on between harmonics, heard as a faint breath.
- TIME 9 (460 ms), REPEATS 6 (60%), MIX 3.5 (35%): a long analogue delay that blurs each step of the sweep into the next.
- Listen for: the steps between overtones smearing together, and a soft breath under the whistle.

context.vcf.reso: In this sound this is how clearly one overtone stands out. Lower it and the overtones blend back into a plain filtered drone; above about 9.3 the filter whistles by itself and no longer follows the harmonics.
context.vcf.freq: The centre of the sweep. The LFO moves the peak either side of this point.
context.vcf.modDepth: How far the peak travels: an octave each way at 2. The higher harmonics of a sawtooth are quieter, so a wider sweep fades at the top.
context.lfo.rate: How long one trip up and down the overtones takes: about half a minute here.
context.lfo.shape: Triangle moves at an even speed. A sine would linger at the top and bottom of the sweep.
context.vca.bias: Keeps the amplifier open so the drone sounds with no key held. At zero the patch only sounds while a key is down.
context.osc1.shape: The sawtooth supplies the harmonics. The filter can only bring out what the oscillator contains.
context.porta.time: The slow slide in pitch when you move to another key.
context.od.level: Pulled back to keep the resonant peak from getting loud.
context.mix.noise: A faint breath that the resonant peak turns into a soft whistle.

tweaks.hear: The separate overtones merge, and the sweep becomes an ordinary slow opening and closing of the filter.
A square wave has only the odd-numbered harmonics, so the whistle now climbs in wider steps.
The body of the drone drops away and the overtone is left almost on its own.
The sweep takes five seconds, and the overtones run up and down like a slow arpeggio.

sounds.name: Soft Pluck with a Tuned Overtone
sounds.ref: In the style of Hiroshi Yoshimura — "Creek" ("Green")
sounds.blurb: Quiet, rounded pluck, a little like a thumb piano, with a hollow ring that stays the same on every note.
sounds.how: One triangle wave supplies a soft tone with few overtones. The character comes from the filter’s resonance, used here as a fixed part of the tone and not as a sweep. FREQ is set so the resonant peak sits on the triangle’s third harmonic, an octave and a fifth above the note, and KEY TRK moves the cutoff with the keyboard so the peak stays on that harmonic for every key. Envelope 2 starts the peak a little higher and lets it drop into place, which gives a soft knock at the front. Envelope 1 has no sustain, so each note dies away like a plucked one.

steps.title: One triangle wave
steps.why:
A single triangle wave makes a soft, rounded tone with few overtones. The filter will add the character later.
- OSC MIX −5: the mixer is a crossfader, and fully left means only Oscillator 1 (the circuit making the tone) is heard.
- SHAPE 3 (triangle): soft, with only odd-numbered harmonics, each much quieter than in a saw. It still has a third harmonic for the filter to find.
- RANGE 8’, TUNE 0: normal pitch, in tune.
- Listen for: a plain, flute-like note that holds while the key is down.

steps.title: Plucked loudness
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). With no sustain, every note dies away by itself like a plucked string.
- A 1.5 (1 ms): still instant to the ear, but enough to take the click off the start.
- D 8 (1.9 s): how long each pluck takes to fade. Shorter makes it a tight marimba-like hit; longer rings on.
- S 0: nothing held, so the note fades even with the key down.
- R 8 (1.1 s): short key presses still ring on after you let go.
- Listen for: each note fading away over about two seconds.

steps.title: Put the resonant peak on the third harmonic
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is set up as a tuned ring: its resonant peak sits on the triangle’s third harmonic, an octave and a fifth above each note.
- MODE low-pass, RESO 8.2: resonance boosts a narrow band at the cutoff. At 8.2 it is strong and narrow. Lower it and the pluck goes plain; near maximum the filter sings by itself.
- FREQ 6 (about 780 Hz): with KEY TRK on this is the cutoff at middle C, three times that note’s pitch. Treat it as a tuning control; small moves matter.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking moves the cutoff with the keyboard, so the peak stays on the third harmonic for every key.
- Listen for: a hollow ring above each note. Switch KEY TRK off and the ring stays at one pitch while the notes move under it.

steps.title: A soft knock at the front
steps.why:
Envelope 2 gives the peak a quick dip into place, which adds a soft knock at the front of each pluck.
- ENV DEPTH 1.5 (15%): how far Envelope 2 lifts the cutoff. Small, so the peak starts about an octave high. More makes a sharper knock.
- A 0, D 5.5 (240 ms), S 0: straight up, then down onto the third harmonic in about a quarter of a second, and nothing held.
- R 5.5 (140 ms): a short release to match.
- Listen for: a small “tok” at the start of each note before the ring settles. Sweep ENV DEPTH to hear it grow or vanish.

steps.title: Clean, with a quiet echo
steps.why:
The last stage keeps the tone clean and adds a quiet echo in the gaps.
- DRIVE 0: the overdrive is always in the path; at zero nothing roughens the tone.
- TIME 8 (330 ms): a medium-long gap, heard as separate echoes.
- REPEATS 4.5 (45%): a few repeats, each darker than the last.
- MIX 3 (30%): echoes well below the dry pluck.
- Listen for: each pluck repeating quietly in the gaps of a sparse line.

context.vcf.freq: In this sound this chooses which harmonic rings. 5.95 is the third harmonic. It is a tuning control here, so small movements matter.
context.vcf.reso: How strongly the chosen harmonic rings. Lower it and the pluck turns plain and soft; near maximum the filter sings by itself.
context.vcf.keyTrk: Keeps the peak on the same harmonic for every key. Without it the ring would stay at one fixed pitch while the notes moved underneath.
context.vcf.envDepth: The size of the knock at the start of each note.
context.env2.d: How quickly the peak drops into place.
context.env1.d: How long each pluck takes to die away.
context.osc1.shape: A triangle has a third harmonic for the filter to boost, but only a quiet one, which is why the ring stays gentle.

tweaks.hear: The ring moves up to the fifth harmonic, two octaves and a third above the note: thinner and more bell-like.
The ring stays at one pitch whatever you play, so some notes ring and others do not.
A sine has no overtones, so the ring almost disappears. Resonance can only boost what the oscillator supplies.
A plain, soft pluck with only a hint of the ring.

sounds.name: Slow Surf from Filtered Noise
sounds.ref: In the style of Suzanne Ciani — the synthesised ocean on "The First Wave: Birth of Venus" ("Seven Waves")
sounds.blurb: Waves of soft noise that rise and fall by themselves with no key held, each one brighter as it peaks, arriving at uneven intervals.
sounds.how: There is no oscillator in this sound. White noise is patched straight into the filter, which takes off the hiss and leaves a low rush. LFO UNI is patched into VCA CV in place of Envelope 1, so the LFO sets the loudness: each slow cycle is one wave, and no key is needed. The same LFO is already wired to the cutoff through MOD DEPTH, so a wave gets brighter as it gets louder. To stop the waves arriving at regular intervals, the sample-and-hold’s random voltage goes through Attenuator 1 into LFO RATE, so some waves come sooner and some later.

steps.title: Patch NOISE → VCF IN
steps.why:
No oscillator is used in this sound. A cable sends white noise straight into the VCF (voltage-controlled filter), which will turn the hiss into surf.
- NOISE → VCF IN: a cable into VCF IN replaces the oscillators at the filter’s input. The jack carries noise at full level; the NOISE knob is not involved.
- Listen for: hold a key and you hear bright white noise. It only sounds while a key is held, because Envelope 1 still controls the amplifier.

steps.title: Filter the hiss down to a rush
steps.why:
The filter takes the fizz off the noise and leaves a low rush, like distant sea.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 5.3 (about 480 Hz): keeps only the low part of the noise. Turn left for a darker, further-off rush; right brings back the hiss.
- RESO 2.5: resonance, a lift at the cutoff that gives the rush a faint pitch. Higher values turn surf into wind.
- KEY TRK off: key tracking would move the cutoff with the keys, but there is no note to follow.
- DRIVE 0: keeps the overdrive stage clean.
- Listen for: hold a key and the hiss becomes a soft roar.

steps.title: Patch LFO UNI → VCA CV
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator, a slow wave that moves other settings) takes over the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier), so each slow cycle becomes one wave and no key is needed.
- LFO UNI → VCA CV: replaces Envelope 1 at the amplifier. LFO UNI only goes upwards from zero, so the amplifier goes from closed to fully open and back. The plain LFO jack would spend half of each cycle below zero, which is silence.
- RATE 1.2 (0.08 Hz), SHAPE sine, KEY SYNC off: one wave every 12 seconds or so. A sine swells and falls away evenly.
- VCA BIAS 1.5 (15%): holds the amplifier slightly open, so a quiet wash remains between waves. At zero there is silence between them.
- Listen for: without touching a key, the rush swells up and dies back.

steps.title: Brighter as it gets louder
steps.why:
The filter now moves with the waves, so each one gets brighter as it peaks. The keyboard gets a job of its own too.
- MOD DEPTH 1.6 (16%): the LFO is already wired to the cutoff; this sets how far. Most of an octave each way, in step with the loudness.
- ENV DEPTH 1.5 (15%): how far Envelope 2 lifts the cutoff.
- Envelope 2 at A 1.6 s, D 1.9 s, S 100%, R 2.6 s: very slow, and fully held while the key is down.
- Listen for: each wave getting brighter as it gets louder. Hold any key and the surf slowly brightens; let go and it darkens again.

steps.title: Patch S&H → ATT1 IN and ATT 1 → LFO RATE
steps.why:
The waves are still regular. The S&H (sample and hold) supplies a slowly wandering random voltage that speeds the LFO up and slows it down, so waves arrive unevenly.
- S&H → ATT1 IN, ATT 1 → LFO RATE: the random voltage goes through Attenuator 1 and is added to the LFO RATE knob.
- 1 at 5: how uneven the timing gets. The LFO can run anywhere from about a quarter to four times its set speed, though rarely at the extremes.
- S&H RATE 0 (0.26 Hz): a new random value about every four seconds.
- GLIDE 10 (1.0 s): slides to each new value, so the speed changes gradually. At zero it would change in sudden steps.
- Listen for: waves now 5 to 25 seconds apart, some close together, some after a long lull.

steps.title: Spread each wave out
steps.why:
A delay at the end blurs the noise, so each wave trails off instead of stopping.
- TIME 7 (240 ms): a medium gap. On noise this does not give clear echoes; it smears the sound.
- REPEATS 5 (50%): a fair number of repeats, each darker than the last.
- MIX 3 (30%): enough to lengthen the tail without washing out the wave.
- Listen for: the back of each wave fading more slowly. Turn MIX to zero to compare.

context.lfo.rate: In this sound one LFO cycle is one wave. 1.2 is about 12 seconds, before the random voltage speeds it up or slows it down.
context.lfo.shape: A sine gives waves that swell and fall away evenly.
context.vcf.freq: How dark the rush is between waves.
context.vcf.modDepth: How much brighter each wave gets at its peak.
context.vcf.envDepth: How far holding a key opens the filter.
context.vcf.reso: Gives the noise a faint pitch. Higher values turn the surf into wind.
context.vca.bias: The level of the wash that remains between waves. At zero there is silence between them.
context.att.1: How uneven the timing of the waves is.
context.sh.glide: Keeps the change of speed gradual. At zero the LFO would change speed in sudden steps.
context.delay.mix: How much of the blurred trail is heard behind each wave.

tweaks.hear: The rush gains a clear whistling pitch that rises and falls with each wave: wind instead of water.
The waves arrive at almost regular intervals, and the pattern soon sounds mechanical.
A wave every three seconds or so: closer to slow breathing.
Brighter, closer surf with more hiss at the top of each wave.

sounds.name: Arpeggio That Fades Itself In and Out
sounds.ref: In the style of Manuel Göttsching — "E2-E4"
sounds.blurb: Slow, soft arpeggio that swells up from silence and sinks back again every twenty seconds, getting brighter as it gets louder.
sounds.how: Attenuator 1 is voltage controlled: a voltage at ATT1 CV turns its level up and down, which makes it a small spare amplifier. Here it works on a control signal, not on audio. Envelope 1 is patched into ATT1 IN, LFO UNI into ATT1 CV, and ATT 1 into VCA CV in place of the usual direct connection. Every note still has its own plucked shape, but the LFO sets how much of it reaches the amplifier, so the whole pattern fades in and out over twenty seconds. The LFO also reaches the cutoff through MOD DEPTH, so the notes brighten as they get louder. The delay fills in behind.

steps.title: Two rounded oscillators
steps.why:
The oscillators (the circuits that make the raw tone) are set to soft, rounded waves for a bell-like base with a slow shimmer from a tiny detune.
- OSC MIX 0 (50 / 50): the mixer is a crossfader; the centre is an equal blend.
- SHAPE osc 1 3.4 (triangle towards sine): very few harmonics, so the notes stay round.
- SHAPE osc 2 3 (triangle), TUNE +0.1 st: a triangle a hair sharp, so the two beat slowly against each other.
- RANGE 8’ on both: normal pitch.
- Listen for: hold a note and hear a gentle, slow pulsing in the tone. Set TUNE osc 2 back to 0 and it goes still.

steps.title: A soft pluck on each note
steps.why:
Both envelopes shape each note into a soft pluck. Envelope 1 feeds the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) for loudness; Envelope 2 feeds the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) for brightness.
- Envelope 1 A 15 ms, D 1.2 s, S 0, R 750 ms: a quick but soft start, then a fade of just over a second with nothing held. Each arpeggio note is a pluck.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 5.8 (about 700 Hz), RESO 1.5: a half-closed filter keeps it mellow. Resonance adds only a faint edge.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking keeps the high notes of the pattern as bright as the low ones.
- ENV DEPTH 2.5 with Envelope 2 A 0, D 540 ms, S 0: opens the filter by about two octaves and closes it in half a second. More depth makes a brighter blip.
- Listen for: a small flash of brightness at the start of each note, then a mellow fade.

steps.title: Patch ENV 1 → ATT1 IN and ATT 1 → VCA CV
steps.why:
The patch bay reroutes Envelope 1 through Attenuator 1 on its way to the amplifier. Attenuator 1 is voltage controlled, so it can act as a spare amplifier for control signals; the next step uses that.
- ENV 1 → ATT1 IN: Envelope 1’s voltage goes into Attenuator 1.
- ATT 1 → VCA CV: replaces the direct connection from Envelope 1 to the amplifier.
- 1 at 7.6: sets the loudest the arpeggio will get. Here the envelope passes at about full strength.
- Listen for: nothing new yet. The arpeggio should sound exactly as it did; if it is quieter, turn ATT 1 up.

steps.title: Patch LFO UNI → ATT1 CV
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator, a slow wave that moves other settings) now turns Attenuator 1 up and down, so the whole arpeggio fades in and out by itself.
- LFO UNI → ATT1 CV: the voltage here sets how much Attenuator 1 lets through, from nothing to full. LFO UNI only goes upwards from zero, so each cycle runs from silence to full and back.
- RATE 0.8 (0.05 Hz), SHAPE sine, KEY SYNC off: one cycle every 20 seconds, an even swell, free-running. The arpeggio is silent for a few seconds at the bottom.
- MOD DEPTH 1.5 (15%): the same LFO is already wired to the cutoff, so notes get brighter as they get louder.
- Listen for: start the riff and leave it. It rises from nothing, peaks bright and sinks away again.

steps.title: Delay for space
steps.why:
A long delay at the end lets the echoes outlast the notes as the pattern fades out.
- DRIVE 0: the overdrive is always in the path; at zero it adds no grit.
- TIME 8.6 (410 ms): long enough for clear echoes between the notes.
- REPEATS 5.5 (55%): how long the echoes last, each one darker than the last on this analogue delay.
- MIX 3 (30%): echoes well behind the notes.
- Listen for: in the quiet part of the cycle, the echoes are the last thing left before silence.

context.att.1: In this sound this is the loudest the arpeggio gets, at the top of the LFO’s cycle. At 7.6 Envelope 1 passes through at about full strength.
context.lfo.rate: How long one fade in and out takes: 20 seconds here.
context.lfo.shape: A sine gives an even swell. The arpeggio is silent for a few seconds at the bottom of each cycle.
context.vcf.modDepth: How much brighter the notes are at the loud part of the cycle than at the quiet part.
context.vcf.envDepth: The small pluck of brightness at the start of each note.
context.env1.d: The length of each note. It is this envelope that the LFO turns up and down.
context.delay.mix: How loud the echoes are. They carry on for a moment after the notes have faded out.

tweaks.hear: The arpeggio swells and fades every five seconds, in and out of step with the pattern.
A long build from silence, then a sudden drop back to nothing.
The quiet notes are very dull and the loud ones clearly brighter, so the pattern seems to come closer and move away.
The whole cycle is quieter, and the silent part lasts longer.

sounds.name: Strings Whose Upper Octave Fades In
sounds.ref: In the style of Angelo Badalamenti — "Laura Palmer’s Theme" ("Twin Peaks")
sounds.blurb: Low, soft string line where each held note starts dark and plain, then gains an upper octave and a little brightness over two seconds.
sounds.how: OSC MIX sets one fixed balance between the oscillators. To change that balance during a note, the patch bay has to do the mixing. Oscillator 1, the low voice, goes straight into summer 1. Oscillator 2, an octave higher, goes through Attenuator 1 first, and Envelope 2 is patched into ATT1 CV, so Attenuator 1 works as a small amplifier that Envelope 2 opens slowly. The summer adds the two and its output goes into VCF IN in place of the normal mix. Short notes are nearly all Oscillator 1. Hold a note and the upper octave arrives gradually, and because Envelope 2 also drives ENV DEPTH, the filter opens a little at the same time.

steps.title: Two softened sawtooths an octave apart
steps.why:
Two sawtooths an octave apart give the string body. Later the patch bay makes the upper one fade in over each note, so for now just set the tones.
- SHAPE osc 1 2.4, osc 2 2.6 (saw towards triangle): the saw’s string-like buzz with some edge taken off. Turn left for brighter strings.
- RANGE osc 1 16’, TUNE 0: the low voice, an octave below normal.
- RANGE osc 2 8’, TUNE a hair sharp: the octave above, detuned too little to show on the chip.
- Listen for: OSC MIX is still fully left from the start patch, so you only hear the low voice. The upper octave comes in once it is patched.

steps.title: Bowed loudness, warm filter
steps.why:
Envelope 1 gives a bowed start through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier), and the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) sets a warm base tone.
- Envelope 1 A 270 ms, D 820 ms, S 80%, R 1.5 s: a soft quarter-second start and a long fade after release.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 6 (about 800 Hz), RESO 1: dark and warm before Envelope 2 opens it later.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking moves the cutoff with the notes, so the top of the line keeps its brightness.
- DRIVE 0, LEVEL 6.5: no grit from the overdrive stage, and its output comes down because the patched mix in the next steps is louder than the normal one.
- Listen for: a slow, soft start to each note, and a warm, rounded tone.

steps.title: Patch OSC 1 → SUM 1(A), OSC 2 → ATT1 IN, ATT 1 → SUM 1(B), SUM 1 → VCF IN
steps.why:
The patch bay replaces the oscillator mixer with a mix you can control from an envelope. Summer 1 adds two signals together, and Attenuator 1 sets the level of one of them.
- OSC 1 → SUM 1(A): the low voice goes in at full level.
- OSC 2 → ATT1 IN, ATT 1 → SUM 1(B): the upper octave goes in through Attenuator 1, so its knob is now Oscillator 2’s level.
- SUM 1 → VCF IN: replaces the normal mix at the filter’s input. OSC MIX no longer does anything.
- 1 at 4: the upper octave is clearly there but quieter than the low voice. More makes a brighter, more organ-like blend.
- Listen for: both octaves now sound together on every note.

steps.title: Patch ENV 2 → ATT1 CV
steps.why:
Envelope 2 now opens Attenuator 1 slowly, so each note starts dark with only the low voice and the upper octave blooms in as you hold it. Attenuator 1 is voltage controlled, which makes it a small amplifier here.
- ENV 2 → ATT1 CV: sets how much Attenuator 1 passes, up to the level of its knob.
- Envelope 2 A 1.9 s: nearly two seconds for the upper octave to arrive.
- D 1.9 s, S 80%, R 1.7 s: it settles just below full and fades out slowly.
- ENV DEPTH 1.2 (12%): the same envelope opens the filter by about an octave as the upper octave comes in.
- Listen for: play a short note, then a long one. The short one is nearly all low voice; the long one grows brighter and gains the octave.

steps.title: A quiet echo
steps.why:
The delay adds a little depth behind the line without getting in its way.
- TIME 7.5 (280 ms): a medium gap, heard as a soft doubling rather than a clear echo on slow lines.
- REPEATS 4 (40%): a few repeats, each darker than the one before.
- MIX 2.5 (25%): low, so the strings stay in front.
- Listen for: a faint trail after each note. Turn MIX to zero to hear how much drier it sounds.

context.att.1: In this sound this is the most the upper octave can reach, once Envelope 2 has fully risen.
context.env2.a: How long the upper octave takes to arrive: nearly two seconds here.
context.env2.s: Where the upper octave settles on a long note, as a share of the ATT 1 setting.
context.vcf.envDepth: How much the filter opens as the upper octave comes in.
context.osc.mix: Bypassed. The cable into VCF IN replaces the mixer, so the balance is set by ATT 1 and Envelope 2.
context.osc2.range: Puts Oscillator 2 an octave above Oscillator 1.
context.env1.a: The soft, bowed start of each note.
context.vcf.freq: The brightness of the strings before Envelope 2 opens the filter.
context.od.level: Pulled back because the patched mix is louder than the normal one.

tweaks.hear: The upper octave is there almost from the start, and the sound is an ordinary two-octave string patch.
On long notes the upper octave ends up nearly as loud as the low voice, so the line seems to rise an octave as you hold it.
A fifth fades in above each held note instead of an octave, which sounds more like an organ stop.
The octave still fades in, but the tone stays as dark as it started.

sounds.name: Soft Keys Whose Brightness Catches Up
sounds.ref: In the style of Harold Budd and Brian Eno — "First Light" ("Ambient 2: The Plateaux of Mirror")
sounds.blurb: Soft, slowly fading keys where a leap upwards starts muted and clears over a second, and a leap downwards starts bright and mellows.
sounds.how: KEY TRK makes the cutoff follow the keyboard at once. This patch makes it follow late. ASSIGN carries the keyboard pitch as a voltage; the slew limiter slows it down, and the result goes into FREQ MOD, with MOD DEPTH at 2 so that one octave on the keys moves the cutoff one octave. KEY TRK itself stays off. The cutoff ends up in the right place for every note, but takes a second or so to get there. After a jump up, the filter is still set for the low note, so the new note begins dull and opens. After a jump down it is still set for the high note, so the new note begins bright and closes, like a firmer touch.

steps.title: Two mellow oscillators
steps.why:
Both oscillators (the circuits that make the raw tone) are set to mellow waves for a soft keys tone that still has a little brightness for the filter to work on.
- OSC MIX 0 (50 / 50): the mixer is a crossfader; the centre is an equal blend.
- SHAPE osc 1 2.7 (saw towards triangle): mostly triangle, with a little saw buzz kept in.
- SHAPE osc 2 3.4 (triangle towards sine): round and soft, for body.
- RANGE 8’ on both, TUNE osc 2 a hair sharp: too little to show on the chip, but it keeps the unison from sounding static.
- Listen for: a soft, electric-piano-like tone that holds while the key is down.

steps.title: A soft strike that fades slowly
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) into a soft strike that fades slowly, like a struck key.
- A 2.5 (3 ms): a few milliseconds, enough to take the click off without softening the start.
- D 8.3 (2.4 s): the note falls over a couple of seconds.
- S 2.5 (25%): it settles low while the key stays down.
- R 8.2 (1.3 s): rings on after release.
- Listen for: each note starting clearly and dying away even while held.

steps.title: A half-closed filter, no key tracking
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is half closed and deliberately does not follow the keyboard, ready for the patch bay to do the tracking late.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 5.7 (about 650 Hz), RESO 1.5: soft and warm, with a faint edge.
- KEY TRK off: key tracking is off because the next step builds its own, slower version.
- ENV DEPTH 1 with Envelope 2 A 0, D 360 ms, S 0: a short lift of brightness, heard as a slight knock at the front of each note.
- Listen for: high notes sound duller than low ones, because the cutoff stays put. The patch fixes that.

steps.title: Patch ASSIGN → SLEW IN and SLEW → FREQ MOD
steps.why:
The patch bay makes the cutoff follow the keys, but late. ASSIGN carries the keyboard pitch as a voltage, and the slew limiter slows its jumps into slides.
- ASSIGN → SLEW IN: the keyboard pitch goes into the slew limiter.
- SLEW → FREQ MOD: replaces the LFO that normally feeds the cutoff.
- SLEW 9 (1.3 s): about a second to settle on each new note. At zero this is plain key tracking.
- MOD DEPTH 2 (20%): one octave on the keys moves the cutoff one octave. At 1 high notes stay a bit duller.
- Listen for: play a low note, then one two octaves higher. The high note starts muffled and clears; jump back down and the low note starts bright and mellows.

steps.title: Clean, with a long quiet echo
steps.why:
The last stage keeps it clean and adds a long, quiet echo.
- DRIVE 0: no overdrive grit.
- TIME 9 (460 ms): a long gap, so each note repeats behind the next.
- REPEATS 5 (50%): several repeats, each darker than the one before.
- MIX 3 (30%): echoes well behind the dry notes.
- Listen for: slow single notes leaving a soft trail under the next one.

context.slew.time: In this sound this is how long the brightness takes to catch up with a new note. At zero the patch behaves like ordinary key tracking.
context.vcf.modDepth: How closely the cutoff follows the keys once it has caught up. At 2 it follows them exactly; at 1 it follows half way, so high notes stay a little duller.
context.vcf.freq: The cutoff for middle C. Every other note ends up the same distance above its own pitch.
context.vcf.keyTrk: Off, because the patch bay is doing the tracking. Switch it on as well and the cutoff moves twice as far as the notes.
context.vcf.envDepth: A slight knock of brightness at the front of each note.
context.env1.d: How long each note takes to fade to its low sustain level.

tweaks.hear: The brightness takes about three seconds to catch up, so after a big leap upwards most of the note is muffled.
The lag is too short to hear, and every note has the same tone, as with KEY TRK.
The moving cutoff becomes easy to follow: a soft "wow" upwards after a rising leap and downwards after a falling one.
The cutoff now moves twice as far as the notes, so high notes finish much brighter than low ones.

sounds.name: Strings Where One Oscillator Arrives Late
sounds.ref: In the style of Stars of the Lid — "Requiem for Dying Mothers, Part 2" ("The Tired Sounds of Stars of the Lid")
sounds.blurb: Soft string line in which one oscillator lands on each new note straight away and the other slides slowly up or down to join it.
sounds.how: PORTA TIME slides both oscillators together. To slide only one, the patch bay has to build the slide itself. ASSIGN carries the keyboard pitch as a voltage, and MULT makes two copies of it. One copy goes through the slew limiter, which makes it lag behind; the other goes through the inverter, which turns it upside down. Summer 1 adds the two, and the result is the difference between the lagging pitch and the real one: large just after a new note, shrinking to nothing as the slew limiter catches up. Through Attenuator 1 that difference is added to Oscillator 2’s pitch. Oscillator 2 therefore starts every note where the last one was and slides into place, while Oscillator 1 is already there.

steps.title: Two softened sawtooths
steps.why:
The oscillators start as a plain string tone: two sawtooths with their edge softened, in unison. The late slide on one oscillator is patched in later.
- OSC MIX 0 (50 / 50): the mixer is a crossfader. Here it is the balance between the oscillator that will jump and the one that will slide.
- SHAPE osc 1 2.4, osc 2 2.6 (saw towards triangle): string buzz with some edge taken off.
- RANGE 8’ on both, TUNE osc 2 a hair sharp: too small to show on the chip, but enough that the unison is not completely still.
- Listen for: a smooth, even string tone.

steps.title: Bowed loudness
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) into a bowed start and a long tail.
- A 6.8 (220 ms): about a fifth of a second. Slow enough to sound bowed, quick enough that the start of the slide is still heard. Much longer and the slide is over before the note is loud.
- D 7 (820 ms), S 8 (80%): eases down a little and holds.
- R 8.3 (1.5 s): a second and a half of fade after release.
- Listen for: a soft swell into each note, and a tail that overlaps the next.

steps.title: A warm filter
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) warms the strings and opens a little as notes are held.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 6.3 (about 1 kHz), RESO 1: warm, with a trace of edge.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking keeps high notes as bright as low ones.
- ENV DEPTH 1.5 (15%): how far Envelope 2 lifts the cutoff.
- Envelope 2 A 440 ms, D 1.9 s, S 50%, R 1.1 s: a slow rise and slow fall, so held notes gently open and settle.
- Listen for: a long note getting slightly brighter after its start.

steps.title: Patch ASSIGN → MULT, MULT 1 → SLEW IN, MULT 2 → INVERT IN
steps.why:
The patch bay starts building a slide for one oscillator only. ASSIGN is the keyboard pitch as a voltage; MULT copies it so it can be treated two ways.
- ASSIGN → MULT: two copies of the keyboard pitch.
- MULT 1 → SLEW IN: the slew limiter turns each jump in pitch into a slide.
- MULT 2 → INVERT IN: the inverter gives the same pitch upside down, with no lag.
- SLEW 9 (1.3 s): a little over a second for the slide to finish. This will be how long Oscillator 2 takes to arrive.
- Listen for: nothing yet. These cables only prepare the two signals.

steps.title: Patch SLEW → SUM 1(A), INVERT → SUM 1(B), SUM 1 → ATT1 IN, ATT 1 → OSC 2
steps.why:
The two signals are added, which leaves only the lag: zero on a held note, and a voltage the size of the jump just after a new one. That goes to Oscillator 2’s pitch, so it arrives late while Oscillator 1 is already there.
- SLEW → SUM 1(A), INVERT → SUM 1(B): summer 1 adds the lagging pitch to the inverted pitch.
- SUM 1 → ATT1 IN, ATT 1 → OSC 2: Attenuator 1 scales the difference and adds it to Oscillator 2’s pitch.
- 1 at 5.1: about half the voltage, because the OSC 2 input moves pitch twice as far as the keyboard does. At 5.1 the slide starts on the previous note; lower starts part way, higher overshoots.
- Listen for: play two notes a fifth apart. One oscillator lands at once; the other slides from the old note to the new one.

steps.title: Clean, with a short quiet echo
steps.why:
The last stage keeps the tone clean and adds a little depth.
- DRIVE 0: no overdrive grit.
- TIME 7.5 (280 ms): a medium gap.
- REPEATS 4 (40%): a few repeats, each darker than the last.
- MIX 2.5 (25%): quiet, behind the line.
- Listen for: a soft trail that keeps the slides audible after you let go.

context.slew.time: In this sound this is how long Oscillator 2 takes to arrive on each new note: a little over a second at 9.
context.att.1: Sets where Oscillator 2’s slide starts from. At 5.1 it starts on the previous note. Lower, and it starts part of the way there; higher, and it starts beyond the previous note and has further to travel.
context.osc.mix: The balance between the oscillator that jumps and the one that slides.
context.osc2.tune: A very small detune, so the two oscillators still beat slowly once the slide has finished.
context.env1.a: A soft start. Make it much longer and the slide is over before the note is loud enough to hear it.
context.vcf.freq: The brightness of the strings.
context.porta.time: Left at zero. It would slide both oscillators, which is the ordinary effect this patch avoids.

tweaks.hear: Oscillator 2 arrives in about a fifth of a second: a quick scoop into each note instead of a long slide.
The slide starts beyond the previous note, so after a leap upwards Oscillator 2 begins lower than where it left off.
Only the sliding oscillator is heard, which sounds like ordinary portamento. Turn fully left and there is no slide at all.
The sliding voice is now an octave below, like a cello following a violin.

sounds.name: Tenor Saxophone Line
sounds.ref: In the style of a tenor saxophone solo
sounds.blurb: Solo lead with the reedy body and slight rasp of a tenor saxophone, played as one long legato line.
sounds.how: A sawtooth carries the body and a pulse tuned a few cents above it beats slowly against it, which is what stops the tone sitting still. The low-pass filter rests near 1 kHz with enough resonance to leave a peak in the middle of the range, where a saxophone is strongest, and KEY TRK keeps the top of the line as bright as the bottom. The rasp comes from the patch bay: Oscillator 1 is patched back into FREQ MOD, so the cutoff is shaken at the pitch of the note itself and the tone gains a hard edge that moves with the melody. A little noise and some overdrive finish the body. Envelope 1 holds at nearly full level and takes about 23 ms to speak, so the line sounds blown rather than struck.

steps.title: A sawtooth with a pulse beside it
steps.why:
A sawtooth and a narrow pulse, slightly apart in tuning, make the reedy body of the sound. The slow beating between them keeps the tone from sitting still, as a player’s breath does.
- SHAPE osc 1 2 (saw), RANGE 8’: the saw carries every harmonic and gives the body.
- SHAPE osc 2 1 (pulse), WIDTH 3.4 (36%): a pulse about a third of the way narrow. Narrower is more nasal and cuts through more.
- TUNE osc 2 +0.1 st: about 14 cents up. At 0 the tone goes still and sounds more like an organ.
- OSC MIX −1.2 (62 / 38): the mixer is a crossfader. Just left of centre keeps the saw in front; further right is thinner.
- Listen for: hold a note and hear the slow beating between the two.

steps.title: Low-pass with a peak in the middle
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) leaves a resonant peak in the middle of the range, where a saxophone pushes hardest. That peak is most of what separates a reed from a plain filtered saw.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 6.4 (about 1.1 kHz): where the peak sits.
- RESO 4.2: resonance, the size of the peak. More sounds more nasal and vocal.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking moves the peak up with the notes so the top of the line does not go dull.
- ENV DEPTH 1.8 with Envelope 2 A 39 ms, D 360 ms, S 65%, R 95 ms: the filter opens by about an octave and a half over the first 40 ms, then settles. That is the reed starting to speak.
- Listen for: a slightly soft onset that brightens into the note.

steps.title: Blown, not struck
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) so each note sounds blown, not struck, and portamento joins the notes.
- A 4.4 (22 ms): takes the front edge off. Shorter than about 10 ms and it starts to sound struck.
- D 360 ms, S 9.5 (95%): a long note holds at nearly full level instead of sagging.
- R 5 (95 ms): the line stops when you stop.
- PORTA TIME 1 (100 ms): portamento, a short pitch slide between notes. Keep it short: a player moving between notes, not a swoop.
- Listen for: slurred notes joining up instead of stepping.

steps.title: A little air in the tone
steps.why:
A thin layer of noise goes into the filter with the oscillators, for the air inside a blown note.
- NOISE 1.4 (14%): white noise mixed in before the filter. It is not meant to be heard on its own.
- Listen for: turn NOISE to 0 and back. Without it the tone is drier and more electronic.

steps.title: Overdrive for the reed edge
steps.why:
The overdrive, always in the path after the filter, adds the reed’s edge. A short, quiet delay puts the line in a room.
- DRIVE 3.2: rounds off the top of the wave and adds harmonics above the filter peak. It also evens out the beating a little.
- TONE 5.5: just above centre keeps some bite. Left is rounder; right is thinner and brighter.
- LEVEL 7.5: the stage’s output level.
- TIME 230 ms, REPEATS 30%, MIX 1.5 (15%): a short echo, kept low, for a sense of space.
- Listen for: a grittier edge on loud held notes, and a small room behind the line.

steps.title: Patch OSC 1 → FREQ MOD
steps.why:
The patch bay adds the rasp. Oscillator 1 shakes the filter cutoff at the pitch of the note, which gives a hard, reedy edge that moves with the melody.
- OSC 1 → FREQ MOD: replaces the LFO that normally feeds the cutoff with Oscillator 1, running at audio rate.
- MOD DEPTH 0.9 (9%): the cutoff moves about half an octave, hundreds of times a second. Above about 2 the tone turns into a growl. The mod wheel no longer reaches it with a cable here, so set it by hand.
- Listen for: no wobble, but a hard, buzzy edge. Pull MOD DEPTH to 0 and back to hear what the cable adds.

context.osc.mix: The balance between the saw body and the pulse. Further right is thinner and more nasal.
context.osc2.tune: The small gap that makes the two oscillators beat. At 0 the tone goes still and sounds more like an organ.
context.osc2.width: How narrow the second oscillator’s pulse is. Narrower is more nasal and cuts through more.
context.vcf.freq: Where the resonant peak sits, and so which part of the range the line pushes hardest.
context.vcf.reso: The size of that peak. This is most of what separates a reed tone from a plain filtered saw.
context.vcf.keyTrk: On, so the peak moves up with the notes and the top of the line stays even.
context.vcf.envDepth: How much the filter opens as each note speaks.
context.vcf.modDepth: The amount of rasp from the cable. Above about 2 the tone turns into a growl. The mod wheel does not reach it: the wheel only turns this knob for the LFO it normally scales, and the cable into FREQ MOD has taken that place, so this one is ridden by hand.
context.env1.a: How long the note takes to speak. Shorter than about 10 ms and it starts to sound struck.
context.env1.s: Held at 9.5 so a long note does not sag.
context.env1.r: Short, so the line stops when you stop.
context.porta.time: The slide between notes. Keep it short: this is a player moving between notes, not a swoop.
context.od.drive: Adds harmonics above the filter peak and evens out the beating between the oscillators.

tweaks.try: Raise from 0.9 to 2.5 while a long note sounds
tweaks.hear: The rasp grows into a growl. This is the knob to ride part-way through a held note rather than set and leave.
The peak moves from a dark, subtone register to a bright, hard one.
From a still, organ-like tone to an obvious wavering.
From a tongued note to a very soft one that arrives late.

sounds.name: Open Trumpet Line
sounds.ref: In the style of an open trumpet solo
sounds.blurb: Bright solo line with the front-heavy bloom of an open trumpet.
sounds.how: One sawtooth does all the work. The character is in the filter: it rests dark, and Envelope 2 opens it by nearly three octaves over the first tenth of a second, which is the lip taking a moment to settle. Some resonance puts an edge on the peak of that bloom. KEY TRK pushes the cutoff up with the notes, so the line gets brighter as it rises, the way a trumpet does. Envelope 1 holds at nearly full level with a short release, and a tenth of a second of portamento joins slurred notes without letting them swoop.

steps.title: One sawtooth
steps.why:
Only Oscillator 1 is used, and it does all the work. The trumpet character comes from the filter later; this step just picks a raw tone with plenty in it.
- OSC MIX −5: the mixer is a crossfader, and fully left means only Oscillator 1 (the circuit that makes the tone) is heard.
- SHAPE 2 (saw): a sawtooth carries every harmonic, which gives the filter something bright to open onto.
- RANGE 8’, TUNE 0: normal pitch, in tune.
- Listen for: a bright, buzzy note. It is too raw for a trumpet until the filter shapes it.

steps.title: A filter that blooms open
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) rests dark, and Envelope 2 opens it quickly on each note. That bloom is the brassy “bwah” of a lip settling into the note.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 5.5 (about 560 Hz): the tone before and after the bloom, dull and covered on its own.
- RESO 3.4: resonance puts an edge on the peak of the bloom. Too much and the note whistles.
- ENV DEPTH 3.4 (34%): Envelope 2 lifts the cutoff nearly three octaves. This is the size of the bloom.
- Envelope 2 A 84 ms, D 420 ms, S 60%, R 95 ms: the rise takes about 85 ms, which reads as a trumpet; much shorter becomes a synth stab. It then settles at a bright level while held.
- Listen for: the “bwah” at the front of each note.

steps.title: Brighter as the line rises
steps.why:
Key tracking makes the filter follow the keyboard, so the line gets brighter as it rises, the way a trumpet does when played higher.
- KEY TRK on: the cutoff moves up with the played note, so the top of the phrase comes out harder than the bottom.
- Listen for: switch KEY TRK on and off while the riff plays. With it off, the high notes sound covered.

steps.title: Held loudness, short release
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier): a tongued start, solid held notes and a quick stop. Portamento joins slurred notes.
- A 3.9 (13 ms): quick enough to sound tongued, slow enough not to click.
- D 360 ms, S 9.5 (95%): long notes hold at nearly full level instead of fading under you.
- R 4.8 (80 ms): the line stops dead when you lift.
- PORTA TIME 0.9 (81 ms): portamento, a short pitch slide between notes. Enough to slur overlapping notes without a swoop.
- Listen for: play legato and hear the notes join; play detached and each one starts clean.

steps.title: A little drive and a short room
steps.why:
The overdrive, always in the path after the filter, adds the hard edge a trumpet has at the top of each bloom. A quiet delay stops it sounding dry.
- DRIVE 3: adds hard upper harmonics when the filter is open. More turns it into a distorted lead.
- TONE 6: above centre keeps those harmonics bright. Left would round them off.
- LEVEL 7.5: the stage’s output level.
- TIME 240 ms, REPEATS 30%, MIX 1.5 (15%): a short, quiet echo, like a small room.
- Listen for: extra bite at the peak of each bloom. MOD DEPTH is still at 0; push the mod wheel to bring the LFO onto the filter for movement on long notes.

context.vcf.freq: The tone at the start and end of each note, before and after the bloom.
context.vcf.envDepth: How far the filter opens: the size of the bloom.
context.env2.a: How long the bloom takes. Around 85 ms it reads as a trumpet; much shorter and it becomes a synth stab.
context.env2.s: The brightness the note settles at while the key is down.
context.vcf.reso: Puts an edge on the peak of the bloom. Too much and the note starts to whistle.
context.vcf.keyTrk: On, so the line brightens as it rises. Switch it off and the top of the phrase sounds covered.
context.env1.s: Held high so a long note does not fade under you.
context.env1.r: Short, so the line stops when you stop.
context.porta.time: A tenth of a second of slide, enough to slur overlapping notes together.
context.od.drive: The hard edge at the top of the bloom.
context.vcf.modDepth: Left at 0, with the LFO already wired to the cutoff through it. The mod wheel turns this knob further, so the movement arrives when you push the wheel and not before.

tweaks.try: Set LFO RATE to 4.8, then push the mod wheel a third of the way up while a long note sounds
tweaks.hear: A vibrato in the brightness fades in as the wheel rises, the way a player leans on a held note.
From a hard stab at one end to a slow swell into each note at the other.
A muted trumpet: the bloom is still there but the note never opens far.
The dark part of each note goes, leaving a bright, thin line with much less bloom.

sounds.name: Clarinet Solo
sounds.ref: In the style of a clarinet in its low register
sounds.blurb: Hollow, woody solo line with a vibrato that fades in by itself as each note is held.
sounds.how: A clarinet is a tube closed at one end, so it makes mostly odd harmonics. A square wave does the same thing, which is why Oscillator 1 is a pulse with WIDTH at the centre. The filter is set high with almost no envelope on it, because the tone of a clarinet barely changes as a note speaks. The interesting part is the vibrato. Three cables send the LFO through Attenuator 1 to both oscillators’ pitch, and Envelope 2 controls how far Attenuator 1 is open. With Envelope 2 given an attack of about three quarters of a second, the vibrato is absent when the note starts and arrives part-way through, which is how a player uses it.

steps.title: A square wave
steps.why:
The hollow, woody part of a clarinet tone comes from a square wave. A clarinet is a tube closed at one end, so it makes mostly odd harmonics, and a square does the same.
- OSC MIX −5: the mixer is a crossfader, and fully left means only Oscillator 1 is heard.
- SHAPE 1 (pulse): the pulse wave, whose tone is set by WIDTH.
- WIDTH 5 (50%): the centre gives a true square, odd harmonics only. Move it either way and the clarinet turns nasal.
- RANGE 8’, TUNE 0: normal pitch.
- Listen for: a hollow, buzzy tone. Nudge WIDTH off centre and hear it get thinner and reedier.

steps.title: Low-pass, high, with no envelope on it
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) takes the fizz off the square but stays fairly open. It does not move as the note speaks, because a clarinet’s tone barely changes; Envelope 2 has another job here.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 6.2 (about 930 Hz): how much fizz is left. Lower gives the darker bottom register.
