- RESO 1: resonance kept low on purpose. A clarinet has no strong peak; adding one makes it a synth lead again.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking keeps the tone even from the bottom of the line to the top.
- ENV DEPTH 0: Envelope 2 has no effect on the filter.
- Listen for: a softer, woodier square with the harsh top gone.

steps.title: Blown loudness
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) so notes sound blown and stop cleanly. Portamento slurs the line.
- A 4.6 (26 ms): how long each note takes to speak. Shorter starts to sound struck.
- D 360 ms, S 10 (100%): a held note stays at one level.
- R 5 (95 ms): the line stops when you stop.
- PORTA TIME 0.9 (81 ms): portamento, a short pitch slide between overlapping notes.
- Listen for: legato notes joined by a small slur.

steps.title: A slow LFO ready for vibrato
steps.why:
The LFO (low-frequency oscillator, a slow wave that moves other settings) is set up for vibrato. Nothing is audible yet: it has no route to the pitch until the cables go in.
- RATE 4.8 (4.74 Hz): about the speed a player uses for vibrato.
- SHAPE 0 (sine): a smooth, even wave, so the pitch rises and falls evenly.
- KEY SYNC on: restarts the LFO on each note, so the vibrato always grows in from the same point in its cycle.

steps.title: Patch LFO → ATT1 IN, ENV 2 → ATT1 CV, ATT 1 → OSC 1+2
steps.why:
The patch bay turns Attenuator 1 into a gate for the vibrato. Attenuator 1 is voltage controlled, so a voltage at ATT1 CV sets how much of its input gets through.
- LFO → ATT1 IN: the vibrato wave goes into Attenuator 1.
- ATT 1 → OSC 1+2: its output goes to both oscillators’ pitch.
- ENV 2 → ATT1 CV: Envelope 2 sets how far Attenuator 1 is open, so the vibrato is only as deep as Envelope 2 is high.
- 1 at 0.7: the widest the vibrato can go, about four tenths of a semitone either way. More sounds wobbly and unmusical.
- Listen for: a gentle vibrato on held notes. For now it arrives almost at once and settles at half depth, because Envelope 2 is still at its default settings.

steps.title: Clean, with a little room
steps.why:
The last stage keeps the tone clean, sets the level and adds a little room.
- DRIVE 0: the overdrive is always in the path. Any grit here turns the woody tone into a synth lead.
- LEVEL 6: a square wave is strong, so the output comes down to sit with other sounds.
- TIME 260 ms, REPEATS 30%, MIX 1.5 (15%): a short delay low in the mix gives the line some space.
- Listen for: a cleaner, slightly quieter clarinet with a faint room behind it.

steps.title: Make Envelope 2 arrive late
steps.why:
Envelope 2 now only opens the vibrato gate, so giving it a slow attack makes the vibrato arrive part-way through each note, the way a player adds it.
- A 8 (720 ms): about three quarters of a second before the vibrato is fully in.
- D 360 ms, S 10 (100%): full sustain, so the vibrato stays once it has arrived.
- R 4 (41 ms): drops away quickly when you let go.
- Listen for: each held note starts straight and the vibrato grows in. Short notes never get any.

context.osc1.width: At the centre this is a true square, which is the odd-harmonic tone the patch is built on. Move it either way and the clarinet turns nasal.
context.vcf.freq: How much fizz is left on the square. Lower is a darker chalumeau register.
context.vcf.reso: Kept low on purpose. A clarinet has no strong peak; adding one makes it sound like a synth lead again.
context.vcf.keyTrk: On, so the tone stays even from the bottom of the line to the top.
context.vcf.envDepth: Zero, because Envelope 2 is being used for the vibrato instead of the filter.
context.env1.a: How long each note takes to speak.
context.env1.s: Full, so a held note stays at one level.
context.env1.r: Short, so the line stops when you stop.
context.porta.time: The slur between overlapping notes.
context.att.1: The widest the vibrato can go. At 0.7 that is about four tenths of a semitone either way.
context.env2.a: How long a note must be held before the vibrato is fully in. At 8 that is about three quarters of a second.
context.env2.s: Full, so the vibrato stays once it has arrived.
context.lfo.rate: The speed of the vibrato, about 4.7 Hz.
context.lfo.keySync: Restarts the LFO on each note, so the vibrato always grows in from the same point in its cycle.
context.od.level: The output level. A square wave is strong, so this sits below the usual setting.

tweaks.hear: The vibrato arrives almost at once at one end, and only on the longest notes at the other.
A much wider vibrato, closer to a folk fiddle than a clarinet.
The square becomes a narrow pulse and the tone turns thin and nasal — nearer an oboe than a clarinet.
A slow, lazy waver at one end and a tight flutter at the other.

sounds.name: Bassoon Solo
sounds.ref: In the style of a bassoon solo
sounds.blurb: Dark, buzzing solo line low down, with a soft front on every note.
sounds.how: The Neutron is at its best low down, and so is a bassoon. Oscillator 1 sits between pulse and sawtooth with its WIDTH narrowed, which gives the double-reed buzz, and a sine beside it, also at 16’, puts weight underneath. The low-pass filter is well closed at about 450 Hz so only the bottom of that buzz gets through, and KEY TRK keeps the upper notes of the line from disappearing. Both envelopes have a soft front: the filter takes about 55 ms to open and the loudness about 40 ms, which is how long the two reeds take to start moving.

steps.title: A narrow pulse with a sine under it
steps.why:
A narrowed pulse blended into a saw gives the double-reed buzz of a bassoon, and a sine an octave below normal puts weight underneath.
- SHAPE osc 1 1.6 (pulse towards saw): mostly sawtooth with some pulse. Towards 2 the buzz smooths out; towards 1 it gets more hollow.
- WIDTH osc 1 3 (32%): narrows the pulse part so it buzzes harder.
- SHAPE osc 2 4 (sine): a clean fundamental with no harmonics of its own.
- RANGE 16’ on both, TUNE 0: an octave below normal, where the Neutron and a bassoon both sit well.
- OSC MIX −2.6 (76 / 24): the mixer is a crossfader. Left of centre keeps the buzz in front; further right is rounder.
- Listen for: a low, bright buzz with a solid bottom.

steps.title: Low-pass, well closed
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is well closed so only the bottom of the buzz gets through. This is the main darkness control.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 5.2 (about 450 Hz): only the first few harmonics pass, so the tone is dark but still clearly buzzing. Above about 6 it turns into a synth bass.
- RESO 2.6: resonance, a small lift at the cutoff that gives the buzz a focus.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking stops the upper notes of the line from going dull.
- Listen for: a dark, covered reed tone. Play high and low and hear the tone stay even.

steps.title: A soft front on the tone
steps.why:
Envelope 2 gives the tone a soft front, how long the two reeds take to start moving.
- ENV DEPTH 1.6 (16%): opens the filter by about one and a quarter octaves.
- A 5.4 (57 ms): how long that opening takes; the length of the soft front.
- D 420 ms, S 60%, R 95 ms: settles back part way while the note is held.
- Listen for: a soft “woh” at the start of each note rather than an edge.

steps.title: Soft front on the loudness too
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) with a soft front of its own. Low notes with a hard start click; this one does not.
- A 5 (39 ms): the soft front on the loudness. Take it to 0 and every low note clicks.
- D 360 ms, S 9.5 (95%): long notes stay solid.
- R 5.2 (110 ms): the line stops when you stop.
- PORTA TIME 1.1 (120 ms): portamento, a pitch slide of about an eighth of a second between notes.
- Listen for: notes that speak softly and slur into each other.

steps.title: A little warmth
steps.why:
The overdrive after the filter thickens the low end, and a short delay gives the line some space.
- DRIVE 1.8: warmth rather than distortion. Above about 4 it turns into fuzz.
- TONE 4: below centre, so the added harmonics stay round and do not fizz.
- LEVEL 7.5: the stage’s output level.
- TIME 210 ms, REPEATS 30%, MIX 1.5 (15%): a short, quiet echo.
- Listen for: a slightly thicker, fuller bottom. Sweep DRIVE up past 4 to hear the point where it stops being a bassoon.

context.osc1.shape: At 1.6 this is a sawtooth with some pulse in it. Towards 2 the buzz smooths out; towards 1 it gets more hollow.
context.osc1.width: How narrow the pulse part is. Narrower buzzes harder, which is the double-reed part of the sound.
context.osc.mix: The balance between the buzz and the sine underneath it. Further right is rounder and less reedy.
context.vcf.freq: The main darkness control. Above about 6 the line stops sounding like a bassoon and starts sounding like a synth bass.
context.vcf.reso: A small lift at the cutoff, enough to give the buzz a focus.
context.vcf.keyTrk: On, so the upper notes of the line keep the same tone as the lower ones.
context.vcf.envDepth: How far the filter opens as the note speaks.
context.env2.a: The length of the soft front on the tone.
context.env1.a: The soft front on the loudness. Take it to 0 and every low note clicks.
context.env1.s: Held high so long notes stay solid.
context.env1.r: Short, so the line stops when you stop.
context.porta.time: The slide between notes.
context.od.drive: Thickens the bottom. Above about 4 it turns into distortion rather than warmth.

tweaks.hear: From a muffled low reed to something much closer to a synth bass.
From a hard, nasal buzz to a rounder, hollower tone.
A hard front on each note. Useful for a staccato passage, wrong for a legato one.

tweaks.try: Press RANGE on Oscillator 1 until 32’ is lit
tweaks.hear: The line drops an octave into contrabassoon territory, with the sine still an octave above it.

sounds.name: Wooden Flute Solo
sounds.ref: In the style of a wooden flute solo
sounds.blurb: Soft, almost pure solo line with a short burst of air at the start of every note.
sounds.how: A flute is nearly a sine wave with air around it, so Oscillator 1 is a triangle and NOISE is turned up a little in the mixer. The chiff — the breathy "ffh" as a note starts — is made by the filter rather than by a second sound source: Envelope 2 throws the cutoff open by more than two octaves and shuts it again in about 80 ms, which lets a short burst of the noise and the upper harmonics through and then takes them away. The rest of the note is the triangle on its own. KEY TRK keeps the tone even up the range, and a short portamento slurs the line together.

steps.title: A triangle
steps.why:
A flute is close to a sine with air around it. A triangle is about as near to that as a plain waveform gets.
- OSC MIX −5: the mixer is a crossfader, and fully left means only Oscillator 1 is heard.
- SHAPE 3 (triangle): a few quiet upper harmonics and nothing else. At 4 (sine) it is softer and more covered; towards 2 it gets reedy.
- RANGE 8’, TUNE 0: normal pitch.
- Listen for: a soft, pure tone that holds while the key is down.

steps.title: Air in the mixer
steps.why:
White noise goes into the mixer as the air around the note. The filter will decide how much of it you hear.
- NOISE 2.2 (22%): on its own this is hiss; behind a triangle it is the air moving past the edge of the instrument. It is also the size of the chiff later.
- Listen for: the note now has a clear hiss on it. The filter is still mostly open, so the hiss is loud for now.

steps.title: Low-pass, fairly open
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) keeps most of the noise out and lets the triangle through almost untouched.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 6.6 (about 1.2 kHz): where the filter settles. Higher lets air through the whole note; lower makes the body purer.
- RESO 3: resonance, a small lift at the cutoff.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking keeps the top of the line from going dull and losing its air.
- Listen for: the hiss drops back to a faint breath behind the tone.

steps.title: The chiff
steps.why:
Envelope 2 makes the chiff, the breathy “ffh” at the start of each note. It throws the filter open and shuts it again at once, letting a short burst of noise and harmonics through.
- ENV DEPTH 3 (30%): the filter jumps more than two octaves.
- A 0, D 4.2 (80 ms): straight up, then back down in about 80 ms. At that length it is a breath; much longer becomes a sweep.
- S 0, R 41 ms: zero sustain, so the air never stays in the note.
- Listen for: a short puff at the start of every note, then the plain triangle.

steps.title: Soft loudness and a slur
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) with a soft start and quick stop. Portamento slurs the line.
- A 4 (15 ms): how softly each note starts.
- D 360 ms, S 9.5 (95%): a long note stays level.
- R 4.9 (87 ms): the line stops when you stop.
- PORTA TIME 0.9 (81 ms): portamento, a short pitch slide, so overlapping notes run together instead of stepping.
- Listen for: legato phrases sliding gently between notes.

steps.title: Clean, with a quiet echo
steps.why:
The last stage keeps the tone clean and puts the flute in a room.
- DRIVE 0: distortion on a near-pure tone shows up as buzz rather than warmth.
- TIME 7.4 (280 ms), REPEATS 3.5 (35%): a medium echo with a few repeats.
- MIX 2 (20%): kept low, behind the line.
- Listen for: a soft echo in the gaps. On long notes, push the mod wheel: MOD DEPTH is at 0, and the wheel brings the LFO onto the filter for a breathy waver.

context.osc1.shape: At 3 this is a triangle. Turn it to 4 for a pure sine, which is a softer, more covered flute; towards 2 it gets reedy and stops sounding like a flute at all.
context.mix.noise: How much air there is to be let through at the start of each note. This is the size of the chiff.
context.vcf.freq: Where the filter settles after the chiff. Higher lets some air through for the whole note; lower makes the body of the note purer.
context.vcf.envDepth: How far the chiff opens the filter.
context.env2.d: How long the chiff lasts. At about 80 ms it is a breath; much longer and it becomes a sweep.
context.env2.s: Zero, so the filter always returns to its resting point and the air does not stay in the note.
context.vcf.keyTrk: On, so notes at the top of the line keep their air instead of going dull.
context.env1.s: Held high so a long note stays level.
context.env1.r: Short, so the line stops when you stop.
context.porta.time: The slur between overlapping notes.
context.od.drive: At 0. Distortion on a near-pure tone shows up as buzz rather than warmth.
context.vcf.modDepth: Left at 0, with the LFO already wired to the cutoff through it. Pushing the mod wheel turns this knob up, which is how the breathy waver comes in part-way through a long note.

tweaks.try: Set LFO RATE to 4.9, then push the mod wheel gently while a long note sounds
tweaks.hear: A waver in the air of the note fades in as the wheel rises, the way a player adds vibrato to a held note.
From a plain electronic tone with a click at the front to a very breathy, almost whistled note.
From a tight "t" at the front of each note to a soft, slow "hoo".
A pure sine. The chiff is still there but the note behind it is completely plain — closer to a recorder than a flute.

sounds.name: Sub Sync Knock
sounds.ref: A struck sub tone with a short woody edge on the front
sounds.artist: Hard sync into a sine sub
sounds.blurb: Low struck knock: a near-sine sub with a short hard-sync edge that falls away in a fraction of a second.
sounds.how: Oscillator 1 is almost a sine, playing low enough to be felt rather than heard. OSC SYNC makes Oscillator 2 restart on every cycle of Oscillator 1, so it adds a formant on top of the sub instead of a second pitch. Envelope 2 goes through Attenuator 1 to Oscillator 2’s pitch input, which drags that formant down from about two and a half octaves above the sub to about nine semitones above it, in 80 ms. That fall is the knock; the sub underneath is the body.

steps.title: A sub that is nearly a sine
steps.why:
Oscillator 1 is a near-sine sub, low enough to be felt. Oscillator 2 is a saw tuned well above it, and will become the knock once sync is on.
- SHAPE osc 1 3.8 (triangle towards sine): mostly sine, a trace of edge, no buzz.
- RANGE osc 1 8’: the riff’s low keys play at written pitch, about 44 to 65 Hz.
- SHAPE osc 2 2 (saw), TUNE +9.6 st: a saw gives the hardest edge later. The wide TUNE knob sets it well above the sub.
- OSC MIX −3.4 (84 / 16): the mixer is a crossfader, leaning towards the sub.
- Listen for: a deep hum with a quiet second note on top, about nine and a half semitones higher. That sour interval goes away in the next step.

steps.title: Switch OSC SYNC on
steps.why:
OSC SYNC is hard sync: Oscillator 1 forces Oscillator 2 to restart its wave on every cycle. Oscillator 2 stops playing its own note and colours Oscillator 1’s instead.
- OSC SYNC on: Oscillator 2 now plays the sub’s pitch. Its TUNE knob sets where the edge sits, not the note you hear. At +9.6 semitones the tone is hard and reedy. Switch it off and the knock turns into a sour chord.
- Listen for: the second note disappears and the sub gains a buzzy, nasal edge locked to it.

steps.title: A short hit
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) into a short hit.
- A 0: instant start.
- D 6.2 (420 ms), S 0: falls away over about 400 ms with nothing held. Long enough for the sub to be felt, short enough that the knocks stay apart.
- R 5.8 (180 ms): a short tail after release.
- Listen for: each note now dies away by itself even if you hold it.

steps.title: Patch ENV 2 → ATT1 IN and ATT 1 → OSC 2
steps.why:
The patch bay sweeps the sync edge with Envelope 2. With sync on, moving Oscillator 2’s pitch changes the tone, not the note, so a fast fall gives a knock.
- ENV 2 → ATT1 IN: Envelope 2 replaces Attenuator 1’s usual input.
- ATT 1 → OSC 2: adds it to Oscillator 2’s pitch only.
- 1 at 7: the sweep is about 21 semitones, from about two and a half octaves above the sub down to the resting edge. This is the size of the knock.
- Envelope 2 A 0, D 4.2 (80 ms), S 0: the sweep falls in a flash. Longer turns it into a sweep.
- Listen for: a hard woody rap at the front of each hit.

steps.title: Low-pass to keep the weight
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) takes the top off the sync edge and keeps the weight.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 4.6 (about 290 Hz): removes the fizz and leaves the thump. Higher lets more of the hard front through.
- RESO 3.2: resonance, a small lift at the cutoff that gives the body a definite pitch.
- KEY TRK off: key tracking off, so the cutoff stays put across the low riff.
- ENV DEPTH 1.5 (15%): the same fast envelope opens the filter for the first few milliseconds, so the knock is not muffled.
- Listen for: a rounder, heavier hit that still has a clear front.

steps.title: Weight
steps.why:
The overdrive, always in the path after the filter, adds overtones above the sub so it can be heard on small speakers.
- DRIVE 4.2: adds harmonics without making the hit longer. Without it the hit is felt more than heard.
- TONE 3: left of centre keeps those overtones rounded.
- LEVEL 8: the stage’s output level.
- Listen for: the knock staying audible on laptop speakers. Turn DRIVE to 0 and the low notes almost vanish there.

context.osc.sync: In this sound this is the whole point. Switch it off and Oscillator 2 becomes a second, badly tuned note and the knock turns into a sour chord.
context.osc2.tune: Where the sync edge rests once the envelope has fallen. Higher is harder and more nasal; at 0 the edge almost disappears.
context.att.1: How far the sync formant sweeps on each hit. This is the size of the knock.
context.env2.d: How long the knock takes to fall. Around 80 ms it is a short rap; longer turns it into a sweep.
context.osc.mix: The balance between the sub and the sync edge. Too far right and the sub goes.
context.osc1.shape: Nearly sine, so almost all the harmonics you hear come from the sync and the overdrive.
context.osc2.shape: A sawtooth gives the hardest sync edge. Towards sine the edge softens and the knock loses its bite.
context.vcf.reso: A small lift at the cutoff, which gives the body of the hit a definite pitch.
context.vcf.freq: How much of the sync edge is kept. Higher lets more of the hard front through.
context.vcf.envDepth: A small lift at the front so the knock is not muffled by the filter.
context.env1.d: The length of the whole hit.
context.od.drive: Adds overtones above the sub. Without it the hit is felt more than heard.
context.od.tone: Left of centre so the added overtones stay rounded.

tweaks.hear: From a soft sub with a faint tick to a hard, hollow rap on the front of every hit.

tweaks.try: Sweep slowly from 0 to 5 while the pattern plays
tweaks.hear: The resting edge climbs through woody, reedy and metallic colours. The sub stays where it is throughout.
The knock stretches into a short downward sweep, closer to a struck spring.
Much more of the sync edge gets through and the sub sits behind a hard buzz.

sounds.name: Hollow Tube Knock
sounds.ref: A knuckle rapped on a length of hollow plastic pipe
sounds.artist: Tone-mod waveform with a collapsing width
sounds.blurb: Dry, hollow knock with a short woody bloom, pitched low in the mid range.
sounds.how: Both oscillators sit near the tone-mod end of the SHAPE morph, which is two sawtooths a set distance apart rather than one waveform. WIDTH sets that distance, from the two sitting on top of one another to half a cycle apart, and at 2.6 they are about a quarter of a cycle apart: hollow, with a strong octave in it. Envelope 2 is patched into ATT2 IN, so Attenuator 2 carries the envelope to both WIDTH inputs instead of the LFO: each hit throws the two sawtooths from a quarter of a cycle apart to past half a cycle and lets them fall back, which is the woody bloom. A band-pass filter keeps only the hollow middle.

steps.title: Two tone-mod waves, close together
steps.why:
Both oscillators sit near the tone-mod end of the SHAPE morph, the Neutron’s own wave. Tone mod is two sawtooths a set distance apart, and WIDTH sets that distance, which gives a hollow tone with a strong octave in it.
- SHAPE 0.4 on both (tone mod towards pulse): must stay near 0. Past about 1.5 WIDTH stops acting strongly and the sweep later does nothing.
- WIDTH 2.6 on both: the two sawtooths about a quarter of a cycle apart. Near 0 the tone is full and low; at 5 it thins out an octave higher.
- TUNE osc 2 1.8 (+4.2 st): deliberately not a clean interval, so it sounds like one struck object rather than a played chord.
- OSC MIX −1 (60 / 40): the mixer is a crossfader; Oscillator 1 leads and Oscillator 2 thickens it.
- Listen for: a hollow, slightly clangy held tone.

steps.title: A short hit
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) into a short hit.
- A 0: instant start.
- D 5.2 (180 ms), S 0: the whole knock is over in under a fifth of a second, even with the key held. Longer makes it ring.
- R 5 (95 ms): a short tail after release.
- Listen for: a thin, dry click with a little tone behind it. The filter has not shaped it yet.

steps.title: Band-pass at about 290 Hz
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) goes to band-pass, which keeps only a band around the cutoff. Taking away the thump below and the fizz above is what makes it sound like a closed tube rather than a drum.
- MODE band-pass: press MODE until the middle lamp lights.
- FREQ 4.6 (about 290 Hz): the pitch of the tube. Lower is a bigger, duller pipe; higher is a small, tight one.
- RESO 5.5: resonance narrows the band and adds a short ring after each hit.
- KEY TRK off, ENV DEPTH 0: the band stays put whatever you play, and no envelope moves it.
- Listen for: the click turns into a hollow “tok” with a slight ring.

steps.title: Patch ENV 2 → ATT2 IN
steps.why:
Attenuator 2 normally carries the LFO to both oscillators’ WIDTH inputs. One cable swaps the LFO for Envelope 2, so each hit sweeps the width and gives the knock a woody bloom.
- ENV 2 → ATT2 IN: Envelope 2 replaces the LFO. No cable is needed at the WIDTH jacks; Attenuator 2 already reaches them.
- 2 at 8.5: the depth of the sweep. Each hit pushes the sawtooths past half a cycle apart, so the tone jumps an octave and falls back.
- Envelope 2 A 0, D 3.8 (57 ms), S 0, R 30 ms: how fast the bloom collapses. Short is a hard rap; longer is a softer knock with a swell.
- Listen for: a quick “dunk” inside each hit. Turn knob 2 to 0 and back to hear it vanish and return.

steps.title: Dry and hard
steps.why:
The overdrive, always in the path after the filter, hardens the front of the knock.
- DRIVE 4.5: pushes the loud start into clipping so the attack is harder.
- TONE 4.2: just below centre, so the extra harmonics do not add fizz on top.
- LEVEL 8: the stage’s output level.
- Listen for: a firmer, drier front on each hit. Turn DRIVE down and the knock softens.

context.osc1.shape: In this sound this must stay near 0. Tone mod is the only shape here that WIDTH acts on strongly, so move it past about 1.5 and the width sweep in the last step stops doing anything.
context.osc1.width: Where the tone rests between hits. Near 0 the two sawtooths sit on top of one another and the knock is full and low; at 5 they are half a cycle apart and it thins out an octave higher.
context.att.2: The size of the width sweep on each hit: the depth of the woody bloom.
context.env2.d: How fast the bloom collapses. Short is a hard rap; longer is a soft knock with a swell in it.
context.osc2.tune: The second tone. Away from a clean interval it sounds like one struck object; at 0 or 2.92 it sounds like a played note.
context.osc.mix: A little left of centre so Oscillator 1 leads and Oscillator 2 thickens it.
context.vcf.freq: The pitch of the tube. Lower is a bigger, duller pipe; higher is a small, tight one.
context.vcf.reso: How narrow the band is, and so how much the knock rings after the hit.
context.env1.d: The length of the whole knock.
context.od.drive: Hardens the front of the hit.

tweaks.try: Turn down to 0, then back up to 8.5
tweaks.hear: Without the width sweep the knock is a flat, static tap. All of the wood is in this one knob.
From a full, boxy knock to a thin tap an octave higher.
The tube changes size: from a deep drainpipe to a short length of tubing.
The bloom disappears. WIDTH and Attenuator 2 have nothing to act on, which shows how much of this sound is the tone-mod shape.

sounds.name: Bending Echo Tick
sounds.ref: A short tock whose repeats climb in pitch as they fade
sounds.artist: Envelope into the delay time input
sounds.blurb: One dry tock that breaks into a run of repeats, each one shorter and higher than the last.
sounds.how: The source is a single 40 ms tock: a narrow pulse through a band-pass filter. Everything after that is the delay. Envelope 2 is patched into DELAY TIME, so each hit stretches the delay to nearly three times its knob setting and then lets it shrink back over a second and a bit. A delay line that is shortening plays its contents back faster, so every repeat comes sooner and sounds higher than the one before it, like a bouncing object settling.

steps.title: A narrow pulse
steps.why:
The source is a thin pulse wave, which gives the band-pass filter plenty of upper harmonics to carve a tock out of.
- OSC MIX −5: the mixer is a crossfader, and fully left means only Oscillator 1 is heard.
- SHAPE 1 (pulse): strong upper harmonics. Triangle and sine would give the filter almost nothing to work with.
- WIDTH 3.4 (36%): left of centre, so the pulse is thin and nasal. Thinner gives the filter more to work with.
- RANGE 8’, TUNE 0: normal pitch.
- Listen for: a buzzy, nasal held tone.

steps.title: Cut it to a tock
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) and cuts the note down to a tock, so everything heard afterwards will be delay.
- A 0: instant start.
- D 3.4 (41 ms), S 0: about 40 ms and gone. Keep it short or the repeats overlap the note itself.
- R 3.4 (25 ms): a very short tail.
- Listen for: a quick click on each key press.

steps.title: Band-pass at about 750 Hz
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) in band-pass keeps only a band around the cutoff, leaving a dry mid-range knock with a pitch to it.
- MODE band-pass, FREQ 5.9 (about 750 Hz): the pitch of the tock and of the whole run of repeats to come.
- RESO 5: resonance gives the tock a definite pitch, which makes the bending in the repeats easy to hear. Lower makes it harder to hear.
- KEY TRK off, ENV DEPTH 0: the band stays put, and no envelope moves it.
- Listen for: the click becomes a woody “tock”.

steps.title: A short delay with many repeats
steps.why:
The delay turns the single tock into a fast stutter. The delay is fed from the amplifier, so the levels before it go up.
- TIME 2 (48 ms): near the minimum, so repeats come fast.
- REPEATS 7.9 (79%): many repeats. Above about 8 they build instead of dying away.
- MIX 7.5 (75%): the repeats are loud against the single dry tock.
- DRIVE 4.5, TONE 5.5, LEVEL 9.5, VOLUME 9: a 40 ms tock has very little energy, and a quiet tock gives quiet repeats, so the overdrive pushes it and both output levels go up.
- Listen for: an even “trrrr” stutter that dies away. It does not bend yet.

steps.title: Patch ENV 2 → DELAY TIME
steps.why:
The patch bay makes the repeats bend. Envelope 2 stretches the delay time on each hit, then lets it shrink; a delay that is shortening plays its contents back faster, so each repeat comes sooner and sounds higher.
- ENV 2 → DELAY TIME: adds Envelope 2 to the TIME knob. At the start of each hit the delay is nearly three times its knob setting.
- Envelope 2 A 0, D 7.6 (1.4 s), S 0, R 690 ms: the delay jumps long and shrinks back over about 1.3 seconds. Short gives a quick chirp; long gives a slow, tumbling fall.
- Listen for: repeats that start spaced out and speed up, climbing in pitch like a ball bouncing to rest.

context.env2.d: In this sound this is how long the run of repeats takes to climb and settle. Short gives a quick chirp; long gives a slow, tumbling fall.
context.delay.time: Where the delay ends up once Envelope 2 has fallen: the gap between the last repeats. Near the minimum they run into one another.
context.delay.repeats: How many repeats you hear. Above about 8 they build instead of dying away.
context.delay.mix: How loud the repeats are against the single dry tock.
context.env1.d: The length of the source tock, about 40 ms. Keep it short or the repeats overlap the note itself.
context.vcf.freq: The pitch of the tock, and so of the whole run.
context.osc1.shape: A pulse, for its strong upper harmonics. Triangle and sine give the filter almost nothing to make a tock from.
context.vcf.reso: How pitched the tock is. Lower makes the bending harder to hear.
context.osc1.width: How thin the pulse is. Thinner gives the filter more to work with.
context.od.level: High, because the delay is fed from the amplifier and a quiet tock gives quiet repeats.
context.out.volume: Up from its usual setting, for the same reason.

tweaks.hear: A single dry tock. Everything else in this sound is the delay.
The repeats climb and settle in about a quarter of the time: a short chirp rather than a tumble.
The repeats stop dying away and pile up into a rising drone.
A slower, wider bounce with the repeats clearly separate.

sounds.name: Grit Scrape
sounds.ref: A dry, grainy rasp with a pitch buried in it
sounds.blurb: Short grainy scrape whose coarseness is set by the key you play, not by a filter.
sounds.how: The sample-and-hold takes readings of white noise and holds each one until the next, at up to 28 readings a second on its own RATE knob. Here Oscillator 2 is patched into S&H CLOCK instead, so it takes a reading on every cycle of the oscillator — a thousand a second and more, and it follows the keyboard. The result is noise chopped into steps at a musical rate, which sounds like coarse grit with a pitch in it. A second cable sends the sample-and-hold straight into the filter as the sound source, so the oscillators are never heard.

steps.title: Oscillator 2 as a clock, not a sound
steps.why:
Oscillator 2 is set up as a clock rather than a sound. It will tell the sample-and-hold when to take readings, so its tuning will set how coarse the grit is.
- SHAPE osc 2 4 (sine): crosses the clock threshold cleanly once per cycle. Saw and pulse can double up at some widths.
- RANGE 8’, TUNE osc 2 5 (+12 st): the clock runs an octave above the played note. Higher gives a finer, hissier scrape; lower a rougher one.
- OSC MIX −5: only Oscillator 1 reaches the mixer, so Oscillator 2 is not heard.
- GLIDE 0: the S&H (sample and hold) output stays in hard steps. Turned up, the grain softens into a warble.
- Listen for: nothing new. You still hear Oscillator 1’s default saw.

steps.title: Patch OSC 2 → S&H CLOCK and S&H → VCF IN
steps.why:
Two cables turn chopped noise into the sound. The S&H takes a reading of white noise and holds it; clocked by Oscillator 2, it does that on every cycle, so the noise is chopped into steps at a musical rate.
- OSC 2 → S&H CLOCK: replaces the S&H RATE knob. Across the riff that is roughly 800 to 3,000 readings a second, and it follows the keys.
- S&H → VCF IN: replaces the filter’s normal input with the stepped signal. The oscillators and the NOISE knob drop out of the path.
- Listen for: a hard, grainy buzz whose pitch changes with the key you play.

steps.title: A narrow band at about 1.4 kHz
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) in band-pass keeps one narrow band of the stepped noise, where the grain reads as a scrape rather than hiss.
- MODE band-pass, FREQ 6.8 (about 1.4 kHz): where the scrape sits. Lower is a rumbling rasp; higher is a dry hiss.
- RESO 8.5: resonance makes the band narrow, so a clear pitch runs through the grit. Below about 5 it spreads out into plain static.
- KEY TRK off: key tracking off, so the band stays put.
- Listen for: the static narrows into a pitched, scratchy tone.

steps.title: A short scrape with a hard front
steps.why:
Both envelopes turn the tone into short scrapes with a hard front. Envelope 1 sets loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier); Envelope 2 flicks the filter.
- Envelope 1 A 0, D 130 ms, S 0, R 68 ms: instant start and gone in about an eighth of a second. This is the length of the scrape.
- ENV DEPTH 2 (20%): how far Envelope 2 pushes the band up.
- Envelope 2 A 0, D 41 ms, S 0: a faster flick, so each scrape starts brighter and settles.
- Listen for: short, bright rasps. Turn ENV DEPTH to 0 and the front goes dull.

steps.title: Harder
steps.why:
The overdrive, always in the path after the filter, squares the steps off and makes the grain coarser. The output comes up because a band-passed stepped signal is quiet.
- DRIVE 5.5: coarser grain. At 0 it sounds smoother, more like filtered noise.
- TONE 6: right of centre keeps the scrape at the top instead of letting it thicken.
- LEVEL 9, VOLUME 7.5: make up the level lost in the narrow band.
- Listen for: a rougher, louder scrape. Sweep DRIVE while playing to hear the grain coarsen.

context.osc2.tune: In this sound this sets how coarse the grain is against the key you play. Higher means more readings per second and a finer, hissier scrape; lower means fewer and a rougher, buzzier one.
context.osc2.shape: A sine gives one clean clock pulse per cycle. Saw and pulse also work, but the clock can double up at some widths.
context.sh.glide: At 0, so the steps stay square. Turn it up and the grain softens into a warble.
context.sh.rate: Does nothing here. The cable into S&H CLOCK has taken over from this knob.
context.mix.noise: Does nothing here either. The cable into VCF IN has taken the mixer out of the path, and the sample-and-hold takes its noise from its own internal connection.
context.vcf.freq: Where the scrape sits. Lower is a rumbling rasp; higher is a dry hiss.
context.vcf.reso: How narrow the band is. High, so a pitch sits inside the grit; below about 5 it spreads out into plain static.
context.vcf.envDepth: The bright front on each hit.
context.env1.d: The length of the scrape.
context.od.drive: Coarsens the grain. At 0 the steps sound smoother and more like filtered noise.
context.out.volume: Up from its usual setting: a band-passed stepped signal carries far less level than an oscillator does.

tweaks.try: Sweep from -5 to 5 while the pattern plays
tweaks.hear: The grain goes from a slow, rattling crunch to a fine, glassy hiss. The played pitch does not change.
The steps slide into one another and the scrape turns into a wet, gurgling texture.
From a low rasp you could use as a body to a thin scrape that sits on top of a track.
The pitch goes and the scrape spreads out into a dry burst of static.

sounds.name: Inverted Rise
sounds.ref: A short struck blip whose pitch springs upwards
sounds.blurb: Bright blip that starts a couple of octaves low and springs up to its resting pitch as it fades.
sounds.how: ENV DEPTH on the front panel can only push the cutoff upwards. The INVERT output carries Envelope 2 turned upside down, so patching it into FREQ MOD does the opposite: each note drags the cutoff two octaves down and lets it spring back. With a narrow, highly resonant band-pass, the filter rings at whatever the cutoff is at that moment, so the ring climbs. A saw and a little noise underneath give it something to ring on.

steps.title: Something for the filter to ring on
steps.why:
A low sawtooth plus noise gives a dense bed with something at every frequency. Neither is really heard later: the band-pass will pick out one narrow slice to ring.
- OSC MIX −5: the mixer is a crossfader, and fully left means only Oscillator 1 is heard.
- SHAPE 2 (saw): every harmonic. A triangle or sine would have nothing up high for the filter to ring on.
- RANGE 32’, TUNE 0: two octaves below normal, so the harmonics are packed close together and the ring stays even.
- NOISE 5 (50%): fills the gaps between the harmonics.
- Listen for: a low, buzzy growl with hiss over it.

steps.title: A narrow band, high up
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) in band-pass keeps only a narrow band high up. With high resonance it rings at the cutoff whenever it is struck, which gives the blip a clear pitch.
- MODE band-pass, FREQ 8.1 (about 3.7 kHz): where the ring sits, and where the climb will end.
- RESO 7.5: resonance narrows the band. Below about 5 it stops ringing and becomes a filtered click.
- KEY TRK off, ENV DEPTH 0: the band stays put, and no envelope moves it.
- Listen for: a thin, whistly hiss with a pitch in it.

steps.title: A short hit
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) into a short hit.
- A 0: instant start.
- D 5 (150 ms), S 0: gone in about a sixth of a second. It has to outlast the climb in the next step, or the top of the sweep is cut off.
- R 4.8 (80 ms): a short tail.
- Listen for: a high, pitched blip on each key press. It does not move yet.

steps.title: Patch INVERT → FREQ MOD
steps.why:
ENV DEPTH on the panel can only push the cutoff upwards. The INVERT jack carries Envelope 2 upside down, so patching it into FREQ MOD drags the cutoff down on each note and lets it spring back.
- INVERT → FREQ MOD: replaces the LFO at the cutoff input. With nothing in INVERT IN, INVERT carries Envelope 2 inverted.
- MOD DEPTH 4 (40%): the cutoff starts about two octaves low, so the ring climbs from around 950 Hz to 3.7 kHz. At 0 the blip is a flat ping.
- Envelope 2 A 0, D 4.6 (110 ms), S 0, R 58 ms: the climb takes about a tenth of a second. Short is a chirp; long is a swoop.
- Listen for: each blip springing upwards. Pull MOD DEPTH to 0 and back to compare.

steps.title: Edge
steps.why:
The overdrive, always in the path after the filter, keeps the blip thin and hard. The output comes up because a narrow band this high carries little level.
- DRIVE 4.5: adds edge to the ring.
- TONE 6: right of centre, so the resonance does not sound round.
- LEVEL 8.5, VOLUME 7.5: make up the lost level.
- Listen for: a sharper, more cutting chirp.

context.vcf.modDepth: In this sound this is how far down the blip starts, and so how far it climbs. At 0 nothing reaches the cutoff at all and the blip becomes a flat ping.
context.env2.d: How long the climb takes. Short is a chirp; long is a slow swoop.
context.vcf.freq: Where the climb ends: the resting pitch of the blip.
context.vcf.reso: How pitched the blip is. Below about 5 it stops ringing and becomes a filtered click.
context.mix.noise: Fills the gaps between the sawtooth’s harmonics so the filter has something to ring on wherever the cutoff happens to be.
context.osc1.range: At 32’ the sawtooth is low and its harmonics are packed close together, which keeps the ring even across the whole climb.
context.osc1.shape: A sawtooth, because it has every harmonic. A triangle or a sine has nothing up at 3.8 kHz for the filter to ring on.
context.env1.d: The length of the blip. It has to outlast the climb or the top of the sweep is cut off.
context.od.tone: Right of centre, to keep the blip thin.
context.out.volume: Up from its usual setting: a narrow band this high up carries very little level.

tweaks.hear: From a flat ping to a blip that springs up through four octaves.
A slow rising swoop instead of a struck blip: useful as a riser under a transition.
The blip settles at a different pitch each time. High settings sit above almost anything else in a track.
The pitch goes and a soft filtered click is left, which shows how much of this sound is the resonance.

sounds.name: Air Ping
sounds.ref: A very high, glassy tick at the top of hearing
sounds.artist: Wide-range oscillator with random filter colour
sounds.blurb: Tiny glassy tick right at the top of the range, a slightly different colour on every hit.
sounds.how: The fourth RANGE setting puts TUNE into a ten-octave mode, so the oscillator can be pushed far above where the keyboard would normally reach. At +51 semitones the riff’s notes land between about 10 and 15 kHz, which is air rather than pitch. A high-pass filter takes away everything below it, and the sample-and-hold — clocked from MIDI GATE so it takes one reading per note — moves that cutoff by up to an octave, so no two ticks have quite the same colour.

steps.title: Push one oscillator into the air band
steps.why:
Oscillator 1 is pushed up into the air band, far above where the keyboard normally reaches, so it sounds like a glassy tick rather than a note.
- RANGE ±10 OCT: press RANGE until all three lamps light. TUNE now covers ten octaves instead of one.
- TUNE 4.3: in this mode about +51 semitones, so the riff lands between roughly 10 and 15 kHz. Careful above about 4.7: the top notes pass 20 kHz and disappear.
- SHAPE 3.4 (triangle towards sine): keeps the tick clean. Saw and pulse have harmonics that fold back this high and sound gritty.
- OSC MIX −5: only Oscillator 1 is heard.
- NOISE 2 (20%): a little hiss for the random filter moves later to act on.
- Listen for: a very high, thin whistle and some hiss. The default low-pass filter still takes much of the top off.

steps.title: High-pass to take away everything else
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) switches to high-pass, which removes everything below the cutoff. It is the floor of the sound.
- MODE high-pass: press MODE until the top lamp lights.
- FREQ 8.9 (about 6.7 kHz): everything below goes, including the low part of the hiss and the overdrive’s lower products.
- RESO 3: resonance, a small lift at the cutoff.
- KEY TRK off, ENV DEPTH 0: the floor stays put.
- Listen for: only air and a bright, glassy whistle left.

steps.title: Cut it to a tick
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) into a tick.
- A 0: instant start.
- D 2.9 (27 ms), S 0: about a fortieth of a second. Past about 4 it stops being percussive and becomes a high whistle.
- R 2.9 (17 ms): almost no tail.
- Listen for: a tiny tick on each key.

steps.title: Patch MIDI GATE → S&H CLOCK and S&H → FREQ MOD
steps.why:
The S&H (sample and hold) takes a random reading of noise. Clocked from the keyboard, it gives one new value per note, and that moves the high-pass floor so each tick has a slightly different colour.
- MIDI GATE → S&H CLOCK: replaces the S&H RATE knob, which now does nothing. MIDI GATE goes high on each key press.
- S&H → FREQ MOD: sends the reading to the cutoff instead of the LFO.
- MOD DEPTH 2 (20%): about an octave either way. More makes the ticks differ more.
- GLIDE 0: no smoothing, so each tick gets its value at once.
- Listen for: a fast run where no two ticks sound quite the same.

steps.title: Bite
steps.why:
The overdrive, always in the path after the filter, thins the tick and makes it cut.
- DRIVE 3: a little grit for bite.
- TONE 7.5: well right, thinning the sound further.
- LEVEL 9: high, because there is very little energy in a sound this short and this high.
- Listen for: the ticks now clear and sharp against a mix.

context.osc1.range: In this sound the wide setting is what makes it possible. In the normal 8’ range the riff would play around middle C and this would be an ordinary click.
context.osc1.tune: How high the tick sits. Careful above about 4.7: the top notes of the riff pass 20 kHz and simply disappear.
context.osc1.shape: Mostly triangle. Saw and pulse have harmonics far above the tick that fold back and sound gritty rather than glassy.
context.vcf.freq: The resting point of the high-pass, around 7 kHz. It is the floor of the sound: everything below it is gone.
context.vcf.modDepth: How much the random reading moves that floor, and so how much the ticks differ from one another.
context.sh.rate: Does nothing here. The cable into S&H CLOCK has taken over from this knob.
context.mix.noise: A small amount of hiss so the random cutoff moves have something broadband to act on.
context.env1.d: The length of the tick. Past about 4 it stops being percussive and becomes a high whistle.
context.od.level: High, to make up for how little energy there is in a tick this short.

tweaks.hear: The tick drops to a bright chime and climbs back up until it is barely there.
Every tick becomes identical. The variation is all from the sample-and-hold.

tweaks.try: Lengthen to 4.5 and set R to 4.5
tweaks.hear: The ticks open into short glassy pings with an audible pitch.
The oscillator drops more than four octaves and the sound becomes a plain click, which shows what the wide range is doing here.

sounds.name: Glass Bell
sounds.ref: Frequency modulation from the patch bay, with the modulator in the ±10 octave range
sounds.blurb: A clear, ringing bell with a shimmer of out-of-tune overtones that fades before the note does.
sounds.how: A bell’s overtones are not whole-number multiples of its note, so a plain waveform cannot make one. Here Oscillator 2 runs at about 3.5 times Oscillator 1’s frequency, which needs the ±10 OCT setting of RANGE: the normal ranges only reach an octave above. Its output goes through Attenuator 1 into Oscillator 1’s pitch, so it shakes that pitch hundreds of times a second and adds overtones that clash gently with the note. Attenuator 1 is voltage controlled, and Envelope 2 at ATT1 CV makes it close as the bell rings, so the shimmer fades first and a purer tone is left. OSC MIX lets a little of Oscillator 2 through as well, as the bell’s own high partial.

steps.title: Two sines, the second 3.5 times higher
steps.why:
Two sines are set up for FM (frequency modulation, one oscillator wobbling another’s pitch very fast). A bell’s overtones are not whole-number multiples of its note, so Oscillator 2 is tuned to about 3.5 times Oscillator 1’s pitch.
- SHAPE 4 (sine) on both: pure tones, so all the overtones will come from the modulation.
- RANGE osc 2 ±10 OCT: press until all three lamps light. The normal ranges only reach an octave up.
- TUNE osc 2 1.8: in this mode about +22 semitones, 3.5 times the pitch. The ratio sets the kind of metal; three times is sweeter, like a chime.
- OSC MIX −3 (80 / 20): the 20% of Oscillator 2 is the steady high partial that makes it a bell.
- Listen for: a plain note with a faint, out-of-tune whistle above it.

steps.title: Patch OSC 2 → ATT1 IN, ATT 1 → OSC 1, ENV 2 → ATT1 CV
steps.why:
The patch bay adds the FM. Oscillator 2 shakes Oscillator 1’s pitch hundreds of times a second, which adds a cluster of clashing overtones, and Envelope 2 will control how much.
- OSC 2 → ATT1 IN, ATT 1 → OSC 1: Oscillator 2, scaled by Attenuator 1, goes to Oscillator 1’s pitch.
- ENV 2 → ATT1 CV: Envelope 2 sets Attenuator 1’s level, so the modulation follows the envelope.
- 1 at 3.5: how hard the pitch is shaken, and so how much shimmer. Above about 5 the strike goes noticeably sharp and slides back into tune.
- Listen for: a metallic, clangy tone at the start of each note.

steps.title: Envelope 2 lets the shimmer fade
steps.why:
Envelope 2 now lets the shimmer fade, so each strike starts bright and metallic and turns purer as it rings.
- A 0: the full shimmer on the strike.
- D 8 (1.9 s), S 0: the clashing overtones die away over about two seconds.
- R 8 (1.1 s): they fade out after release too.
- Listen for: hold a note. The clang softens while the note carries on underneath.

steps.title: A long ring and a little echo
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) so each note rings out like a struck bar. The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) stays open, and a quiet echo fills the gaps.
- Envelope 1 A 0, D 9 (4.3 s), S 0, R 8.5 (1.7 s): no sustain, so the bell fades by itself over about four seconds.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 7.8 (about 3 kHz), RESO 0: open, taking off only the very top.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking keeps high notes as bright as low ones.
- TIME 330 ms, REPEATS 40%, MIX 2 (20%): a quiet echo about a third of a second behind.
- Listen for: a long, clear ring that dies away on its own.

context.osc2.range: In this sound: the ±10 OCT setting, which is what lets Oscillator 2 sit 3.5 times above Oscillator 1. In 8’ TUNE stops at one octave up.
context.osc2.tune: In this sound: the ratio between the two oscillators, and so the kind of metal. 1.58 (an octave and a fifth up, 3 times) is sweeter and more like a tuned chime; the settings in between clash more.
context.att.1: In this sound: how hard Oscillator 2 shakes Oscillator 1, so how much shimmer each strike has. Above about 5 the strike also goes noticeably sharp and slides back into tune, because this kind of modulation raises the average pitch.
context.env2.d: In this sound: how long the shimmer lasts before the tone turns pure.
context.env1.d: In this sound: how long each bell rings. With no sustain it is also what you hear after you let go.
context.osc.mix: In this sound: mostly Oscillator 1. The 20% of Oscillator 2 is the steady high partial that makes it a bell rather than a chime.

tweaks.hear: The bell passes through glassy, gong-like and clanging tones as the ratio changes.
The shimmer lasts as long as the note: a harder, more metallic bell.
The steady high partial goes and only the fading shimmer is left: softer, more like a glass struck with a spoon.

sounds.name: Reed Piano with Amp Bark
sounds.ref: In the style of a 1970s Wurlitzer electric piano played through a small amplifier
sounds.blurb: A warm electric piano that growls when a key is struck and turns clean as the note dies away.
sounds.how: An electric piano played through a small amplifier breaks up on the loud start of each note and cleans up as the note fades. On the Neutron the overdrive normally sits before the amplifier, so it always sees the same level and the grit never changes. Three cables swap the two round: the filter feeds the amplifier, the amplifier feeds the overdrive, and the overdrive feeds the delay. Now Envelope 1 sets how hard the overdrive is pushed, so the growl follows the loudness of the note. Few synths let you change the order of their modules at all.

steps.title: A soft, reedy wave
steps.why:
One soft, reedy wave is the body of the electric piano. It needs just enough edge for the overdrive to bite on later.
- OSC MIX −5: the mixer is a crossfader, and fully left means only Oscillator 1 is heard.
- SHAPE 2.7 (saw towards triangle): mostly triangle with some saw in it. Rounder than a saw, with some edge left.
- RANGE 8’: normal pitch.
- Listen for: a mellow, organ-like held tone.

steps.title: A filter that softens after the strike
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is bright on the strike and softens straight after, like a hammer hitting a reed.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 6.2 (about 930 Hz), RESO 1: a warm resting tone.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking keeps high notes as bright as low ones.
- ENV DEPTH 3 (30%): how bright the strike is.
- Envelope 2 A 0, D 6.3 (460 ms), S 0: open at once and closed again within half a second.
- Listen for: a bright “plink” at the front of each note that mellows.

steps.title: A piano-like fall
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) into a piano-like fall: loud at the strike, then a quiet hum.
- A 0: instant start.
- D 7.2 (970 ms): how quickly the note falls from the strike.
- S 2 (20%): the quiet level held notes settle at.
- R 5.5 (140 ms): notes stop as the key comes up.
- Listen for: each note hitting hard and dropping away while held.

steps.title: Patch VCF 1 → VCA IN, VCA → OD IN, OVERDRIVE → DELAY IN
steps.why:
Three cables swap the amplifier and the overdrive round. Normally the overdrive sits before the amplifier, so the grit never changes. Now the amplifier comes first, so the loud strike pushes the overdrive into growl and the quiet tail stays clean.
- VCF 1 → VCA IN, VCA → OD IN, OVERDRIVE → DELAY IN: filter to amplifier, amplifier to overdrive, overdrive to delay.
- DRIVE 4.5: how loud a note must be before it breaks up. Higher and even the tail growls.
- TONE 4.5: the colour of the growl. Left is woolly and dark; right thinner and more cutting.
- LEVEL 7: now the final volume, with only the delay after it.
- Listen for: a bark on each strike that cleans up as the note fades.

context.od.drive: In this sound: how loud a note has to be before it breaks up. Higher and even the tail growls; lower and only the hardest part of the strike does.
context.od.tone: In this sound: the colour of the growl. Left is a woolly, darker bark; right is a thinner, more cutting one.
context.od.level: In this sound: the final volume. With the overdrive last in line, nothing comes after it but the delay.
context.env1.d: In this sound: how quickly the note falls from the growling strike to the clean hum.
context.env1.s: In this sound: the quiet level held notes settle at, well below the point where the overdrive bites.
context.vcf.envDepth: In this sound: how bright the strike is. The overdrive adds its own brightness on top.
context.env2.d: In this sound: how quickly the strike softens.

tweaks.hear: Every note growls all the way through: an amplifier turned right up.
Held notes stay loud enough to keep breaking up, closer to an organ than a piano.
Almost a sine: a softer, rounder piano, and the overdrive has less to grip.

sounds.name: Melody over Its Own Drone
sounds.ref: In the style of a hurdy-gurdy or bagpipes: a tune over a steady drone note
sounds.blurb: A singing line with vibrato over a low, reedy drone that holds still beneath it.
sounds.how: PARAPHONIC gives each oscillator its own key: hold a low note first and Oscillator 2 keeps it, while Oscillator 1 follows every key you play on top. So one synth plays a drone and a tune at once. They still share one filter and one envelope, so the tune is played legato, with a short glide between notes. The vibrato goes only on the tune: the LFO, turned right down by Attenuator 2, is patched into OSC 1, not OSC 1+2, so the drone underneath stays perfectly steady.

steps.title: A soft voice and a reedy drone
steps.why:
PARAPHONIC gives each oscillator its own key, so one synth plays a drone and a tune at once: hold a low note first and Oscillator 2 keeps it while Oscillator 1 follows the tune.
- SHAPE osc 1 3.4 (triangle towards sine): the tune, a clear singing tone.
- SHAPE osc 2 2.3 (saw towards triangle): the drone, mostly saw for a reedy buzz.
- RANGE osc 2 16’: the drone sounds an octave below the key that holds it.
- OSC MIX −1.5 (65 / 35): the mixer is a crossfader, balancing tune against drone.
- PARAPHONIC on: two notes at once, one per oscillator, sharing one filter and one envelope. Switch it off and both oscillators jump to every note.
- Listen for: hold a low key, then play a tune above it. The low note stays put.

steps.title: Shared filter, sustained notes, a little glide
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) and Envelope 1 are shared by both voices, so they are set to hold the drone steadily and let the tune play legato.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 6.8 (about 1.4 kHz), RESO 1.5: takes the fizz off the drone. Lower is a darker drone.
- KEY TRK off, ENV DEPTH 0: the drone’s tone does not change as the tune moves.
- Envelope 1 A 63 ms, S 100%, R 330 ms: a soft start and full sustain, so the drone holds while the key is down.
- PORTA TIME 1.2 (140 ms): portamento, a short slide into each tune note. The drone does not move, so it does not glide.
- Listen for: tune notes gliding briefly over a steady drone.

steps.title: Vibrato on the tune only: ATT 2 → OSC 1
steps.why:
Attenuator 2 already carries the LFO (low-frequency oscillator, a slow wave that moves other settings). Patching it to Oscillator 1 alone gives the tune vibrato and leaves the drone steady.
- ATT 2 → OSC 1: reaches only Oscillator 1, not OSC 1+2.
- 2 at 0.9: the vibrato depth, just under half a semitone.
- LFO RATE 4.8 (5.02 Hz), SHAPE sine: about 5 Hz, close to a singer’s vibrato.
- Listen for: the tune wavering while the drone underneath stays perfectly still.

steps.title: A little space
steps.why:
A quiet echo stands in for the room.
- TIME 8 (330 ms): about a third of a second between echoes.
- REPEATS 4 (40%): a few repeats, each darker than the last.
- MIX 2 (20%): quiet, behind the line.
- Listen for: a faint trail after tune notes, filling the space above the drone.

context.osc.para: In this sound: what lets one synth hold a drone and play a tune. Switch it off and both oscillators jump to every note.
context.osc2.range: In this sound: 16’ puts the drone an octave below the key held for it, well under the tune.
context.osc.mix: In this sound: the balance between the tune (Oscillator 1) and the drone (Oscillator 2).
context.att.2: In this sound: the depth of the vibrato. It reaches only Oscillator 1, because that is where the cable goes.
context.lfo.rate: In this sound: the speed of the vibrato, about 5 Hz, close to a singer’s.
context.porta.time: In this sound: the short slide between tune notes. The drone does not move, so it does not glide.
context.vcf.freq: In this sound: one filter for both voices. Lower is a darker, more distant drone; higher lets the drone’s buzz through.

tweaks.hear: The drone becomes a nasal, bagpipe-like buzz.
A wide, operatic vibrato on the tune, while the drone stays still.
The tune slides slowly between notes, like a bowed string.

sounds.name: Tone-Mod Ensemble Strings
sounds.ref: In the style of a 1970s string ensemble
sounds.blurb: Soft, shimmering strings that sound like several players, from just two oscillators.
sounds.how: The tone mod position of SHAPE, fully left, is the Neutron’s own waveform: two sawtooths added together, with WIDTH setting how far apart they start. Attenuator 2 carries the LFO to WIDTH, and while WIDTH moves, one sawtooth keeps sliding past the other. A sawtooth that keeps sliding ahead is running slightly faster, so each oscillator sounds like two detuned sawtooths, the usual recipe for a string ensemble. A triangle LFO moves WIDTH at a steady speed, so the detune stays steady and only flips direction at each turn. PARAPHONIC gives two-note chords.

steps.title: Tone mod on both oscillators
steps.why:
Both oscillators go to tone mod, the Neutron’s own wave at the far left of SHAPE: two sawtooths added together, with WIDTH setting how far apart they start. Moving WIDTH later will make each oscillator sound like two detuned saws.
- SHAPE 0 (tone mod) on both: WIDTH only works strongly here. Turn to 2 (plain saw) and the shimmer later stops.
- WIDTH 1.7 and 2.4: the sawtooths a fifth and a quarter of a cycle apart, a little different on each, so the two oscillators colour the sound differently. Near 5 the note loses its bottom octave.
- RANGE 8’ on both, OSC MIX 0 (50 / 50): same octave, equal blend on the crossfader.
- PARAPHONIC on: two held keys each get their own oscillator, sharing one filter, for two-note chords.
- Listen for: a bright, buzzy, still tone. The movement comes next.

steps.title: Move WIDTH with ATT 2
steps.why:
Attenuator 2 carries the LFO (low-frequency oscillator, a slow wave that moves other settings) to both WIDTH inputs with no cable. While WIDTH moves, one sawtooth keeps sliding past the other, which sounds like detuning.
- 2 at 4.5: how far the LFO moves WIDTH, about 12 points either way, and so how strong the shimmer is.
- RATE 3.8 (1.59 Hz): faster moves WIDTH faster, which is the same as a wider detune. Slower gives a gentle beating.
- SHAPE 1 (triangle): moves WIDTH at a steady speed, so the detune stays steady and only flips direction at each turn. A sine would make it come and go.
- Listen for: the tone starting to shimmer like a section of players. Turn knob 2 to 0 and it goes still.

steps.title: Soft bowing
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) softens the top, and Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) so chords are bowed in and out.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 7.2 (about 1.9 kHz), RESO 1: takes the fizz off without dulling the strings.
- KEY TRK on, ENV DEPTH 0: the cutoff follows the keys, and no envelope moves it.
- Envelope 1 A 270 ms: the bow. Longer makes chords swell in.
- D 150 ms, S 100%, R 1.1 s: full level while held, and about a second to fade after release.
- Listen for: chords that fade in softly and overlap as they change.

steps.title: A little space
steps.why:
A quiet echo adds depth behind the chords.
- TIME 8.5 (390 ms): about 0.4 seconds between echoes.
- REPEATS 4 (40%): a few repeats, each darker than the last.
- MIX 2 (20%): kept low so the strings stay in front.
- Listen for: a soft trail after each chord. Turn MIX to zero to compare.

context.osc1.shape: In this sound: fully left, the tone mod wave. Turn it to 2 (a plain sawtooth) and the shimmer stops, because WIDTH no longer does anything.
context.osc1.width: In this sound: where the two sawtooths sit relative to each other when the LFO is at rest. Near 5 they are half a cycle apart and the note loses its bottom octave.
context.att.2: In this sound: how far the LFO moves WIDTH, and so how strong the detuned shimmer is.
context.lfo.rate: In this sound: faster moves WIDTH faster, which is the same as a wider detune. Slower gives a gentle, slow beating.
context.lfo.shape: In this sound: a triangle, which moves WIDTH at a steady speed. A sine slows down at each turn, so the detune comes and goes.
context.osc.para: In this sound: two-note chords, one note on each oscillator, through one shared filter.
context.env1.a: In this sound: the bow. Longer makes the chords swell in.

tweaks.hear: A fast, wide shimmer, closer to a string machine with its ensemble effect turned up.
The shimmer stops: each oscillator is one still tone, which shows what the moving WIDTH was doing.

tweaks.try: Turn slowly from 1 to 5 on a held chord
tweaks.hear: The tone thins towards a hollow, octave-up sound as the two sawtooths move half a cycle apart.

sounds.name: Singing Sync Voice
sounds.ref: A soft vocal lead from hard sync on a sine
sounds.blurb: A rounded, voice-like lead whose vowel opens a little at the start of each note.
sounds.how: Hard sync makes Oscillator 2 restart each time Oscillator 1 does, so Oscillator 2 always sounds at Oscillator 1’s pitch and its own tuning sets which harmonics stand out. That fixed peak is what a voice’s vowel is. Sync is usually heard as a harsh, tearing sweep because it is used on a sawtooth. The Neutron’s SHAPE also works on the synced oscillator, so here Oscillator 2 is set between triangle and sine, which gives a soft, round peak instead. Envelope 2, through Attenuator 1, lifts Oscillator 2’s tuning several semitones as each note starts, so the vowel opens and settles.

steps.title: A soft synced oscillator
steps.why:
OSC SYNC (hard sync) makes Oscillator 2 restart each time Oscillator 1 does, so it always plays Oscillator 1’s pitch and its own tuning sets which harmonics stand out: a fixed peak, like a vowel. With soft waves instead of saws, the sync sounds sung, not torn.
- SHAPE osc 1 4 (sine), RANGE 8’: a plain sine for body and pitch.
- SHAPE osc 2 3.6 (triangle towards sine): mostly sine, which keeps the sync soft. Towards 2 (saw) it becomes the familiar tearing sync lead.
- RANGE osc 2 ±10 OCT, TUNE 1: press RANGE until all three lamps light. TUNE 1 here is about an octave up, putting the peak on the second and third harmonics. Higher moves the vowel from “oo” towards “ee”.
- OSC SYNC on, OSC MIX 2 (30 / 70): mostly the synced oscillator.
- Listen for: a round, vocal “oo” tone at the pitch you play.

steps.title: Patch ENV 2 → ATT1 IN, ATT 1 → OSC 2
steps.why:
The patch bay makes the vowel open at the start of each note. Envelope 2 lifts Oscillator 2’s tuning; with sync on that moves the peak, not the pitch.
- ENV 2 → ATT1 IN, ATT 1 → OSC 2: Envelope 2, scaled by Attenuator 1, goes to Oscillator 2’s pitch.
- 1 at 4: about 8 semitones of lift. This is how far the vowel opens.
- Envelope 2 A 270 ms, D 820 ms, S 60%, R 220 ms: a quarter of a second to open, then it settles part way.
- Listen for: each note sliding from “oo” to a brighter vowel and relaxing back.

steps.title: Vibrato: ATT 2 → OSC 1+2
steps.why:
Attenuator 2 carries the LFO (low-frequency oscillator, a slow wave that moves other settings). Patched to both oscillators’ pitch at a low level it gives vibrato, and because Oscillator 2 is synced, the vowel moves with it, as a singer’s does.
- ATT 2 → OSC 1+2: the LFO to both pitches.
- 2 at 0.8: about a third of a semitone either way.
- RATE 4.9 (5.64 Hz), SHAPE sine: a natural vibrato speed and smooth wave.
- Listen for: held notes wavering in pitch and colour together.

steps.title: A sung phrase
steps.why:
The last step shapes the phrasing. The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) takes the edge off the sync, and Envelope 1 on the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) makes notes start and stop like a voice.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 7.4 (about 2.2 kHz), RESO 0, KEY TRK on: just trims the top, evenly across the range.
- Envelope 1 A 63 ms, D 150 ms, S 90%, R 220 ms: a soft start and a short, natural tail.
- PORTA TIME 1 (100 ms): portamento, a short slide between notes.
- TIME 280 ms, REPEATS 35%, MIX 2 (20%): a quiet echo behind the line.
- Listen for: phrases that slur and breathe like a wordless singer.

context.osc.sync: In this sound: what keeps Oscillator 2 at the played pitch. Switch it off and the envelope bends Oscillator 2’s pitch instead of its tone.
context.osc2.shape: In this sound: mostly sine, which is what makes this sync soft. Towards 2 (sawtooth) it becomes the familiar hard, tearing sync lead.
context.osc2.tune: In this sound: the vowel. Higher settings put the peak on higher harmonics, from a round "oo" towards a thin "ee".
context.osc2.range: In this sound: the ±10 OCT setting, so TUNE can take the peak more than an octave above the note.
context.att.1: In this sound: how far the vowel opens at the start of each note.
context.env2.a: In this sound: how slowly the vowel opens.
context.osc.mix: In this sound: mostly the synced oscillator. More Oscillator 1 adds a plain sine under the voice.

tweaks.hear: The vowel moves from a dark, closed sound to a bright, nasal one.
The same patch turns into a hard sync lead, which shows how much the sine shape is softening it.
Each note starts with a clear "wow" as the vowel opens wide.

sounds.name: Oboe Line
sounds.ref: In the style of an oboe solo
sounds.blurb: A nasal, singing reed line with a soft start and a gentle vibrato.
sounds.how: An oboe’s lowest harmonic is weaker than the ones above it, which gives its thin, nasal tone. The tone mod position of SHAPE can do that on its own. It adds two sawtooths a set distance apart, and when that distance is close to half a cycle the fundamental of one nearly cancels the other’s, while the second and third harmonics come through strongly. WIDTH at 3.9 does it here. A fixed filter with some resonance at about 1.5 kHz, not following the keyboard, acts like the body of the instrument, and a breath of noise and a gentle vibrato finish it.

steps.title: Tone mod with WIDTH at 3.9
steps.why:
Tone mod, the Neutron’s own wave at the far left of SHAPE, adds two sawtooths a set distance apart. With that distance near half a cycle, the fundamental nearly cancels and the upper harmonics lead, which is the thin, nasal tone of an oboe.
- OSC MIX −5: the crossfader fully left, Oscillator 1 alone.
- SHAPE 0 (tone mod): on the pulse shape the same WIDTH would give a hollow square-like tone instead.
- WIDTH 3.9: the fundamental is faint and the note sits in its upper harmonics. Lower is fuller, like a clarinet or sax; nearer 5 it thins to an octave-up whistle.
- RANGE 8’: normal pitch.
- Listen for: sweep WIDTH from 0 to 5 and hear the bottom drop out, then return it to 3.9.

steps.title: A fixed body and a breath
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is a fixed body with a peak that does not follow the keys, as on an acoustic instrument. Envelope 2 opens it a little as each note speaks, and a trace of noise adds breath.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 6.9 (about 1.5 kHz): the body. Lower gives a darker cor anglais; higher a brighter reed.
- RESO 3: resonance, how strongly that body stands out.
- KEY TRK off: key tracking off, so the body stays fixed as the line moves.
- ENV DEPTH 1.5 with Envelope 2 A 24 ms, D 360 ms, S 50%: a small lift as the note starts.
- NOISE 1 (10%): the breath. Keep it low or it turns to hiss.
- Listen for: a nasal reed with a slight breathy edge.

steps.title: Tongued notes, slurred together
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) like a tongued reed, and portamento slurs the line.
- A 4.8 (32 ms): softens the front of each note.
- D 150 ms, S 9 (90%): held notes stay nearly full.
- R 4.5 (63 ms): phrases stop cleanly.
- PORTA TIME 0.8 (64 ms): portamento, a short slide from one note into the next.
- Listen for: legato notes joined by a small slur.

steps.title: Vibrato: ATT 2 → OSC 1+2
steps.why:
Attenuator 2 carries the LFO (low-frequency oscillator, a slow wave that moves other settings). Patched to both oscillators’ pitch it gives a gentle vibrato.
- ATT 2 → OSC 1+2: the LFO to both pitches.
- 2 at 0.8: about a third of a semitone. It also nudges WIDTH very slightly, which only adds movement.
- RATE 4.9 (5.32 Hz), SHAPE sine: about 5 Hz, a smooth, player-like speed.
- Listen for: held notes wavering gently. Turn knob 2 to 0 and the line goes straight.

context.osc1.width: In this sound: how much of the fundamental is cancelled. Lower is fuller and closer to a clarinet or saxophone; nearer 5 it thins to an octave-up whistle.
context.osc1.shape: In this sound: fully left, the tone mod wave. On the pulse shape the same WIDTH gives a hollow, square-like tone instead.
context.vcf.freq: In this sound: the body of the instrument, at about 1.5 kHz. Lower gives a darker cor anglais; higher a brighter, more cutting reed.
context.vcf.reso: In this sound: how strongly that body stands out.
context.vcf.keyTrk: In this sound: off, so the body stays fixed as the line moves, as on an acoustic instrument.
context.mix.noise: In this sound: the breath. Keep it low or it turns to hiss.
context.att.2: In this sound: vibrato depth. It also nudges WIDTH very slightly, which only adds to the movement.

tweaks.hear: The fundamental comes back: a rounder, fuller reed, more like a soprano saxophone.
A darker, more veiled tone, closer to a cor anglais.
A plain, straight tone, the way an oboe sounds in a slow orchestral line.

sounds.name: Gliding Chord Pad
sounds.ref: Paraphonic chords with portamento, where each voice slides to its own new note
sounds.blurb: A slow, warm pad whose two voices slide from one chord to the next, often one up while the other goes down.
sounds.how: On a monophonic synth portamento slides one note. With PARAPHONIC on, each oscillator has its own note, and each slides separately to its next one. Change a two-note chord and one voice can rise while the other falls, crossing the gap in about a second and a half. A monophonic synth can only slide one line. The chords here are played legato, so the envelope never restarts and the pad is one unbroken sound. A slow LFO on the filter keeps the brightness moving, and a long delay fills in behind.

steps.title: Two mellow oscillators, one per note
steps.why:
Two warm oscillators, one per note. With PARAPHONIC on, each oscillator takes one of two held keys, which is what later lets each voice glide on its own path.
- SHAPE osc 1 2.6, osc 2 2.8 (saw towards triangle): warm, with some edge left.
- RANGE 8’ on both, OSC MIX 0 (50 / 50): same octave, equal blend on the crossfader.
- PARAPHONIC on: two notes at once, sharing one filter and one envelope.
- Listen for: hold a two-note chord and hear both notes, one on each oscillator.

steps.title: A long portamento
steps.why:
Portamento makes pitch slide between notes. In paraphonic mode each oscillator slides separately, so changing a chord can send one voice up and the other down.
- PORTA TIME 4 (1.6 s): about a second and a half to reach each new note. This is the whole idea of the sound. Switch PARAPHONIC off and both voices slide together to the top note.
- Listen for: play one chord, then another legato. The voices melt from one into the next, sometimes crossing.

steps.title: A dark filter that breathes
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) keeps the pad dark, and the LFO (low-frequency oscillator, a slow wave already wired to the cutoff) opens and closes it gently.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 6 (about 800 Hz): the warmth of the pad. Raise it and the slides are easier to follow.
- RESO 3, KEY TRK on, ENV DEPTH 0: a little edge, cutoff following the keys, and no envelope movement.
- MOD DEPTH 1.5 (15%): how far the LFO moves the cutoff. Keep it low: this is slow movement, not a wobble.
- RATE 1.5 (0.11 Hz), SHAPE sine: one smooth cycle about every nine seconds.
- Listen for: the pad slowly brightening and darkening while you hold a chord.

steps.title: Slow swell and a long echo
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) into a slow swell, and a long delay keeps old chords sounding under new ones.
- Envelope 1 A 720 ms, S 100%, R 1.7 s: fades in over most of a second and fades out slowly.
- TIME 9 (460 ms): a long gap between echoes.
- REPEATS 6 (60%): high, so each chord’s echoes last into the next.
- MIX 3 (30%): behind the pad.
- Listen for: chord changes blurring together under a wash of echoes.

context.porta.time: In this sound: how long each voice takes to reach its new note. It is the whole idea of the sound.
context.osc.para: In this sound: gives each oscillator its own note, so each glides on its own path. Switch it off and both voices slide together to the top note.
context.vcf.modDepth: In this sound: how far the slow LFO moves the cutoff. Keep it low: this is breathing, not a wobble.
context.lfo.rate: In this sound: one slow cycle about every nine seconds.
context.delay.repeats: In this sound: high, so the echoes of each chord last into the next.
context.vcf.freq: In this sound: the warmth of the pad. Raise it and the slides become easier to follow.

tweaks.hear: The voices take about four seconds to arrive, so you hear the slide more than the chords.
Both oscillators play the top note and slide together: a single gliding line.
A vocal, ringing edge follows the filter as it breathes.

sounds.name: Nylon-String Pluck
sounds.ref: In the style of a nylon-string guitar played softly
sounds.blurb: A soft, round plucked string that mellows as it rings, with quiet echoes behind it.
sounds.how: A string plucked at one fifth of its length has no fifth harmonic, because that harmonic has a still point exactly where the finger pulls the string. A pulse wave with a width of one fifth leaves out the same harmonics, so WIDTH works like the point along the string where you pluck. The filter then does what the string does as it rings: Envelope 2 opens it at the pluck and lets it close slowly, so the tone starts bright and softens. The echoes come back a little darker each time.

steps.title: A pulse plucked a fifth of the way along
steps.why:
A string plucked a fifth of the way along has no fifth harmonic. A pulse wave with a width of one fifth leaves out the same harmonics, so WIDTH works like the point on the string where you pluck.
- OSC MIX −5: the crossfader fully left, Oscillator 1 alone.
- SHAPE 1 (pulse): the wave WIDTH acts on.
- WIDTH 1.7 (20%): the pluck point. Towards 0 is near the bridge, thin and bright; at 5 it is mid-string, hollow and soft.
- RANGE 8’: normal pitch.
- Listen for: a bright, nasal held tone. The filter and envelope make it a string next.

steps.title: Bright at the pluck, softer as it rings
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) does what a string does as it rings: bright at the pluck, softer as it goes. Envelope 2 opens it and lets it close.
- MODE low-pass, FREQ 5.2 (about 450 Hz), RESO 1: a low, soft resting tone.
- KEY TRK on: key tracking keeps high notes as bright as low ones.
- ENV DEPTH 3 (30%): opens the filter by more than two octaves. This is how hard the string is plucked; more is a steel-string attack.
- Envelope 2 A 0, D 540 ms, S 0, R 330 ms: bright at once, mellowing over about half a second.
- Listen for: a clear pluck at the front of each note, then a rounder tone.

steps.title: A fading string
steps.why:
Envelope 1 shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) so each note fades by itself like a plucked string.
- A 0: instant start.
- D 8 (1.9 s), S 0: about two seconds of ring, even with the key held. This is how long each string rings.
- R 7.5 (750 ms): a little shorter, as if a finger touched the string when you let go.
- Listen for: each note dying away naturally.

steps.title: Echoes on the offbeat
steps.why:
The delay is timed to fall between the notes, and each repeat comes back a little darker, as analogue echoes do.
- TIME 9.1 (470 ms): a dotted eighth at 96 bpm, so the echoes land off the beat.
- REPEATS 4 (40%): a few repeats.
- MIX 2.5 (25%): quiet enough to sit in the gaps the phrase leaves for them.
- Listen for: echoes answering each pluck in the spaces.

context.osc1.width: In this sound: where the string is plucked. Towards 0 is near the bridge, thin and bright; at 5 it is the middle of the string, hollow and soft.
context.vcf.envDepth: In this sound: how hard the string is plucked. More is a brighter, steel-string attack.
context.env2.d: In this sound: how quickly the brightness fades from the pluck.
context.env1.d: In this sound: how long each string rings.
context.delay.mix: In this sound: the level of the echoes. The phrase is written to leave gaps for them.

tweaks.hear: The pluck moves from near the bridge (thin and wiry) to the middle of the string (hollow and soft).
